signals.title: `IcebergLocalDefinition::object_storage_type` incorrectly set to `azure` instead of `local`
signals.text: _Found via ClickGap automated review. Please close or comment if this is incorrect or needs adjustment._ _Retrospective finding from a historical scan of [PR #68210](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68210) (merged 2024-08-27). Confirmed on current codebase — close with a note if already fixed._ ### Describe what's wrong `icebergLocal` table function throws `BAD_ARGUMENTS: Disk type doesn't match with table engine type storage` when used with a Local object storage disk via `SETTINGS disk = 'local_disk_name'` **Root cause:** StorageObjectStorageDefinitions.h:77 — `IcebergLocalDefinition::object_storage_type = "azure"` is a copy-paste error from `IcebergAzureDefinition`. Should be `"local"` to match `DeltaLakeLocalDefinition` and `IcebergLocalClusterDefinition`. **Why we believe this is a bug:** TableFunctionObjectStorage::getConfiguration (line 108-114) validates that Definition::object_storage_type matches the disk's object storage type. For icebergLocal with a Local disk: Definition::object_storage_type='azure' != 'local', causing the check to fail. **Affected locations:** - `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageDefinitions.h:77` — object_storage_type = "azure" in IcebergLocalDefinition - `src/TableFunctions/TableFunctionObjectStorage.cpp:114` — Validation throws BAD_ARGUMENTS when object_storage_type != "local" **Impact:** Users cannot use `icebergLocal` table function with a Local object storage disk. The `SETTINGS disk = 'local_disk'` feature is completely broken for `icebergLocal`, while it works for `deltaLakeLocal` and `icebergS3`. ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `9821949fd80`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Using clickhouse client to reproduce: -- First verify a Local object storage disk exists: -- SELECT name, object_storage_type FROM system.disks WHERE object_storage_type = 'Local' -- Then run: -- SELECT 1 FROM icebergLocal(path = 'test', SETTINGS disk = '<local_disk_name>') -- Expected: should proceed to check if path exists -- Actual: BAD_ARGUMENTS: Disk type doesn't match with table engine type storage ``` ### Expected behavior ``` Should proceed past disk type validation (and then fail on path not existing or similar) ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Code: 36. DB::Exception: Disk type doesn't match with table engine type storage. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` ### Additional context **Suggested fix:** Change `object_storage_type = "azure"` to `object_storage_type = "local"` in `IcebergLocalDefinition` struct at StorageObjectStorageDefinitions.h:77. **Analysis details:** Confidence HIGH | Severity P1 | Testability: `STATELESS_SQL` Found during automated review of [PR #68210](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68210). --- _ClickGapAI · Confidence: HIGH · Severity: P1 · Finding: `h_pr68210_001`_

signals.title: DeltaLake Logical error: 'No version found in table state snapshot'
signals.text: ### Describe the bug Seems not related to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/102037 Reading a persistent DeltaLake (or Iceberg) table through a code path that does **not** call `updateExternalDynamicMetadataIfExists()` reaches `IDataLakeMetadata::iterate()` with a storage snapshot whose `datalake_table_state` is empty. `iterate()` treats this as impossible and throws `LOGICAL_ERROR`, which aborts the server: ``` <Fatal> : Logical error: 'No version found in table state snapshot'. DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel::iterate (DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel.cpp:331) -> DataLakeConfiguration<…, DeltaLakeMetadata>::iterate (DataLakeConfiguration.h:294) -> StorageObjectStorageSource::createFileIterator (StorageObjectStorageSource.cpp:287) -> ReadFromObjectStorageStep::createIterator / initializePipeline ``` Found by BuzzHouse on master `26.6.1.694` via `SELECT * FROM d2.t284` on a `DeltaLakeS3` table that had been through many ALTER/mutation/cluster-function operations. ## Root cause A persistent data-lake table's in-memory metadata gets its snapshot version pinned (`setDataLakeTableState`) only inside `updateExternalDynamicMetadataIfExists()` (`StorageObjectStorage.cpp:397`). The analyzer calls it on the table it resolves (`IdentifierResolver.cpp:335`), so a *direct* SELECT is fine. But several read paths build the child storage snapshot straight from `getInMemoryMetadataPtr()` **without** that call: - `StorageMerge` — `StorageMerge.cpp:730` (and `:414`) - cluster/distributed table-function reads on the executing node - (the materialized-view target path used to have this bug; it was fixed by adding the update call — `StorageMaterializedView.cpp:400`) When the table is reached first through one of these, the snapshot carries no `datalake_table_state`, and `iterate()` throws instead of falling back. The throw is also asymmetric with its sibling in the *same file*: `DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel::prepareReadingFromFormat()` (`DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel.cpp:505-511`) handles the identical missing-version case **gracefully** by falling back to the version from settings. `iterate()` should do the same. Iceberg is identical: `IcebergMetadata::iterate()` (`IcebergMetadata.cpp:1023`) throws `"Can't extract iceberg table state from storage snapshot"` under the same condition. ## Relationship to prior findings Same bug *class* as the Iceberg over-assertions filed in #107316 — a `LOGICAL_ERROR` guarding an invariant that is actually reachable from normal SQL. Here the invariant is "the storage snapshot always carries a pinned table-state version", which is false for read paths that skip `updateExternalDynamicMetadataIfExists`. ### How to reproduce With clickhouse binary in the PATH and the server running, run this script: ```bash set -u BIN=clickhouse # 26.6.1.694, has delta-kernel TABLE=contrib/delta-kernel-rs/kernel/tests/data/table-without-dv-small P="/var/lib/clickhouse/user_files" rm -rf "$P" && mkdir -p "$P" cp -r "$TABLE" "$P/delta1" ABS="$P/delta1/" echo "=== control: direct SELECT pins state, works ===" "$BIN" --client --multiquery " SET allow_experimental_delta_kernel_rs=1; CREATE TABLE ok ENGINE = DeltaLakeLocal('$ABS'); SELECT count() FROM ok; " echo "=== repro: merge() is the SOLE first access -> aborts ===" "$BIN" --client --multiquery " SET allow_experimental_delta_kernel_rs=1; CREATE TABLE t ENGINE = DeltaLakeLocal('$ABS'); SELECT * FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t\$') ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 5; " echo "exit=$? (134 = SIGABRT = reproduced)" ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace Stack trace: ``` <Fatal> : Logical error: 'No version found in table state snapshot'. <Fatal> : Format string: 'No version found in table state snapshot'. <Fatal> : Stack trace (when copying this message, always include the lines below): 0. /ClickHouse/contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__exception/exception.h:115:14: Poco::Exception::Exception(String&&, int) @ 0x0000000027021373 1. /ClickHouse/src/Common/Exception.cpp:139:7: DB::Exception::Exception(DB::Exception::MessageMasked&&, int, bool) @ 0x0000000014bdab29 2. /ClickHouse/src/Common/Exception.h:171:100: DB::Exception::Exception(String&&, int, String, bool) @ 0x000000000d189cd6 3. /ClickHouse/src/Common/Exception.h:57:54: DB::Exception::Exception(PreformattedMessage&&, int) @ 0x000000000d189798 4. /ClickHouse/src/Common/Exception.h:189:77: DB::Exception::Exception<>(int, FormatStringHelperImpl<>) @ 0x0000000014bd9279 5. /ClickHouse/src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel.cpp:331:15: DB::DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel::iterate(DB::ActionsDAG const*, std::function<void (DB::FileProgress)>, unsigned long, std::shared_ptr<DB::StorageInMemoryMetadata const>, std::shared_ptr<DB::Context const>) const @ 0x0000000018ab9f3d 6. signals.title: [CI crash] Pure-virtual call in dumpPipeline/printPipeline for a streaming (STREAM) query on teardown (debug build)
signals.text: ## Description The `AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted)` job crashes with `SIGABRT` (a pure-virtual call) while dumping the pipeline for a streaming (`STREAM`) query over a `MergeTree` table. This is unrelated to the codec whose test the targeted fuzzer mutated — the crashing query reads no data columns (`SELECT 'Int32' FROM t_pco STREAM`), and the crash is entirely inside generic streaming-query + pipeline-diagnostics code. Found via the targeted fuzzer on PR https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110613 (report: `PR -> AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted)`, sha `7898ce1800f75471f816553d3e341f7adbe61719`). ## Crash ``` (from thread 1165) (query_id: ae177a58-...) (query: SELECT 'Int32' FROM t_pco STREAM) Received signal Aborted (6) ... 6. libcxxabi/src/abort_message.cpp:66 7. libcxxabi/src/cxa_virtual.cpp:16 (__cxa_pure_virtual) 8. src/Processors/IProcessor.h:139 DB::IProcessor::getUniqID() const 9. src/QueryPipeline/printPipeline.h:74 DB::printPipeline<...>(...) 10. src/Processors/Executors/PipelineExecutor.cpp:771 DB::PipelineExecutor::dumpPipeline() const 11. src/Processors/Executors/PipelineExecutor.cpp:229 DB::PipelineExecutor::execute(...) 12. src/Processors/Executors/CompletedPipelineExecutor.cpp:43 DB::threadFunction(...) ``` ## Root cause In a debug build, `PipelineExecutor::execute()` wraps the run in `try/catch`, and on any exception it logs `dumpPipeline()` (guarded by `#ifndef NDEBUG`, `PipelineExecutor.cpp:229`). `dumpPipeline` → `printPipeline` walks the graph and, for every output port, calls `next.getUniqID()` on the connected downstream processor (`printPipeline.h:74`). `getUniqID` calls the virtual `getName()` (`IProcessor.h:139`). The pure-virtual dispatch (`__cxa_pure_virtual`) means a processor reachable through a port is being destroyed / no longer alive at the time of the dump. For a long-running streaming query that is cancelled or torn down (here the query had been running ~4 minutes and the crash coincides with the server being shut down at the end of the fuzzer run — the client log shows `Connection reset by peer` / `Connection refused` around the same time), the pipeline graph still references a processor whose derived part has already been destructed. This is a **debug-only** path: release builds do not call `dumpPipeline`, so they surface the original exception instead of crashing. It is also **codec-independent** — it reproduces for any `MergeTree` table (`SELECT '...' FROM <mt> STREAM` returns rows on a release build; the crash needs the debug diagnostics + teardown timing). ## Reproduction - Debug build. - `SET enable_streaming_queries = 1;` - A `MergeTree` table `t`. - `SELECT '<const>' FROM t STREAM` while the query is cancelled / times out / the server shuts down mid-execution, so `PipelineExecutor::execute()` throws and reaches the `dumpPipeline()` diagnostics path. ## Notes - `enable_streaming_queries` is an experimental feature (`STREAM` table modifier). - Fix direction: `dumpPipeline`/`printPipeline` should not dereference processors reachable only through ports without a guaranteed lifetime, or the streaming-query teardown must keep the graph's processors alive until the executor stops; alternatively, the diagnostics should tolerate a partially-destroyed graph.

signals.title: `AggregatingStep` and `MergingAggregatedStep` don't serialize `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` into the query plan
signals.text: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/b849a6c2d9c8d3e4f6a6372c3c80b611f777036b/src/Processors/QueryPlan/AggregatingStep.cpp#L965-L996 `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte` is declared as a query plan serialization setting (default 1) and read on deserialization (AggregatingStep.cpp line 1135, MergingAggregatedStep.cpp line 318), but neither `AggregatingStep::serializeSettings` nor `MergingAggregatedStep::serializeSettings` writes it. Every other `Aggregator::Params` field they carry is written (`min_hit_rate_to_use_consecutive_keys_optimization`, two-level thresholds, `enable_producing_buckets_out_of_order_in_aggregation`, ...), this one is read-only. So with `serialize_query_plan = 1`, a plan built with `serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte = 0` round-trips as 1: the node executing the deserialized plan aggregates with the trailing zero byte while the initiator runs without it. The setting exists exactly to keep the string serialization format consistent across a cluster of incompatible versions, silently dropping it on the wire defeats that. Since 25.12. Fix: add `settings[QueryPlanSerializationSetting::serialize_string_in_memory_with_zero_byte] = params.serialize_string_with_zero_byte;` to both `serializeSettings` (AggregatingStep.cpp line 965, MergingAggregatedStep.cpp line 194). Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/90880 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #112131 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1435` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Stale set skip index read after ALTER MODIFY COLUMN whose mutation was killed aborts index analysis
signals.text: ## Describe the bug A `set` skip index over a column that has had `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN` change its type can be read against parts that still hold the old serialization, aborting the server in debug and sanitizer builds: ``` Logical error: 'Sizes of nested column and null map of Nullable column are not equal after deserialization (null map size = 1, nested column size = 0)' ``` ``` SerializationNullable::deserializeBinaryBulkWithMultipleStreams src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationNullable.cpp:178 MergeTreeIndexGranuleSet::deserializeBinary src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexSet.cpp:129 MergeTreeIndexReader::read src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexReader.cpp:167 MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor::filterMarksUsingIndex src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor.cpp:2710 ``` The `Nullable` wording is incidental. With a non-Nullable target type the same defect surfaces as `Code: 12 PARAMETER_OUT_OF_BOUND` in `ColumnVector<T>::insertRangeFrom`, so keying on the `Nullable` message understates the bug. ## How to reproduce ClickHouse version: `master` (reproduced on 26.8.1.1, debug build). ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, value String, INDEX i (value) TYPE set(0) GRANULARITY 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id PARTITION BY id SETTINGS add_minmax_index_for_numeric_columns = 0, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, '10'), (2, '20'), (3, '300'); SYSTEM STOP MERGES t; SET alter_sync = 0, mutations_sync = 0; ALTER TABLE t MODIFY COLUMN value Nullable(UInt64); -- the ALTER mutation is removed before it materializes KILL MUTATION WHERE table = 't' SYNC FORMAT Null; SELECT count() FROM t WHERE value = 300; -- aborts ``` This is not transient. Every later query against the table aborts until the parts are rewritten. `OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL` clears it, and `SETTINGS use_skip_indexes = 0` returns the correct answer. Reading the column itself still works, so the data is intact and the fault is confined to skip-index analysis. ## Expected behaviour The type-incompatible index is excluded from index analysis for parts that predate the type change, and the query returns the correct result, as it does when the mutation is allowed to finish. ## Root cause Exclusion is driven by `getAlterConversionsForPart(...)->getAllUpdatedColumns()` feeding `canUseIndex` (`MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor.cpp:1108-1117` and `:764`). `canUseIndex` returns success unconditionally when that name set is empty, so the stale granule is read. Two independent situations leave the name set empty: 1. The mutation is still pending, but the read snapshot drops it, because `MergeTreeData.cpp:12000` sets `need_alter_mutations = apply_mutations_on_fly || apply_patch_parts`. With both off the `READ_COLUMN` entry is absent from the snapshot. This is what https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106988 fixes. 2. The mutation was killed. The entry is gone from `system.mutations` entirely, so the name set is legitimately empty regardless of `need_alter_mutations`, while the table metadata keeps the new column type and the old parts keep the old index. Not covered by #106988. Measured on a debug `master` build: | case | result | |---|---| | killed mutation, `Nullable(UInt64)` | abort, `null map size = 1, nested column size = 0` | | killed mutation, plain `UInt64` | `PARAMETER_OUT_OF_BOUND` in `ColumnVector::insertRangeFrom` | | killed mutation, `alter_column_secondary_index_mode` at default | abort | | pending mutation, `apply_mutations_on_fly = 0, apply_patch_parts = 0` | abort (case 1) | | pending mutation, default settings | correct result | | mutation allowed to finish, or no ALTER at all | correct result | `alter_column_secondary_index_mode` is not required to trigger this, so it is not specific to the recent index-rebuild work. The exclusion decision currently trusts a mutation entry that `KILL MUTATION` can remove. A durable fix should compare what the part actually holds against what the table metadata now declares, rather than inferring it from pending mutations. ## CI history 35 rows across 24 distinct pull requests since 2026-05-01, of which 4 have `pull_request_number = 0` (`master`), on `arm_tsan`, `amd_tsan`, `amd_debug`, `arm_debug`, `arm_release`, `amd_msan` and `arm_asan_ubsan`. STIDs `6726-6874`, `6726-6444`, `6726-6673`, `6726-36f1`, `6726-4d8b` and `6726-38f2` are this same defect in different buckets. On 2026-08-07 alone the message produced all of `6726-6874` (11 rows), `6726-6444` (5), `6726-6673` (4), `6726-4d8b` (3) and `6726-38f2` (1), so searching on any single STID misses most of the family. In CI the kill is not issued by the failing test. On the occurrence below, an unrelated concurrent test (`02558_system_processes_elapsed.sh`, running `kill query where current_database = currentDatabase()`) had its statement mutated by the AST fuzzer into `KILL MUTATION WHERE current_database = currentDatabase() SYNC`, which removed 9 mutations across three databases, including those of the victim table in `03702_alter_column_modify_secondary_index_drop.sh`, two seconds before the abort. That cross-database reach is why the carrier pull request is always unrelated. Example report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108096&sha=25f51f1fddd05350d9c5aa1231aa0e7ee6fc676f&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 Reported from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108096#issuecomment-5098842183. Related but distinct: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101832 is in the same function, but `block.clear()` there runs only on the `rows_to_read == 0` early return and costs filtering effectiveness downstream. Here the fault is upstream of any granule reuse. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #112484 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1470` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Parquet and ORC do not push predicates into Tuple subcolumns
signals.text: ### Describe the issue Parquet and ORC filter pushdown works for a top-level column but is lost when the identical values are stored in a `Tuple` subcolumn. With one million ordered rows: | Format and predicate | Input read | |---|---:| | Parquet: `id = 555555` | 1 of 91 row groups | | Parquet: `tup.1 = 555555` | all 91 row groups | | ORC: `id = 555555` | 10,000 rows | | ORC: `tup.1 = 555555` | 1,000,000 rows | `id` and `tup.1` contain identical `UInt64` values. ### Version `26.8.1.404` ### Reproducer The automated reproducer generates both fixtures, captures `--print-profile-events`, prints the result counts and reader metrics, and asserts the differences: Run python script [repro_format_nested_and_orc_cast_pushdown.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30543252/repro_format_nested_and_orc_cast_pushdown.py) Output: ```text case result selected_rows_raw rows_per_pass read_row_groups pruned_row_groups parquet_direct 1 3372 1686 1 90 parquet_tuple 1 2000000 1000000 91 0 orc_direct 1 20000 10000 0 0 orc_tuple 1 2000000 1000000 0 0 orc_noop_toUInt64 1 2000000 1000000 0 0 All result and ProfileEvents assertions passed. ``` `clickhouse-local` includes both schema inference and query execution in `SelectedRows`, so the script prints the raw counter and the corresponding per-pass value. Parquet row-group counters are emitted directly. Expanded manual steps follow. Generate the files: ```bash clickhouse local \ --output_format_parquet_row_group_size 10000 \ --output_format_parquet_data_page_size 4096 \ --output_format_parquet_write_page_index 1 \ --output_format_parquet_write_bloom_filter 1 \ --query " SELECT number AS id, tuple(number, toString(number % 31)) AS tup FROM numbers(1000000) INTO OUTFILE '/tmp/nested_pushdown.parquet' TRUNCATE FORMAT Parquet" clickhouse local \ --output_format_orc_row_index_stride 10000 \ --query " SELECT number AS id, tuple(number, toString(number % 31)) AS tup FROM numbers(1000000) INTO OUTFILE '/tmp/nested_pushdown.orc' TRUNCATE FORMAT ORC" ``` Compare Parquet predicates: ```bash clickhouse local --print-profile-events --query " SELECT count() FROM file('/tmp/nested_pushdown.parquet', Parquet) WHERE id = 555555 SETTINGS max_threads=1 FORMAT Null" clickhouse local --print-profile-events --query " SELECT count() FROM file('/tmp/nested_pushdown.parquet', Parquet) WHERE tup.1 = 555555 SETTINGS max_threads=1 FORMAT Null" ``` Relevant output: ```text # id = 555555 ParquetReadRowGroups: 1 ParquetPrunedRowGroups: 90 # tup.1 = 555555 ParquetReadRowGroups: 91 ParquetPrunedRowGroups: 0 ``` Compare ORC predicates: ```bash clickhouse local --print-profile-events --query " SELECT count() FROM file('/tmp/nested_pushdown.orc', ORC) WHERE id = 555555 SETTINGS max_threads=1 FORMAT Null" clickhouse local --print-profile-events --query " SELECT count() FROM file('/tmp/nested_pushdown.orc', ORC) WHERE tup.1 = 555555 SETTINGS max_threads=1 FORMAT Null" ``` Relevant output, including the schema-inference pass: ```text # id = 555555 SelectedRows: 20000 # tup.1 = 555555 SelectedRows: 2000000 ``` ### Parquet statistics are present `ParquetMetadata` reports valid min/max statistics for physical path `tup.1`. The nested scan is therefore not caused by missing file statistics. ### Expected behavior Predicates on supported primitive Tuple/Nested subcolumns should be translated to their physical Parquet/ORC paths and used for row-group or row-index pruning, the same as equivalent top-level columns. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #113383 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1477` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->
signals.author: PedroTadim

signals.title: Paimon tables partitioned by `TIMESTAMP` cannot be read: "scale 6 is not supported, only support scale <= 3"
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong Any read of a Paimon table that is partitioned by a `TIMESTAMP` column with precision greater than 3 fails with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`, before a single row is produced: ``` Code: 36. DB::Exception: scale 6 is not supported, only support scale <= 3. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` Precision 6 is not an unusual choice — it is what everybody gets by default: * In Paimon, a bare `TIMESTAMP` is `TIMESTAMP(6)`. * Spark's `TIMESTAMP` and `TIMESTAMP_NTZ` always map to Paimon `TIMESTAMP(6)`, so no Spark DDL can produce a partition column that ClickHouse is able to read. * ClickHouse itself defaults to precision 6 when the Paimon type string carries no precision (`Types.h`). So in practice *every* timestamp-partitioned Paimon table is unreadable. Only partition values are affected: the same column reads fine when it is not a partition key. ### How to reproduce * Which ClickHouse server versions are incompatible: 26.8.1.491 (`e61186d9a13`), master * Non-default settings: `allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine = 1` Create the table with Spark (`pyspark` 4.0.2, `org.apache.paimon:paimon-spark-4.0_2.13:1.4.1`): ```python spark = ( SparkSession.builder .config("spark.sql.extensions", "org.apache.paimon.spark.extensions.PaimonSparkSessionExtensions") .config("spark.sql.catalog.p", "org.apache.paimon.spark.SparkCatalog") .config("spark.sql.catalog.p.warehouse", WAREHOUSE) .config("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "UTC") .getOrCreate() ) spark.sql("CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS p.d") spark.sql("CREATE TABLE p.d.ts6 (id INT, ts TIMESTAMP_NTZ) PARTITIONED BY (ts)") spark.sql("INSERT INTO p.d.ts6 VALUES (1, TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456')") # Control: the same column type, but not a partition key. spark.sql("CREATE TABLE p.d.plain (id INT, ts TIMESTAMP_NTZ)") spark.sql("INSERT INTO p.d.plain VALUES (1, TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456')") ``` The written schema confirms the precision: ```json { "id" : 1, "name" : "ts", "type" : "TIMESTAMP(6)" } ``` Then read both tables: ```sql SET allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine = 1; SELECT * FROM paimonLocal('<warehouse>/d.db/ts6'); -- Code: 36. DB::Exception: scale 6 is not supported, only support scale <= 3. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) SELECT * FROM paimonLocal('<warehouse>/d.db/plain'); -- 1 2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456 ``` ### Expected behavior `SELECT * FROM paimonLocal('<warehouse>/d.db/ts6')` returns `1 2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456`, like the non-partitioned control table does. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 5. Paimon::BinaryRow::getTimestamp(int, int) @ BinaryRow.cpp:192 6. Paimon::getPartitionString(Paimon::BinaryRow&, DB::PaimonTableSchema const&, String const&) @ Utils.cpp:246 7. Paimon::getBucketPath(String const&, int, DB::PaimonTableSchema const&, String const&) @ Utils.cpp:293 8. DB::PaimonManifestEntry::DataFileMeta::DataFileMeta(...) @ PaimonClient.h:203 9. DB::PaimonManifestEntry::PaimonManifestEntry(...) @ PaimonClient.h:287 11. DB::PaimonTableClient::getDataManifest(...) 12. DB::PaimonMetadata::getManifest(String const&, long) const @ PaimonMetadata.cpp:520 ... 17. DB::DataLakeConfiguration<DB::StorageLocalConfiguration, DB::PaimonMetadata>::iterate(...) ``` ### Root cause `BinaryRow::getTimestamp` only implements Paimon's *compact* timestamp encoding and gives up otherwise — `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Paimon/BinaryRow.cpp:185`: ```cpp DateTime64 BinaryRow::getTimestamp(Int32 pos, Int32 scale) { if (scale <= 3) { return DateTime64(getFixedSizeData<Int64>(pos)); } /// TODO: support larger precision throw DB::Exception(ErrorCodes::BAD_ARGUMENTS, "scale {} is not supported, only support scale <= 3", scale); } ``` Paimon splits the value once the precision exceeds 3 (`BinaryRow.getTimestamp` → `MemorySegmentUtils.readTimestampData` in `paimon-bundle-1.4.1`): the 8-byte field slot then holds `(sub_offset << 32) | nanoOfMillisecond`, and the epoch milliseconds live in the variable-length area at `offset + sub_offset`. That layout is visible in the manifest of the table above — the partition blob is ``` 00000001 0000000000000000 40F5060010000000 7BD75A6198010000 arity null bits field slot millis ``` i.e. `sub_offset = 16`, `nanoOfMillisecond = 456000`, and the `Int64` at `offset(4) + 16 = 20` is `1753980000123` = `2025-07-31T16:40:00.123` — together, `2025-07-31T16:40:00.123456`. ### A second defect on the same path Accepting the wider encoding is not sufficient on its own: both callers of `getTimestamp` hardcode scale 3 for the value they get back, so the partition value would then be off by three orders of magnitude. * `Utils.cpp:164` — `DecimalField<DateTime64>(partition.getTimestamp(i, type->getScale()), 3)` * `Utils.cpp:246` — `formatDateTime(partition.getTimestamp(i, type->getScale()), 3, type->getTimeZone())` The second one builds the partition directory name, which must reproduce byte for byte what Paimon wrote. Paimon names partition directories with Java's `LocalDateTime.toString()` (`Timestamp.toString()` → `toLocalDateTime().toString()`), which drops the seconds when both they and the fraction are zero and prints 0, 3, 6 or 9 fractional digits depending on the value. The directories written by the reproducer show all of those cases: ``` ts=2025-07-31T16%3A00 -- 16:00:00 ts=2025-07-31T16%3A40 -- 16:40:00 ts=2025-07-31T16%3A40%3A00.000456 ts=2025-07-31T16%3A40%3A00.123 ts=2025-07-31T16%3A40%3A00.123456 ``` Passing `type->getScale()` instead of the literal `3` covers precision up to 6, because `writeDateTimeText<..., /*cut_trailing_zeros_align_to_groups_of_thousands=*/true>` already reproduces that rule. It does not cover precision 7 to 9: `writeDateTime64FractionalText` only ever emits 3 or 6 digits, so a nanosecond partition value is silently truncated rather than printed with 9 digits. ```sql SELECT toDateTime64('2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456789', 9, 'UTC') SETTINGS date_time_64_output_format_cut_trailing_zeros_align_to_groups_of_thousands = 1; -- 2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456 (Java would print 2025-07-31T16:40:00.123456789) ``` ### Impact Read-only failure, no data loss and no abort.
signals.author: PedroTadim

signals.title: Row policy on the shard-local table is bypassed with `serialize_query_plan = 1` on a non-local replica
signals.text: 🕵 **Describe the bug** With `serialize_query_plan = 1`, a read shipped to a non-local replica of a `Distributed` table bypasses the row policy defined on the shard-local table: the receiving server deserializes an already-built read plan, so it never applies its own row policies. With `serialize_query_plan = 0` (text shipping) the same query is filtered correctly. This matters because defining the policy on the underlying local table is the documented way to filter reads that go through a `Distributed` table (`docs/en/sql-reference/statements/create/row-policy.md`), so the workaround silently returns unfiltered rows in this mode. **How to reproduce** Version: 26.8.1.1 (reproduced on `master`, commit `bde560d7b00`). Server config: a cluster `self` with one replica pointing back at the server itself, and `<process_query_plan_packet>1</process_query_plan_packet>`. ```sql CREATE TABLE rp_leaf (x UInt32, y UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x; INSERT INTO rp_leaf SELECT number, number FROM numbers(10); CREATE TABLE rp_dist AS rp_leaf ENGINE = Distributed('self', currentDatabase(), rp_leaf); CREATE ROW POLICY rp_l ON rp_leaf FOR SELECT USING y < 5 TO CURRENT_USER; SELECT count() FROM rp_dist SETTINGS prefer_localhost_replica = 0, serialize_query_plan = 0; -- 5, correct SELECT count() FROM rp_dist SETTINGS prefer_localhost_replica = 0, serialize_query_plan = 1; -- 10, policy skipped SELECT count() FROM rp_leaf; -- 5, correct ``` **Expected behavior** Both remote reads return `5`. Either the shipped plan carries the filter, or the receiving server re-applies its local row policies to the deserialized plan, or plan shipping is refused when the shard-local table has a row policy that applies (fail close). **Additional context** Two stateless tests already pin `serialize_query_plan = 0` for exactly this reason: - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04498_row_policy_role_scope_interserver.sh` - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04652_nested_merge_prewhere_type_mismatch.sql` (added by https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112326) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112326
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: `date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'` clamps to the whole second, not to the maximum representable value
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe what's wrong With `date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'`, an out-of-range value is clamped to the whole second and the sub-second component is discarded. The result is therefore below the maximum representable value of the target type, at every scale. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce `253402300800` is `10000-01-01` UTC, out of range at every scale. The check does not assume where the boundary sits — it adds 999999 µs to the saturated value and shows the result is still representable and strictly greater, proving the saturated value was not maximal. Run on `26.2.19.43`, `26.7.1.1315` (latest stable) and master `26.8.1.287`: ```sql SELECT toDateTime64(253402300800, 6) AS saturated, saturated + toIntervalMicrosecond(999999) AS still_representable, still_representable > saturated AS saturation_was_not_maximal SETTINGS date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'; -- 26.7.1.1315 and master 26.8.1.287: -- 9999-12-31 23:59:59.000000 | 9999-12-31 23:59:59.999999 | 1 -- 26.2.19.43 (narrower DateTime64 range, same defect): -- 2299-12-31 23:59:59.000000 | 2299-12-31 23:59:59.999999 | 1 ``` The same shortfall appears at every scale — on `26.7.1.1315` and master `26.8.1.287`: ```sql SELECT toDateTime64(253402300800, 6) SETTINGS date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'; -- 9999-12-31 23:59:59.000000 expected 9999-12-31 23:59:59.999999 SELECT toDateTime64(253402300800, 8) SETTINGS date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'; -- 4892-10-07 21:52:48.00000000 expected 4892-10-07 21:52:48.54775807 SELECT toDateTime64(253402300800, 9) SETTINGS date_time_overflow_behavior = 'saturate'; -- 2262-04-11 23:47:16.000000000 expected 2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807 ``` ### Expected behavior `saturate` should clamp to the maximum representable value of the target type, including its sub-second component — the values given in the comments above. ### Error message and/or stacktrace No exception is raised — the returned value is simply below the type maximum. ### Additional context The maxima differ by scale for two different reasons: at scale 6 the bound is the supported date range (`9999-12-31 23:59:59.999999`), while at scales 8 and 9 it is the `Int64` tick range (`9223372036854775807` ticks, i.e. `4892-10-07 21:52:48.54775807` and `2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807`). In all three cases the clamp discards the fractional part rather than clamping to the true maximum tick. Underflow clamps to the true minimum correctly (`toDateTime64(-62167219201, 6)`, checked on `26.2.19.43` and master `26.8.1.287`), so the defect is specific to the **upper** bound. A note for anyone re-testing at scale ≤ 7: #107907 widened `DateTime64` to `[0000-01-01, 9999-12-31]`, so a literal such as `'9999-12-31 22:59:59'` is now *in range* and is returned exactly, and no longer exercises the saturate path. An out-of-range value also cannot be written as a `String` at that scale, because a 5-digit year fails at the parser first (`Code: 41 ... unexpected number of decimal digits: 5`) — hence the numeric literal above. Related: #100471, #101131 (the same setting ignored for numeric sources — a different defect), #111524.
signals.author: samay-sharma

signals.title: Paimon tables with a nullable ARRAY or MAP column cannot be read: "Nested type ... cannot be inside Nullable type"
signals.text: A Paimon table containing a nullable `ARRAY` or `MAP` column cannot be read at all: schema parsing wraps the composite type in `Nullable`, which ClickHouse forbids, so `DESC` and `SELECT` throw an exception before any data is read. Since Paimon columns are nullable by default (e.g. any Spark-created table with an array column), this makes fairly ordinary Paimon tables entirely unreadable — the exception is raised while parsing the table schema in `PaimonMetadata::create`, so it affects the whole table, not just queries touching the offending column. **How to reproduce** Write a Paimon table with a nullable array column (Paimon 1.1.1, Spark 3.5): ```sql -- spark-sql with org.apache.paimon:paimon-spark-3.5:1.1.1, -- spark.sql.catalog.paimon = org.apache.paimon.spark.SparkCatalog, -- spark.sql.catalog.paimon.warehouse = file:/tmp/paimon_wh CREATE TABLE paimon.default.t (f ARRAY<INT>) TBLPROPERTIES ('file.format'='parquet'); INSERT INTO paimon.default.t VALUES (array(1,2)); ``` Read it with ClickHouse (master, commit `7c826d816cd5`): ``` $ clickhouse local --query "DESC paimonLocal('/tmp/paimon_wh/default.db/t')" Code: 43. DB::Exception: Nested type Array(Nullable(Int32)) cannot be inside Nullable type. (ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT) ``` The same error occurs via `paimonS3` / `paimonAzure` and the `Paimon*` table engines. A nullable `MAP` column fails identically with `Nested type Map(...) cannot be inside Nullable type`. **Root cause** `Paimon::DataType::parse` in `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Paimon/Types.h` wraps the result in `DataTypeNullable` when the Paimon field is nullable, including for the `ARRAY` and `MAP` branches: ```cpp if (real_type == "ARRAY") { ... type.clickhouse_data_type = std::make_shared<DataTypeArray>(nested_type.clickhouse_data_type); if (nullable) type.clickhouse_data_type = std::make_shared<DataTypeNullable>(type.clickhouse_data_type); } ``` `DataTypeNullable`'s constructor rejects composite nested types (`src/DataTypes/DataTypeNullable.cpp`), hence the exception. The `Nullable` wrap should be skipped for `ARRAY` and `MAP` (reading a null array/map as empty), which is how the Iceberg and Delta Lake type mappers handle nullable composites. The existing test fixtures (`tests/queries/0_stateless/data_minio/paimon_all_types`) never hit this because their array/map fields are declared non-nullable. The new Paimon type-matrix E2E test works around it with `NOT NULL` composite columns for now. Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/102343 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #113450 - Backported to: `26.7.4.30`, `26.6.3.39`, `26.5.7.51` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fall back to local execution when a plan step does not support distributed execution (`make_distributed_plan`)
signals.text: `make_distributed_plan=1` builds a multi-stage distributed plan whose fragments are shipped to workers by serializing the query plan. Not every `IQueryPlanStep` supports serialization: the base class already has `isSerializable` (default `false`, `src/Processors/QueryPlan/IQueryPlanStep.h`), and `assertFragmentSerializable` in `src/Processors/QueryPlan/QueryPlan.cpp` checks each stage fragment up front. However, when a non-serializable step is found, the query **fails** with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED`: `make_distributed_plan cannot distribute this query: step '...' is not serializable for remote execution`. There are also several ad-hoc throws for other unsupported shapes (`WITH TOTALS` / `ROLLUP` / `CUBE` / extremes in `optimizeTree.cpp`, `GROUPING SETS` and `max_rows_to_group_by` in `makeDistributed.cpp`, etc.). **Proposal** Introduce a systematic check of all steps of the plan for distributed-execution support before distributing it, and if any step is unsupported fall back to normal local execution, exactly as if `make_distributed_plan=0`, instead of throwing: 1. Run the check once on the whole plan before the `tryMakeDistributed*` transforms (not per-fragment after the fact), based on `isSerializable` plus the existing ad-hoc conditions, so the decision is made before the plan is rewritten with exchanges. 2. On failure, log the offending step (as the parallel-replicas fallback already does: `Keeping the plan fragment local: step '...' is not serializable for remote execution` in `applyParallelReplicas.cpp`) and continue with the ordinary single-node plan. 3. Keep a way to get the old strict behavior (e.g. a setting like `distributed_plan_fallback_to_local_execution`, or reusing the error under a "throw" mode), so tests and users who want to be sure the plan is actually distributed can still assert it. 4. Convert the scattered `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` throws in `optimizeTree.cpp` / `makeDistributed.cpp` / `assertFragmentSerializable` to the same mechanism, so the supported/unsupported decision lives in one place.

signals.title: Custom-key parallel replicas over a Merge table with a Distributed child: children are offloaded to a finalized stage (CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE, logical error in GroupingAggregatedTransform)
signals.text: 🕵 Reading a `Merge` table (or the `merge` table function) with custom-key parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_mode = 'custom_key_sampling'` or `'custom_key_range'`) fails with an exception when the common processing stage of the children is `WithMergeableState` — for example, when one of the underlying tables is a `Distributed` table. ```sql CREATE TABLE t_mrg_ck_1 (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k AS SELECT number FROM numbers(100000); CREATE TABLE t_mrg_ck_2 (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k AS SELECT number FROM numbers(100000); CREATE TABLE t_mrg_ck_3 (k UInt64) ENGINE = Distributed('test_shard_localhost', currentDatabase(), 't_mrg_ck_1'); SET enable_parallel_replicas = 1, max_parallel_replicas = 3, cluster_for_parallel_replicas = 'test_cluster_one_shard_three_replicas_localhost', parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree = 1, parallel_replicas_mode = 'custom_key_sampling', parallel_replicas_custom_key = 'k'; SELECT count() FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t_mrg_ck_'); ``` ``` Code: 70. DB::Exception: Conversion from UInt64 to AggregateFunction(count) is not supported: while converting source column `count()` to destination column `count()`: Child table: default.t_mrg_ck_1. (CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE) ``` Depending on the aggregate function, it instead trips an assertion in the pipeline — an exception in debug and sanitizer builds (found by the AST fuzzer, STID `3970-479a`): ```sql SELECT 47, quantileExactInclusive(visibleWidth(['1', '2'])) IGNORE NULLS FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t_mrg_ck_') GROUP BY ALL LIMIT 973; ``` ``` Logical error: 'Chunk should have AggregatedChunkInfo/ChunkInfoWithAllocatedBytes in GroupingAggregatedTransform.'. ``` **Root cause.** The `Distributed` child reports `WithMergeableState` from its `getQueryProcessingStage`, so `StorageMerge::getQueryProcessingStage` sets the common stage of all children to `WithMergeableState`, and `ReadFromMerge::createPlanForTable` plans each `MergeTree` child through an interpreter with `SelectQueryOptions(WithMergeableState)`. Inside that child interpreter, the custom-key branch of `PlannerJoinTree` (`src/Planner/PlannerJoinTree.cpp`, the `canUseParallelReplicasCustomKey` block) offloads the child query to the replicas at the hard-coded stage `WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`, ignoring the requested `to_stage`. The child plan therefore produces finalized rows (post-aggregation, post-`LIMIT`) where the parent `ReadFromMerge` pipeline expects partial aggregation states: `convertAndFilterSourceStream` throws `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` when the finalized type differs from the state type, and when the types coincide structurally, the chunks without `AggregatedChunkInfo` reach `GroupingAggregatedTransform` and trip the assertion. Only the analyzer path is affected (`enable_analyzer = 0` returns correct results). Reproduced on current master (verified on a binary with no unrelated changes); found by the targeted AST fuzzer on https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972 (which is unrelated: the failure reproduces without `parallel_replicas_allow_merge_tables`, a setting that does not exist on master), report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110972&sha=ac0a584ce316ace31f4dbc16b38e1262a2344751&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29 The custom-key offload should be skipped when the requested `to_stage` is below `WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`: a plan that must stop at a partial stage cannot accept a finalized remote read. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #113742 - Backported to: `26.7.4.29`, `26.6.3.42`, `26.5.7.52`, `26.3.18.31`, `25.8.30.19` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Server crash in `applyRangeFilterFromAST`: `Pipe::getHeader` on an empty per-layer pipe
signals.text: The AST fuzzer running inside stateless/stress tests crashes the server in `applyRangeFilterFromAST` (`src/Processors/QueryPlan/PartsSplitter.cpp`) when the per-layer pipe built by `readByLayers` is empty: `Pipe::getHeader` dereferences the pipe's null `header`. The ASan+UBSan build reports it as undefined behavior, the TSan builds as a segmentation fault: ``` /ClickHouse/contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__memory/shared_ptr.h:574:12: runtime error: reference binding to null pointer of type 'element_type' (aka 'const DB::Block') #0 std::shared_ptr<DB::Block const>::operator*() const #1 DB::Pipe::getHeader() const src/QueryPipeline/Pipe.h:45:46 #2 DB::applyRangeFilterFromAST(DB::Pipe&, ...) src/Processors/QueryPlan/PartsSplitter.cpp:1230:34 #3 DB::readByLayers(DB::SplitPartsByRanges, ...) src/Processors/QueryPlan/PartsSplitter.cpp:1263:9 #4 DB::ReadFromMergeTree::readByLayers(...) src/Processors/QueryPlan/ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:1242:18 #5 DB::ReadFromMergeTree::spreadMarkRanges(...) src/Processors/QueryPlan/ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:3654:16 #6 DB::ReadFromMergeTree::initializePipeline(...) src/Processors/QueryPlan/ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4549:16 ... #9 DB::QueryAnalyzer::evaluateScalarSubqueryIfNeeded(...) src/Analyzer/Resolve/evaluateScalarSubqueryIfNeeded.cpp:277:63 #11 DB::QueryAnalyzer::resolveTableFunction(...) src/Analyzer/Resolve/QueryAnalyzer.cpp:4670:13 ... #33 DB::executeASTFuzzerQueries(...) src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp:2375:27 SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior /ClickHouse/contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__memory/shared_ptr.h:574:12 ``` `readByLayers` calls `applyRangeFilterFromAST` on every pipe returned by the reading step getter, and a layer can produce an empty `Pipe` (a default-constructed `Pipe` has a null `header`). An empty pipe is legal downstream - `Pipe::unitePipes` starts with `removeEmptyPipes` - so the filter simply has nothing to apply to. Observed in CI on two unrelated pull requests, so it is not caused by either of them: - https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=99639&sha=e3675c072cc6c7cb1184a060d9c872ac519c78a2&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29 (`Stress test (amd_asan_ubsan)`, `Stress test (amd_tsan)` and `Stateless tests (amd_tsan, s3 storage, parallel, 3/3)`, 2026-08-03), see https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99639 - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103182 (2026-08-05) `applyRangeFilterFromAST` was introduced on `master` on 2026-06-19 by commit `f29978c7cd7e` ("Read per-bucket PK-range layers on the distributed-read worker"). There is no deterministic reproducer: both occurrences come from the AST fuzzer, and the exact fuzzed query is not recoverable from the logs (the server dies before it is logged as finished). <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #114177 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1483` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup does not work with views
signals.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the situation `optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup` (#91164) rewrites `dictGet(dict, attr, key) = const` into a key-column filter that the primary index can use. This rewrite happens when the `dictGet(...)` call is written directly in the query. It does not happen when the same predicate is expressed as a filter on a **view** column that is itself defined as `dictGet(...)`. The view case falls back to a full-table scan. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Found on 26.7 ### How to reproduce ```sql CREATE TABLE dim_source ( dim_id UInt64, dim_code String ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY dim_id; INSERT INTO dim_source SELECT number, substring(lower(hex(sipHash64(number))), 1, 8) FROM numbers(1000); CREATE DICTIONARY dim_dict ( dim_id UInt64, dim_code String ) PRIMARY KEY dim_id SOURCE(CLICKHOUSE(TABLE 'dim_source')) LAYOUT(HASHED()) LIFETIME(MIN 0 MAX 0); CREATE TABLE fact ( dim_id UInt64, created_at DateTime, metric Float64 ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY dim_id; INSERT INTO fact SELECT number % 1000, now() - number, rand() / 1e9 FROM numbers(1000000); INSERT INTO fact SELECT number % 1000, now() - number, rand() / 1e9 FROM numbers(1000000); INSERT INTO fact SELECT number % 1000, now() - number, rand() / 1e9 FROM numbers(1000000); CREATE VIEW fact_v AS SELECT dim_id, dictGet('dim_dict', 'dim_code', dim_id) AS dim_code, created_at, metric FROM fact; ```sql SET optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup = 1; -- (1) works: dictGet() written directly in the query EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT * FROM fact WHERE dictGet('dim_dict', 'dim_code', dim_id) = assumeNotNull((SELECT dim_code FROM dim_source WHERE dim_id = 723)); -- ┌─explain──────────────────────────────────┐ -- 1. │ Output: dim_id, created_at, metric │ -- 2. │ │ -- 3. │ ReadFromMergeTree (rnorgren.fact) │ -- 4. │ Read type: Default │ -- 5. │ Parts: 3 | Granules: 3 │ -- 6. │ Output: dim_id, created_at, metric │ -- 7. │ Prewhere filter │ -- 8. │ Prewhere filter column: dim_id = 723 │ -- 9. │ Indexes: │ -- 10. │ PrimaryKey │ -- 11. │ Keys: │ -- 12. │ dim_id │ -- 13. │ Condition: (dim_id in [723, 723]) │ -- 14. │ Parts: 3/3 │ -- 15. │ Granules: 3/369 │ -- 16. │ Search Algorithm: binary search │ -- 17. │ Ranges: 3 │ -- └──────────────────────────────────────────┘ -- (2) fails: identical predicate, but via a view column aliasing dictGet() EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT * FROM fact_v WHERE dim_code = assumeNotNull((SELECT dim_code FROM dim_source WHERE dim_id = 723)); -- ┌─explain───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ -- 1. │ Output: dim_id, dictGet('rnorgren.dim_dict'_String, 'dim_code'_String, dim_id), created_at, metric │ -- 2. │ │ -- 3. │ ReadFromMergeTree (rnorgren.fact) │ -- 4. │ Read type: Default │ -- 5. │ Parts: 3 | Granules: 369 │ -- 6. │ Output: dim_id, dictGet('rnorgren.dim_dict'_String, 'dim_code'_String, dim_id), created_at, metric │ -- 7. │ Prewhere filter │ -- 8. │ Prewhere filter column: dictGet('rnorgren.dim_dict', 'dim_code', dim_id) = '4810f1b6' │ -- 9. │ Indexes: │ -- 10. │ PrimaryKey │ -- 11. │ Condition: true │ -- 12. │ Parts: 3/3 │ -- 13. │ Granules: 369/369 │ -- 14. │ Ranges: 3 │ -- └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` ### Expected performance Both `EXPLAIN` plans show the primary index pruned to the matching `dim_id`, e.g.: ``` PrimaryKey Condition: (dim_id in [723, 723]) Parts: 3/3 Granules: 3/369 ``` ## Actual behavior Query (1) prunes correctly. Query (2) does not — `PrimaryKey Condition: true`, all parts and granules are read, despite the `Prewhere filter column` being identical to query (1)'s once the view's `dim_code` alias is inlined. This suggests `InverseDictionaryLookupPass` runs before the query-plan-level predicate pushdown that inlines a view's projection expression into the outer filter, so it never sees the combined `dictGet(...) = const` shape when the predicate originates outside the view. ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

signals.title: Function `gzipDistance`
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Use case Text classification and similarity _without embeddings_ ### Describe the solution you'd like (based on an idea from @thevar1able) This [blog post](https://backdrifting.net/post/068_text_classification_gzip) ([corresponding paper](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.426.pdf)) describes using gzip for calculating text similarity. We could have a function `gzipDistance(text1, text2)` (similar to the existing hamming, jaro, etc. distance functions). The smaller the result, the more similar both texts are. ### Describe alternatives you've considered The new function `aiSimilarity`, but it is doing expensive remote LLM calls. signals.title: Buffer table silently discards an acknowledged INSERT when the destination schema drifts (DROP / re-CREATE) before the deferred flush
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse QA (durability testing) ### Describe what's wrong An `INSERT` into a `Buffer` table is acknowledged as soon as the rows land in the in-memory buffer; the write to the destination table happens later (background threshold flush, or `OPTIMIZE`). If the destination's schema *diverges* in that window, the flush silently discards the acknowledged rows and reports success — the client that received the `INSERT` acknowledgement never sees any error. Two variants lose whole acked rows during normal, server-healthy operation: - the destination is dropped and re-created with a column set that has **no name in common** with the buffer → the whole buffered block is discarded; - the destination is **dropped** (a migration step) before the flush fires → the whole buffered block is discarded. `StorageBuffer::writeBlockToDestination` logs these two cases at `<Error>` level — i.e. the code treats them as error conditions — but then `return`s normally, so `flushBuffer` counts the flush as successful and clears the buffer (`src/Storages/StorageBuffer.cpp:1085-1089` for the missing-destination case, `:1120-1124` for the no-common-columns case). Only a thrown exception restores the block to the buffer, so the rows are gone from everywhere with only a server-log line. A third, milder variant is documented (a dropped destination column silently drops that column's acknowledged values while the rows survive — `StorageBuffer.cpp:1103-1127`; documented at `docs/en/engines/table-engines/special/buffer.md`), so this report is about the two **whole-block** losses, which the docs do not cover. This is the same durability class as #112394 (Buffer losing buffered rows on graceful shutdown), but a distinct mechanism: here the server stays up and healthy, and the trigger is an ordinary destination schema change (`DROP`/re-`CREATE`/`ALTER`) between the acknowledgement and the deferred flush. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Reproduces on 26.8.1.1. `StorageBuffer::writeBlockToDestination` carries the same discard-with-log logic on current `master`. ### How to reproduce `clickhouse-server` 26.8.1.1, single node, default settings. ```sql CREATE TABLE dst (k UInt64, v String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k; -- Buffer thresholds set high so no auto-flush fires before the drift; a -- production Buffer with ordinary thresholds hits the same discard on its -- background flush. CREATE TABLE buf AS dst ENGINE = Buffer(currentDatabase(), 'dst', 1, 3600, 7200, 1000000, 2000000, 100000000, 200000000); INSERT INTO buf SELECT number, concat('payload_', toString(number)) FROM numbers(50); -- The INSERT is acknowledged. The rows are visible through the buffer: SELECT count() FROM buf; -- 50 SELECT count() FROM dst; -- 0 (not flushed yet) -- An ordinary destination migration: drop and re-create with a different schema. DROP TABLE dst; CREATE TABLE dst (a UInt64, b String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; OPTIMIZE TABLE buf; -- flush; returns success SELECT count() FROM dst; -- 0 -> the 50 acknowledged rows are gone ``` The whole-block loss also reproduces when the destination is simply dropped and not re-created before the flush. ### Expected behavior An acknowledged `INSERT` should not be silently lost while the server is healthy. At minimum the flush should not report success when it discards an acknowledged block: the discard is already recognized as an error internally (it is logged at `<Error>`), so it should surface to a place the client or an operator can observe (an exception that keeps the block buffered and retries, or a failure counter / `system.errors` entry), rather than clearing the buffer and returning success. ### Error message and/or stacktrace Server log only; nothing is returned to the client. From a run of the reproduction: ``` <Error> StorageBuffer (default.buf): Destination table default.dst have no common columns with block in buffer. Block of data is discarded. <Error> StorageBuffer (default.buf): Destination table default.dst doesn't exist. Block of data is discarded. ``` ### Additional context Reproduced 5/5 with a non-vacuity control (no drift → all 50 rows flush) and the acknowledged rows proven present through the buffer before the drift. Code references are against `master` at `aa3ccbf5e7df`.

signals.title: S3 multipart complete: a NoSuchUpload is rewritten to success on key existence alone, silently losing an acknowledged fixed-key INSERT
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse QA (durability testing) ### Describe what's wrong When an S3 `CompleteMultipartUpload` returns `NoSuchUpload`, `DB::S3::Client::CompleteMultipartUpload` disambiguates by **key existence only**: it issues a `HeadObject` on the target key and, if any object exists there, rewrites the outcome to a fabricated success — with no upload-id, ETag, size, or version cross-check against the upload that just failed (`src/IO/S3/Client.cpp:531-551`): ```cpp if (!outcome.IsSuccess() && outcome.GetError().GetErrorType() == Aws::S3::S3Errors::NO_SUCH_UPLOAD) { auto check_request = HeadObjectRequest().WithBucket(bucket).WithKey(key); auto check_outcome = HeadObject(check_request); /// if the key exists, than MultipartUpload has been completed at some of the retries /// rewrite outcome with success status if (check_outcome.IsSuccess()) outcome = Aws::S3::Model::CompleteMultipartUploadOutcome(Aws::S3::Model::CompleteMultipartUploadResult()); } ``` The rewrite is meant for the benign retry-idempotency case (a lost complete response where an earlier attempt already completed). But key existence is not proof that *this* upload completed. If the target is a **fixed key that already holds a prior object** (an overwrite via `s3_truncate_on_insert = 1`, or a foreign writer) and this multipart upload was genuinely aborted between create and complete — e.g. by an `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` bucket lifecycle rule (a widely recommended, common configuration) racing a slow/large INSERT, or by a concurrent abort — then `CompleteMultipartUpload` legitimately returns `NoSuchUpload`, the `HeadObject` finds the **prior** object, the outcome is rewritten to success, and the INSERT is **acknowledged while zero of its rows are durable**. The old object is served forever; the client sees no error. The secondary guard `check_objects_after_upload` is off by default (`src/IO/S3Defines.h`) and even when on it checks key existence + size only. Scope: fixed-key writes — `s3()` / `S3` engine, especially with `s3_truncate_on_insert = 1`. MergeTree-over-S3 uses unique random keys, so a `HeadObject` there fails and the error propagates correctly (no loss). Distinct from #112419 (two concurrent same-key INSERTs) and #113179 (local metadata rewrite). ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Reproduces on 26.8.1.1. `Client::CompleteMultipartUpload` carries the same key-only rewrite on current `master`. ### How to reproduce `clickhouse-server` 26.8.1.1 against an S3 endpoint (MinIO), default settings. A fault proxy in front of the endpoint fails the `CompleteMultipartUpload` (POST with `uploadId=`) once with `NoSuchUpload`, **without forwarding** it — so the upload stays genuinely incomplete and the prior object at the key survives (the faithful stand-in for a lifecycle-aborted upload). ```sql -- 1. Seed a small OLD object at the fixed key (single PUT): INSERT INTO FUNCTION s3('http://.../bucket/mpu/obj.csv', 'CSV', 'tag String, filler String') SETTINGS s3_truncate_on_insert = 1 SELECT 'OLD', repeat('x', 50) FROM numbers(100); -- 2. Arm the proxy to fail the next CompleteMultipartUpload with NoSuchUpload -- (unforwarded), then INSERT a LARGE NEW object to the SAME key. The size -- (>32 MiB, the default s3_max_single_part_upload_size) forces a multipart -- upload, so CompleteMultipartUpload is called: INSERT INTO FUNCTION s3('http://.../bucket/mpu/obj.csv', 'CSV', 'tag String, filler String') SETTINGS s3_truncate_on_insert = 1 SELECT 'NEW', repeat('x', 50) FROM numbers(900000); -- ^ returns SUCCESS -- 3. Read the key back: SELECT countIf(tag = 'NEW'), countIf(tag = 'OLD') FROM s3('http://.../bucket/mpu/obj.csv', 'CSV', 'tag String, filler String'); -- 0 100 -> the acknowledged NEW rows are gone; the OLD object is served ``` Control (no fault): the same large NEW INSERT lands the 900000 NEW rows and 0 OLD — the multipart write path and truncate work; the loss is caused by the rewrite. ### Expected behavior An acknowledged INSERT must not be silently lost. When `CompleteMultipartUpload` returns `NoSuchUpload`, the `HeadObject` disambiguation should confirm the object at the key is *this* upload's result before rewriting to success — e.g. compare the ETag against the multipart tags already known to the writer, or the object size against the total written, rather than treating mere key existence as proof. If it cannot be confirmed, the complete should fail (so the INSERT errors and can be retried), not be reported as success. ### Error message and/or stacktrace None — the INSERT returns success. The only trace is that a later read of the key returns the pre-existing object's content instead of the inserted rows. ### Additional context Reproduced **5/5** with a non-vacuity control (no fault → the NEW object lands) and the INSERT acknowledged (`rc = 0`) in every faulted iteration. Code references are against `master` at `aa3ccbf5e7df`.

signals.title: toUnixTimestamp() in ORDER BY silently loses primary-key pruning starting in 26.7 (regression from 26.6)
signals.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour For a MergeTree table whose sorting key includes `toUnixTimestamp(<DateTime64 column>)`, a plain range filter on the raw column (e.g. `WHERE event_ts >= '2026-06-15'`, no cast, no function wrapper) uses the primary key to prune granules on ClickHouse `26.4` through `26.6`. Starting with the first `26.7` release, the identical query against the identical table and data no longer prunes via the primary key at all. `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` shows `PrimaryKey Condition: true`, meaning every granule in the matched parts is read. This persists through the current 26.8 master build. Partition-level (Min-Max) pruning is unaffected in all versions; only the primary-key contribution is lost starting in 26.7. No exception is thrown and no incorrect results are returned. This is a silent loss of an optimization, not a correctness bug. ORDER BY keys using `toDate(<col>)` or `toStartOfHour(<col>)` on the same table/data do not show this regression — they continue to prune correctly on every version we tested, `26.4` through `26.8`. The issue appears specific to `toUnixTimestamp()`. I also checked the new `use_partition_minmax_for_primary_key_pruning` setting (present in `26.8`, absent in `26.5`) as a possible cause, since its description sounded related. Toggling it on/off made no difference to the broken query, so it does not appear to be the cause. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Not affected: `26.4.5.143, 26.5.6.113, 26.6.1.1193, 26.6.2.160` Affected (regression introduced here): `26.7.1.1315` (first `26.7` release) — confirmed present through `26.7.3.19` and the current `26.8` master build (`26.8.1.1181, built ~2026-08-11`) The break happens between the `26.6` branch cut and the first `26.7` release. ### How to reproduce How to reproduce - Interface: clickhouse local (also reproduces in clickhouse-server; tested via official release binaries downloaded from GitHub Releases for each version, arm64) - Non-default settings: index_granularity = 128 on the table (lowered only so a 100k-row table produces enough granules to observe pruning; not related to the bug) - Minimal repro (single-column ORDER BY, no composite key needed) `CREATE TABLE t (id UInt8, ts DateTime64(3)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY toUnixTimestamp(ts); INSERT INTO t SELECT number, now() - toIntervalDay(180) + toIntervalMinute(number) FROM numbers(1000000); EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT count() FROM t WHERE ts >= now() - toIntervalDay(30);` - Full repro matching the original investigation (composite key, closer to a real schema): `CREATE TABLE events_base ( platform String, application String, event_name String, event_ts DateTime64(3, 'UTC'), user_id String ) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO events_base SELECT ['ios','android','web'][1 + rand() % 3] AS platform, ['checkout','billing','onboarding'][1 + rand() % 3] AS application, ['click','view','purchase','error'][1 + rand() % 4] AS event_name, toDateTime64('2026-03-01 00:00:00', 3, 'UTC') + toIntervalSecond(rand() % 14083200) AS event_ts, toString(rand()) AS user_id FROM numbers(100000); CREATE TABLE events_tounix ( platform LowCardinality(String), application LowCardinality(String), event_name LowCardinality(String), event_ts DateTime64(3, 'UTC'), user_id String ) ENGINE = MergeTree() PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(event_ts) ORDER BY (platform, application, event_name, toUnixTimestamp(event_ts)) SETTINGS index_granularity = 128; INSERT INTO events_tounix SELECT * FROM events_base; EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT sum(length(user_id)) FROM events_tounix WHERE event_ts >= '2026-06-15';` On 26.4, 26.5, and 26.6, the PrimaryKey block of the EXPLAIN output is: `PrimaryKey Keys: toUnixTimestamp(event_ts) Condition: (toUnixTimestamp(event_ts) in [1781481600, +Inf)) Parts: 3/3 Granules: 283/340` On 26.7.1.1315 and every version since, the same query against the same table gives: `PrimaryKey Condition: true Parts: 3/3 Granules: 340/340` ### Error message and/or stacktrace Expected performance: `toUnixTimestamp(event_ts)` should continue to be usable by the primary key for range pruning when the query filters on the raw `event_ts` column, exactly as it did on 26.4–26.6 and as demonstrated in ClickHouse's own docs example at https://clickhouse.com/docs/knowledgebase/why_is_my_primary_key_not_used (which uses `ORDER BY (code, toUnixTimestamp(timestamp))` as its worked example). On affected versions, queries that previously read a few hundred granules out of many thousand now read every granule in the matched parts, which will show up as a significant, silent latency/cost regression for anyone using this documented pattern. ### Related issues and pull requests Related: - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97746 - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/95125 - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/docs/knowledgebase/why_is_my_primary_key_not_used (Not confirmed as the same root cause, but same subsystem/time window: PR #97746, merged Feb 25 2026 into 26.3.1.43+, reworked KeyCondition.cpp's handling of monotonic-function atoms for DateTime64 columns. In review, @nihalzp explicitly flagged toUnixTimestamp() as having a known, deliberately-deferred issue — a DECIMAL_OVERFLOW on out-of-range values used as a PARTITION BY key — left for a follow-up PR. That's a different symptom (partition key, thrown exception) from this regression (ORDER BY key, silent loss of pruning, no exception), but it's the same function and the same code path, so it may be relevant context for whoever picks this up.) ### Additional context The issue might surface if we run a diff on `src/Storages/MergeTree/KeyCondition.cpp` between the v26.6.1.1193-stable and v26.7.1.1315-stable tags, since the regression is present in the very first 26.7 release.

signals.title: INSERT on a DDL-lagging Replicated-database replica silently skips an un-applied materialized view's cascade, permanently losing the acknowledged rows from the MV target
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse QA (durability testing) ### Describe what's wrong An `INSERT` into a table inside a `Replicated` database is acknowledged by the replica that receives it, and that replica alone fires the source table's materialized-view cascade. It captures the set of dependent views from its **local** catalog (`DatabaseCatalog::getDependentViews`). If that replica is **behind on the Replicated-database DDL log** and has not yet applied a `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` entry, its local catalog has no MV — so the acknowledged `INSERT` writes only the source table, and the MV target table never receives the rows. This is permanent: after the DDL log catches up and the MV is created on that replica, the earlier acknowledged rows are **not** back-filled. The client that received the `INSERT` acknowledgement sees no error. The streaming-ingestion path guards exactly this situation. `DatabaseCatalog::getReadyDependentViews` (`src/Interpreters/DatabaseCatalog.cpp:1148`) returns an empty set — refusing to process — when the dependency graph is only partially loaded, with the comment *"Return empty to prevent streaming engines from processing with a partial dependency graph, which would permanently lose data for views not yet loaded."* The plain-`INSERT` path does not use that guard: `InsertDependenciesBuilder` reads the unguarded `getDependentViews` (`src/Interpreters/InsertDependenciesBuilder.cpp:898` and `:984`). So a Kafka/S3Queue/RabbitMQ consumer with a not-yet-loaded view is held back, but a plain `INSERT` on the same replica proceeds and silently drops the cascade. The realistic trigger is a replica that is recovering / catching up on the Replicated-database DDL log (the `unsynced_after_recovery` window, `src/Databases/DatabaseReplicatedWorker.cpp:630`) while already answering queries, and a client that inserts into an existing source table on it — for example a direct connection, or a load balancer that has not yet drained the lagging replica. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — reproduces on 26.8.1.1, and the code path is identical on current `master` (`0eb5eba20b92`). ### How to reproduce Two-replica `Replicated` database on one Keeper. The DDL lag is made deterministic with the `PAUSEABLE` failpoint `database_replicated_stop_entry_execution` (`src/Databases/DatabaseReplicatedWorker.cpp:628`), which pauses a replica's DDL worker in `initAndCheckTask` before it executes the next log entry — so the replica is held with the source and target tables applied but the `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` entry pending. (The failpoint only makes the window exact; the same loss occurs whenever a replica genuinely lags on that DDL entry while taking inserts.) ```sql -- On both replicas r1 and r2: CREATE DATABASE rdb ENGINE = Replicated('/clickhouse/rdb', 's1', 'r1'); -- 'r2' on the other -- Applied on both replicas (before the hold): CREATE TABLE rdb.src (id UInt64, v UInt64) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree ORDER BY id; CREATE TABLE rdb.dst (id UInt64, v UInt64) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree ORDER BY id; -- Hold r2's DDL worker on the NEXT entry (the CREATE MV): -- (on r2) SYSTEM ENABLE FAILPOINT database_replicated_stop_entry_execution; -- On r1: create the MV. r1 applies it; r2 is paused on the entry, so r2 has no MV. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW rdb.mv TO rdb.dst AS SELECT id, v FROM rdb.src; -- Direct an INSERT at the lagging replica r2 (which has src but not mv): INSERT INTO rdb.src VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30); -- acknowledged SELECT count() FROM rdb.src; -- 3 on both replicas (RMT replication) SELECT count() FROM rdb.dst; -- 0 -> the acknowledged rows never reached the MV target -- Release r2's DDL worker so it finally creates the MV: -- (on r2) SYSTEM DISABLE FAILPOINT database_replicated_stop_entry_execution; SELECT count() FROM rdb.dst; -- still 0 -> no back-fill; the rows are gone from the MV target ``` Observed with the reproduction rig, 5/5 runs, both controls green: - **bug** — r2 held on the CREATE MV entry, INSERT directed at r2: INSERT acknowledged, `src` = 30 on both replicas, `dst` = 0 on both replicas before and after releasing the hold. - **non-vacuity control** — no hold, INSERT on r2 after r2 has the MV: `dst` = 30 (the cascade fires). - **positive control** — r2 held, INSERT directed at r1 (which has the MV): `dst` = 30 (the cascade fires on the receiving replica). ### Expected behavior An acknowledged `INSERT` should not silently skip a materialized view whose `CREATE` has already been committed to the Replicated-database DDL log. The plain-`INSERT` cascade path should apply the same partial-dependency-graph protection the streaming path already has (`getReadyDependentViews`): if the receiving replica has not yet loaded a dependent view that the DDL log says exists, the `INSERT` should be delayed until the view is loaded, or fail loudly, rather than being acknowledged with the cascade silently dropped. ### Error message and/or stacktrace None — the `INSERT` is acknowledged and no error is logged; the rows are simply absent from the MV target. ### Additional context Distinct from #111935 (recovery *drops MV inner-table data*) and #111818 (refreshable-MV records refresh success before durability): here the server is healthy, the MV target is an ordinary explicit table, and the trigger is an ordinary DDL-log lag between the acknowledged `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` and a replica that receives an `INSERT` before applying it. Code references are against `master` at `0eb5eba20b92`.

signals.title: Failed INSERT INTO s3(...) PARTITION BY leaves a durable read-visible prefix; default hive strategy silently duplicates it on retry
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse QA (durability testing) ### Describe what's wrong A failed `INSERT INTO FUNCTION s3(...) PARTITION BY <key>` (and the equivalent object-storage table engines) is **not atomic and leaves a durable, read-visible prefix of the partitions it had already written**, while the statement reports failure. `PartitionedSink` finalizes one object per partition value **sequentially**, with no rollback of the partitions committed before the one that fails: ```cpp // src/Storages/PartitionedSink.cpp:120-125 void PartitionedSink::onFinish() { for (auto & [_, sink] : partition_id_to_sink) { sink->onFinish(); // each StorageObjectStorageSink::onFinish -> finalizeBuffers -> write_buf->finalize() (the durable PUT / CompleteMultipartUpload) } } ``` Each child `StorageObjectStorageSink::onFinish` (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageSink.cpp:89-119`) finalizes (PUTs) its own object. If the PUT of partition *k* throws, the exception propagates out of the loop; the partitions finalized **before** *k* are already durable and immediately listable/readable, and nothing deletes them or records that only a prefix landed (`cancelBuffers` only aborts the not-yet-finalized buffers). So the error's implied "nothing happened" contract is a lie. The consequence on the **default** partition strategy is silent duplication on a natural retry. `file_like_engine_default_partition_strategy` defaults to `HIVE` (`src/Core/Settings.cpp:7754`), and `HiveStylePartitionStrategy::getPathForWrite` appends a fresh `generateSnowflakeID()` to every filename: ```cpp // src/Storages/IPartitionStrategy.cpp:383 path += std::to_string(generateSnowflakeID()) + "." + Poco::toLower(file_format); ``` so every attempt writes new object keys. A client that treats the failed INSERT as "nothing happened" and re-submits it therefore **duplicates every partition that survived the first attempt** — there is no dedup for object-storage writes and no exists-check that can catch it (the keys differ each time). A client that does *not* re-submit is left with silently half-applied state. The `WILDCARD` strategy (an explicit `{_partition_id}` placeholder in the path) fails safe instead of duplicating: the retry recomputes the same keys and the exists-check rejects it (`Code: 36 ... already exists, enable s3_truncate_on_insert`), which is fail-closed but still leaves the client permanently half-applied and unable to tell which partitions survived without listing the bucket. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — reproduced deterministically on 26.8.1.1. The code paths (`PartitionedSink::onFinish`, `StorageObjectStorageSink::finalizeBuffers`, `HiveStylePartitionStrategy::getPathForWrite`, and the `HIVE` default) are all present on current `master`. ### How to reproduce A durability rig reproduces both facets 3/3 with controls (MinIO behind a fault proxy that returns a non-retryable `403 AccessDenied` on **one** partition's PUT — the classic least-privilege / transient-denial to a single prefix — and a single clean server). `N = 300` rows over 3 partition values `p = number % 3`. **Facet 1 — a failed INSERT leaves a read-visible prefix (WILDCARD path, deterministic):** 1. `INSERT INTO FUNCTION s3('http://.../base/{_partition_id}/data.parquet', ..., 'Parquet', 'id UInt64, p UInt64') PARTITION BY p SELECT number AS id, number % 3 AS p FROM numbers(300)`, with the proxy denying PUTs to the key of the partition that finalizes **last**. 2. The INSERT fails (`Code: 499 ... S3_ERROR`), yet the two partitions finalized before it are durable and queryable through the object store, while the faulted partition is absent. - **Clean control** (proxy disarmed): the 3-partition INSERT round-trips all 300 rows. - **Isolation control** (same fault, but `INSERT ... PARTITION BY p ... WHERE p = <faulted>` — a single partition, no fan-out): the INSERT fails and **nothing** is durable, proving the surviving prefix in step 2 is the fan-out's doing. **Facet 2 — the default HIVE strategy silently duplicates on retry:** 1. Same INSERT into a non-wildcard path (default `partition_strategy = hive`), denying PUTs to one partition's `p=<v>/` prefix. 2. The INSERT fails; a `SELECT count()` over the whole prefix returns **200** (the two surviving partitions). 3. The client re-submits the identical INSERT (its natural response to a failed op). It succeeds, and `SELECT count()` over the prefix now returns **500** — 300 unique rows plus the **200-row surviving prefix duplicated** (fresh snowflake filenames, no dedup, no exists-check). ### Expected behavior A failed `INSERT ... PARTITION BY` should not silently leave a durable, read-visible subset of its partitions with the statement reporting failure. Either the partitioned write should roll back the partitions it already committed on failure (so the error's "nothing happened" contract holds), or the surviving prefix should be recorded/surfaced so the outcome is not silently half-applied — and in particular, on the **default** hive strategy a natural client retry of a failed partitioned INSERT should not silently duplicate the rows of the partitions that survived the first attempt. Honest caveat: object-storage writes through the `s3`/`azureBlobStorage` table functions and engines are not transactional, and at-least-once export is a known property. What this report isolates is the specific, undocumented combination — a failed multi-partition INSERT leaves a **query-visible** durable prefix, and the **default** hive strategy makes an ordinary retry duplicate that prefix with no dedup and no way to be idempotent — which is a data-integrity footgun distinct from the concurrent-writer clobber already filed as #112419. ### Error message and/or stacktrace `Code: 499. DB::Exception: ... (S3_ERROR)` on the faulted INSERT; `Code: 36 ... Object in bucket ... already exists (...enable s3_truncate_on_insert)` on the wildcard retry.
