signals.title: Adaptive Aggregator
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New adaptive algorithm for parallel `GROUP BY` (controlled via setting `enable_adaptive_aggregator`, enabled by default): each thread aggregates into its own hash table until it holds `adaptive_aggregator_freeze_threshold` keys and then freezes it, so frequent keys keep updating the small cache-resident tables with no coordination, while rare keys are routed by their hash into per-bucket backlogs and aggregated exactly once, inside the bucket-parallel merge. ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1465` (included in `26.8` and later)
signals.author: nihalzp

signals.title: Fix lazy materialization OOB and a Merge LOGICAL_ERROR from unused text index virtual columns
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111422 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix an out-of-bounds read (release) / logical error (debug) in the lazy materialization optimization, and a logical error in `Pipe::unitePipes` for `Merge` tables, when the direct-read-from-text-index optimization leaves an unused index virtual column in the read header of a `MergeTree` table with multiple `text` indexes. ### Description Closes #111422. `TextIndexDAGReplacer::replace` rewrites text-search predicates into `__text_index_*` virtual columns, recording one per rewritten node, then runs `removeUnusedActions()`. When the rewrite keeps a different index's virtual column (or the original expression), the first virtual's input becomes unreferenced, but `result.added_columns` was not re-filtered, so `createReadTasksForTextIndex` still appended that orphaned column to the `ReadFromMergeTree` output header. `removed_columns` was already reconciled against the surviving inputs; `added_columns` was not, and that asymmetry is the bug. The fix drops from `added_columns` any virtual column whose input did not survive, reusing the surviving-inputs set already computed for `removed_columns`. The reading step's header then matches what the plan consumes, and a redundant index read goes away. One orphaned column causes two user-visible failures, both fixed: 1. **Lazy materialization out-of-bounds read** (the reported issue). `optimizeLazyMaterialization2` builds its `required_columns` mask positionally from the input headers above the reading step, which never contain a read-only virtual column. The mask ends up shorter than that step's header and the pass indexes a `std::vector<bool>` past its end: out-of-bounds read in release, `cols.size() == required_columns.size()` assertion in debug. 2. **`Merge` table logical error.** With `text` indexes on both `mapKeys(map)` and `mapValues(map)`, the `mapKeys` virtual wins the predicate and the `mapValues` one is left registered but unreferenced. Under `SELECT count()` nothing else is read, so the dead virtual becomes the indexed child's only output column while a non-indexed sibling's header stays empty. `Pipe::getCommonHeader` picks the first non-empty header and `unitePipes` asserts the empty sibling against it: `Block structure mismatch in Pipe::unitePipes stream`, a server abort in debug and sanitizer builds. `02346_text_index_bug111422` covers the first shape. The new `04563_text_index_merge_heterogeneous_children` covers the second, which the first cannot reach (no `merge()`, no bare `count()`). It pins the two runner-randomized settings it depends on per setting, not with a blanket tag. <details> <summary>Validation of the new test</summary> Debug build of this branch, memory-capped server, per-slot ports. | arm | build id | result | |---|---|---| | master `f9801d5649` (no fix) | `c29b56ab…` | aborts: `Block structure mismatch in Pipe::unitePipes stream: different number of columns` (`Block.cpp:308` <- `Pipe.cpp:316` <- `QueryPipelineBuilder.cpp:263`) | | this branch, reconciliation loop removed | `fd96fd28…` | aborts: `Column __text_index_idx_map_values_equals_… already added for reading` (`ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4765`); via the test runner: `ClickHouse server died` | | this branch, unmodified | `a0a422da…` | passes byte-for-byte, and 50/50 randomized runs | The pre-fix signature differs between the two bases because this branch's merge-base predates the `already_has_direct_read` re-entry gate (`optimizeDirectReadFromTextIndex.cpp`, `6253632d8da4`): without that gate the pass visits the step twice and the same over-registration trips the duplicate guard before a pipe is united. Same defect, two assertions. Both pinned settings were verified load-bearing and effective: with the pins removed, a client injecting `query_plan_direct_read_from_text_index=0` or `query_plan_text_index_add_hint=0` turns the `EXPLAIN` assertion vacuous (`1 0` -> `0 0`); with the pins present the test matches the reference under either injection and under both together. Full `text_index` suite on this branch, base vs with the new test: 157 -> 158 tests, 7 -> 6 failures, **zero new failures**. All shared failures are environmental on a bare slot server (missing stateful `test.hits` dataset, no `localhost:9000`, and four debug-build 600s timeouts). </details>
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Preserve unchanged TOAST values in MaterializedPostgreSQL
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/83517 Preserve PostgreSQL columns encoded as unchanged TOAST references in `MaterializedPostgreSQL` replication instead of replacing them with default values. The consumer resolves the previous value from an earlier row in the same replication buffer when possible. Otherwise, it reads the current row from the nested `ReplacingMergeTree` by replica identity, batching key lookups to avoid a query per value. The old replica identity tuple is used when an update changes the key. An unchanged TOAST value in a replica identity column is rejected because the replication message does not contain a value that could identify the row. The integration test covers a regular update, multiple updates of the same row in one PostgreSQL transaction, and a replica identity change. The user-facing documentation is updated for both `MaterializedPostgreSQL` engines. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `MaterializedPostgreSQL` now preserves unchanged PostgreSQL `TOAST` values during updates instead of replacing them with default values.
signals.author: OrpheusAgent

signals.title: keeper: Increase default `write_snapshot_version` to 8 and make it hot-reloadable
signals.text: Version 6 is a bit of a ticking bomb as it stops working after 2^31 requests. Hot-reloading helps in this scenario: * `write_snapshot_version` is 6 (writes 31-bit sequence numbers for znodes) * some znode's sequence number grows above 2^31, and the server stops writing snapshots but otherwise stays fully functional, * you don't notice for a week * then you notice and want to increase `write_snapshot_version` to 7 * you increase+restart one server * but there's a week's worth of log entries for this server to catch up on, so it takes forever to catch up * until it catches up you can't restart other servers without losing availability * you're stuck, oops With this you can change the setting in the config file without restarting servers, so the valuable accumulated in-memory state gets snapshotted and not lost. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required)

signals.title: Use Gaussian centroids for truncated QBit codes
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109405 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110911 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve reduced-precision `L2DistanceTransposedQuantized`, `cosineDistanceTransposedQuantized`, and `dotProductTransposedQuantized` by reconstructing `p < 8` `QBit(Int8)` codes with Gaussian conditional-mean prefix centroids. Full precision (`p = 8`) remains bit-exact; reduced-precision approximate distances may change, and recall/latency gains are workload-dependent. ### Motivation The existing reduced-precision path selects one middle fine Lloyd-Max reconstruction level for every truncated prefix. That value is not the conditional mean of the complete Gaussian interval represented by the prefix. This change uses the conditional mean `(phi(lo) - phi(hi)) / (Phi(hi) - Phi(lo))` which minimizes scalar MSE for that prefix under the standard-normal source model of the existing Lloyd-Max codec. The 127 positive values are evaluated from the existing `Float32` boundaries at high precision, rounded once to `Float32`, stored as hexadecimal literals, and mirrored exactly for negative prefixes. This keeps the hot distance loop as one LUT lookup and avoids platform-dependent libm work during LUT initialization. ### Validation - A new stateless regression fails on the exact official `26.7.1.1315` binary for all 20 reduced-precision centroid/sign checks and passes its `p = 8` control. The candidate passes all 20 checks and the control. - An independent all-raw probe covers every raw byte and every `p = 1..8`: expected level counts, finiteness, symmetry, prefix-block invariance, index-order monotonicity, independent Gaussian means (maximum 0 ULP), and bit-exact legacy `p = 8` reconstruction. - An engine probe covers all raw bytes and precisions, non-strided and `QBit(Int8, 16, 8)`, `used_dims` 8/16, dot/L2/cosine, and `optimize_qbit_distance_function_reads` 0/1. Partial-read modes match bitwise; bounded SimSIMD tolerances are used for L2/cosine. - Debug `programs/clickhouse` build passes. Updated `04504_transposed_distance_quantized` and new `04628_qbit_lloyd_max_prefix_centroid` match their references with empty stderr in clean `clickhouse local` paths. On 103,000 source-disjoint Nomic embedding vectors (768 dimensions, 200 queries, four randomized-Hadamard seeds), scalar coordinate MSE decreases at every changed precision. The transformed-space retrieval proxy is deliberately reported separately because it is not a production ClickHouse latency benchmark: | `p` | scalar MSE delta | recall@10 delta (pp) | hit@1 delta (pp) | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | -3.83% | 0.000 | 0.000 | | 2 | -3.49% | -0.250 | -0.375 | | 3 | -0.89% | +0.538 | +0.750 | | 4 | -15.17% | +1.738 | +1.625 | | 5 | -17.70% | +1.300 | +1.875 | | 6 | -24.08% | +0.800 | +0.125 | | 7 | -44.32% | +0.588 | +0.250 | | 8 | unchanged | 0.000 | 0.000 | There is no universal retrieval improvement claim: `p = 2` regresses slightly in this proxy. There is also no latency claim until a matched Release-build p50/p95 benchmark is available. The intentional compatibility boundary is numerical output at `p < 8`; function signatures, storage, and `p = 8` results are unchanged.

signals.title: Implement PromQL functions clamp(), clamp_min(), clamp_max() and round()
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `clamp`, `clamp_min`, `clamp_max`, and `round`. ### Description Implements four PromQL functions previously reported as not implemented: - `clamp(v, min, max)`, `clamp_min(v, min)`, `clamp_max(v, max)` — new `applyClampFunction` converter mapping to `greatest`/`least` SQL with explicit guards, because vectorized `least`/`greatest` in ClickHouse treat NaN as the largest value and ignore NULLs, which would corrupt NaN sample values and missing points. Prometheus special cases are reproduced exactly: `min > max` returns an empty vector, and a NaN bound propagates NaN. - `round(v[, to_nearest])` — new `applyRoundFunction` converter; replicates Prometheus inverse arithmetic (`floor(v * (1/to_nearest) + 0.5) / (1/to_nearest)`), including ties rounding toward `+Inf` and NaN propagation for `to_nearest = 0` or NaN. Both drop the metric name from results, matching Prometheus. Non-constant scalar bounds (for example, `clamp(v, time()*0-1, 2)`) are supported. No parser changes were needed; arity is enforced by each converter. The embedded support matrices for `prometheusQuery` and `prometheusQueryRange` list the new math functions and retain the implemented range functions `increase`, `changes`, and `resets`. **Semantics verified against Prometheus 3.5.0** for bound combinations `(0, 1)`, `(0, 1e12)`, `(1e12, 0)`, `(1e12, 1e12)`, and fractional `to_nearest`. **Testing**: adds `test_clamp` and `test_round`, plus conversion and aggregation regressions for empty scalar handling and a runtime scalar `quantile` parameter outside `[0, 1]`.
signals.author: valerypetrov

signals.title: Support the NetCDF format
signals.text: Adds support for the [NetCDF](https://www.unidata.ucar.edu/software/netcdf/) format, a self-describing binary format for multidimensional arrays that is the standard way climate, weather, oceanographic and other scientific data is distributed. There is a lot of public data in it (ERA5, CMIP, NOAA, Copernicus), and until now the only way to query it with ClickHouse was to convert it first. Reading is supported for the three "classic" versions of the format: CDF-1, CDF-2 (64-bit offset) and CDF-5 (64-bit data), and writing produces CDF-2 or CDF-5, whichever the data needs. The files are parsed directly, so there is no new dependency. A NetCDF-4 file, which is an HDF5 file with a different data model on top, is recognized and reported with a message that says how to convert it. **Data model.** Every variable of a file becomes a column, and the rows enumerate the Cartesian product of all the dimensions that the variables use; a variable that does not use some of them is repeated along them. The `to_dataframe` method of `xarray` produces a table with the same columns and the same set of rows, though possibly in a different order: `to_dataframe` puts the dimensions in alphabetical order by default, while ClickHouse keeps the order of the dimensions of the variables. So a file with the dimensions `time`, `lat`, `lon` and the variables `time(time)`, `lat(lat)`, `lon(lon)`, `temperature(time, lat, lon)` reads as a table with four columns and `time * lat * lon` rows. The classic format has no string type, so a `char` variable is read as a String whose length is the last dimension of the variable, when that dimension serves only as the length of the strings; a dimension that anything else in the file uses as a real axis stays in the row space, and such a `char` variable is read as one character per row. Only the variables that a query needs are read, the number of rows comes from the header (so `count()` does not read any data), and an input that cannot be seeked is read into memory instead. **Writing.** Every column becomes a variable over a single dimension named `row`, so a file written by ClickHouse is read back with the same column names and the same rows; the types come back as the closest types of the classic format (a `FixedString` as a `String`, an `Enum` or a `LowCardinality` column as the type it wraps, dates and times as plain numbers, a `Nullable` column as its base type unless read with `input_format_netcdf_fill_value_as_null`). The version of the format is chosen automatically: CDF-5 when a column needs a type that only CDF-5 has or takes more than 4 GiB, CDF-2 otherwise. A `Nullable` column is written with the `_FillValue` attribute, and a column with dates or times gets the `units` attribute of the CF conventions, so `xarray` decodes it back into timestamps. **Settings.** `input_format_netcdf_fill_value_as_null` reads the values equal to the `_FillValue` (or `missing_value`) attribute of a variable as NULL, which is how the CF conventions mark missing data such as sea surface temperature over land. `input_format_netcdf_add_dimension_columns` adds a column with the index along every dimension that has no coordinate variable of the same name, for the files that have none. **Testing.** The test files in `tests/queries/0_stateless/data_netcdf` were written by the netCDF C library, not by this code. Beyond the two functional tests, during development the reader was compared value by value against an independent reference implementation for all three format versions, the output was checked by opening it with the netCDF C library for every supported type family, and 321 truncated and bit-flipped files were fed to the reader — all of them either parsed or failed with a clean error, with no crashes. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support the `NetCDF` format for both reading and writing. It is a self-describing binary format for multidimensional arrays, widely used for climate, weather and other scientific data. Reading supports all three classic versions of the format (CDF-1, CDF-2 and CDF-5), and writing produces CDF-2 or CDF-5, whichever the data needs. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: Measure the compressed size of aggregate states in `estimateSizeOfCompressedState`
signals.text: `Aggregator::estimateSizeOfCompressedState` estimates how many bytes the aggregate states would take when a replica sends them to the initiator, which is how automatic parallel replicas decides whether distributing a query pays off. It builds a `CompressedWriteBuffer` over a `NullWriteBuffer`, but serializes the sampled states into the `NullWriteBuffer` directly and then reads that buffer's counter: ```cpp NullWriteBuffer wb; CompressedWriteBuffer wbuf(wb); // never written to ... aggregate_functions[j]->serialize(place + offsets_of_aggregate_states[j], wb); ... wbuf.finalize(); res += it ? static_cast<size_t>(table.size() * wb.count() / ((it + period - 1) / period)) : 0; ``` So nothing is ever compressed and, despite the function's name and its own `We only interested in the size of compressed state` comment, it returns the plain serialized size. `recordAggregationStateSizes` then stored that single number as all three of `bytes`, `sample_bytes` and `compressed_bytes`, which pins the compression ratio of the aggregation-state statistics to 1. `recordAggregationStateColumnSizes`, documented as `Mirrors the logic of Aggregator::estimateSizeOfCompressedState` for in-order aggregation, feeds the same `AggregationState` counters via `estimateCompressedColumnSize` and does measure the compressed size - so two producers of one statistic disagreed on what it means. This change serializes the sample through the compressing buffer and returns the sample's uncompressed and compressed sizes alongside the extrapolated total, letting the existing compression-ratio machinery in `RuntimeDataflowStatisticsCacheUpdater` apply the states' real ratio. Taking the ratio from the sample rather than compressing the extrapolated size also keeps the per-compressed-block framing overhead out of the extrapolation, where multiplying it by `table.size() / num_samples` would have inflated it. **Effect on the estimate.** Only queries whose output is dominated by compressible aggregate states move. That is exactly the shape that showed up as a CI failure of `03634_autopr_output_bytes_estimation` on master: `query_28` (`MIN(Referer)` states over a two-level hash table with many groups) estimated 59335657 bytes against a recorded 23722663, a ratio of 2.4996 that left the test's 2.5x bound no margin. Reading the estimates out of the failing job's server log, the ten other queries in that test match their recorded values within 1.00..1.41x, because their output is dominated by aggregation keys or by output columns, both of which were already measured compressed. So the recorded values expect the compressed size and this defect is why that one entry looked wrong. **Two small-sample corrections found while validating this in CI.** The compressed format writes a checksum and a block header in front of every block, so a sample of a few bytes comes out of `CompressedWriteBuffer` larger than it went in and the derived ratio drops below one, *inflating* the estimate. With an early conversion to a two-level hash table (`group_by_two_level_threshold=1`, which the test randomization sets) every one of the 256 buckets holds a handful of states and every per-bucket sample is dominated by that framing, which is what made `04034_autopr_dataflow_cache_reuse_between_different_queries` fail on the first run of this pull request: the two cache-reusing queries lost parallel replicas. When the states are really sent, the framing is amortized over `min_compress_block_size` of data, so such a sample is now reported as incompressible rather than as expanding, keeping the ratio at 1 - exactly what the caller assumed before the ratio was measured at all. The new test `04653_autopr_state_size_estimate_small_buckets` pins `group_by_two_level_threshold` to 1 and fails without that. Reviewing the same statistic end to end also turned up the mirror-image defect on the in-order-aggregation side, reported in review: `recordAggregationStateColumnSizes` totalled `IColumn::byteSize`, which for a `ColumnAggregateFunction` whose states live in a foreign arena (as `AggregatingInOrderTransform` hands them over) counts one pointer per row, so arena-backed states - `min(String)`, `groupArray`, `uniqExact` - were under-counted. That column is now sized from its serialized states too, sampling at most as many of them as the hash-table producer samples per bucket. **Recorded values.** The values in `03634_autopr_output_bytes_estimation` are empirical and need `test.hits`, so they are re-measured from this PR's own CI run rather than guessed - the test reports every query that lands outside the 2.5x band, and I will update whatever it reports. `query_1` and `query_20` are single `count()` states whose estimate becomes the ~29-byte compressed-block framing instead of a 2-3 byte varint; the test's `NOT (res.2 < 100 AND res.3 < 100)` guard already covers those. Verified so far: both changed translation units pass a full `-fsyntax-only` typecheck against master. The estimate itself is validated by CI, since reproducing it needs the stateful dataset. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111981 That PR is the interim, test-only fix for the master CI failure linked below: it re-records `query_28` as the ~58 MB the estimator currently reports. **The two changes touch the same line and are mutually exclusive.** If #111981 merges first, this PR must set `query_28` back to the post-fix measurement (expected to land near the original 23722663); if this PR merges first, #111981 should be closed as unnecessary. https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=5baed0f5a10c333cd220b9646d6ef4647425079d&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%20parallel%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the estimation of the size of aggregate states used by automatic parallel replicas: it measured the serialized size of the states instead of their compressed size, overestimating how much data a replica would send for queries that aggregate into large, compressible states.
signals.author: alexey-milovidov

signals.title: Fix signed integer overflow in Keeper coordination timeouts
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106961 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes signed integer overflow when a Keeper coordination timeout such as `operation_timeout_ms`, `session_timeout_ms` or `startup_timeout` is set to a very large value. Converting the millisecond count to nanoseconds, and adding it to the current time to form a deadline, could both overflow, so the wait expired immediately instead of waiting for the configured time, and the server aborted in builds with the undefined behaviour sanitizer. ### Description Found while sweeping the Keeper half of #106961, scoped out of it because coordination timeouts need a different bound from query-execution waits ([scope-out comment](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106961#issuecomment-5050311603)). #### What goes wrong A millisecond timeout reaches a `std::chrono` expression whose common type is `nanoseconds`, represented as `Int64`. Two operations there overflow, both undefined behaviour: the `count() * 1000000` conversion in `__chrono/duration.h`, and the deadline addition `steady_clock::now() + d` reached from `condition_variable::wait_for` and `std::future::wait_for`. A configured value in `[9223372036855, 9223372036854775]` is stored faithfully and still overflows the conversion. The wrapped deadline lies in the past, so a wait configured to be long gives up immediately. Under `-fno-sanitize-recover=all`, set for sanitizer builds, it aborts the server instead: `signed integer overflow` at `__chrono/duration.h:93`, [example report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108468&sha=90aff18153638c03d5c74142a927349b3c3405b4&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29), symbolizing into `ConcurrentBoundedQueue::popImpl` at one of the lines changed here. #### What I changed Saturation at the unsafe conversion, in the callee owning the timeout, bounded at `(INT64_MAX / 2) / 1000000`, about 146 years. No setting is capped: `e90238828006b0` ("Allow to use bigger timeouts for zookeeper") fixes this bug class by widening the conversion and leaving the value alone. Half the range, because each site then adds `steady_clock::now`, so a bound that only just fits the conversion still wraps after days of uptime; `AtomicStopwatch::secondsToNanoseconds` does the same. Twenty sites: waits and `steady_clock` comparisons in `KeeperServer`, `KeeperContext`, `KeeperDispatcher` and both request dispatchers; three via `ConcurrentBoundedQueue::tryPop`/`tryPush`, fixed inside the queue; two at the `open_client_req_stream` boundary into NuRaft. The three boundaries keep deliberately different rules, detailed below. #### Tests 14 unit tests in `src/Common/tests/gtest_saturated_wait_duration.cpp` and `src/Coordination/tests/gtest_keeper_saturated_wait.cpp`; these timeouts have no SQL surface. The oracle is behavioural: the wait's predicate is satisfied shortly after the wait begins, so an unfixed build fails instantly on its wrapped deadline. That discriminates on every build type and covers `UINT64_MAX`, which produces no sanitizer report at all. Each production change was confirmed load-bearing by reverting it alone. #### Not in this PR - `contrib/NuRaft/src/asio_service.cxx` does the same conversion for its other callers; being a submodule it needs a separate pull request against the fork first. - #106961 adds `DB::saturatedMilliseconds` with a one year policy bound and touches the same two `ConcurrentBoundedQueue` lines. The helpers can converge once it merges; a one year cap would be wrong here. - `src/Coordination/Changelog.cpp` builds five `milliseconds` values from three raw `UInt64` changelog settings, one of which (`log_readahead_serve_wait_timeout_ms`) reaches a `wait_until`. Same conversion, different setting family, file untouched here, and I have not measured a consequence there. <details> <summary>The three boundary rules, and which waits are actually unsafe</summary> - **Waits** get the half-range bound, two-sided, non-positive clamped to zero, which is what `wait_for` does with a non-positive duration anyway, so no shutdown path can newly block. The two dispatchers already read this setting into different types on `master`, `int64_t` in `KeeperRequestDispatcher` and `uint64_t` in `KeeperRequestDispatcherOld`, so a negative count saturates to zero on the signed sites and to the bound on the unsigned ones. Those declarations are untouched; on `master` both are undefined behaviour instead. - **`min_session_timeout`/`max_session_timeout` in `KeeperTCPHandler`** only get their `* 1000` made safe, at the full `Poco::Timespan::TimeDiff` range. This is not a wait: it is copied into the replicated request, stored in `session_and_timeout` and the expiry queue, and compared at full microsecond value, so clamping it would change expiry policy. The wait on this path is bounded inside `getSessionID`. The handshake reply is a protocol `int32`, so a `session_timeout_ms` above `INT32_MAX` already diverges between server and client on `master`, identically; widening that field is separate. - **The NuRaft boundary** saturates only the upper end, converting to unsigned first exactly as the `uint64_t` parameter does today. NuRaft arms its timers only when the count is nonzero, so mapping a negative count to zero would silently disable the timer, which is worse than the overflow. `condition_variable::wait_for` without a predicate is already safe, going through `__safe_nanosecond_cast`; the undefined behaviour is only in the predicate overload, which every one of these sites uses. `std::future::wait_for` is unsafe regardless, being `wait_until(now() + rel)` with no checked cast. `sleep_for` is safe, so the two Keeper `sleep_for` sites are untouched, and `KeeperServer.cpp`'s `operation_timeout_ms * 2` never enters `std::chrono`. Both test files also build against the merge-base tree, because `Bugfix validation (unit tests)` overlays them there without the fix and reports a compile failure as inconclusive. Cases naming the new helper, and the two reaching the private `interruptibleSleep`, compile only where the header exists; the rest are unconditional. </details>

signals.title: Keep the function name of a stack frame attributed to a libc++ `__functional` header
signals.text: Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/57201 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100419 `collapseDemangledNames` replaced a stack frame's function name with `?` whenever the frame's source location was a file in a directory ending in `functional`. The intent was to hide `std::function` plumbing frames, whose demangled names spell out the whole captured lambda type and say nothing the neighbouring frames do not already say. But the file of a frame is the source line the *instruction* maps to, which is not necessarily where the enclosing function is defined. An ordinary function can have individual instructions attributed to a libc++ `__functional` header - an inlined `std::function` operation, or compiler-generated code reported with line 0 - and then its name was dropped too, which loses the only useful part of the frame. This PR requires the symbol to name the `std::function` plumbing as well: the type-erasing wrappers (`std::__function::__func`, `__value_func`, `__policy_func`, ...) and the type erasure of `std::function` itself - its `operator()`, its copy, move and callable-taking constructors and assignment operators, and its destructor. The ordinary members of `std::function` (`swap`, `target_type`, `operator bool`, the `nullptr` reset `operator=(std::nullptr_t)`, the empty-constructing `function()` / `function(std::nullptr_t)`, ...) do work of their own, so they keep their names too. Those are still displayed as `?`, exactly as before; every other frame keeps its name - not only an ordinary `DB` function, but also a meaningful libc++ symbol that happens to live in a `__functional` header, such as `std::hash<String>::operator()` from `__functional/hash.h`, or the generic invocation helpers `std::invoke` / `std::__invoke` / `std::mem_fn`, which are not `std::function`-specific and whose frames can name the callable they dispatch to. This is much more likely in a build with ThinLTO enabled, where `std::function` calls are inlined across translation units, so it went unnoticed for a long time: `amd_cfi` is the only integration-test build with ThinLTO on, and its `test_crash_log` failure is what surfaced it. In that build, the frame that actually terminated the server was displayed as ``` 8. contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__functional/function.h:0:7: ? @ 0x1c01f41f ``` both in the fatal log and in `trace_full` in `system.crash_log`, where `0x1c01f41f` is inside `DB::executeQuery` (the symbol resolves correctly - only the display suppressed it). Official release builds also use ThinLTO, so the same frames were being anonymised for users. `collapseDemangledNames` becomes a static member of `StackTrace` so that the heuristic is covered by a unit test in every build, rather than only by the weekly ThinLTO job. Fixes `test_crash_log/test.py::test_crash_log_extra_fields[terminate_with_exception-trace_full]` and `[terminate_with_std_exception-trace_full]`, seen in https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=b05161aa67d75ad84151a392f3e87156efd42842&name_0=WeeklyCFI&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28amd_cfi%2C%202%2F4%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a stack frame being displayed as `?` instead of its function name in fatal log messages and in the `trace_full` column of `system.crash_log`. It affected frames of ordinary functions that have code attributed to a libc++ `__functional` header, which is common in release builds. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1334` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.4.44`, `26.5.7.57` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend
signals.text: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106136 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes silently missing rows when a query filters on `intDiv(constant, key)` or `divide(constant, key)`. Primary-key and partition analysis reports the wrong direction of monotonicity for a constant divided by a key column, so matching granules are pruned away and the query returns fewer rows with no error. Also fixes `intDiv` with an unsigned constant dividend whose high bit is set, stops claiming monotonicity when a `Decimal` operand makes the division compute in the decimal's native width, and stops key analysis from raising `Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long` for a valid query that divides an `IPv4`/`IPv6` constant by a key column. ### Description `FunctionBinaryArithmetic::getMonotonicityForRange` reports the direction of `c / x` incorrectly in its `const / variable` branch, so `KeyCondition::applyMonotonicFunctionsChainToRange` inverts the transformed range exactly when it must not, the range matches no granule, and matching rows are dropped with no error and exit code 0. Reproduced at completely default settings (no `SETTINGS` clause), 20000-row `Int32`-keyed MergeTree: ```sql SELECT count() FROM t WHERE intDiv(toInt32(-1000000), a) >= 11; -- keyed MergeTree: 0 ENGINE = Memory oracle: 10909 ``` #### Root cause For `f(x) = c / x` on an interval excluding 0, `d/dx (c/x) = -c/x²`, whose sign is `-sign(c)` for every `x != 0` — the `x²` denominator is positive on both sides of 0. So the direction is governed by `sign(c)` alone and is the *same* on the negative and the positive branch; only the values differ. The code instead treated the two arms as needing opposite polarity, which is the intuition that `1/x` "flips" across the branches. It does not: it is monotone on each branch separately, which is exactly why the strict range-sign guards are there. The two arms are now one return with a single `!is_constant_positive`, and the strict guards are kept verbatim. Fixing only that is not sufficient, and on its own would be *worse* than the current code for one shape. Three further defects live in the same branch: * **Unsigned constant dividend.** `intDiv` casts the dividend through `make_signed_t` whenever either operand is a signed integer (`DivisionUtils.h`), so an unsigned constant whose high bit is set divides as negative — `intDiv(toUInt8(200), x)` is `intDiv(toInt8(-56), x)` — while the raw `Field` still compares as positive. The boundary is `2^(8 * width - 1)` of the dividend's own width (verified for 8/16/32/64/128/256-bit dividends; the divisor width is irrelevant). This is reachable with no cast at all, because the literal `200` is `UInt8`. On a *negative* range the un-negated arm is accidentally correct for this shape, so adding the missing `!` alone would turn a correct answer into a wrong one. A new `intDivConstDividendReinterpretsNegative` helper corrects the effective sign; it deliberately does not reuse the existing `intDivConstReinterpretsNegative`, whose width early-out has the opposite polarity here. * **`Decimal` operand.** With a `Decimal` on either operand and no `Float` operand, the division computes in the decimal's native width (`DecimalBinaryOperation` casts both operands to `NativeResultType` and substitutes the integral operation even for `divide`). The divisor is then truncated, so `intDiv(toDecimal32(1000, 0), x)` is periodic in `x` with period `2^32` and not even monotonic. Nothing is claimed for that combination, mirroring the rejection the sibling `variable / constant` branch already performs. A `Decimal`/`Float` pair is exempt: it is converted to `Float64` before the operation, never truncates, and is itself a carrier of the direction defect, so those shapes are fixed rather than rejected. The rejection is deliberately keyed on the operand types and not on the constant's value, so it also covers a *zero* dividend and therefore runs ahead of the `constant == 0` fast path. That ordering is load-bearing: the truncation moves where the quotient is defined, so a range that strictly excludes 0 can still contain a point where the function is undefined, which is exactly what the zero-constant guard assumes away. With `Decimal32` the divisor truncates to `Int32`, so `intDiv(toDecimal32(0, 0), key)` over an `Int64` key range around `2^32` raises `ILLEGAL_DIVISION`; letting the zero guard win would claim monotonicity, prune the raising row away, and return a silent answer instead. Pinned by `c5iv`. * **Non-numeric operand (pre-existing exception on a valid query).** `IPv4`/`IPv6` are substituted with `UInt32`/`UInt128`, so their declared width does not describe the arithmetic, and their raw `Field` cannot be compared with a numeric zero. Two existing comparisons against zero therefore raise `Code: 169 BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD "Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long"` during key analysis today: one in the single-value fast path (reached when a granule's min equals its max) and one in the zero-constant guard (reached otherwise). Both roles are affected — `intDiv(toIPv4('192.168.0.1'), numeric_key)` and `intDiv(1, ipv4_key)` — and one of them fires even when the key range spans 0. A numeric gate hoisted above the fast path removes both; after it each query returns the correct rows with no pruning. Placing the gate inside the `const / variable` block would cover only the second site, which the new test pins at two granularities. Scope note: "both roles" here means the IP value as the dividend constant and as the key column, both with the constant on the left. The mirror shape, an IP constant as the *divisor* (`intDiv(numeric_key, toIPv4(...))`), still raises the same exception, as do `plus`/`minus`/`multiply` with an `IPv4`/`IPv6` operand. Both are pre-existing (measured byte-identical on `origin/master`) and are tracked separately rather than widened into this PR, since a correct fix for them also has to touch the `multiply` arm and the shared fast path. #### Behaviour changes to be aware of * **Two pre-existing key-analysis exceptions disappear.** As above, a non-numeric operand now reports non-monotonic instead of raising, so the query succeeds unpruned. This is a scope extension beyond "fix the direction", included because those same comparisons against zero are the mechanism being corrected and an exception on a valid query is a bug either way. * **Pruning is lost for `Decimal` shapes with no `Float` operand.** Measured with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1`: | shape | before | after | |---|---|---| | `Decimal32(0)` key, `intDiv(toInt32(-1000), a) = -25`, positive range | `Granules: 2/4` | `Granules: 4/4` | | `UInt64` key, `intDiv(toDecimal32(1000, 0), a) = 250` | `Granules: 2/4` | `Granules: 3/4` | | `Int64` key, `intDiv(toDecimal32(0, 0), a) = 5`, range around `2^32` | `Granules: 0/2` | `Granules: 2/2` | The first two queries return the same rows before and after — the index simply stops filtering. The third is the zero-dividend case: it must stop pruning, because the pruned plan silently returned `0` for a query that correctly raises `ILLEGAL_DIVISION`. This mirrors the decision already shipped for the `variable / constant` branch, where the same truncation applies. `Decimal`/`Float` pairs keep pruning and are additionally fixed. No committed reference in the repository changes. * **Everything else keeps pruning.** Strictly-positive ranges with a signed constant, both-unsigned operands, `Float` divisors, and unsigned key ranges crossing the divisor's own `2^(8W-1)` are all unaffected. That last group is worth naming: the *values* jump across the wrap while the *order* is preserved, which satisfies the non-strict definition of `Monotonicity`, so rejecting them would delete pruning that is correct today. The new test pins them, with plan-level assertions. #### Testing `04651_intdiv_const_variable_monotonicity` compares a keyed MergeTree against an identical `ENGINE = Memory` table on the same data, so each of its 82 count rows prints `1` when index-based pruning agrees with the full-scan ground truth. It covers both range signs for both functions and both constant signs, unsigned dividends at several widths, `Decimal` in either role plus the `Decimal`/`Float` exemption, `Float64`/`LowCardinality`/`Nullable` keys, ranges that span zero or have zero as an endpoint, the unsigned wrap shapes, and the `IPv4`/`IPv6` cases at two granularities. Twelve further rows assert with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` that the surviving shapes still prune (so the fix cannot silently degrade into "no pruning at all") and that the zero-dividend `Decimal` shape stops pruning — 94 asserted rows in total. On a master-HEAD binary the test fails: 28 rows print `0` and it then aborts with `Code: 169 BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD`. On this branch it passes, including 50/50 runs with randomized settings. Each of the four edits was mutation-tested individually — reverting the negation, the sign correction, the `Decimal` rejection, the `Float` exemption, the numeric gate, the gate's hoisted position and its role restriction each make specific named rows fail. `index_granularity` decides whether the range handed to `getMonotonicityForRange` is strictly negative, strictly positive or spans zero, so it is pinned per DDL and the test carries `no-random-merge-tree-settings` with that reason stated inline.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Add cardinality estimation for `startsWith`, `endsWith` String predicates
signals.text: The condition selectivity estimator previously handled string predicates poorly: `startsWith` / `endsWith` fell back to the generic unknown-condition factor (0.33), and every `LIKE` pattern got one flat factor (0.1) regardless of shape. This PR estimates both families through one shared mechanism. These two predicate families must land together: the analyzer pass `LikePerfectAffixRewritePass` (enabled by default via `optimize_rewrite_like_perfect_affix`) rewrites `col LIKE 'p%'` → `startsWith(col, 'p')` and `col LIKE '%s'` → `endsWith(col, 's')` *before* the where-optimizer runs. Only with both halves present does the same logical predicate get the same estimate regardless of that setting. ## What's included **`startsWith` / `endsWith` estimation** (all 8 variants, incl. `CaseInsensitive`/`UTF8`): pattern-shape heuristics scaled by literal length (UTF8 variants count code points), with statistics-based NULL-share handling for `Nullable` columns and FixedString(N) impossibility detection (needle longer than N ⇒ 0 rows). **Constant `LIKE` / `ILIKE` / `NOT [I]LIKE` pattern classification:** | Pattern shape | Estimate | |---|---| | `'abc'` (exact, case-sensitive) | equality range — uses real per-column statistics (uniq/countmin) | | `'abc'` (exact, ILIKE) | equality heuristic (`default_cond_equal_factor`) | | `'abc%'` / `'%abc'` / `'%abc%'` | prefix 0.25^n / suffix 0.35^n / contains 0.45^n (n = literal length, capped at 4), never above the legacy 0.1 fallback | | `'%'`, `'%%'` | matches every non-NULL row | | `x LIKE NULL` | SQL NULL for every row ⇒ 0 TRUE rows, NOT-safe | | `LIKE ... ESCAPE 'c'` | normalized via `likePatternWithCustomEscapeToLikePattern`, same argument restrictions as `FunctionsStringSearch` | | `'_'`, multi-segment (`'%a%b%'`), trailing `\` | unsupported ⇒ legacy 0.1 fallback | Escape-sequence semantics of the classifier mirror `likePatternToRegexp()` exactly (`\%`, `\_`, `\\`; unknown escapes keep the backslash literal). Exact `LIKE` on `FixedString(N)` is only treated as equality when the literal is exactly N bytes, because `=` ignores trailing NUL padding while `LIKE` matches all N bytes. **Three-valued-logic correctness for same-column combinations:** the `Selectivity` model tracks how each predicate behaves on the column's NULL rows, so combinations like `col LIKE '%' AND col IS NOT NULL` or `(pred OR col IS NULL) AND col IS NULL` are estimated with NULL-domain correlation instead of assuming independence. **Bug fix in clause merging:** `RPNElement::tryToMergeClauses` now counts `column_selectivities` carriers in its single-carrier merge arm. Without this, a nested same-column sub-clause such as `(startsWith(ns, 'abc') OR ns IS NULL) AND ns IS NOT NULL` flattened through the opposite logical operator and lost its grouping, estimating 0 rows instead of ~117/10000 (this was visible as a failing expectation in `Statistics.StringPredicateFunctionSelectivity`). ## Testing - `Statistics.StringPredicateFunctionSelectivity` — startsWith/endsWith across String, Nullable(String), FixedString, UTF8, negation, and same-column `IS [NOT] NULL` combinations (AST and DAG paths). - `Statistics.LikePatternSelectivityWithMetadata` — exact/prefix/suffix/contains/match-all, NULL patterns, ESCAPE normalization, escaped wildcards, FixedString length rules, and nested same-column OR/AND grouping. - `04266_statistics_basic_prewhere` — end-to-end EXPLAIN-based PREWHERE ordering checks for both predicate families, including nullable correlation and FixedString exact-length cases. ## Limitations / follow-ups - ILIKE affix patterns reuse the case-sensitive constants; a case-insensitive match is somewhat less selective, but the estimator has no case-distribution statistics yet. - LIKE literal length is counted in bytes (the UTF8 `startsWith`/`endsWith` variants count code points). - Padding-aware FixedString exact-LIKE estimates (matching a `String` equality literal against NUL-padded values) are left for a follow-up, noted in code comments. - Multi-segment patterns (`'%a%b%'`) keep the legacy fallback; they could later be estimated as a product of contains factors. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve PREWHERE condition ordering by using statistics-based selectivity estimates for `startsWith` and `endsWith` string predicates, including case-insensitive and UTF-8 variants.
signals.author: cv4g

signals.title: Keep an S3Queue file retryable after losing the race for its `processing` node
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `S3Queue`/`AzureQueue` skipping a file forever after losing the race for its `processing` node in Keeper: if the other processor released the file without committing it, the file was not retried by this table until the server restart. ### Description Found during the review of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108977 (the regression test there has to accept losing one file for exactly this reason). When `ObjectStorageQueueIFileMetadata::trySetProcessing` fails because the `processing` node in Keeper already exists, that node belongs to another processor - another server, or another table on the same server. `afterSetProcessing` then updated the local `FileStatus` to `Processing`, and since the non-processable checks in `trySetProcessing` and `prepareSetProcessingRequests` treat `Processing` as terminal, every later attempt short-circuited on that cached state without ever rechecking Keeper. Unlike `Processed` and `Failed`, `Processing` is not backed by a persistent Keeper node: the foreign processor can release the file without committing it - it can die, or fail the file and reset the node. Stale `processing` node cleanup does not evict `local_file_statuses` either; only the processed/failed node cleanup (`ObjectStorageQueueMetadata.cpp`) does. So the file stayed skipped by this table until its file status was evicted from the cache or the server was restarted. The cached `Processing` state is now remembered as a timestamped observation of the foreign `processing` node (`FileStatus::onProcessingByAnotherProcessor`): it is still reported in `system.s3queue`, and it is respected - the file is skipped without touching Keeper - while the observation is fresh (the new table setting `foreign_processing_node_cache_ttl_seconds`, 5 minutes by default; zero means to always check Keeper). After that, the next attempt probes Keeper again and refreshes the observation if the node is still there, so a file released without a commit is retried within the timeout, while a file being processed by another server costs at most one Keeper probe per timeout instead of one per listing pass. As soon as the foreign processor commits the file, the next probe fails on the `processed` (or `failed`) node instead and the state becomes terminal again. `afterSetProcessing` also keeps the cached state untouched when it is already `Processing` and not marked as foreign: in that case the node belongs to a concurrent local processor sharing this `FileStatus` (tables on the same server using the same Keeper path, insert threads), and its owner updates the state on commit. The cached observation participates in the listing pre-filter (`FileIterator::filterProcessableFiles`) as well: a file with a fresh foreign-`Processing` observation is dropped from the batch before the `processed`/`failed` multi-read is built, so the fresh observation avoids Keeper requests on the listing path too. The terminal states which that pre-filter does discover in Keeper are written back into the cached `FileStatus` (unless the state is owned by an active local processor, whose owner updates it on commit), so `system.s3queue_metadata_cache` follows Keeper instead of keeping a stale `Processing` after another processor has committed the file. The write-back replaces the whole cached record, not only the status: the per-attempt data of an abandoned local attempt is cleared, and a file failed by another processor carries the exception and retries from the `failed` node. The write-back is skipped when the cached state already equals the discovered terminal state: such a record describes a finished local attempt (its `rows_processed` and timings must survive relistings). A cached `Failed`, however, also describes retriable local attempts (`retries < loading_retries`), so it is kept only when its retry count matches the `failed` node payload: when another processor exhausts the retries after a retriable local failure, the cached record follows the terminal node instead of keeping the stale local exception. The set-processing probe (`trySetProcessing`/`prepareSetProcessingRequests`) follows the same contract: when it discovers a `processed`/`failed` node (which can appear after the pre-filter ran), it returns the metadata of that node and `afterSetProcessing` refreshes the whole cached record with the same guards, instead of flipping only the status. A skipped file is not simply dropped from the current listing pass: the file iterator keeps it in a recheck list (also filled when `trySetProcessing`/`prepareSetProcessingRequests` observe a foreign `processing` node), and every batch boundary of the pass takes the files whose observation has expired and runs them through the regular filtering. Within a long listing pass the TTL is therefore honored with batch granularity; files whose observation is still fresh when the listing is exhausted are dropped with the iterator, because the observation timestamps live in the shared file status cache and the next pass re-queues them with the original deadlines. The TTL bounds the retry latency even on an otherwise idle queue, where the polling backoff after zero-row cycles can far exceed it: the streaming task schedules its next cycle no later than the earliest pending recheck deadline. That wake-up cap applies only to cycles which actually consume the iterator: a `SYSTEM STOP`/`SYSTEM PAUSE`d table and a table with `s3queue_disable_streaming` never consume it, so a recheck left pending by an earlier active cycle would stay overdue and make the background task reschedule with a zero delay in a tight loop. In `Ordered` mode a foreign-held file also blocks the later files of its ordering domain (the scope of one `processed` pointer: a bucket, and a partition within it when partitioning is used) for the current listing pass. Without this, committing a later file advances the `processed` pointer past the held file, and the next listing pass drops it as already processed - losing it forever if the foreign processor never commits it. The file iterator records foreign-held files per ordering domain and drops the later files of the domain both at the listing pre-filter and before handing a file out (a file returned for retry releases its `processing` node); they are re-listed by the next pass. A held file stops blocking its domain as soon as this server wins its `processing` node or a terminal state for it is discovered in Keeper. With several processing threads sharing one ordering domain (`buckets = 1`), the block alone is not enough: it is recorded only when the set-processing attempt of the held file fails, and a later file handed out to another thread before that could still be committed first. The file iterator therefore registers a file whose set-processing outcome is not yet known at hand-out time (following the hand-out order), and a later file of the domain waits until the outcomes of the smaller files are known before starting its own attempt - so the set-processing attempts of one domain serialize for the duration of one Keeper round trip, and a foreign-held discovery blocks the later files before any of them starts processing. `foreign_processing_node_cache_ttl_seconds` is a per-table setting: `ObjectStorageQueueMetadataFactory` shares a single `ObjectStorageQueueMetadata` between all tables with the same `keeper_path`, so the value is not kept there - it travels from `StorageObjectStorageQueue` through `FileIterator` to `ObjectStorageQueueMetadata::getFileMetadata`, and each table uses (and reports in `system.s3_queue_settings`) the value from its own DDL. The setting can be changed on a live table with `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY SETTING`: the storage keeps the value in an atomic member which the file iterators read through a reference, so the new value (for example, zero, to get a stuck file retried immediately) applies to the running streaming task without recreating the table. Tests: `tests/integration/test_storage_s3_queue/test_foreign_processing_node.py` emulates the foreign processor with a real `processing` node in Keeper, checks that the file is not committed while that node exists, removes it, and asserts that the file is then processed - without the fix the count stays one short. A second test in the same file creates two tables sharing one `keeper_path` with different values of the setting and checks both the reported value and the retry window. A third test emulates the foreign processor committing one file and failing another, and asserts that `system.s3queue_metadata_cache` reports `Processed` (respectively `Failed`, with the exception of the processor which failed the file) instead of a stale `Processing`, and that neither file is ingested by this table. A fourth test checks that `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY SETTING` shortens the retry window of an already-running table. A fifth test repeats the retry scenario in `ordered` mode, with the foreign processor holding the lexicographically greatest file, asserting that the max processed path does not swallow the skipped file. A sixth test holds the only file of the queue with a two-minute polling backoff configured and asserts that it is retried within the TTL after its holder releases it, not after the backoff. A seventh test parks the `ordered` set-processing attempt at a failpoint between the initial state read and the multi request, fails the file from a fake foreign processor inside that window, and asserts that the cached record carries the exception of the `failed` node instead of an empty one. An eighth test feeds the table a file it cannot parse (a retriable local failure), writes the terminal `failed` node from a fake foreign processor, and asserts that the cached record follows its payload. A ninth test holds a file in the middle of the ordering domain in `ordered` mode and asserts that the later files wait for it: only the files before it are processed until the foreign `processing` node disappears, then the held file and the files after it follow. A tenth test runs two processing threads over one ordering domain, parks the set-processing attempt of the smallest file at a failpoint (the file is held by a fake foreign processor), and asserts that the other thread does not ingest the later files while the outcome of the smallest file is unknown, and that no file is lost after the holder releases it. An eleventh test pauses a table which has a pending foreign-processing recheck and asserts that it keeps its paused backoff instead of rescheduling in a tight loop. `src/Storages/ObjectStorageQueue/tests/gtest_file_status_foreign_processing.cpp` covers the shared `FileStatus` state machine, including the same-server contention case and the reset of the per-attempt data (exception, processed rows, processing end time) of a previous local attempt when the file becomes observed as processed by another processor, and the whole-record refresh on a terminal node discovered by the set-processing probe. The members added by the fix are referenced from `if constexpr (requires ...)` branches, so the gtest also compiles at the merge base (where it fails at runtime), which is what the `Bugfix validation (unit tests)` job checks. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108977

signals.title: Implement PromQL functions sum_over_time(), avg_over_time() and count_over_time()
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `sum_over_time()`, `avg_over_time()` and `count_over_time()`. ### Description Implements three PromQL range-vector functions previously reported as not implemented. `sum_over_time`, `avg_over_time` and `count_over_time` are three different projections of the same `(sum, count)` accumulator, so they share one new header (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSumCountAvg.h`) with a single invertible `Summary{sum, count}` monoid (merge adds both fields, unmerge subtracts them), plugged into the existing generic `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSlidingSum` sliding-window fast path — the same infrastructure already proven by `rate`/`increase`/`delta`. No changes were needed to the generic grid/bucket machinery (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesBase.h`) or to `checkArgumentTypes` (all three take a single range-vector argument, the existing default). Registered `timeSeriesSumToGrid`/`timeSeriesAvgToGrid`/`timeSeriesCountToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the three `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`, matching `rate`/`increase`/`delta`'s convention. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0.** **Testing**: new SQL-level test (`04628_timeseries_sum_avg_count_over_time.sql`) plus cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering all three functions, an empty-window case, a window narrower than the step (grid points with no sample must be absent/NULL, not zero), and a nested `avg_over_time(rate(...)[2m:10s])` case. This flips 19 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed.
signals.author: valerypetrov

signals.title: Implement PromQL functions max_over_time() and min_over_time()
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `max_over_time()` and `min_over_time()`. ### Description Implements `max_over_time(v range-vector)` and `min_over_time(v range-vector)`, previously reported as not implemented. Unlike `sum`/`count`, max/min are not invertible monoids, but they are commutative and associative (merge = `max(a, b)`/`min(a, b)`), so the new header (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesExtremumOverTime.h`, templated on a bool `is_max_`) reuses `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSlidingSum`'s existing non-invertible sliding-window fallback (the same two-stacks/recompute machinery already shipped and tested via `deriv`/`predict_linear`) — no new windowing logic was needed. `Bucket == Summary` directly, following `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesToGridSparse`'s (`last_over_time`'s) simplest-case shape, since max/min don't depend on sample order. The comparison is NaN-aware (`candidate > current || isnan(current)`), matching Prometheus's own "a NaN currently held as the running extremum is unconditionally overwritten by the next sample" semantics. Registered `timeSeriesMaxToGrid`/`timeSeriesMinToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the two `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`, matching `rate`/`increase`/`delta`'s convention. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0.** **Testing**: new SQL-level test (`04628_max_min_over_time_timeseries_functions.sql`) including an `AggregatingMergeTree` serialize/deserialize/merge round-trip, plus cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering both functions over a series with decreases (so results differ meaningfully from `last_over_time`), including a more complex nested query. This flips 13 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed.
signals.author: valerypetrov

signals.title: Implement PromQL functions stddev_over_time() and stdvar_over_time()
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `stddev_over_time()` and `stdvar_over_time()` (population standard deviation/variance). ### Description Implements `stddev_over_time(v range-vector)` and `stdvar_over_time(v range-vector)`, previously reported as not implemented. **Key Technical & Numerical Stability Highlights**: 1. **Welford's Algorithm & Chan's Parallel Merge**: Uses a running centered-moment `{count, mean, m2}` accumulator ($M_2 = \sum (x - \bar{x})^2$) in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesVarianceOverTime.h` updated per sample via Welford's formula and merged pairwise via Chan et al.'s parallel merge algorithm. This avoids catastrophic cancellation on large-magnitude counter series (e.g. byte counters $\sim 5 \times 10^8$, where raw $\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2 / N$ loses all precision and produces false zeroes or negative variances). 2. **Prometheus Staleness Handling**: Implements full Prometheus stale-marker (`0x7ff0000000000002`) semantics. Stale markers are flagged at ingestion (`is_stale_marker`), excluded from range-vector aggregations (`WHERE NOT is_stale_marker`) so target disappearance does not pollute range windows with NaNs, while remaining detectable by instant selectors to correctly report series absence. 3. **Non-Invertible Two-Stacks / Recompute Strategy**: Avoids floating-point `unmerge` subtraction on moments to prevent numerical cancellation and drift over long sliding windows. Registered `timeSeriesStddevToGrid`/`timeSeriesStdvarToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the two `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`. **Verified numerically against Prometheus 3.5.0**: verified bit-for-bit accuracy against Prometheus 3.5.0 live responses, including cross-architecture (ARM64 vs x86_64) ULP tolerance handling in CI. **Testing**: SQL-level test (`04628_variance_timeseries_functions.sql`) covering empty/single/multi-sample windows and `AggregatingMergeTree` round-trips, plus integration cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` (including stale-marker ingestion and instant/range evaluations). This flips 12 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed.
signals.author: valerypetrov

signals.title: Support PromQL timestamp() function on both vector selectors and general expressions
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: `timestamp()` is now implemented for both direct selectors and general expressions, matching Prometheus 3.5.0 semantics. ### Description `timestamp(<expression>)` previously threw `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. This PR implements `timestamp()` support for both direct vector selectors and general instant vector expressions (e.g. `timestamp(test)`, `timestamp(test offset 1m)`, `timestamp(test * 1)`, `timestamp(-test)`, `timestamp(timestamp(test))`). Matching Prometheus 3.5.0 semantics: - For direct instant vector selectors (plus optional direct `offset`/`@` modifiers), extracts the raw sample timestamp from storage via `timeSeriesTimestampToGrid`. - For general instant vector expressions (binary math, unary operators, comparisons, nested `timestamp()` calls), evaluates the argument as an instant vector and returns the query step evaluation timestamp ($T_{\text{eval}}$) for each present sample. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0**, including the timestamp-unit conversion (seconds, not milliseconds). **Testing**: Added integration test cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering bare vector selectors, offset/@ modifiers, binary math, unary minus, and nested `timestamp()` calls.

signals.title: Fix data corruption when inserting into an Iceberg table through a materialized view
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109838 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed data corruption when inserting into an Iceberg table reached through a `MATERIALIZED VIEW`. The data file was written against the target's `CREATE`-time column types instead of its live Iceberg schema, so a `DateTime` value was stored as a bare Avro `int` and read back as microseconds, and with `DateTime64(0)` or `DateTime64(9)` the file could not be read back at all. As a consequence, `INSERT INTO <materialized view>` against a target whose Iceberg schema is wider than the view's declared columns now raises `TYPE_MISMATCH` instead of writing a corrupt row. ### Description `InsertDependenciesBuilder::observePath` captures each dependency node's metadata with a bare `getInMemoryMetadataPtr`, never calling `updateExternalDynamicMetadataIfExists`. `InterpreterInsertQuery::execute` does make that call, but only for the root insert target, which is why a direct `INSERT INTO <iceberg>` is correct. An Iceberg materialized view target therefore keeps its `CREATE`-time types, and that stale snapshot flows through `createSink` and `StorageObjectStorage::write` into the Avro format header, where `DateTime` shares the `UInt32` arm and is emitted as a bare `avro::IntSchema()` with no logical type. The reader maps the Iceberg `timestamp` primitive to `DateTime64(6)`, so a value written as 5 seconds is read back as 5 microseconds. The fix is one guarded call in `observePath`, restoring for dependent sinks the invariant `InterpreterInsertQuery` already establishes for the root target. Only `Avro` is affected. This is the structural gap #104917 documented but only symptom-fixed. Every insert corrupts, not only the first. Any read of the target, even a `DESCRIBE`, performs the refresh itself and persists it, which is why this went unnoticed and why a corrupt prefix survives. **One user-visible behaviour change:** `INSERT INTO <mv>` (into the view, not its source) against a widening-typed target now raises `TYPE_MISMATCH` instead of corrupting silently. That limitation is neither new nor data-lake specific: on master the same `Code: 53` appears once anything has read the target, and plain `MergeTree` behaves identically for `DateTime` -> `DateTime64(6)`. It is fail-closed: 0 rows, 0 data files. A separate task tracks it. New stateless test `04652_iceberg_mv_target_stale_schema_write.sh`: 14 assertions, 11 moving when the fix is reverted, 3 controls that must stay correct either way. 50 runs with the default randomization and 50 without are green. <details> <summary>Measured round trip, same declared type, unmodified master build</summary> | declared type | direct `INSERT INTO <iceberg>` | through a `MATERIALIZED VIEW TO <iceberg>` | |---|---|---| | `DateTime` | `2020-01-02 03:04:05.000000` | `1970-01-01 00:26:17.934245` | | `DateTime64(3)` | `2020-01-02 03:04:05.123000` | `1970-01-19 06:18:54.245123` | | `DateTime64(0)` | `2020-01-02 03:04:05.000000` | file cannot be read back (`Code: 36`) | | `DateTime64(9)` | `2020-01-02 03:04:05.123456` | file cannot be read back (`Code: 36`) | | `Nullable(DateTime)`, `Array(DateTime)`, `Tuple(a DateTime)`, `Map(String, DateTime)` | correct | corrupt | | `DateTime64(6)`, `Date`, `Date32`, integers, floats, `String`, `UUID` | correct | correct | Only `Avro` is affected, and not because the other writers ignore the declared type: `Parquet` and `ORC` write a self-describing physical unit, so a stale header costs precision rather than the value, while `Avro`'s `DateTime` arm emits no logical type at all. Physical oracle, independent of how the reader interprets the file: for the same declared `DateTime` column the Avro data file carries `{"type":"long","logicalType":"timestamp-micros"}` on the direct path and a bare `"type":"int"` through the view. The two unreadable scales land as `{"type":"bytes","logicalType":"decimal","scale":0}` and `...,"scale":9}`, the `Decimal` fallback the `Avro` writer takes for a `DateTime64` scale other than 3 or 6. </details> Reported at https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109838#discussion_r3662399031. There is no upstream issue for it. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1478` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Fix SimpleAggregateFunction Native header dropping an explicit nested aggregate version
signals.text: Fix SimpleAggregateFunction Native header dropping an explicit nested aggregate version Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes reading a `SimpleAggregateFunction` column whose value type holds an `AggregateFunction` declared with an explicit version `0`, such as `SimpleAggregateFunction(anyLast, AggregateFunction(0, sumMap, Array(UInt64), Array(Decimal32(2))))`. The `Native` type header omitted that version, so a reader re-parsing the announced type saw the function's default instead and could not read the data back: `SELECT` failed with `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` on `StripeLog`, and the column could not be reloaded by `Set`/`Join`, restored from a `Memory` backup, or read from a `Native` file, which was left empty. ### Description **Root cause.** `SimpleAggregateFunction(f, T)` is stored as the storage type `T` plus a custom name caching its own copy of `T`. Version `0` is never printed, so a leaf declared `AggregateFunction(0, ...)` prints a versionless spelling, and the alias rebuilds its value type by parsing that spelling back, where the missing token reads as the function's default. The version walker leaves an explicit version alone, so nothing corrects it: the header announces the default over a version-`0` payload, and for `sumMap` the two versions differ in width, so the reader over-consumes. **The change** stays at the transport boundary. `NativeWriter::write` renders the header from both type trees: syntax from the cached side, which alone remembers spellings such as `Nested(...)`, and versions from the live side. One rendering feeds the stream and index headers so they cannot drift apart. `getName()`, the type factory, the version walker and `NativeReader` are untouched, so `CREATE`, `ATTACH` and on-disk data are unchanged. **Scope after #112052.** That PR made the walker re-version the alias customization, which covers a leaf pinning no version: it is stored with the default spelled out, so header and payload already agree. What remains, and what this PR fixes, is the explicit version-`0` declaration. Verified against a master build carrying #112052 and none of this change: that case fails `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` there and round trips here. The test marks its regression arms; the wrapper and engine cases stay as round-trip coverage. **Known adjacent gap.** The same shape below a `Variant` fails identically on plain master. Covering it means mirroring the walker's discriminator-order and refuse-on-collapse semantics for an experimental type, which is a separate change; `NativeFormat.mdx` records the behaviour.
