signals.title: Precompute hashes and prefetch for fixed-size-keys aggregation methods
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104475 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): For the `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256` family of aggregation methods (several fixed-size keys packed into one integer), precompute the per-row canonical hashes in one pass over the batch-packed keys and reuse them to software-prefetch the target bucket and to skip rehashing the key in `emplace`. Previously the look-ahead prefetch computed every key and its hash twice per row. --- This extends the precomputed-hash + prefetch mechanism that #104475 introduced for the `prealloc_serialized` family to `HashMethodKeysFixed` (multi-key `GROUP BY` over numeric columns, e.g. ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q32). When the whole block of keys is batch-packed upfront (`prepared_keys`), the per-row canonical hashes are computed in one pass on the first `emplace`/`find` call and reused both for the look-ahead prefetch and for the insert itself, replacing the generic look-ahead in `Aggregator::executeImplBatch` that builds every key holder and hashes it a second time per row. Details: - The runtime gates mirror `prealloc_serialized`: batch-packed keys available, `enable_software_prefetch_in_aggregation`, and the `min_bytes_for_prefetch` hash-table size threshold (checked lazily on the first call, when `Data` is known). Nullable and low-cardinality variants never use `prepared_keys` and are excluded at compile time. - A new concept `HasPrefetchByHashMemberFunc` compiles the path out for tables without hash-addressed buckets (`FixedHashTable` behind `keys16`). Set, JOIN and `arrayUniq`-style callers of `HashMethodKeysFixed` pass no settings context, so nothing changes for them. - `HashMethodSerializedContext` carried only the settings and is now the shared `HashMethodSettingsContext`, also used by `HashMethodKeysFixed::createContext`. - `HashTable::isEmptyCell` (the `findKey` short-circuit for precomputed hashes, used in the `no_more_keys` mode) is made zero-key-aware: the zero key is stored outside the buffer, so an empty cell at the key's place proves nothing when the zero key is present. The existing user (`prealloc_serialized`) never produces empty keys, so this was latent; an all-zeros fixed key is common (the ClickBench `hits` table has a `SearchEngineID = 0, ClientIP = 0` group). Correctness was verified against an unpatched build of the same commit on the full ClickBench `hits` dataset (identical single part, 99,997,497 rows): full-result checksums for `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256`, nullable keys and `prealloc_serialized`; the all-zero key group; the `no_more_keys` path (`max_rows_to_group_by` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`); and external aggregation (spill + merge). All results are identical. An honest note on measured impact, from the investigation written up in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638#issuecomment-5285053418: in a local interleaved A/B on a (noisy, shared) 96-core aarch64 box, this change measures neutral on ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q35 — the generic look-ahead prefetch already covered these methods, so the remaining saving is one packed-key load plus one CRC per row. The issue's local reproduction numbers for these queries turned out to be dominated by an unrelated effect (the memory-based `max_threads` cap from #100383, which the pre-#100383 baseline build does not have — details in the issue). The perf tests that exercise these exact shapes (`tests/performance/clickbench.xml` Q30/Q31/Q32, `group_by_fixed_keys.xml`, `hash_table_sizes_stats.xml`) should be the arbiter on dedicated hardware.

signals.title: Support aggregate functions in the trivial GROUP BY LIMIT optimization
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114637 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114695 The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT n` optimization (`optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`, default `true`) now also fires for projections **with aggregate functions**, e.g. ClickBench Q17 (`SELECT UserID, SearchPhrase, COUNT(*) FROM hits GROUP BY UserID, SearchPhrase LIMIT 10`), while keeping the aggregate values of the returned keys **exact**. **Why it was restricted.** The settings-based rewrite (`max_rows_to_group_by = n + offset` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`) enforces the cutoff per aggregation stream: a key kept by one stream and rejected by another loses the other stream's rows and comes out of the merge with an undercounted value. Returning an unspecified subset of the groups is fine for `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`; returning wrong values is not. **How it works now (shared kept keys, zero hot-path cost).** The streams aggregate completely normally until the first one exceeds `n + offset` distinct keys (the pre-existing per-block `checkLimits`). That stream publishes a frozen seed of exactly `n + offset` kept keys with empty aggregate states (`ManyAggregatedData::SharedKeptKeys`); every stream then rebuilds its hash table to exactly that key set — keeping the states it accumulated for the kept keys, dropping the rest — and continues on the pre-existing `no_more_keys` path against a table of `n + offset` keys. Streams that finished consuming before the freeze are rebuilt by the last stream before the merge. Every row before the freeze is aggregated normally and every later row of a kept key finds its key in the rebuilt table, so the merged values are exact; the dropped keys are absent from every rebuilt table and never reach the result. The rebuild reuses the existing two-stage machinery (`convertToChunks(final = false)` + `mergeOnBlock`), so the hot aggregation loops in `Aggregator.cpp` are untouched. **Where it fires.** The cutoff is detected in the planner and enabled only when the node performs the complete aggregation itself (first and second stage): partial states sent to a remote initiator would be merged with other nodes' states, whose kept keys differ, and the values would be undercounted again — across nodes instead of across threads. On the shards of distributed queries and on the replicas of parallel-replicas reading it stays off. The settings-based rewrite of `OptimizeTrivialGroupByLimitPass` remains for aggregate-free projections (it is sound cross-shard). For the 8/16-bit key methods (fixed hash maps bounded by the key space) the cutoff stays inert and the aggregation is complete and exact. External aggregation is disabled when the cutoff is armed (spilled buckets would bypass the restriction); memory stays bounded by roughly `n + offset` keys plus one block of keys per stream. **Guards for wrong results of the existing optimization.** The shape check (shared between the pass and the planner, `getTrivialGroupByLimit`) now also rejects `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions and `arrayJoin` in the projection. These consume or filter the groups after the aggregation, and all four cases were verified to return wrong results on master with the default settings (e.g. `SELECT DISTINCT intDiv(k, 25000) FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 3` returned 1 row instead of 3; `SELECT count() OVER () FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 5` returned ~100 instead of 100000). Test `04837` pins all four in both the top-level (pass) and subquery (planner) forms. The guards are also submitted separately as the minimal backportable bug fix https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114695 (issue https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114693); whichever merges second needs a trivial conflict resolution. **Measured** on a 96-core aarch64 box, `SELECT number % 100000000 AS k, count() FROM numbers_mt(200000000) GROUP BY k LIMIT 10`: 0.06–0.13 s with the optimization vs 0.37–0.94 s without (interleaved hot runs on a shared machine). The values of the returned keys match the full aggregation exactly (verified by the `04836` join-against-truth tests for `UInt64`/`String`/`LowCardinality`/`Nullable`/two-key shapes, `count`/`sum`/`min`/`max`/`uniqExact`, with `OFFSET`, under single-stream and 16-stream execution, from aggregate projections, and over `remote()`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT n` optimization (setting `optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`) now also applies to queries with aggregate functions in the projection, such as ClickBench Q17: once any aggregation thread exceeds `n + offset` distinct keys, all threads are restricted to a single shared set of kept keys, so the hash tables stay small while the aggregate values of the returned keys remain exact (about 2x on ClickBench Q17). Additionally, the optimization no longer fires for queries with `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions, or `arrayJoin` in the projection, where it could return wrong results. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Parallelize single-level to two-level conversion in Aggregator::prepareVariantsToMerge
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114640 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107490 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/pull/1360 When some per-thread aggregation states convert themselves to two-level mid-scan, `Aggregator::prepareVariantsToMerge` converts all the remaining single-level variants **sequentially on one thread**. Initializing a two-level variant allocates and zeroes 256 bucket tables, and there is one variant per query thread, so on machines with many cores this serial loop dominates short aggregation queries. This regime became reachable after #107490: the accurate aggregation memory accounting makes `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes` (default 50 MB) engage for queries with **few groups but heavy states** (e.g. `uniqExact` over ~300 groups, where the states sum to hundreds of MB while the hash tables stay tiny). Previously the query-tracker delta under-reported such memory (each thread batches up to `max_untracked_memory` before propagating), so the threshold effectively never fired for this shape. Once it fires mid-scan, only the variants that happen to execute a block after the crossing convert themselves (measured: ~25 of 192 on ClickBench Q11), and the merge preparation then serially converts the remaining ~170. Effect on ClickBench (`c7a.metal-48xl`, 192 cores), hot runs, bisected and measured via manual ClickBench dispatches (evidence and result files in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/pull/1360): | build | Q10 | Q11 | |---|---|---| | master `c79b0d9227e` (4 min before #107490) | 0.133 | 0.092 | | master `32129f76fca` (4 min after #107490) | 0.297 | 0.165 | | master 07-11 (`ab8535b3ab0`) | 0.391 | 0.213 | | master 07-11 + `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes=0` | 0.093 | 0.102 | | pre-#107490 + `group_by_two_level_threshold=1` (uniform early conversion) | 0.132 | 0.095 | The last two rows show the cost is specifically the serial merge-prep conversion after a mid-scan flip: disabling the bytes trigger recovers fully, and uniform early conversion (which happens in parallel, each thread converting its own variant during the scan) is also fast. The daily ClickBench dashboard shows the same regression on both `c7a.metal-48xl` and `c8g.metal-48xl` (192 physical cores) since 2026-07-19, and not on machines with 96 or fewer physical cores. The fix converts the remaining single-level variants in parallel on the aggregator thread pool, following the existing `ThreadPoolCallbackRunnerLocal` pattern used elsewhere in the file. Converting distinct variants concurrently is safe: `AggregatedDataVariants::convertToTwoLevel` touches only the variant's own members. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Parallelize the single-level to two-level conversion of per-thread aggregation states before merging. This fixes a 2-3x regression of short `GROUP BY` queries with heavy aggregate states (e.g. `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)`, ClickBench Q10/Q11) on machines with very many cores, introduced in 26.7 development builds when the aggregation memory accounting was made accurate. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1469` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix wrong results of the trivial GROUP BY LIMIT optimization with DISTINCT, QUALIFY, window functions or arrayJoin
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114693 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114690 The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT` optimization (`optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`, default `true` since 26.5) caps the aggregation at `LIMIT + OFFSET` distinct keys, which is only sound when the LIMIT directly cuts the produced groups. The shape check missed four constructs that consume or filter the groups **between** the aggregation and the LIMIT, and each of them returned wrong results with default settings (verified on master; reproducers in the issue and in the added test): - `DISTINCT` collapses the projected groups: `SELECT DISTINCT intDiv(k, 25000) FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 3` returned **1 row instead of 3**. - A window function in the projection is evaluated over all groups (`hasWindow` only catches the named `WINDOW` clause, not an inline `OVER ()`): `SELECT count() OVER () FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 5` returned **~100 instead of 100000**. - `arrayJoin` in the projection can drop rows (empty arrays), so the kept groups may produce fewer rows than the LIMIT while more groups exist: **1 row instead of 10**. - `QUALIFY` filters the groups after the aggregation: **0 rows instead of 10** (a `QUALIFY` on plain group keys alone is pushed down below the aggregation and was not affected; a window function in the projection keeps it in place). The pass now skips these shapes. https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114690 contains the same guards as part of a shared shape-check helper; whichever merges second needs a trivial conflict resolution, and this separate pull request keeps the wrong-results fix minimal and backportable on its own. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results of the trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT` optimization (setting `optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`) for queries with `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions, or `arrayJoin` in the projection: these consume or filter the groups after the aggregation, so capping the aggregation at `LIMIT + OFFSET` keys could return too few rows or wrong values. The optimization no longer applies to such queries. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1479` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Support PromQL histogram_fraction for classic histograms
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL: support `histogram_fraction()` for classic histograms.** ### Description **What was missing** Prometheus supports `histogram_fraction(lower, upper, b)` for estimating the fraction of observations between two bounds. ClickHouse previously rejected this function in TimeSeries PromQL queries. **What this PR adds** - **Add:** support for classic Prometheus bucket series. - Reuses the existing classic histogram handling used by `histogram_quantile`. - Matches Prometheus behavior for interpolation and bucket edge cases. - Keeps different histogram metric names separate during aggregation. - Removes the input metric name from the result. Example: ```promql histogram_fraction(0.1, 0.5, http_request_duration_seconds_bucket) ``` ### Why this matters **This is used for real latency and SLO queries**, not only parser compatibility. - **Pyrra:** generates `histogram_fraction()` in native-histogram latency SLO rules. See the [query generator](https://github.com/pyrra-dev/pyrra/blob/main/slo/promql.go#L761-L784) and [example SLO config](https://github.com/pyrra-dev/pyrra/blob/main/examples/pyrra-connect-latency.yaml#L14-L20). - **Grafana SLO:** uses it in a [request-latency SLI query](https://grafana.com/docs/plugins/grafana-slo-app/latest/sli-examples/latency/). - **Grafana Mimir:** documents it for calculating the [fraction of requests in a latency range](https://grafana.com/docs/mimir/latest/visualize/native-histograms/). - **Prometheus:** uses it for [fraction and Apdex calculations](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/). Without this function, PromQL copied from these workflows fails in ClickHouse. ### Scope - **Supported:** classic `*_bucket` histogram series. - **Supported:** constant scalar lower and upper bounds. - **Not supported yet:** native histogram samples. - **Not supported yet:** non-constant bound expressions. Native histogram samples are not supported by the current TimeSeries Engine. This PR intentionally covers the classic bucket form first. ### References - [Prometheus histogram functions](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#histogram_fraction) - [Prometheus classic histogram implementation](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/quantile.go) ### Changes - **Function support:** add `histogram_fraction` to the TimeSeries function registry and support documentation. - **Execution:** add a Prometheus-compatible classic histogram fraction aggregate. - **Shared logic:** reuse the histogram SQL-building pipeline with `histogram_quantile`. - **Precision:** preserve Float64 bound literals for Float32 tables and exact cumulative-count differences for large UInt64 counts. ### Tests - **Interpolation:** normal buckets, `rate()` input, negative bucket bounds, and bounds inside buckets. - **Bucket edges:** exact boundaries, degenerate buckets, `+Inf`, `NaN`, malformed `le`, and out-of-range bounds. - **Grouping:** range queries with multiple histogram groups and `sum by (le)` aggregation. - **Input validation:** invalid argument types and non-constant bounds. - **Float32:** regression coverage for precision near an `le` boundary. - **UInt64:** regression coverage for one-count differences above `2^53`. - **Compliance:** add classic histogram fraction queries to the PromQL compliance cases. - **Checks:** `git diff --check` and Python syntax validation for the integration test files.

signals.title: Do not prune with an invalid polygon in pointInPolygon key analysis
signals.text: Do not prune with an invalid polygon in pointInPolygon key analysis <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114630 (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed rows missing from the result of a `SELECT` filtered by `pointInPolygon` over a MergeTree primary key when the polygon argument is an invalid constant literal and `validate_polygons = 0`. Primary key analysis derived granule pruning from a polygon it never validated, and dropped granules holding matching rows. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114630 ### Description Two defects, both making primary key analysis prune from a polygon that disagrees with the one `pointInPolygon` evaluates. **Invalid ring.** The constant ring was never checked with `boost::geometry::is_valid`, unlike `parseConstPolygon` and the GeoParquet pruning path. `bg::correct` does not repair a self-intersection, so the unusable ring reached `bg::intersects`, whose relate-based answer disagrees with the grid algorithm the function evaluates. On the reporter's reproducer: 849 rows against 875 for the same data with a key permitting no such atom, 26 lost. Both argument forms are affected, correcting the issue text: they reach the same lambda, as the reporter's own three-argument case (794 against 820) shows. **Invalid assembly (found in review).** Holes are not stored, so the filter tests the shell alone, which over-approximates the function only while the assembled shell-plus-holes shape is valid. A valid *concave* shell with a self-intersecting hole loses rows: an L-shaped shell with a bowtie hole returned 3446 against 3556, the 110 missing rows all in the shell's notch, which the shell excludes but the assembly includes. A convex shell cannot expose this, having no notch outside its own outline. Both are fixed by validating the shape the function itself validates and declining the atom otherwise, so no pruning happens and the scan returns the correct rows. This mirrors `GeoBbox.h`, which refuses a pruning bbox rather than throwing; index analysis must not raise user errors. Neither check is gated on `validate_polygons`: with validation enabled the query already fails earlier, so gating would keep the bug for exactly the users who can reach it. `force_primary_key = 1` now raises `INDEX_NOT_USED` on these shapes, no key atom being left to force. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Debug build, both directions, Build IDs asserted against the running servers. | Case (`validate_polygons = 0`) | Before | After | Expected | |---|---|---|---| | bowtie ring, 2-arg, both modes | 849 | 875 | 875 | | bowtie ring, 3-arg with hole, both modes | 794 | 820 | 820 | | rows lost / gained | 26 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | | valid concave shell + bowtie hole, both modes | 3446 | 3556 | 3556 | | rows lost, that case | 110 | 0 | 0 | | degenerate 2-point ring | 8 | 8 | 8 | | valid convex ring | 1681 | 1681 | 1681 | | valid ring, granules | 289/1250 | 289/1250 | unchanged | | valid shell + valid hole, granules | 85/1250 | 85/1250 | unchanged | | invalid ring, granules | 188/1250 | 1250/1250 | no pruning | | invalid assembly, granules | 733/1250 | 1250/1250 | no pruning | Every shape newly declined is already rejected by the function under the default `validate_polygons = 1`, verified per shape, so pruning changes only under the explicit opt-out. Valid shapes keep pruning: interior hole, two disjoint holes, holes sharing a vertex, clockwise and explicitly-closed holes, concave shell with interior hole, and the existing with-holes minmax test. The test fails on the unpatched binary with exactly the pre-fix counts and passes 50/50 randomized. Of 153 selected `polygon`, `key_condition`, `primary_key_index`, `geo_` and `minmax_index` tests, 15 failed and none is attributable: 9 fail identically unpatched, and 6 are order or sandbox-config flakes measured on both binaries. </details> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1487` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: CI: run the full test suite only when review threads are resolved
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114724 While a PR has unresolved review threads, running the full test suite is a waste: the code is expected to change again once the review comments are addressed. This PR implements the gate requested in the issue: - A new `review_threads.py` pre-hook in the `Config Workflow` counts the PR's unresolved review threads (via GraphQL `reviewThreads`) and stores the state in the workflow kv data. While threads are unresolved, `should_skip_job` runs only builds and the preliminary checks (`Style check`, `Fast test`), plus the `Code Review` job — the AI review keeps re-checking pushed code and resolves its own addressed threads, which is what re-triggers the full suite automatically. - The `can_be_merged.py` post-hook re-checks the live thread state at finish time and turns the `Mergeable Check` red while threads are unresolved, or while only the limited pipeline ran (even if the threads were resolved mid-run — the full suite still has not run). The per-run verdict is recorded in a new `Review Threads` commit status, which doubles as immediate feedback on the PR. This also makes the decision on the AI review's comments once they are ready, as suggested in the issue: comments posted during the run are seen by the finish-time check. - A new `Rerun On Review Threads` workflow detects state changes and re-runs the last completed `PR` workflow run for the current head commit whenever the recorded verdict disagrees with the live state (thread resolved/unresolved, new review comments, the override label added/removed). Previously succeeded jobs are restored from the CI cache, so the re-run only executes the previously skipped jobs. Review-thread events on PRs from forks carry a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so they are relayed through a trivial `Review Threads Signal` workflow and handled on its `workflow_run` completion in the trusted default-branch context; `PR` workflow completions are watched too, to catch threads resolved while a run was still in flight. A safety cap (5 attempts per run) prevents any reconciliation bug from re-running one workflow forever. - The gate can be bypassed with the new `ignore-unresolved-threads` label (fetched fresh from the API, so adding the label and re-running works; the label also triggers the re-run automatically). `ci-force-all` still bypasses job filtering, so it runs the full suite, but it does not bypass the merge gate for unresolved threads. - `retry_infra_failures.yml` learned to not treat a `Finish Workflow` failure caused by this merge gate as an infrastructure failure. - Failure direction: if the thread state cannot be fetched at config time, nothing is skipped (fail toward more testing); at finish time the check fails close (the `Mergeable Check` goes red). The `ignore-unresolved-threads` label has been created in the repository. Documentation: a new `Review threads check` section in `docs/resources/develop-contribute/contribute/continuous-integration.mdx`. Tests: `ci/tests/test_review_threads_gate.py` pins the decision functions and their integration into `should_skip_job` (what is skipped, what keeps running, the merge-gate truth table, the commit-status description budget). ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signals.title: CI: run only the selected tests in the sanitizer functional tests in PRs
signals.text: The sanitizer flavors of `Stateless tests` ran the whole suite in every pull request: 17 jobs for the ASan/UBSan, TSan and MSan builds. Under the assumption in the issue - that the stress tests with sanitizers are a stronger check than a plain functional run - those jobs now run only the tests selected for the change. The new `selected tests` option of `ci/jobs/functional_tests.py` runs an ordinary functional test run over the subset that `Targeting` already computes for the targeted check: the tests the pull request changes, the tests that already failed in this pull request, and the tests covering the changed lines according to the coverage database. Unlike the `targeted` check, it does not rerun that selection many times - it is a plain run with a shorter list of tests. The selection is a few hundred tests, so the batches of the full-suite jobs collapse into a single job per flavor: 17 jobs become 8. What still covers the whole suite in a pull request: the debug and plain binary functional test jobs, and the stress tests, which run the functional tests under every sanitizer with heavy concurrency and randomized settings. The master workflow is unchanged and keeps running the full suite in every flavor. Also in this change: * When the selection cannot be fetched (the coverage database or the GitHub diff is unavailable), the job fails rather than silently run an unbatched, weaker version of the former sanitizer configuration. Retrying restores the intended selected-test run. * Tests the job flavor would never run (`no-parallel` tests in a `parallel` job and vice versa) are dropped from the selection, and the job is skipped when nothing is left for it. * `clickhouse-test` exits with code 1 when every test it was given is filtered out - e.g. all the selected tests are tagged `no-tsan` in a TSan job. For a run over an explicit list of tests (flaky, targeted, `selected tests`) that is now reported as SKIPPED instead of a failure; for a full-suite run it stays a failure, since there it means a broken filter. Unit tests for the new logic are in `ci/tests/test_selected_tests_run.py`. `.github/workflows/pull_request.yml` was regenerated via `python3 -m ci.praktika yaml`. ### Verification in this pull request's own CI This pull request changes no source file and no test under `tests/queries`, so nothing is relevant to select and the new jobs correctly report SKIPPED. To exercise the path that actually runs a subset, commit 85362432c858e0cd9aadbf57f2895888b9d35863 temporarily touched `00001_select_1.sql` (reverted in the following commit). On that commit, with all builds served from the cache: * `Stateless tests (amd_tsan, parallel, selected tests)` and `Stateless tests (amd_asan_ubsan, distributed plan, parallel, selected tests)` ran, and the report shows the three selection passes followed by the single selected test - `00001_select_1 OK 1.01s`. * `Stateless tests (amd_asan_ubsan, db disk, distributed plan, sequential, selected tests)` skipped, because the only changed test is parallel-safe and the flavor filter left it nothing to run. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114730&sha=85362432c858e0cd9aadbf57f2895888b9d35863&name_0=PR Possible follow-up, not done here: once the test list is short, the job start dominates the run - in the TSan run above, `Start ClickHouse Server` (which prepares the stateful datasets `test.hits`, `test.visits`, TPC-DS and TPC-H) took 324 seconds out of a 418-second job. Skipping the stateful preparation when no stateful test is selected needs a reliable way to tell, so it is left out of this change. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114725 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ...

signals.title: Adaptive lazy execution of short-circuit function arguments (continues #73776)
signals.text: This continues #73776 by @lgbo-ustc, whose branch was ~17 months behind `master` and could no longer be merged mechanically (27 conflicting files in the hottest central code). The author's commits are preserved; on top of them this reconciles the change with the current `master` and reworks the plumbing. Short-circuit evaluation decides *statically* which arguments of `and`, `or`, `if` and `multiIf` are executed lazily. Lazy execution is not free: the rows which are not needed are filtered out and the result is expanded back to the original size. When the filtered out part is small, or the argument itself is cheap, this overhead is larger than the work it saves. This adds an opt-in adaptive mode: the execution of every function is profiled (elapsed time and processed rows), and every 20000 rows the decision is revisited per action - lazy execution is turned off when the estimated cost of the full execution is lower than the measured cost of the lazy execution, and turned back on when the per-row cost of the action grows significantly. Actions whose function can throw an exception on invalid input values (for example `intDiv(1, 0)`) are never switched to eager execution, so the short-circuit protection is preserved. The mode is disabled by default and enabled with the new experimental setting `enable_adaptive_short_circuit_lazy_execution`. Changes on top of the original branch: * The flag no longer travels through `ExpressionStep`/`FilterStep` constructors, the query plan optimizations, the planner and the step serialization. It lives in `ExpressionActionsSettings` next to `enable_lazy_columns_replication`, which removes ~20 files from the change and all the ripple through `QueryPlan/Optimizations`. * `ExpressionActions::execute` and `executeOnColumns` stay `const`; the free `executeAction` became a member with three virtual hooks (`shouldExecuteLazily`, `executeFunction`, `finalizeBlockExecution`) which `AdaptiveExpressionActions` overrides. * The profile plumbing follows the current `IExecutableFunction` chain, including `executeWithoutReplicatedColumns`, which did not exist when the branch was written. * `is_no_except` is computed only when the setting is enabled, so nothing changes for the default path. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental setting `enable_adaptive_short_circuit_lazy_execution`, which enables dynamic evaluation of whether a short-circuit function's argument should be lazily executed. The execution of the functions is profiled at runtime, and the lazy execution of an argument is disabled when it costs more than executing the argument on all the rows. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/73776

signals.title: Build Debian packages for the release builds only
signals.text: The `Stress test` was the only job installing the Debian packages of the debug, sanitizer and CFI builds, and it can take the plain `clickhouse` binary instead — that binary is built and uploaded for every build type anyway. Every other consumer of the packages (`Install packages`, `Compatibility check`, `Upgrade check`, the server Docker images and the release jobs) runs on a release build. So the release builds keep their packages, and nine of the eleven packaging steps go away, together with the `DESTDIR` install that copies the whole binary, and the upload and download of the resulting packages. The stress test now sets up the paths the packages own from the binary: `install_binary` in `stress_tests.lib` symlinks `/usr/bin/clickhouse*` at it, installs the default `config.xml` and `users.xml`, and unpacks the self-extracting archive up front — decompressing a sanitizer build under `clickhouse start` would eat into its wait for the pid file and race any concurrent `clickhouse local`. `install_packages` stays for the upgrade check, which installs an actual release. Symbolization is unaffected: `clickhouse_split_debug_symbols` leaves `programs/clickhouse` untouched and strips only the copy it installs, so the binary artifact carries its debug info even for a release build. For the sanitizer builds `clickhouse-common-static-dbg` was empty to begin with, since they do not set `SPLIT_DEBUG_SYMBOLS`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signals.title: Do not read FINAL merging columns that the output header no longer carries
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/91849 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` ("Unexpected number of kept output positions after removing unused columns from `ReadFromMergeTree`") raised by a `SELECT ... FINAL` whose `PREWHERE` uses a column that `FINAL` needs for merging (`ver`, `is_deleted`, `sign`) and which does not select that column. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/91849 ### Description A `SELECT ... FINAL` whose `PREWHERE` consumes a merging column it does not select fails with `LOGICAL_ERROR: Unexpected number of kept output positions after removing unused columns from ReadFromMergeTree`. `removeUnusedColumns` added back to the read set every `getColumnsRequiredForMergingFinal` column, including ones `PREWHERE` had consumed and the output header no longer carried. `kept_output_positions` is sized from the old header, so the header recomputed from the widened read set was longer and tripped the count assertion. That widening is redundant: `initializePipeline` already appends the sorting-key columns plus `is_deleted`/`sign`/`version` for `FINAL`, and passes `original_column_names` separately so the extras are projected back off. So retain a merging column at analysis time only when the output header has it. The header keeps its size, `kept_output_positions` stays correct, and the assertion is kept. This is option 1 of the two I put to @antaljanosbenjamin above, reached by not widening the read set at all, so no position mapping is rebuilt and no grown root header has to be reconciled. Say so if you would rather the general fix (option 2) land. It also drops the first version's `canRemoveUnusedColumns` exclusion, so pruning now applies where that version declined it. The merge still gets its key columns: `is_deleted` stays in the read set, and every merging mode returns the same deduplicated rows as with `query_plan_remove_unused_columns = 0` on multi-part tables. Test `04906` covers both entry points, four merging modes, the optimizer-moved `PREWHERE`, the two late header rebuilds and duplicate output names, and asserts pruning still applies. Found by the AST fuzzer and the stress test on unrelated pull requests; also reproduces on a plain `FROM t FINAL`. - `AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107305&sha=1a49e7372d0f969cd06d7ba237d8eb3b3461e814&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29 - `Stress test (arm_asan_ubsan, s3)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108069&sha=77f495e71c33bb2c27441fa12f9deb0fdb7e24f2&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1463` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Remove `WINDOW VIEW`
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/61069 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113493 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114097 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/75191 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/88706 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The experimental `WINDOW VIEW` feature is removed, together with the `WATCH` statement and the `windowID` function. It has been non-functional since version 24.12 (inserts into the source table were silently not delivered to window views) and was never supported by the analyzer, which is enabled by default since 24.3. The settings `allow_experimental_window_view`, `window_view_clean_interval`, `window_view_heartbeat_interval`, and `wait_for_window_view_fire_signal_timeout` are kept as obsolete no-ops. The time-window functions `tumble`, `tumbleStart`, `tumbleEnd`, `hop`, `hopStart`, and `hopEnd` are kept. If you still have window views defined, drop them before upgrading: a server that finds a window view in its metadata fails to start (`Cannot parse definition from metadata file ... (SYNTAX_ERROR)`), the same way the removal of the `Lazy` database engine behaves. Similar functionality will be reimplemented on top of streaming queries (issue [#114738](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738)). The removal, in detail: - `src/Storages/WindowView/` (`StorageWindowView`, `WindowViewSource`, `StorageBlocks`), `WatermarkTransform`, the `ParserCreateWindowViewQuery` parser, and the whole `WATCH` statement stack (`ParserWatchQuery`, `ASTWatchQuery`, `InterpreterWatchQuery`, the `IStorage::watch` virtual) — window views were the last implementor of `watch`, and the `WATCH` statement was already documented as deprecated. - The `ASTCreateQuery` watermark/lateness fields and their AST JSON serialization and validation. The `clickhouse_json` boundary fails closed rather than silently reinterpreting legacy payloads: `ASTCreateQuery::readJSON` rejects a set `is_window_view`, watermark strategy or `allowed_lateness` flag and the `watermark_function` / `lateness_function` children (otherwise such a payload deserialized as an ordinary `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` and was executed as an immediate-population table create), while `ASTViewTargets::readJSON` rejects the `Inner` target kind, which nothing produces any more and which formatted back to parser-impossible `INNER ENGINE ...` SQL. Both are covered by `04892_ast_json_removed_window_view_state`; the `PushingToWindowViewSink` and `ViewType::WINDOW` branches in `InsertDependenciesBuilder`; window-view special cases in `InterpreterCreateQuery`, `InterpreterInsertQuery`, `StorageFactory`, `DatabaseOrdinary`, `DatabaseReplicated`, `DDLDependencyVisitor`, `QueryFuzzer`, BuzzHouse, and the ArrowFlight table-type mapping. - The `windowID` function and the `UInt32` single-argument forms of `tumbleStart`/`tumbleEnd`/`hopStart`/`hopEnd` (they only accepted `windowID` output). The rest of the time-window function family stays, since these are ordinary functions usable in a regular `GROUP BY` and are exactly the vocabulary for the streaming-queries replacement. - The keywords `WATCH`, `EVENTS`, `ALLOWED_LATENESS`, and `STRICTLY_ASCENDING` (the `WATERMARK` keyword stays: the streaming-queries `WATERMARK FOR` clause uses it), the error code `QUERY_IS_NOT_SUPPORTED_IN_WINDOW_VIEW`, and the corresponding fuzzer dictionary and ANTLR grammar entries. - Kept for compatibility: `QueryViewsLogElement::ViewType::WINDOW` (so existing `system.query_views_log` tables keep their schema) and `ViewTarget::Inner` (so old DDL log entries still parse), following the same pattern as the `LIVE VIEW` removal. - The `allow_experimental_window_view` constraint in `tests/docker_scripts/stress_tests.lib` is kept (only the constraint, not the profile value, which would mark an obsolete setting as changed and add a `system.warnings` entry): the upgrade check runs the previous release's suite under the previous release's binary, whose window-view tests are not dropped afterwards because `--upgrade-check` implies `--fake-drop`, and the leftover metadata would then stop the new server from starting. - Tests: the four remaining window-view tests are removed. The pure time-window-function coverage of `01049_window_view_window_functions` moved to a new `04891_time_window_functions` test, which also pins the new `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` behavior of `tumbleStart(UInt32)`. - Docs: the `Window View` section of `CREATE VIEW`, the `WATCH` page (with its navigation entries and locale twins) are removed and the old-slug redirects retargeted; the window-view entries are removed from the generated settings/functions reference pages (second commit, hence the `pr-autogenerated-docs` label): the `window-view.mdx` settings page, the four settings' entries in the pages/manifest/navigation/settings explorer, and the `windowID` section of `time-window-functions.mdx`. The unrelated drift accumulated on master since the last nightly regeneration is deliberately not included; the nightly docs-autogen job will pick it up. Why now: the feature has been non-functional since Dec 2024 — commit `ceae84c87a2` removed the explicit view-dependency registration and `DDLDependencyVisitor` never extracted the source table of a `CREATE WINDOW VIEW`, so inserts into the source table were silently not pushed to window views, and direct inserts failed with `std::out_of_range` (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113493). Nobody noticed for ~1.5 years. It was never ported to the analyzer (with `enable_analyzer = 1`, the default, existing window views load permanently inert), its tests were removed in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/73822 because they were inherently flaky, and it kept costing triage time (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114097 is a recent server SIGSEGV through `getSourceTableSelectQuery`). The full assessment, including the plan for reimplementing this functionality on top of streaming queries (`SELECT ... FROM t STREAM`, `WATERMARK FOR`, emit-on-watermark windowed aggregation), is in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114738. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Support DEFINER / SQL SECURITY for dictionaries
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85293 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support `DEFINER` and `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` for dictionaries, like for views. A dictionary with a local `CLICKHOUSE` source can name the user whose privileges its load runs with, instead of storing a user and password in `SOURCE(...)`. Rotating that user's password no longer breaks the dictionary. ### Description A dictionary with a `CLICKHOUSE` source authenticates every load with the credentials in `SOURCE(...)`, so rotating that password breaks all later reloads. A deployment issuing short-lived credentials must embed a long-lived one, or load as `default` with excess authority. Name the identity instead: `DEFINER = dict_owner`, with no `USER`/`PASSWORD` in `SOURCE(...)`. The load then runs with that user's privileges, consults no credential, and is bounded by the definer's settings constraints. It reuses the view definer machinery, inheriting the `SET DEFINER` grant check and the guard against dropping a live definer. `04869_dictionary_definer.sh` covers rotation against a stored-credential control, privilege and settings bounding, `SET DEFINER`, the metadata round trip, every rejection, and locality both ways, each arm mutation-verified. Scoped to a **local** `CLICKHOUSE` source, as @ pufit confirmed on the issue: any other authenticates against a foreign system with credentials a locally resolved identity cannot replace, so the clause is rejected at `CREATE` time. Locality is decided on the effective configuration, resolving named collections and `PORT tcpPort()` first; an unprovable source is rejected too. `DEFINER` is the only accepted type and must name somebody: `INVOKER` because a dictionary loads from a background pool with no invoker, `NONE` because nothing consults the type at load time. A dictionary without the clause is unchanged; `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = Dictionary(...) SQL SECURITY ...` keeps failing closed. Three limits come from the shared UUID-keyed definer registry, and each is master's behaviour for views today: an ephemeral `<user>:definer` clone can go uncollected when a `CREATE` is rejected late or the object leaves a UUID-bearing database; drop protection does not apply in `Memory` or `Ordinary` databases; and a `DROP USER` racing a `CREATE` can pass its dependency check before the object registers (over 60 attempts, 21 hits for views on master against 2 for dictionaries here).

signals.title: Do not let a post-run coverage diagnostic discard a finished test run's exit code
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `NightlyCoverage` shards exit 1 after every test has already passed. CIDB gets a pseudo-test row `clickhouse-test` / FAIL whose whole context is `clickhouse-test exited with code 1`, while the report shows the shard `OK` with `Failed: 0`. On master: 83 such rows in 30 days, 26 nights, all 8 shards, 6 of them on one nightly. Cause: `main()`'s post-run coverage block printed one diagnostic line built from two `FINAL` aggregates over `system.coverage_log`, the only two statements in that block outside a `try/except`. `clickhouse_execute` defaults to `timeout=30` and re-raises after 5 retries, and the aggregates sit at that cap: the job's own exporter runs the same aggregate over the same 23.4-25.4M rows in 20-29s. The `TimeoutError` propagates out of `main()`, so `sys.exit(exit_code.value)` never runs and Python exits 1 with every result already collected. That costs a red job for a non-failure, and an exit status that no longer separates a test failure from a teardown timeout. The statement is deleted rather than guarded because in this job it is a vestigial duplicate: `CoverageExporter.do()` re-runs the identical aggregate about 30s later, prints a strict superset of the numbers, and raises when the row count is zero. Nothing reads `cov_rows`/`cov_tests`. A local run drops the export stage, so it loses the line rather than seeing it duplicated. Validated locally: the extracted block exits 1 before the change and 0 after, with negative controls confirming the probe is specific to this timeout. Every remaining `clickhouse_execute` in the post-run block is now guarded (checked by AST). The pre-run block is untouched: it is meant to fail the run when coverage is broken. Two siblings are left alone: `coverage_indirect_calls` is redundant the same way but already guarded, and `reportCoverage` is unguarded but no CI job passes `--report-coverage`. CI report, shard 3/8 of the 2026-08-13 nightly: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=3da3cf323b91553960bdf55780a3b94e9deb5793&name_0=NightlyCoverage&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_llvm_coverage_per_test%2C%20per_test_coverage%2C%203%2F8%29

signals.title: Replace the AggregatingInOrderTransform cancellation test with a failpoint integration test
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110104 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107941 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110104 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107941 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `04512_aggregation_in_order_cancellation.sh` guards the per-key-interval cancellation check from #110104, but asserts on aggregation CPU as a multiple of scan CPU after a shell-issued `KILL`. It prints `not cancelled in time` on master again: 6 such failures on 2026-08-13 (2 on master, 4 on unrelated PRs), 5 on `amd_asan_ubsan, distributed plan, parallel`. Eighth rewrite of the assertion. The oracle prices the window between "rows are read" and "the `KILL` flips `is_cancelled`", and two `clickhouse-client` startups sit on that path; `04410_primes_source_cancellation.sh:48-49` records ~8 s for one invocation on a loaded sanitizer build. On all five failures that printed the CPU diagnostics the checkpoint was firing, stopping at 48-75 % of the loop, not 100 %: only the window grew, and the shell cannot close it, since read progress is published only after the source's `work()` returns (`ExecutionThreadContext.cpp:57-75`). So this adopts the mechanism `LimitByTransform` already uses (`e20a67394329867` and follow-ups): a `PAUSEABLE_ONCE` failpoint on interval 6, after the cancellation check and inside the loop, a `LOG_TEST` marker in the existing cancellation branch, and an integration test that pauses there, kills, resumes and asserts the marker appears exactly once. No timing, no threshold, no free constant. Exactly once, not merely present: `is_cancelled` latches, so dropping only the `return` prints the marker once per remaining interval (94 here) while every other assertion still passes. Mid-loop matters for the same reason: a pre-loop pause resumes straight into the first `isCancelled()`, staying green with that check hoisted out of the loop, which is what #110104 fixed. All three mutations (checkpoint deleted, check hoisted, `return` deleted) redden the new test, the failpoint still pausing in each so no arm is vacuous. Removing `SYSTEM ENABLE FAILPOINT` fails loudly; `test_limit_by_transform_kill_query` stays green. Hot-path cost is not measurable, and dropping the 40 M-row fixture removes its `max_estimated_execution_time` exposure. `04409_skip_index_build_cancellation.sh` has a weaker form of the same pattern (bounded `KILL ... SYNC` at `timeout 10`); left unchanged.

signals.title: Do not consult the query context when building a CAST
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109946 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR: Context has expired` exception when a stored expression containing `accurateCastOrDefault` or a `to<Type>OrDefault` function is evaluated after the query that created it has finished, for example a `MATERIALIZED` column default on `INSERT` or a mutation expression. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109946 `CastOverloadResolverImpl` inherited `WithContext`, which holds only a `weak_ptr<const Context>`, and its `buildImpl` passed `getContext()` to `createFunctionBaseCast`. That is safe only during analysis, while a caller still holds a strong `ContextPtr`. #109946 made `FunctionCastOrDefault` store that resolver as a member and call `build()` at execute time. The `ActionsDAG` keeps the resolver alive but nothing keeps its context alive, and both affected paths build the DAG from a function-local `Context::createCopy` that dies on return (`inplaceBlockConversions.cpp:230` for materialized-column defaults, `MutationsInterpreter.cpp:1762` for mutations). Evaluating such an expression later throws `Context has expired`: an exception in release builds, a server abort under debug and sanitizers. This captures the conversion settings in the resolver's constructor, while the context is provably alive, and has `buildImpl` consume that snapshot. `FunctionCast` used its `ContextPtr` for nothing but `settings(context, ...)`, so the snapshot moves one step earlier in the same call chain rather than being introduced. The resolver now holds no context at all, so the `WithContext` exception for this file in `various_checks.sh` is removed. The two build paths keep their distinct `DateTimeOverflowBehavior`: `Saturate` for `createInternalCast`, `Ignore` for `buildImpl`. Sharing one snapshot between them would silently change date-time conversion. Since a snapshot replaces a live context, every context-derived conversion setting was compared before and after and is byte-identical, including all three `date_time_overflow_behavior` modes, `cast_keep_nullable`, `precise_float_parsing`, the IPv4/IPv6 error settings and timezone substitution. `04510_accurateCastOrDefault_settings` from #109946 passes unchanged. The new test aborts a master server at `CastOverloadResolver.cpp:195` and passes with this change, 50/50 green under randomized settings. The defect rides along with #109946, so it is present wherever that landed: 26.7 (#114689, merged); the 25.8, 26.3 and 26.5 backports are still open. <details> <summary>CI provenance</summary> `Logical error: Context has expired`, STID `1805-460a`, first seen 2026-08-13 22:45:16 UTC, about four hours after #109946 merged. The frame pair `CastOverloadResolverImpl::buildImpl` + `Context has expired` has no earlier occurrence in the 90 days CIDB retains. | when (UTC) | check | where | |---|---|---| | 2026-08-14 02:20:39 | [Stress test (arm_release)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=17d2798b962607ded301a9cab913c8ca70a33409&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_release%29) | master, `17d2798b9626` | | 2026-08-14 01:49:18 | [AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114666&sha=dc79add25489c923c36b67be101b349bb964b190&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29) | unrelated PR | | 2026-08-14 00:02:12 | [Stress test (amd_tsan)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114131&sha=06852ededde08f411d205aea05f6a78dbadaf55c&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_tsan%29) | unrelated PR | | 2026-08-13 22:50:06 | [AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted, old_compatibility)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100374&sha=50f4e25e8e3204407e724392592231c2ac54151c&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29) | unrelated PR | | 2026-08-13 22:45:16 | [AST fuzzer (arm_asan_ubsan)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112679&sha=a2d3810c4df7a6d108a1a5b207e779cc41ae7e86&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29) | unrelated PR | The master row is bucketed as STID `1805-4810` because an STID is a stack hash, but it carries both discriminating frames and `17d2798b9626` contains #109946. </details>

signals.title: Fix TopK filtering dropping NULL and NaN rows from the answer
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113406 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107074 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` silently omitting rows that belong in the answer when TopK filtering is active. A `Float32`/`Float64`/`BFloat16` column holding `NaN` was affected at default settings; nested-`NULL` types such as `Array(Nullable(T))` and `Map(K, Nullable(V))` were affected under `ASC NULLS FIRST` and `DESC NULLS LAST` with `use_top_k_dynamic_filtering_for_variable_length_types` enabled. A sort column containing `JSON`, `Variant` or `Dynamic` at any depth was affected in either direction, and additionally raised a `LOGICAL_ERROR` for `Tuple(Dynamic)` and `Tuple(Variant(...))`. ### Description TopK filtering must order values the way the sorter does. Three mechanisms broke that. `__topKFilter`'s fast path compares through `lessOrEquals`/`greaterOrEquals`. For a composite type those resolve to `GenericComparisonImpl`, which hardcodes the nan/nulls-direction hint to "NULLs and NaNs are greatest", contradicting `ORDER BY` whenever `nulls_direction` is -1. For a float, IEEE comparison leaves `NaN` unordered against everything including itself, so a `NaN` row fails both comparators in every direction. `use_skip_indexes_for_top_k` loses the same rows independently, via `MinMaxGranuleItem::operator<`. Third, a runtime-typed sort column. The threshold reaches `TopKThresholdTracker` as a bare `Field` (`IColumn::get`), which keeps a `Variant`/`Dynamic` payload without its discriminator, while `ColumnVariant::compareAt` ranks by discriminator first. Measured on one constant value per part: `Tuple(Dynamic)` returned `(0)` for `ORDER BY v DESC LIMIT 2` where the answer is `(1000)`, and `Tuple(Variant(UInt64, UInt8))` returned `(3)` for `ASC` where it is `(900)`. Both hold a single runtime type, so mixed alternatives are not required. Floats and nested `NULL`s are routed to the existing general path, which honours `nulls_direction`, and floats are added to the two skip-index gates. Runtime-typed columns instead install no filter, since no comparison here can recover the discriminator. Both predicates recurse over the type rather than listing wrappers, and test the sort column's own type, so sorting on a static subcolumn such as `v.f` of `JSON(f Float64)` keeps the filter. Cost: no pruning for float or runtime-typed sort columns. On a NaN-free `Float64`, 10M rows, `ORDER BY f ASC LIMIT 10` goes from 7 ms to 15 ms and reads 10M rows instead of 81,920; integers are unaffected. The two `TODO`s in the code note what would recover it. The test runs 42 carriers on and off and requires each pair to agree, 12 of them controls. Each guard term is mutation-checked: reverting it reddens only the arm it exists for.

signals.title: Extract reusable `ActionsDAG` lineage
signals.text: Extract a reusable `ActionsDAG` lineage computation into `actionsDAGUtils`. The new `traceActionsDAGLineage` traces every `ActionsDAG` output to at most one input via a single iterative, memoized traversal. Each hop is classified as `Identity`, `ValuePreserving`, or the weaker `DistinctValuesBound` (output NDV bounded by input NDV plus `ndv_delta`), and results are keyed by input/output positions, so they stay unambiguous under duplicated column names. `remapColumnStats` in the join-order optimizer is rewired onto the new API, replacing its hand-rolled `propagatesNdv`/`backTrackColumnsInDag` walk. Besides the extraction, this improves the call site: - One lineage walk per `ActionsDAG` instead of one full DFS per statistics column: complexity drops from `O(#stats × DAG)` to `O(DAG + #outputs)` when several columns carry statistics. - No wasted walks for statistics names that match no DAG input — previously the full DFS still ran and its result was discarded. - The common case of absent statistics stays free by construction: an explicit `mapped.empty()` guard skips the (now unconditional) lineage walk entirely. - The remap itself becomes a straight loop over the lineage vector with two hash lookups per traceable output, dropping the per-name set/map bookkeeping. The computed statistics values are unchanged: the hop classification is ignored by `remapColumnStats` (only traceability and `ndv_delta` matter there), and the `ndv_delta` logic — NULL-collapsing hops add one distinct value, with the same overflow guard — is identical. The position-based keying is a robustness property of the reusable API for future consumers; this consumer still keys statistics by column name. New unit tests cover the lineage kinds (`Identity` vs `ValuePreserving` vs `DistinctValuesBound`) and the position-based disambiguation of duplicated input/output names. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): - Not for changelog

signals.title: Hold the table lock across a lightweight UPDATE pipeline
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104431 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a server abort (`Logical error: Part patch-... doesn't exist`) when a `DROP TABLE` runs concurrently with a lightweight `UPDATE` on a `ReplicatedMergeTree` table. The update now holds the table's shared lock until its patch part is committed, so the `DROP` waits instead of removing it. ### Description Reported by @ alexey-milovidov on #104431: an `Upgrade check (amd_release)` abort with no fix on master, STID `3208-458f`, 4 hits on 4 unrelated PRs in 6 days ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=104431&sha=7970f08a82eaf2ad5217d57a7796ae1c5e920030&name_0=PR&name_1=Upgrade+check+%28amd_release%29)). **What breaks.** A lightweight `UPDATE` racing a `DROP TABLE` aborts the server, release builds included: `Transaction::commit`'s `modifyPartState` sits in `NOEXCEPT_SCOPE`, whose catch-all is `std::terminate`. **Root cause.** `InterpreterUpdateQuery::execute` takes `lockForShare` into a function-local holder and parks only the *storage* in the returned pipeline; `QueryPlanResourceHolder` keeps `storage_holders` and `table_locks` separately, so the lock dies when `execute()` returns, long before the sink commits the patch part. A concurrent `DROP` then takes the exclusive lock, `dropAllData()` clears `data_parts_indexes`, and the commit cannot find its own part. It needs a UUID-less database (`Memory`/`Ordinary`), where `DROP` removes data inline, hence the intermittency. **The change.** Move the already-acquired lock into the pipeline's resources, as the INSERT path does at `InterpreterInsertQuery.cpp:1297`. Three entry points: `InterpreterUpdateQuery::execute`, `InterpreterAlterQuery::executeToTable`, and `StorageAlias::updateLightweight`, which resolves a *different* storage and so needs the target's own lock, as `StorageAlias::read` does. `DELETE FROM` rewrites to `UPDATE` and is covered transitively. A concurrent `DROP` or `DETACH` now waits for an in-flight lightweight update, as it already does for `INSERT`. `TRUNCATE` takes no exclusive lock for `MergeTree`. **Validation.** New test `04905_lwu_drop_race_table_lock.sh`, one arm per fixed carrier. A pauseable failpoint parks the replicated sink between the patch-part rename and the commit, while the update still holds the lock; the arm then drops the table and waits for the drop to block on that lock. Nothing is timed, so an arm cannot miss a window or pass quietly. Aborts without the fix, passes with it, 50/50 green. <details> <summary>Both-directions matrix (every cell measured, Build IDs asserted against the running server)</summary> | binary | `UPDATE` | `ALTER ... UPDATE` | via `Alias` | |---|---|---|---| | base (fix reverted) `ea8e869d` | ABORT | ABORT | ABORT | | interpreters only `3651f11d` | pass | pass | ABORT | | full fix `1884b944` | pass | pass | pass | The middle row is the control that shows the `StorageAlias` change is necessary: with both interpreter fixes applied, the alias arm is the only one that still aborts. The lock demonstrably serializes the two queries: with the sink parked after the patch-part rename, the `DROP` becomes a waiting writer and stays one until the sink is released, then completes. Deadlock check: the change only extends the lifetime of a *Read* acquisition, and no sink on this path takes the table lock. `update_sequential_consistency = 1` and a following `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` both complete normally. </details>

signals.title: Preserve non-clonable sources for deferred set builds
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619#issuecomment-5230196558 The speculative ordered-set build used for index analysis consumed non-clonable source plans before it knew whether the set was complete. If a `ReadFromRemote` pipeline stopped on an unavailable shard before `Set::finishInsert`, the deferred build had no source left and `FunctionIn` received a not-ready set. Preserve non-clonable local sources by skipping the speculative index optimization and letting `DelayedCreatingSetsStep` perform the authoritative build. The regression test uses the deterministic five-part `test_unavailable_shard` reproducer from the linked issue comment and verifies that `ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED` propagates normally. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix queries with an `IN` subquery over unavailable remote shards potentially raising the `Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument` logical exception instead of the underlying connection exception.

signals.title: Add byte-weighted bytes_to_do and progress to system.mutations
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114678 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `system.mutations` now exposes byte-weighted mutation progress: `bytes_to_do` (the on-disk size of the data parts that still need to be mutated) and `progress` (an estimated finished fraction from 0 to 1, including the live fraction of the parts currently being rewritten). Part counts are a poor work proxy — parts are unequal in size and a regular merge can retire many pending parts at once — so the byte view is the honest one; the docs gain an "Estimating mutation progress" section with an equivalent parameterized-view recipe for older releases. Implements the conclusion of the research on the issue in two layers: **Columns** (`bytes_to_do` UInt64, `progress` Float64 in `system.mutations`): derived on read like `parts_to_do` — no persisted state, no replication protocol or znode format change. For plain `MergeTree` the sizes ride along the existing per-part scan in `getMutationsStatus`; for replicated tables the queue keeps returning name-only statuses under its state lock and the storage resolves sizes afterwards, so no parts lock is ever taken under the queue mutex (parts gone by then were retired and contribute nothing). The in-flight fraction comes from the merge list (`system.merges` rows with `is_mutation = 1`). Values are estimates by nature: a merge can retire pending parts at any moment, making `progress` jump forward. **Docs**: an "Estimating mutation progress" section on the `system.mutations` page explains why part-count percentages mislead and ships a parameterized-view recipe computing the same number on releases without the columns (the view was validated live against a running mutation, including a merge collapsing 9 pending parts mid-run), plus cross-links from `system.merges`, `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`, and the knowledge base. The stateless test asserts exact values on both engines: with merges stopped (which parks mutation tasks), `bytes_to_do` equals the active parts' total size and `progress` is 0; after completion the entry reports 0 and 1. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signals.title: Reuse the previous row's result for equal consecutive rows in Set execution
signals.text: The per-row execution of `x IN <set>` (`Set::executeImplCase`) hashes the full key for every row — SipHash128 for hashed multi-column keys. When the key columns are clustered (e.g. they are a primary-key prefix, so the data arrives sorted), consecutive rows form long runs of equal values, and the previous row's result can be reused after a cheap raw-byte comparison instead of repeating the hash+probe. With this change, when all key columns are non-nullable fixed-width (tuples are flattened element-wise), each row's raw bytes are compared with the previous row's, and on equality the previous result is reused, skipping the hash+probe entirely. Motivation: in SQL transpiled from PromQL selectors over `TimeSeries` tables, the per-row `id IN (tags subquery)` filter computes SipHash128 of a 24-byte `Tuple(UInt64, UUID)` per row into a `HashSet<UInt128>`. On tsbench, a PromQL benchmark over the ClickHouse `TimeSeries` engine (30 days of scrape data at 15s step, scale 1 = 1.06 billion samples / 6112 series, Ryzen 9950X, query result cache disabled, best of 3), this filter took ~17.5% of CPU of a 30-day rate query scanning 69M rows. With this change the hashing disappears from the profile (~3% of cheap byte comparisons remain), and raw-selector benchmark queries improved 1.4–2.3x. The optimization is generic: any `IN` over clustered/sorted key columns benefits; for unclustered data the added cost is a few loads per row. Bitwise comparison is applied only to POD column layouts (fixed-width raw bytes in one contiguous buffer, tuples flattened element-wise), where bitwise equality implies key equality; strings, arrays, `Nullable` and other non-POD layouts keep the existing path. The new performance test `tests/performance/set_in_clustered_keys.xml` covers both the clustered case (runs of equal consecutive keys) and the unclustered regression control (consecutive rows always differ). Note: tsbench scale-64 validation is in progress; numbers will be added before merge. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up execution of `IN` over clustered (e.g. sorted by primary key) columns by reusing the previous row's result for equal consecutive rows.

signals.title: Type `IN (subquery)` over `LowCardinality` consistently in the old analyzer
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114229 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100226 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `LOGICAL_ERROR: Unexpected return type from tuple. Expected Tuple(..., UInt8). Got Tuple(..., LowCardinality(UInt8))` when a `LowCardinality` column compared with `IN (subquery)` is read through `tuple(...)` across a subquery boundary and `enable_analyzer = 0`. With the old analyzer, `x IN (subquery)` over a `LowCardinality` column now returns `LowCardinality(UInt8)`, the same type as `x IN (literal list)` and the same as with `enable_analyzer = 1`. ### Description The old-analyzer half of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114229, whose test is tagged `no-old-analyzer`. Reproducer, broken since 26.6 and still broken on master: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (s LowCardinality(String)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY s; INSERT INTO t VALUES ('a'); SET enable_analyzer = 0; SELECT tuple(*) FROM (SELECT s, s IN (SELECT 'a') AS f FROM t); -- Code: 49. Unexpected return type from tuple. Expected Tuple(LowCardinality(String), UInt8). -- Got Tuple(LowCardinality(String), LowCardinality(UInt8)). (LOGICAL_ERROR) ``` **Root cause.** The general typing rule wraps a result in `LowCardinality` only when at most one argument is a full `LowCardinality` column and no argument is a full ordinary column (`IFunctionOverloadResolver::getReturnType`, `src/Functions/IFunction.cpp:797`). The two passes over the same expression disagree: - during execution the set is a constant column (`ColumnSet` is always wrapped in `ColumnConst` since https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100226) and a `Set`-typed argument counts as constant since https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114229, so `in` returns `LowCardinality(UInt8)`; - during analysis the set from a subquery is not built yet, so `in` is replaced with `inIgnoreSet` and the left operand is passed twice as the stand-in for the missing set (`src/Interpreters/ActionsVisitor.cpp`). Two full `LowCardinality` arguments fail the `num_full_low_cardinality_columns <= 1` condition, so the result types as plain `UInt8`. The outer query records `UInt8` for that column and the pipeline delivers `LowCardinality(UInt8)`, so `columnMatchesType` rejects the `tuple` result in `executeActionForPartialResult` during `ActionsDAG::updateHeader`. `DESCRIBE (subquery)` and `EXPLAIN header = 1` disagreeing on the type is the quick diagnostic. In a release build this is a query error; in debug and sanitizer builds it aborts the server. **Change.** The stand-in for the missing set is a constant `UInt8` instead of the left operand. It is indistinguishable from the real `Set` argument in every dimension the typing rule inspects — it is constant, so it is skipped by both `LowCardinality` counters; it is not `Nullable`, so it does not affect the null wrapper; and `FunctionIn::getReturnTypeImpl` only reads `arguments[0]`. Analysis and execution therefore agree by construction, for all eight `in` / `notIn` / `nullIn` / `notNullIn` × `global` variants and for every operand shape, not only the one in the reproducer. The `IgnoreSet` variants never look at their second argument. A `Set`-typed stand-in would mirror execution more literally, but `getRootActionsNoMakeSet` feeds window-definition expressions into an executed plan (`src/Interpreters/ExpressionAnalyzer.cpp:1562`), which can be serialized for distributed execution, and a `ColumnSet` with no set behind it would be dereferenced there. A `UInt8` constant cannot be. **Visible type change**, mirroring what https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114229 did for the analyzer: with `enable_analyzer = 0`, `toTypeName(x IN (subquery))`, `DESCRIBE` of such a subquery, `EXPLAIN` headers, and column types of `CREATE ... AS SELECT` over such an expression now show `LowCardinality(UInt8)` instead of `UInt8`. Values do not change. **Validation.** New stateless test `04894_in_subquery_lowcardinality_type_old_analyzer` asserts, for both analyzers, that the literal-set and subquery-set forms have the same type, that the type recorded for the subquery column is `LowCardinality(UInt8)`, and that `tuple(*)` over that column across a subquery boundary works, with `IN` / `NOT IN` `count()` controls. Its first two arms fail and the `tuple(*)` arm aborts a debug server without the change.
