signals.title: Apply HAVING without aggregation in the old analyzer
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113760 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results with `enable_analyzer = 0` when a query has a `HAVING` clause but no aggregation: the condition was silently ignored and excluded rows were returned. `HAVING` is now merged into `WHERE` for such queries, matching the new analyzer. ### Description With `enable_analyzer = 0`, a `SELECT` that has a `HAVING` clause but no aggregation silently discarded the condition and returned rows it excludes. Over a MergeTree table holding 1, 2, 3: ```sql SELECT a FROM t HAVING a > 999 SETTINGS enable_analyzer = 0, enable_optimize_predicate_expression = 0; -- returned 1, 2, 3; the new analyzer returns nothing ``` Root cause: the old analyzer builds and executes a `HAVING` filter only in its aggregation branch (`appendHaving` is called under `if (need_aggregate)`, and `executeHaving` is reachable only from inside `else if (expressions.need_aggregate)`), so without aggregation the clause is never applied. What normally hides this is `PredicateExpressionsOptimizer` moving non-aggregate conjuncts to `WHERE`, i.e. a performance optimizer was load-bearing for correctness with no interpreter fallback. It also fails at default settings when a stateful conjunct makes `tryMovePredicatesFromHavingToWhere` bail out, so `HAVING a > 999 AND blockNumber() >= 0` reproduces with `enable_analyzer = 0` alone. This merges `HAVING` into `WHERE` in `TreeRewriter::analyzeSelect` when the query does not aggregate, the canonicalization the new analyzer already performs in `Planner.cpp:2231-2238`. The interpreter, `ExpressionAnalyzer` and `PredicateExpressionsOptimizer` are unchanged. The site sits after `getAggregates` and `getWindowFunctions` so `NOT_AN_AGGREGATE` and `ILLEGAL_AGGREGATION` keep being raised, after `PredicateExpressionsOptimizer` so the default path is a no-op, and outside the `ast_optimizations_allowed` gate so it also applies on shards. Validation: `EXPLAIN` shows no `Filter` step before; after the fix the predicate reaches the storage and prunes (`Parts: 0/1`). 33 query shapes now agree across the old analyzer, the old analyzer with the rewrite enabled and the new analyzer; 20 disagreed before. `NOT_AN_AGGREGATE`, `ILLEGAL_AGGREGATION` and the `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` for `WITH TOTALS` without aggregation are unchanged and pinned by the new test. Distributed and `remote()` queries were checked on a two-shard cluster. The 44 stateless tests setting `enable_optimize_predicate_expression` pass, 589 further `HAVING` and `*analyzer*` tests show no regression.

signals.title: Keep 04896_orfill_merge_group_by_overflow_any on the projection merge path at any granularity
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114740 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `04896_orfill_merge_group_by_overflow_any` fails deterministically whenever the test runner randomizes `index_granularity_bytes` small: ``` Code: 117. DB::Exception: Projection p is specified in setting force_optimize_projection_name but not used. (INCORRECT_DATA) ``` Seen at four different values (7801, 9281, 49209 and locally at 1024), so it reds unrelated PRs' CI (most recently #112889 and #76867), and the arm stops covering the null-place `mergeBatch` segfault it was added for in #114740. A throw is not coverage. The optimizer is correct here. The table declares two projections, and `p` stores four aggregate states where `p2` stores one; granule sizing charges an aggregate-state column at its serialized width, so at small `index_granularity_bytes` `p` reads more marks than the base table and than `p2`, and is dropped (`optimizeUseAggregateProjection.cpp:1036` and `:1048`). At coarse granularity every candidate floors to one granule per part, the marks tie, and `p` wins only because it is declared first. The fix removes both comparisons from the fixture rather than constraining the randomizer: `index_granularity = 1` on the table makes the base and every projection read one row per granule, so a projection's mark count no longer depends on state width. The `sumOrNull` arm, the only one where `p2` is a candidate at all, also names `p` as preferred, which reduces the candidate list to one entry before any cost comparison. `force_optimize_projection_name = 'p'` is kept, so each arm still asserts that `p` specifically was used. `index_granularity_bytes`, `min_bytes_for_wide_part` and `use_const_adaptive_granularity` stay randomized. This matches `04063` and `04365`, the other tests using this pin. Validated: all four culprit values pass; 5 arms x 36 setting combinations (Compact and Wide) pass with the pinned projection applied; 50/50 runs with and without randomization; and the pre-fix binary still segfaults in `AggregateFunctionOrFill::mergeBatch` with this fixture, so the defect stays covered. `.reference` is unchanged.

signals.title: Coordinate a read with pinned block numbers in classic parallel replicas
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114263 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/97557 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results when a `SELECT` with `select_sequential_consistency = 1` on a `ReplicatedMergeTree` table runs with classic (task-based) parallel replicas. Every replica performed a complete local read clamped to the quorum boundary instead of a coordinator-assigned slice, so rows were returned once per participating replica. ### Description `StorageReplicatedMergeTree::read` routes a `select_sequential_consistency = 1` query into `readLocalSequentialConsistencyImpl`, which called `MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor::read` with `enable_parallel_reading` hardcoded to `false`. The setting is propagated to the followers, so each follower took that same branch: `read_task_callback` was never installed, the follower never announced its parts, and it read the whole pinned range locally. The initiator then merged N complete copies. On a 5-part `ReplicatedMergeTree` with a pinned boundary of 12000 rows and `max_parallel_replicas = 3`, `count()` returned 36000 and `sum()` was likewise tripled, with no exception and no warning. It scaled exactly linearly with `max_parallel_replicas`, and `uniqExact` stayed correct, confirming pure per-replica duplication. Reaching the defect requires turning off one of the optimizations that would otherwise bypass this read path: `optimize_trivial_count_query = 0` for `count()`, since at its default the planner serves the count from `totalRows()` and disables parallel replicas, or `parallel_replicas_local_plan = 0` or `parallel_replicas_prefer_local_replica = 0` for data reads. All three are documented, settable per query, and leave the wrong result silent. The fix passes `canUseParallelReplicasOnFollower()` at that call site, exactly as the sibling `readLocalImpl` already does for the non-pinned path, so the pinned read participates in coordination instead of being silently excluded from it. The boundary stays computed and applied: when it binds it comes from ZooKeeper and is identical on every replica (measured on two replicas holding different part sets, 7 and 6 active parts, both clamping to the same block), and with no quorum node it is the replica's own maximum, which excludes nothing it owns. Validation: new test `04912_pr_classic_pinned_block_numbers` fails on master and passes with the change, 50/50 green under randomized settings. Full matrix in the validation-gate comment below. Out of scope, neither introduced nor altered here: the plan-based path with `parallel_replicas_local_plan = 0` (#114263), and divergent part sets with no quorum node (#105710).

signals.title: Report RabbitMQ container recreations absorbed by the startup retry
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114415 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114434 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description #114415 made the RabbitMQ readiness waiter recreate a container that fails to start and try again, turning a 21-case module abort into a passing run. When the second attempt succeeds, every channel that could record the first failure closes at once: artifact collection is gated on a failing suite (`if failed_suits:`), the report log strips setup logs from passed tests (`--report-log-exclude-logs-on-passed-tests`), and `job.log` never carried harness logging. The recovered failure survives only as an anomalous duration on the module's first test: +123.5 s against a p99 of 13.4 s over 7774 runs of that test and lane. So a retry-absorbed run discards exactly the diagnostics #114415 added to show where a hang is stuck. Now: - the waiter copies the failed attempt's `rabbit.log` out of the instance directory before recreating the container (that directory is removed on teardown) and emits a stable `RABBITMQ_RECREATE` token. The copy is named per process, cluster, waiter call and attempt, because S3 upload keys use the basename alone; - at job end the script counts those tokens across the per-worker pytest logs, puts the count in `Result.info` and attaches the preserved logs, whatever the outcome. The failure-gated paths are left alone. A recreation is not itself a verdict, so only `info` and `files` are touched: status and labels stay as the test results set them, and the count is appended after the job's own `Failures: N/M` summary rather than replacing it. Forcing a retry on a healthy host passes, and the count reaches `result_*.json` with the 107,336 B broker log attached. The same run with the reporting removed attaches nothing; a run that never retried writes no count; a forced-red run keeps its `Failures: 1/1`. `test_system_stop.py` is 21 passed. Both sides are unit-tested, each arm checked against a mutation of the code it pins.

signals.title: Add RadixHashJoin: a radix-partitioned hash join
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106023 `parallel_hash` probes one shared two-level hashtable. Once the build side outgrows last-level cache every probe lookup is a cold miss, and after the per-slot maps are merged at the end of the build phase the two-level split does nothing to shrink the working set. This adds `radix_join`: radix-partition the build side into many small hashtables that each stay cache-resident, then stream the probe side against them in budgeted waves, so that while a leaf table is in cache it is hit by a long run of probe rows instead of one lookup at a time. Each leaf is a real `HashJoin`, so join semantics aren't reimplemented — only the partitioning and the scheduling around it. v1 handles `INNER ALL` equi-joins with a single equality clause (no `OR`) over fixed-width columns; anything else falls back to `parallel_hash`. Design notes are in `RadixHashJoin.h`. ## The probe side is not fully materialised This is the part that departs from a textbook radix join, and it is the point of the design. A classic partitioned hash join shuffles the *entire* probe side down to leaf depth before it probes anything, which puts its memory floor at `|build| + |probe|` and means no output appears until the whole probe input has been read and scattered. Here the probe side is buffered only up to a budget. When the budget fills, that wave of buffered rows is scattered, probed against the leaves it touches, and emitted; the probe buffer is dropped, and the cycle repeats. The leaf hashtables persist across waves — only the probe buffer is recycled. So transient memory is bounded by the budget rather than by probe cardinality, and rows start flowing downstream well before the probe side has been consumed. The budget is `radix_join_probe_buffer_fraction` of the bytes the build side accumulated (stored rows plus leaf tables), default **0.15**, with a floor of `radix_join_probe_buffer_min_bytes` (default 512 MiB) and an optional cap from `radix_join_probe_buffer_max_bytes`. On the sweep below that works out to a 0.5-6.9 GiB probe buffer; at the widest shape measured, a classic fully-materialising implementation would instead have had to hold ~119 GiB of shuffled probe stream. The trade-off is time, and it is worth being explicit about the direction: full materialisation scatters the probe side once and touches each leaf table once, whereas a leaf that receives rows in several waves gets re-read once per wave, so bounded memory is bought with extra cache traffic. Turning `radix_join_probe_buffer_fraction` (or `radix_join_probe_buffer_max_bytes`) up trades back toward the classic behaviour, and at a budget large enough to hold the whole probe stream the eviction cycle never fires and this degenerates to a classic partitioned hash join. Every number below is at the default budget; I have not measured the fully-materialising end of that range. ## Benchmarks ### What was measured Two generated tables joined on one `UInt64` key, `INNER JOIN ... USING (k)`. Three properties of the join were varied: - **How big the build side is** — 32M, 64M, 128M, 256M or 500M rows. - **How much bigger the probe side is** — 1, 2 or 4 probe rows per build row. - **How wide the rows are** — every row is the 8-byte key plus 0, 1, 3 or 7 further 8-byte columns, so **8, 16, 32 or 64 bytes per row**, chosen independently for the two sides. Only the columns counted here are projected out of the join, so these widths are what the join actually moves. That is 5 x 3 x 4 x 4 = 240 join shapes, each run at `max_threads` of 16, 32, 64 and 96: **960 measured points**. Every point is checked against `parallel_hash` for an identical result (960/960 completed, zero checksum mismatches). Hardware: 4 identical ARM64 VMs — Neoverse-V2 (Graviton 4), 96 cores on one socket and one NUMA node, 64 KiB L1d and 2 MiB L2 per core, 36 MiB shared L3, 371 GiB RAM. Sweep tag `radix-sweep-202608140814`. Settings pinned: `join_algorithm` to the algorithm under test, `enable_analyzer = 1`, `enable_join_runtime_filters = 0`. Multiplying row counts by row widths gives the one quantity that organises every result below — **how many bytes the probe side carries for each byte of build side**: probe bytes / build bytes = (probe rows x probe row width) / (build rows x build row width) Across the sweep this spans 1/8 (a 64-byte build row against an equal number of 8-byte probe rows) to 32 (an 8-byte build row against four times as many 64-byte probe rows). It does not depend on how big the build side is, which is why build size below is a separate axis from it. Speedup always means `parallel_hash` time / `radix_join` time, so above 1 is a `radix_join` win. Aggregates are geometric means. ### Why this range of shapes The build sizes start high enough that every point is already past the cache cliff this algorithm exists to address: at the bottom of the range, a 32M-row key-only build reserves a 1 GiB leaf-table budget — 28x the 36 MiB L3 — so there is no point in the sweep that `parallel_hash` could have kept cache-resident. From there the range spans 16x in build size, enough to put both the crossover and the peak inside it. It stops at 500M rows because the per-row costs of both algorithms have flattened out well before that (see below), not because of a hardware limit — the heaviest single point peaks at 63.6 GiB, 17% of the box. ### Headline `radix_join` wins **793/960 (82.6%)**, median winning factor 1.62x. | threads | radix wins | gmean speedup | gmean latency, radix | gmean latency, `parallel_hash` | |--------:|-----------:|--------------:|---------------------:|-------------------------------:| | 16 | 200/240 | 1.28x | 2676 ms | 3421 ms | | 32 | 197/240 | 1.31x | 1634 ms | 2145 ms | | 64 | 193/240 | 1.47x | 1202 ms | 1770 ms | | 96 | 203/240 | 1.88x | 1133 ms | 2133 ms | The best single point is 5.73x: 96 threads, 500M build rows, one probe row per build row, a 64-byte build row and a 16-byte probe row — 3446 ms against 19747 ms. The worst is 0.14x, in the band described under "Known weak spot". ### Where it wins How many bytes the probe side carries per byte of build side predicts the outcome almost by itself, monotonically across two and a half orders of magnitude: | probe bytes per byte of build side | 1/8 | 1/4 | 1/2 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | gmean speedup | 2.93x | 2.67x | 2.08x | 1.74x | 1.41x | 1.19x | 1.04x | 0.99x | 0.91x | | radix wins | 20/20 | 60/60 | 112/120 | 164/180 | 173/200 | 145/180 | 83/120 | 31/60 | 5/20 | That ordering is what the algorithm predicts. `radix_join` shuffles both sides. The build-side shuffle is amortised — paid once, then repaid by every probe row that hits a cache-resident leaf. The probe-side shuffle is pure added cost, repaid by nothing. So the advantage decays as the probe side grows relative to the build side, and the crossover sits near 8: `radix_join` is ahead while the probe side carries up to roughly 8 bytes per byte of build side, and behind past that. Per side, the same thing stated two ways: a **wide build row** is the strongest predictor of a win (64-byte build rows win all 240 of their shapes, gmean 2.57x; key-only 8-byte build rows manage 1.05x), and a **wide probe row** is the strongest predictor of a loss (8-byte probe rows average 1.87x, 64-byte probe rows 1.29x). Build size is the second axis, and it is not monotone: the advantage rises sharply from 32M to 64M rows, peaks around 128M-256M, and gives some back at 500M. The low end is the algorithm not having enough build side to pay back the partitioning, plus the bug below. The decline at the top bounds how far this result extrapolates. Two measured facts produce it, pulling in opposite directions: 1. **`parallel_hash`'s cost per build row is already flat across the whole sweep** — 17.97, 18.17, 18.44, 18.44, 17.07 ns per build row at 32M, 64M, 128M, 256M and 500M. Whatever penalty it pays for falling out of cache is fully saturated before the sweep even starts, which is what the 28x-L3 figure above would predict. A larger build side therefore hands `radix_join` no additional penalty to recover. 2. **`radix_join`'s own cost per build row climbs after 128M** — 10.40, 10.64, 11.42 ns per build row at 128M, 256M and 500M. One curve flat and the other rising is the whole arithmetic of the decline: the speedup falls 12-15% from 256M to 500M in every band, and extrapolating, the two would meet somewhere above this sweep. I have not measured where. I also have not investigated *why* (2) happens — it is an observation, not a diagnosis. The number of leaf partitions does grow with the build side over that range (8192, 16384 and 32768 for a key-only build side), which is the obvious thing to look at first, but I have not confirmed it is the cause. What it is *not* is a change in the depth of the radix plan: that is two passes at every point in this sweep, and a third pass would need more than 1024^2 partitions, which is around 10^10 rows away. ### Thread scalability This is the case the algorithm was built for. Going from 64 to 96 threads, `parallel_hash` gets *slower* on 197 of the 240 shapes — 20% slower in the geometric mean, 1770 ms to 2133 ms pooled — while `radix_join` keeps improving on all but 20 of them. The regression is a build-side effect, and the sweep can show that much without a phase breakdown. It scales cleanly with how wide the build row is — 96-thread over 64-thread latency of 0.97, 1.19, 1.30, 1.41 for 8-, 16-, 32- and 64-byte build rows — while being flat in probe row width (1.19, 1.19, 1.23, 1.21) and *shrinking* as probe rows per build row grows (1.29, 1.22, 1.11 for 1, 2 and 4). A cost that tracks build-side bytes and gets diluted by added probe work sits on the build side. `radix_join`'s build side writes only per-lane block stores, never a shared map, and its leaf tables are immutable once built. ### Known weak spot Of the 167 losing points, 52 fall in one reproducible band. With a 32M-row build side and a build row of 16 or 32 bytes, `radix_join` costs 40-73 ns per build row, against 3-7 ns for the *same shape* at every larger build size — up to 14x its own family: | probe rows per build row | build row | probe row | at 32M rows | at 64M+ rows | factor | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 2 | 16 B | 8 B | 60.8 ns/row | 4.3 ns/row | 14.3x | | 2 | 32 B | 8 B | 72.9 ns/row | 5.7 ns/row | 12.7x | | 1 | 32 B | 16 B | 45.4 ns/row | 4.4 ns/row | 10.3x | Two things point at plan selection rather than bandwidth. It is non-monotonic in the build row width at a fixed byte ratio — 8-byte build rows are healthy, 16 and 32 are pathological, 64 is healthy again — and the affected points do not respond to threads at all: 1.04x going from 16 to 96 threads, against 1.92x for the healthy 32M points. That suggests the leaf-count/pass-plan heuristic picking a bad plan in a narrow band of small build sizes. These are the visible sub-parity outliers in the first plot. Not diagnosed further. The remaining 115 losses are mostly the regime the model expects to lose: 68 of the 72 losses at 64M build rows and above are where the probe side carries 4 or more bytes per byte of build side, and the probe-side shuffle cannot be repaid. Excluding only the 52 pathological points, the sweep reads 793/908 (87.3%) at gmean 1.60x. ### Memory `radix_join` costs 1.35x peak memory over `parallel_hash` on average (median 1.34x, worst 1.83x), from holding the scattered build side plus the leaf tables. It is highest on the smallest build sides (32M rows: 1.49x) and lowest on the largest (500M: 1.21x). ### Reproducing The harness is in this PR: `bep/tools/join_mergetree_bench.py` runs the SQL sweep above — the four axes are `--cardinalities`, `--ratios`, `--build-payload-columns` / `--probe-payload-columns` (the 0/1/3/7 extra columns per row) and `--threads`. `src/Common/benchmarks/hash_join_bandwidth_model.cpp` is the standalone build/probe/scatter bandwidth microbenchmark. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental JOIN algorithm `radix_join`, a radix-partitioned hash join for joins whose build side is too large to stay cache-resident. Enable with `SET join_algorithm = 'radix_join'`. It supports `INNER ALL` equi-joins with a single equality clause whose key and payload columns are all fixed-width, non-nullable and non-`LowCardinality`; other queries fall back to `parallel_hash`.

signals.title: Support ROLLUP, CUBE, GROUPING SETS and grouping() with make_distributed_plan
signals.text: Support `ROLLUP`, `CUBE`, `GROUPING SETS` and the `grouping` function under `make_distributed_plan`. 11 of the 99 TPC-DS queries use `ROLLUP`. - `RollupStep` and `CubeStep` are serialized (query plan serialization version 7), so they can run in a worker stage, for example below a distributed `ORDER BY`. - The `grouping` function specializations hold their parameters inside the function object and cannot be serialized. The distributed results of all new stateless tests are verified against non-distributed execution of the same queries. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support `ROLLUP`, `CUBE`, `GROUPING SETS` and the `grouping` function in queries executed with `make_distributed_plan = 1`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signals.title: Take referential dependencies into account in DROP DATABASE table order
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114917 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97057 `InterpreterDropQuery::executeToDatabaseImpl` sorts the tables of a database being dropped in reverse topological order, so that a dependent is always dropped before the tables it depends on, and if the server crashes mid-drop, the remaining tables keep their dependencies intact and can be loaded on restart. Previously the ordering took only loading dependencies into account (#97057); now it takes the union of loading and referential dependencies (loading dependencies are mostly a subset of referential ones, but that is not enforced anywhere, so we merge both). This implements the TODO added in #114917, and the comment in `DatabaseCatalog::checkTableCanBeRemovedOrRenamedUnlocked` now simply documents the invariant. Like #97057, this comes without a functional test: within a single `DROP DATABASE`, dependents from the same database are deliberately ignored by the dependency check, so the drop order is not observable without crash injection in the middle of `DROP DATABASE`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `DROP DATABASE` now drops tables in reverse topological order of both loading and referential dependencies (previously only loading dependencies), so a crash in the middle of `DROP DATABASE` cannot leave a table whose dependencies were already dropped. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1488` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix an unkillable hang when dropping a low-sorting-name TimeSeries table
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114259 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a hang when dropping a `TimeSeries` table whose name sorts lexicographically below its inner tables' names, for example `` DROP TABLE `-ts` `` or dropping a materialized view declared with `ENGINE = TimeSeries`. The drop self-deadlocked on the DDL guard and could not be cancelled with `KILL QUERY`. ### Description `DROP TABLE` of a `TimeSeries` table never returned and could not be killed when the table's own qualified name sorted below its inner tables' names: ```sql SET allow_experimental_time_series_table = 1; CREATE TABLE `-ts` ENGINE = TimeSeries; DROP TABLE `-ts`; -- hung forever ``` A materialized view's inner name is `.inner_id.<uuid>`, which always sorts below `.inner_id.metrics.<uuid>`, so dropping an `MV ... ENGINE = TimeSeries` hung too. **Root cause.** `executeDropQuery` takes the DDL guard for the inner table, then synthesizes an `ASTDropQuery` for that same table without setting `no_ddl_lock`, so the nested interpreter takes the guard for the identical name again. `DDLGuard::table_lock` wraps a non-recursive `std::mutex`, so the thread deadlocks against itself. A mutex wait is not a cancellation point, so `KILL QUERY` could not land and the guard stayed held for the server's lifetime. `need_ddl_guard = true` comes from one call site, `StorageTimeSeries::dropInnerTableIfAny`, which requests the inner guard only when the parent name sorts first. That predicate is correct and is kept: guards must be taken in increasing name order. Only its comment was wrong, claiming the inner name is "almost always less", which holds for `MaterializedView` but not `TimeSeries`. **The change.** `executeDropQuery` now sets `no_ddl_lock = need_ddl_guard`, so the inner name is guarded exactly once, by the caller, across the nested execute. `InterpreterCreateQuery` sets the same field for the same reason. The fix is inert for the other ten call sites, which all take the `need_ddl_guard = false` default. The `ddl_guard` null check is pre-existing hardening. **Validation.** Both shapes time out before the fix and succeed after, while a high-sorting-name control passes on both builds. Eight concurrent drops serialize and complete and the name is reusable afterwards, so the guard is still taken and released. New test `04920` covers both shapes and asserts no inner table is left behind.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Fix `rows_before_limit_at_least` under parallel replicas local plan (#113279)
signals.text: ### Problem Closes #113279 With parallel replicas enabled (`parallel_replicas_local_plan = 1`, the default), queries with a `LIMIT` incorrectly report `rows_before_limit_at_least = 0`, even when `exact_rows_before_limit = 1`. Under `parallel_replicas_local_plan = 0` or standard non-parallel execution, the exact total rows before limit is correctly reported. ### Root Cause When building the local replica plan for parallel replicas, the query is planned at `QueryProcessingStage::WithMergeableState`. However, `createLocalPlanForParallelReplicas` (`src/Processors/QueryPlan/ParallelReplicasLocalPlan.cpp`) previously initialized `select_query_options.is_local_shard_plan` checking only `processed_stage == QueryProcessingStage::WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`. Because `is_local_shard_plan` evaluated to `false`, `addPreliminaryLimitStep` in `src/Planner/Planner.cpp` did not invoke `limit->markAsShardLimit()` on the local branch's preliminary `LimitStep`. During pipeline initialization in `initRowsBeforeLimit` (`src/QueryPipeline/QueryPipeline.cpp`), this unmarked limit transform was treated as a query-level accounting boundary rather than an internal shard limit, terminating the processor traversal early without attaching the rows-before-limit counter to the local input pipeline. Consequently, when the reading coordinator routed read granules to the local replica, the statistics counter remained 0. ### Solution In `createLocalPlanForParallelReplicas`, mark `select_query_options.is_local_shard_plan` as true when `processed_stage` is either `WithMergeableState` or `WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`. This ensures the preliminary limit on the local replica branch is recognized as a shard limit, allowing `initRowsBeforeLimit` to traverse through it and attach the counter to the local input stream, matching remote replica behavior. ### Test Plan - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/02590_parallel_replicas_local_plan_rows_before_limit.sh` and reference asserting `rows_before_limit_at_least` returns the correct row count under `parallel_replicas_local_plan = 1`.

signals.title: Apply a row policy to a read shipped as a serialized query plan
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112891 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a `SELECT` row policy on a shard-local table being ignored when the read is shipped to the executing replica as a serialized query plan (`serialize_query_plan = 1`, with `process_query_plan_packet` enabled there). Reads through a `Distributed` table with `prefer_localhost_replica = 0`, and reads over parallel replicas, returned rows the policy excludes. Closes #112891. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112891 **What breaks.** With a policy `USING y < 5` on a 10-row MergeTree table, `SELECT count()` through a `Distributed` table returns 10 instead of 5 and `SELECT DISTINCT y` returns 0..9. Parallel replicas leak the same way once remote replicas get read tasks. **Root cause.** The initiator resolves the policy into `SelectQueryInfo::row_level_filter`, since a MergeTree table accepts filter push-down into the read. When the plan is built for shipping, the leaf becomes a placeholder `ReadFromTableStep`, which has no field for that filter, so it is never serialized; on the executing node `replaceReadingFromTable` rebuilds the read with a hand-built `SelectQueryInfo` that never sets it. Each side assumes the other applied the policy. **The change.** Such a read is now rebuilt through the reconstructed-query path `resolveStorages` already uses for remote and `Merge` storages. That path runs the ordinary planner, so the policy is resolved in the executing node's own access context, and the read-column widening, the `FINAL` deferral and the PREWHERE ordering come with it. No wire format change and no version bump. Reads without a policy keep the direct path. The initiator cannot make this decision: effective policies resolve per node. **Residual, pre-existing and not introduced here.** A policy existing only on the receiver is still missed where the initiator pushes no policy into the read: storages without PREWHERE support (`Memory`, `View`) and those whose PREWHERE-column contract is not `nullopt` (`Buffer`, `File`, data lakes). Those behave exactly as on master. Replanning them would double-apply the filter step the initiator already shipped, and telling the two apart needs the plan to carry whether that step was emitted. So the fix assumes the shards behind one `Distributed` table use engines with the same PREWHERE contract. **Validation.** Three stateless tests (`Distributed`, parallel replicas, column grants), all failing on master. <details> <summary>Arms run on both binaries</summary> Measured on a debug build of base `63b0a472f4b62ac2` and of this branch. | arm | base | fix | |---|---|---| | `count()` / `sum(x)` / `sum(y)` / subquery, `serialize_query_plan = 1` | 10 / 45 / 45 / 10 | 5 / 10 / 10 / 5 | | `SELECT DISTINCT y` | 0..9 | 0..4 | | parallel replicas `sum(x)` / `count()` / `max(y)` | 548895757384 / 1046417 / 1111952 | correct on all three | | explicit `PREWHERE` + policy | 8 | 3 | | policy on `LowCardinality` / `Nullable` / `Array` / `ALIAS` / `MATERIALIZED` column | 10 each | matches the non-serialized result | | always-false policy | 10 | 0 | | `FINAL`, both `apply_row_policy_after_final` values | disagrees with the non-serialized path | agrees | | policy on `Memory` (push-down refused, must keep the direct path) | 5 | 5, and a nondeterministic policy is applied exactly once | | `additional_table_filters` on the read table, nondeterministic | applied once | applied once | | `additional_table_filters` on a table only the policy's subquery reads | n/a, policy not applied at all | applied, agreeing with `serialize_query_plan = 0` | | policy on the `Distributed` table itself | `ILLEGAL_PREWHERE` | same code and outcome; the message drops its now-stale `serialize_query_plan` advice | | `max_rows_to_read = 1` | returns 10 silently | `TOO_MANY_ROWS`, matching the non-serialized path | | no policy, `serialize_query_plan` 1 and 0 | 10 / 10 | 10 / 10 | Existing row-policy and serialized-plan tests pass unchanged, including `03743_apply_row_policy_after_final_safety`, `04652_prewhere_final_move_skipped_when_deferred`, `03006_parallel_replicas_prewhere` and `03302_analyzer_distributed_filter_push_down`. The new `Distributed` test is 50/50 stable under randomized settings. </details>

signals.title: Honour do_not_block_pipeline_on_failure for every non-ok job status
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107115 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109071 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description A job that sets `do_not_block_pipeline_on_failure` still blocked its whole downstream closure whenever it ended `ERROR` rather than `FAIL`. The two consumers disagreed. `hook_html.py:224` gates on `not result.is_ok()`, so dependees were correctly not marked `DROPPED`. `runner.py:910` gated on `result.is_failure()`, which is `FAIL`/`XPASS` only, so an `ERROR` was never exempted and the job emitted `pipeline_status=failure`. Every dependent job's guard is `!contains(needs.*.outputs.pipeline_status, 'failure')` over a transitive `needs`, so that one token skips the entire closure. The case that hits it: an integration shard exhausts its 7200 s parallel-phase budget and appends a synthetic `Timeout` child while every real test passes. One non-ok child means `force_ok_exit = True`, so the job declares itself non-blocking, but the same timeout sets the error flag and `set_error()` makes the status `ERROR`. That skipped 107 of 175 results on #107115 and 112 of 177 on #109071, including all five `Bugfix validation (*)` jobs. Because those never ran, `new_tests_check.py` read them as `PENDING` and failed `Finish Workflow` with "it's not actually a regression test for the fix", reporting a timeout in an unrelated shard as a verdict on the author's regression test. 8 occurrences across 8 PRs and 5 of the 6 shards in 30 days. `runner.py` now uses the same predicate as `hook_html`, extracted so it is reachable from a test. They have been asymmetric since the `runner.py` consumer was added in `b35b5fd41f28412`. `functional_tests.py:1527` passes the same flag after a path that can also end `ERROR`, so it is fixed by the same line. **Merge-blocking is unchanged.** `ready_for_merge` is computed from `job.allow_failure` alone (`native_jobs.py:1102-1117`) and never reads this flag; all six shards are `allow_failure=False`, so a failing shard still blocks the merge and still reports red. Only downstream dispatch changes. `new_tests_check.py` is left as it is: its strict check is correct once the jobs actually run. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Every mutation below was applied to production code and the suite re-run. | arm | mutation | result | |---|---|---| | 0 | the fix | 45 passed | | A | predicate reverted to `is_failure()` (pre-fix behaviour) | 11 failed, incl. the end-to-end shard shape | | B | exemption made unconditional, flag ignored (negative control) | 14 failed (every `flag=False` row) | | C | `hook_html` predicate drifted to `is_failure()` | 1 failed (the agreement pin) | | D | output site re-derives the status inline, helper left unused | 1 failed (the delegation pin) | | E | merge gate made to read the flag | 1 failed (the merge-gate pin) | | F | emitted token hardcoded, or overridden after the call | 1 failed each (the emit pin) | Arm B is what rules out a vacuous oracle: a test that ignored the flag would stay green. Arms D, E and F each redden exactly one test, pinning the seams nothing else covers: the call site the extraction created, the token actually emitted, and the merge computation the paragraph above rests on. The new test parametrizes every non-ok member of `Result.Status` (`FAIL`, `ERROR`, `XPASS`, `DROPPED`, `UNKNOWN`, `PENDING`, `RUNNING`) and all three ok members against flag on/off, asserts the two consumers reach the same verdict, reproduces the measured production shape (903 `OK` + 17 `SKIPPED` + 1 `Timeout`), and pins `allow_failure=False` on the six shards. Full `ci/tests`: 972 passed / 31 skipped / 8 failed with the fix, versus 927 / 31 / 8 on pristine `runner.py`. The same 8 pre-existing environment failures on both arms (`clickhouse was not found in PATH`); the delta is the new tests. Exactly two production `complete_job(` call sites pass this flag, and both are covered by this one line. The only other writer of `pipeline_status` is the config job's unconditional `success`. The remaining `is_failure()` uses are test-level row filtering or rendering, not job-level gating. </details>

signals.title: Codex tries to learn from its mistakes
signals.text: The unattended PR continuation workflow made two kinds of unsafe decisions. It incorrectly closed PR #114849 after confusing commit visibility with containment by the current `master`, and it force-pushed PR #111032 from a malformed single-parent commit that changed 673 files and deleted 26,457 lines. Require an explicit base-branch ancestry check and a separate current-state check so reverted changes are not considered integrated. Before committing or pushing, the workflow must inspect the staged and complete PR diffs, preserve the existing remote head as an ancestor, and stop on unexplained scope changes. A `pre-push` hook now enforces fast-forward-only updates and rejects branch deletion even if an agent attempts a force-push. An audit of recent automation activity found eight account-level force-pushes since 2026-08-13. PR #111032 was the only malformed large-diff outlier; the other seven replacement heads changed 2–8 files. The audit also found a smaller scope failure in PR #104495, where conflict resolution accidentally staged three unrelated untracked test files. The new explicit-path staging rule and staged-diff inspection cover that failure mode. The safety hook was tested in a throwaway repository: normal fast-forward updates were accepted, while non-fast-forward updates, branch deletion, and the exact PR #111032 rewrite were rejected. Shell syntax and ShellCheck validation also pass. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114849 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111032 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104495 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not for changelog.

signals.title: Retry transient GitHub errors in the `good-prs` skill
signals.text: Make the `good-prs` skill survive transient GitHub API errors. A full report makes roughly two GraphQL calls per pull request — several hundred per run — so hitting at least one transient GitHub failure is close to certain. The script aborted the whole run on the first one, which threw away all the API quota already spent. Three consecutive runs died this way: on `HTTP 503`, on `API rate limit already exceeded`, and on `HTTP 504`. This adds a shared `gh_retry` wrapper used by both per-pull-request helpers: - Transient failures (`HTTP 408`, `429`, any `5xx`, gateway timeouts, connection resets, TLS handshake errors) are retried with exponential backoff. - Secondary rate limits back off more aggressively. - A primary rate-limit rejection waits for the hourly window to reset, using the unmetered `rate_limit` endpoint, capped so a run always terminates. The fail-loud design is preserved. An error that will never fix itself (auth, unknown pull request, bad flag) still aborts on the first attempt, and a transient error that outlives every retry still aborts — in both cases with the original `gh` diagnostic. A row is never silently dropped from the report. Two tests were added to `test.sh`: a pull request whose checks fail twice with `HTTP 503` is retried and still rendered (exactly three calls), and a permanent error is attempted exactly once. `GH_RETRIES` and `GH_RETRY_DELAY` make the suite exercise the retry path without sleeping. All tests pass. This only touches `.claude/skills/good-prs/`, a developer-facing helper script; there is no change to ClickHouse itself. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1472` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix signed integer overflow reading Iceberg decimal bounds
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114929 Decoding a `Decimal` column bound from an Iceberg manifest ran in `int64_t` regardless of how wide the bound was, in `deserializeFieldFromBinaryRepr` (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/ManifestFileIterator.cpp`). Three steps overflow: * the big-endian accumulation `unscaled_value = (unscaled_value << 8) | byte`, once the bound is more than eight bytes wide; * the sign extension `sign_extension <<= (str.size() * 8)`, which shifts by 64 or more for a bound of eight bytes or more; * the scaler loop `scaler *= 10`, which computes `10^scale` and leaves `int64_t` at scale 19. A `Decimal(38, 30)` column reaches all three: its bounds are 14 bytes wide. Bounds are parsed for every column of a manifest entry, so any query with a filter is enough and the filter does not have to touch the decimal column. A build with the undefined behaviour sanitizer aborts, as reported in the issue. Only `Decimal32` and `Decimal64` bounds are ever turned into a `Field` (everything else already returned `std::nullopt` a few lines below), and both fit into `Int64`. So the fix decodes exactly those and rejects anything wider before the arithmetic, which keeps the observable behaviour: a bound that used to be computed and then discarded is now not computed at all. Two smaller defects in the same expression are fixed along the way: * the sign extension is skipped when the value already fills all 64 bits. Previously it shifted an `int64_t` by 64, which is undefined; on the usual targets the shift count is taken modulo 64, so `-1` was left unchanged and OR-ing it in turned every eight-byte negative bound into `-1`. That is a wrong bound, not just undefined behaviour, and a wrong bound prunes files that do contain matching rows. * the widening `unscaled_value += scaler` and the narrowing to `Int32` are range checked. The bound comes from the manifest and is not validated against the declared precision, so a malformed manifest could otherwise wrap it into a bogus bound. ### Testing `tests/queries/0_stateless/04907_iceberg_decimal_bounds_overflow.sh` reads a `Decimal(38, 30)` Iceberg table with a filter. The table is the one attached to the issue, produced by Spark, repacked without the Spark checksum files and embedded as base64: ClickHouse cannot write a decimal column to Iceberg (`Unsupported type for iceberg Decimal(38, 30)`), so the test cannot build it itself. Because the overflowed bound was discarded anyway, the query results are the same before and after this change; the test fails before the fix only under the undefined behaviour sanitizer, and pins the results everywhere else. I verified the reproducer and the resulting query output against the official master build `26.8.1.1463`; I have not built this branch locally, so the compile and the sanitizer runs are left to CI. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes reading Iceberg tables whose manifests carry `Decimal` column bounds that do not fit into 64 bits, such as those of a `Decimal(38, 30)` column. Such a bound is now ignored instead of being decoded into a meaningless value, and a negative bound stored in eight bytes is no longer read as `-1`, which could skip files that do contain matching rows.

signals.title: Mask credentials of the Azure data lake table engines
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114939 `IcebergAzure`, `DeltaLakeAzure` and `PaimonAzure` appear in neither branch of the table engine dispatch in `FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder::findTableEngineSecretArguments` (`src/Parsers/FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder.cpp`): the S3 branch lists the S3 family lake engines (`DeltaLake`, `DeltaLakeS3`, `Hudi`, `Iceberg`, `IcebergS3`, `Paimon`, `PaimonS3`, `S3Queue`) and the Azure branch lists `AzureBlobStorage` and `AzureQueue`. With no branch matching, none of the three engines has any argument marked secret, so the storage account key stays verbatim in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, in `system.tables.engine_full` and in the logged query text, at the default `format_display_secrets_in_show_and_select = 0` and without the `displaySecretsInShowAndSelect` privilege. Both spellings leak: the `AccountKey=` inside a connection string and the positional `account_key` of the five argument form. The three engines take the same leading arguments as `AzureBlobStorage`, and `findAzureBlobStorageTableEngineSecretArguments` already handles both spellings, so this routes them to it. The Azure *table functions* (`icebergAzure`, `deltaLakeAzure`, `paimonAzure` and their `*Cluster` variants) were already dispatched there, which is why a `CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT * FROM icebergAzure(...)` masked while the engine did not. As the issue notes, this is not a regression: `git log -S "IcebergAzure"` over the secret finder's history is empty, so the engines were never masked. `findBackupNameSecretArguments`, the other dispatch in the same file, is left alone: it resolves a `BACKUP ... TO` destination, and the lake engines are not backup destinations. ### Testing `tests/queries/0_stateless/04908_azure_lake_engines_secret_mask.sh` covers all three engines and both argument spellings against an unreachable endpoint, so no Azure endpoint or emulator is needed: * `DeltaLakeAzure` defers reading the table when the columns are given, so its `CREATE` succeeds and `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and `system.tables.engine_full` are asserted directly. * `IcebergAzure` and `PaimonAzure` read their metadata while the table is created, so theirs fail against that endpoint. The masking happens when the query is formatted for the log, before the failure, so for those two the assertion is that the logged query text carries no key. Against the official master build `26.8.1.1463` the test prints the raw account key in all four `SHOW CREATE` and `engine_full` rows and reports 4 logged queries containing it; the committed reference is the masked output with 0. I have not built this branch locally, so the compile and the test run are left to CI. The Azure part of `tests/integration/test_mask_sensitive_info/test.py` is untouched: it runs against Azurite, and these three engines need a real table to exist there, which the unreachable-endpoint approach above avoids. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `IcebergAzure`, `DeltaLakeAzure` and `PaimonAzure` table engines now hide the Azure storage account key in `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and in `system.tables.engine_full`, as the `AzureBlobStorage` engine already did. Previously any user allowed to run `SHOW CREATE TABLE` or read `system.tables` could see the key of such a table.
signals.author: yussypu

signals.title: Mask the Azure shared access signature carried in a url argument
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114946 A storage account url is a documented, working way to authenticate: when the url contains a `?`, `processURL` (`src/Disks/DiskObjectStorage/ObjectStorages/AzureBlobStorage/AzureBlobStorageCommon.cpp`) takes everything after it as `sas_auth`, and `tests/integration/test_storage_azure_blob_storage/test.py::test_sas_token` exercises exactly that form. `maskAzureConnectionString` (`src/Parsers/FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder.cpp`) skips any argument starting with `http`, so the token stayed verbatim in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, in `system.tables.engine_full` and in `system.query_log.query` at the default `format_display_secrets_in_show_and_select = 0`. The same credential spelled as a connection string (`...;SharedAccessSignature=...`) was hidden, and the positional `account_key` was hidden, so the url spelling was the one gap. A shared access signature is a bearer credential: whoever holds it gets the access it was issued for until it expires. This masks the `sig` parameter, the HMAC over the signed fields and the only part of the token that cannot be guessed. The remaining parameters (`sv`, `sp`, `se`, `sr`, ...) grant nothing without it and stay visible, which keeps the url diagnosable, the same way `maskPresignedURLParameters` keeps a presigned S3 url readable. The new `maskAzureSASSignature` sits next to it in `src/Common/maskURIPassword.h` and is written the same way. The url argument is replaced in place (`result.replaced_arguments`) rather than hidden whole, and the function keeps returning `false`, so a positional `account_key` in the same call is still masked by the caller. That is the mechanism the S3 url masking already uses, and it composes with the other masking. All the call sites of `maskAzureConnectionString` are covered by the one change: the `AzureBlobStorage` and `AzureQueue` engines, and the `azureBlobStorage` table function with its `*Cluster` and named collection forms. If masking the whole query string is preferred over masking only `sig`, that is a one line change here; I went with the narrower one because the other parameters are not secret and are useful in a log. ### Testing `tests/queries/0_stateless/04909_azure_sas_url_secret_mask.sql` covers the engine through `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and `system.tables.engine_full`, and the table function and its cluster variant through `EXPLAIN QUERY TREE run_passes = 0`, which leaves them unresolved so nothing is read. A url with no signature in it is asserted to be left alone. The `CREATE` needs no reachable endpoint: with a shared access signature the engine skips the container probe. Against the official master build `26.8.1.1463` every one of those surfaces prints the signature verbatim; the committed reference is the same output with `sig=[HIDDEN]`. I also compiled `maskAzureSASSignature` standalone and checked it over multiple occurrences, a fragment, an empty value, a missing `=`, and the near-miss names `signature`, `xsig` and `SIG`. I have not built this branch, so the compile and the test run are left to CI. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): When an Azure shared access signature is passed inside the url of the `AzureBlobStorage` engine or the `azureBlobStorage` table function, its `sig` value is now hidden in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, `system.tables.engine_full` and `system.query_log`. Previously the whole token was stored and displayed in plain text, even though the equivalent connection string spelling was already hidden. The rest of the signature stays visible so the url is still readable in a log.

signals.title: Bound the waits in 02932_refreshable_materialized_views_1 and report refresh state on expiry
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105987 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105987 Requested by @ alexey-milovidov in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105987#issuecomment-5302349211, after a private-sync run of `Stateless tests (amd_asan_ubsan, distributed cache, meta in keeper, s3 storage, parallel, 2/2)` hung in this test with the active query `select * from rmv_a order by x`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description **The problem.** Every wait in this test is an unbounded loop with no deadline and no diagnostic, and some predicates can never become true: the first waits for a refresh to succeed, but with `refresh every 2 second` a failing refresh retries forever, so the predicate never holds and the `exception` column that says why is never read. The test just times out, naming nothing. `-- $LINENO` was also single-quoted at two of the three sites emitting `select * from rmv_a order by x`, and the third had no marker, so the one query a report can quote was untraceable. **The change.** One `wait_for` helper for all ten client-side waits and the unguarded read. Each poll is capped by the budget remaining, a failing client fails the wait rather than being retried as a mismatch, and on expiry the test prints the awaited query, expected and actual values, why the wait expired and `system.view_refreshes` including `exception`, then exits 1. All three `order by x` sites now carry a line number. I bound every wait, not just the two loops I first offered on that thread: the observed hangs pin lines 42, 91 and 145. One wait costs at most 30s (20s polling, then SIGKILL grace and the bounded dump), inside the 60s Fast test cap, against a slowest measured wait of 2.65s on ASAN. It bounds one wait, not the script, since the harness timer is per-test. `SYSTEM WAIT VIEW` is left alone: `RefreshTask::wait` has no deadline and no cancellation check, so bounding it client-side would park a server thread. **Validation.** With a failing refresh armed, the test previously spun silently until killed; it now reports in 20s with the pinned line and the exception. Passing-path stdout is byte-identical to the unchanged `.reference`; 50/50 runs pass on debug and ASAN.

signals.title: Avoid merge conflicts in the append-only lists of events, metrics and failpoints
signals.text: Two pull requests that each add a `ProfileEvents`, `CurrentMetrics` or `FailPoint` entry almost always add it at the same place - the end of the list - and Git reports that as a conflict, even though keeping both entries is always the right resolution. GitHub then marks the pull request as conflicting and it has to be resolved by hand. Marking the file `merge=union` in `.gitattributes` makes Git keep both sides instead, which is exactly the wanted resolution. This is already done for `src/Core/SettingsChangesHistory.cpp`. A union merge resolves *every* overlapping region by keeping both sides, so it is only safe for a file that contains nothing but such a list. Each list is therefore moved into its own `.inc` file, and only those files are marked, so a union merge can never silently duplicate or interleave ordinary code: - `src/Common/ProfileEventsList.inc` - `src/Common/CurrentMetricsList.inc` - `src/Common/FailPointsList.inc` The other idea considered was padding the entries apart with blank or backslash lines. That does not help: Git reports a conflict whenever both sides insert different text at the same point, however much unchanged context surrounds it, and insertions a line or two apart already merge cleanly today. This is written down in a comment in each list so it does not get retried. The last entry of `APPLY_FOR_FAILPOINTS` had no trailing backslash, so adding an entry edited that line instead of inserting after it - under a union merge that would duplicate the line and truncate the macro. All three lists now end the same way, with every entry a self-contained line, so appending is always a pure insertion. `src/Common/ErrorCodes.cpp` is deliberately left alone, and `.gitattributes` says why: an error code is a value in the public protocol, and a union merge there would silently keep two entries with the same number. The change is a pure text move, verified as such: - the preprocessed expansion of each list is byte-identical before and after, warning-clean under `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` (the failpoints are checked with four distinct category macros, so a miscategorised entry would show up); - all three translation units compile with production flags with no new warnings, and their symbol tables are unchanged (1703 / 544 / 470 symbols); - `ci/jobs/scripts/check_style/check_cpp.sh` reports nothing; - two branches that each append an entry to all three lists now merge cleanly, keeping both entries, and the merged lists still preprocess with no duplicates. The same scenario on `master` today conflicts. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signals.title: Do not regenerate part names from part infos for tables with the deprecated syntax
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/87206 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103537 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112457 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `BAD_DATA_PART_NAME` ("Trying to get part name in new format for old format version") on a `ReplicatedMergeTree` created with the deprecated positional syntax under `allow_deprecated_syntax_for_merge_tree`. A mutation could be reported as done on a replica that had not applied it, and the table could stay readonly after a restart. ### Description Reported by @ alexey-milovidov on #112457 ([`Upgrade check (amd_release)` report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112457&sha=f888781eb610bfabdc8c8675d835b99482bec8a2&name_0=PR&name_1=Upgrade%20check%20%28amd_release%29)). No related open issue found. A table created with `ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree(date, key, granularity)` uses date-based (V0) part names. `MergeTreePartInfo::getPartNameAndCheckFormat` cannot produce one, because the min/max dates it needs are not part of a `MergeTreePartInfo`, so it throws. Two `ActiveDataPartSet` entry points take only an info and regenerate the name that way; each had exactly one caller, and both callers already held the name and threw it away. This change passes the name at both call sites, as in `536b611c96a757e`, which fixed the `ATTACH PARTITION` instance of this bug. V0 name formatting is untouched, and current-format tables are unaffected because the name-taking overload re-parses to the same info and runs the same insertion code. The linked report contains both failures: - `ReplicatedMergeTreeQueue::getPartNamesToMutate` builds `mutation.parts_to_do`. The throw left it empty, so a mutation reported `is_done` on a replica that never mutated its part, and `mutations_sync = 2` returned success while that replica still served pre-mutation values. Regressed by #87206, which changed `produced_parts` to hold infos instead of names. - `StorageReplicatedMergeTree::checkPartsImpl` builds the set of empty unexpected parts. The throw aborted `ReplicatedMergeTreeAttachThread`, leaving the table readonly. Regressed by my own #103537, which replaced a name-based call with an info-based one. The V0 gap in `MergeTreeData::restorePartFromBackup` that the throw-site comment describes is a different code path, absent from both stacks, and is not addressed. A new stateless test asserts `parts_to_do` on the frozen replica: it fails on master (`parts to do 0`) and passes here (`parts to do 2`), and 50/50 randomized runs pass. `checkPartsImpl`'s state needs parts fabricated on disk, so that half is covered by three V0 cases added to `gtest_active_data_part_set.cpp`, all of which fail with this change reverted. `00062_replicated_merge_tree_alter_zookeeper_long` and `00652_replicated_mutations_zookeeper` still pass.

signals.title: Do not drop the whole GROUP BY when unwrapping injective functions of constants
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104863 (same logical error, closed earlier without this cause identified) ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results for a `GROUP BY` whose only key is an injective function of constants, for example `SELECT 1 FROM t GROUP BY materialize(NULL)`. Such a key was removed by `optimize_injective_functions_in_group_by`, which left the query with no `GROUP BY` and no aggregation at all, so it returned one row per input row instead of one row per group. Over a `Merge` table that mixes a local and a remote child the same cause also raised the logical error `Chunk info was not set for chunk in GroupingAggregatedTransform`. ### Description `unwrapInjectiveFunctionsInKeys` unwraps an injective function to its arguments and skips constant arguments, so a key that is an injective function *of a constant* unwraps to nothing and is dropped. `OptimizeGroupByInjectiveFunctionsPass` assigned that result unconditionally: when such a key was the only one and the query had no aggregate function, `GROUP BY` became empty and the query stopped aggregating. Under a `Merge` table mixing a child that aggregates with one that does not, the un-aggregated child's raw chunks reach a merge transform that requires aggregate state; both wordings of the message occur, `GroupingAggregatedTransform` and `MergingAggregatedTransform`, depending on `distributed_aggregation_memory_efficient`, and one fix closes both. Found by the fuzzers, e.g. [AST fuzzer (amd_debug)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=94148&sha=8eb1df1331f7fd5dcf93b4b0e975e56685b6f732&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%29). The fix assigns the unwrapped list only when it is non-empty, which is what `OptimizeLimitByInjectiveFunctionsPass` already does for `LIMIT BY` and what the non-analyzer `TreeOptimizer::optimizeGroupBy` does via `appendUnusedGroupByColumn`. Of those three sibling paths only the analyzer's `GROUP BY` pass lacked the guard. The shared helper is unchanged, so `LIMIT BY` is unaffected. A per-key variant was deliberately not used: it would weaken the optimization when another key survives, and it is the branch added in 462445c2c201a5f and removed the next day in 355909eb3a415b7. `GROUP BY materialize(NULL), k` still groups by `k` alone. Affected queries now return a different row count, which is the point of the fix. Across 25 shapes the patched default is byte-identical to running with `optimize_injective_functions_in_group_by = 0`, where before it diverged on 7 of them; `enable_analyzer = 0` and a plain `GROUP BY NULL` key agree. The old behaviour stays reachable with that setting. The new test fails on master and passes here.

signals.title: Report the real error when an in-place `IN`-set build destroys its source
signals.text: `FutureSetFromSubquery::buildOrderedSetInplace` speculatively builds the set of an `IN` subquery during index analysis. A subquery whose source plan cannot be cloned - a read from a remote cluster, for example - takes the destructive path there, which consumes the source plan. When that build then throws, the set can never be built again: `build` returns a null plan, every caller takes that for "nothing left to build", and the query keeps running with an unready set until `FunctionIn` reports the logical error `Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument for function 'in'`. That is exactly what happens whenever a caller deliberately ignores an in-place build failure. Statistics-based part pruning is such a caller: it logs the failure and keeps reading the part whose condition it could not evaluate. So ```sql SELECT count() FROM t WHERE a IN (SELECT a FROM clusterAllReplicas('cluster_with_an_unavailable_replica', currentDatabase(), t)) ``` reported `Not-ready Set` instead of the connection error, which aborts the server in a build with `abort_on_logical_error`. The failure of a destructive in-place build is remembered now and rethrown from `build` instead of returning a null plan, so the query fails with the real reason - the same error it fails with when no in-place build is attempted at all. This is the cause of the recurring master `Stress test` failure `Logical error: Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument for function 'A (STID: 0250-3e49)`, seen on `arm_release` and `arm_msan` a few times a day since 2026-07-23: CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=2926be24e6102daae60b8f44c88969495a76ec3c&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_release%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107924 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix the logical error `Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument for function 'in'` for a query with an `IN` subquery reading from a remote cluster: the query now fails with the actual error from the subquery, such as a connection failure.

signals.title: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend
signals.text: This supersedes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112156, whose fork branch no longer accepts maintainer updates. Credit to @groeneai for the original implementation. signals.title: Implement geo-location awareness during fetching
signals.text: <!--- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): - Implement geo-location awareness during fetching This PR try to solve the issue in #52398. When you have a cross-ocean ClickHouse deployment and each region has multiple ClickHouse replicas, the cross-ocean network bandwidth could become expensive. For example, you have two replicas in `US` and two replicas in `APAC`, once you insert data to a replica in `APAC`, both `US` replicas will try to fetch parts from the `APAC` node, which double the necessary cross-ocean network bandwidth. We introduce a new component, `ReplicatedMergeTreeGeoReplicationController` that enable the following replication architecture: ``` US1 (region leader) <-----------------------> APAC1 (region leader) | | US2 (follower) APAC2 (follower) ``` Each region will have a regional leader and multiple followers. During replication, all replicas still pull log entries from ZooKeeper log queue to its queue, no matter which replica publish the entry. However, when replaying the log entries, if fetching needed, following constraints will apply: 1. A region leader can fetch part from any replica (inside and outside of the region) 2. A follower can only fetch part from the leader If the target part is not ready on the leader, followers will defer execution of the log entry (default 20 seconds). If a follower waits for a leader for too long (default 900 seconds), it will stop waiting and try to fetch on any replica (or check if the part is broken). The leader is per-table. After being elected, the leader will maintain a _lease_ in ZooKeeper, so other node know that there is a leader. All replicas within a region will run leader election if leader is absented (currently leader election is done with ZooKeeper). Additional ZooKeeper nodes per replicated table: - `/path_to_table/regions/{region}` - `/path_to_table/regions/{region}/leader_election`: leader election node for the region `region` - `/path_to_table/regions/{region}/leader_lease`: ephemeral node, current leader of the region - `/path_to_table/replicas/{replica}/{$REGION}`: ephemeral node, ZooKeeper information about the region of current replica You can enable this feature by setting `geo_replication_control_region` when create replicated table. ```xml <clickhouse> <replicated_merge_tree> <geo_replication_control_region>APAC</geo_replication_control_region> <!-- values defined by user --> </replicated_merge_tree> </clickhouse> ``` ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!--- Directly edit documentation source files in the "docs" folder with the same pull-request as code changes or Add a user-readable short description of the changes that should be added to docs.clickhouse.com below. At a minimum, the following information should be added (but add more as needed). - Motivation: Why is this function, table engine, etc. useful to ClickHouse users? - Parameters: If the feature being added takes arguments, options or is influenced by settings, please list them below with a brief explanation. - Example use: A query or command. --> > Information about CI checks: https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/development/continuous-integration/

signals.title: group_by_each_block_no_merge setting
signals.text: ### Changelog category: - New Feature ### Changelog entry: Added the `group_by_each_block_no_merge` setting (off by default). When enabled, a query with `GROUP BY` is processed in a streaming fashion: aggregation is performed, finalized, and flushed for every block of data, without fully merging the partial results. The exact output is plan-dependent and not deterministic in general. This is intended for special cases such as populating a materialized view with `POPULATE`, where the partial results are merged later in the background. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/9604 ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) The setting is documented in `src/Core/Settings.cpp` (rendered into the settings reference). > Information about CI checks: https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/development/continuous-integration/

signals.title: Implemented SIEVE eviction in cache framework
signals.text: Implements the `SIEVE` cache eviction policy in the cache framework (`CacheBase`), available alongside the existing `LRU` and `SLRU` policies. `SIEVE` is a simple, scan-resistant eviction algorithm: a single "hand" walks a FIFO queue of entries and evicts the first entry whose `visited` flag is clear, clearing the flag as it passes set entries. See the paper for details: https://junchengyang.com/publication/nsdi24-SIEVE.pdf This continues the original work by @Vectorshine, brought up to date with `master`: - Reworked `SIEVECachePolicy` to match the current `ICachePolicy` interface (`CurrentMetrics` tracking, `maxCount`, `contains`, per-entry `OnRemoveEntryFunction`), mirroring `LRUCachePolicy`. - Fixed a bug in `remove` where the stored queue iterator was advanced in place and the wrong node was erased. - Added unit tests in `gtest_sieve_cache.cpp`, including a step-by-step test of the eviction logic. - Randomized the mark and uncompressed cache policy across `LRU`, `SLRU` and `SIEVE` in stateless functional tests (`ci/jobs/functional_tests.py`) and the stress test (`tests/docker_scripts/stress_runner.sh`). `SIEVE` is only implemented for the `CacheBase`-backed caches, so the filesystem cache (backed by `FileCachePolicy`) is not randomized to it, and it is excluded during bugfix validation, which runs downloaded master-side binaries. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58910 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new cache eviction policy `SIEVE`. It can be selected for the in-memory caches backed by `CacheBase`, such as the mark cache and the uncompressed cache, via the corresponding `*_cache_policy` server settings (for example, `mark_cache_policy` and `uncompressed_cache_policy`). It is not available for the filesystem cache. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)
signals.author: Vectorshine
