signal.title: Promote ConstantValue to Core with Field-free value accessors
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113051 --> Continue removing `DB::Field` from constant handling by promoting the owning single-constant type to a shared primitive with `Field`-free value accessors. ### What - **Move `ConstantValue` from `Analyzer/` to `Core/`.** It bundles `{size-1 ColumnConst, DataTypePtr}`. It carries a `DataTypePtr`, and `DataTypes` depends on `Columns`, so `Core` is the correct layer (this also removes a lower layer having to reach up into `Analyzer` for the type). It stays deliberately distinct from `ColumnWithTypeAndName` (size-1 const invariant, no name, scalar accessors). - **Add value accessors** that read row 0 of the size-1 column without materializing a `Field`: `isNull`, `getUInt`, `getInt`, `getFloat64`, `getBool`, `getDataAt`. `ConstantNode` gains matching delegators, and `ConstantNode::getValue` now delegates to a single transitional `ConstantValue::getField`. - **`evaluateConstantExpressionAsColumn` now returns `ConstantValue`** instead of `std::pair<ColumnPtr, DataTypePtr>`. Callers updated: `numbers`/`primes`/`generateSeries`/`values` table functions, `ActionsVisitor`, `InterpreterSelectQuery` (LIMIT/OFFSET), prometheus/timeSeries selectors, and the gtest. The two `getStringConstArgument` helpers now read the value directly via `isNull`/`getDataAt`. ### Behavior No user-visible change: the value is the same size-1 const column with the same exact type, just bundled and readable without a `Field`. `ConstantValue`'s `Field` constructor and `getField` remain as the only `Field` entry/exit while the analyzer still folds constants into `Field`s; a later phase removes them. ### Verification `gtest_convert_column_to_type`, `gtest_evaluate_constant_expression`, and a `numbers`/`generate_series`/`values`/`LIMIT` (integer + fractional)/`IN` stateless spot-check. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113051 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not for changelog: internal refactor toward removing `DB::Field`; no user-visible behavior change. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1480` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Reject Delta Lake partition column absent from the table schema
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114462 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` when reading a Delta Lake table whose `metaData.partitionColumns` names a column that `metaData.schemaString` does not declare. Such metadata is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` on the delta-kernel reader and `INCORRECT_DATA` on the legacy reader, whenever the table or its schema is read from a snapshot, not only when the query carries a predicate. ### Description Requested by @ PedroTadim in #114462. `partitionColumns` and `schemaString` are independent fields of externally supplied metadata and nothing cross-checked them, so a mismatch was reported as `LOGICAL_ERROR`, which aborts on debug and sanitizer builds. Paimon already threw `BAD_ARGUMENTS` here. - delta-kernel reader: validate in `TableSnapshot::initOrUpdateSchemaIfChanged`, where both values first exist, beside the existing empty-schema rejection. Previously an unfiltered `SELECT *` succeeded and only a predicate threw, since `PartitionPruner` is built only when a filter exists. That site keeps `LOGICAL_ERROR`, now a genuine internal invariant. - legacy reader: `LOGICAL_ERROR` -> `INCORRECT_DATA` where an `add` action's `partitionValues` names an undeclared key, in the JSON-log and checkpoint branches. It also validates `partitionColumns` where `metaData` is loaded, in both branches, so a snapshot with no `add` action to resolve is rejected too. That check compares logical names: a parsed legacy schema is keyed by column-mapping physical names, so comparing against it would reject well formed column-mapped tables. Iceberg is unaffected: it resolves partitions by numeric `source_id` field ids, not by name. Change-data-feed reads go through `TableChanges`, which resolves no partition name, and are out of scope. Behaviour change: such a table was readable without a predicate, and on the legacy reader also with no `add` action; it is now rejected for every query that reads it. It is malformed per the Delta protocol. One case is left alone, unchanged from master: on a table with an explicit column list a bare `count()` is answered from transaction-log row counts, which resolve no column name, so it is not rejected, while reading any column from it is. Validated with the new stateless test `04877`: every failure arm fails on a targeted revert of the line it covers, including a well formed column-mapped control that must keep reading. Also 50/50 randomized runs and the `delta_lake` suite.
signal.author: groeneai

signal.title: SQLancer: track sqlancer main, deduplicate findings, fail the job on them
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes Not user-facing. ### Description Three fixes to the nightly SQLancer job (`NightlySQLancer`, every 3 days). #### 1. Fuzz `ClickHouse/sqlancer` `main`, not a hardcoded commit The image pinned `ClickHouse/sqlancer@a62ea509`, so oracle work landing in the fork never reached CI. Pointing the Dockerfile at a branch is not enough: praktika rebuilds an image only when its directory digest changes, so a branch fetched at image-build time freezes at whatever `main` was when the Dockerfile was last edited — worse than an explicit pin, because it silently lies about what is being fuzzed. Instead: - the image clones `main` as a **warm cache** and keeps `.git` plus the maven repository under `/sqlancer` (world-writable, so the job's non-root user can extend it); - `sqlancer_job.sh` **re-clones and rebuilds `main` at job start** (~1 min with the warm maven repo) and falls back to the baked build if GitHub or Maven is unavailable; - the resolved commit is printed and included in the job info, so a finding stays attributable after `main` moves. Overrides for a one-off run: `SQLANCER_REF`, `SQLANCER_REPO`, `SQLANCER_BUILD_AT_RUNTIME=0`. #### 2. Readable output: one artifact per finding, deduplicated Before, the job log was ~3600 progress lines for a 5h run plus, for every finding, the whole reproducer state dump that SQLancer's `AlsoWriteToConsoleFileWriter` mirrors to stderr — impossible to read, and the reproducers were only available as one tarball of everything. Now the console shows one progress line per ~5 minutes and a summary (~20 lines for a clean run); the full fuzzer output remains an artifact. Findings are reported individually **and** deduplicated: - Each `logs/clickhouse/databaseN.log` is exactly one finding (`StateLogger.logException` writes the stack trace plus that database's whole `CREATE`/`INSERT`/…/`SELECT` sequence, then the worker continues under a fresh database name), so each is copied out and attached as its own artifact. - New `ci/jobs/scripts/sqlancer_failures.py` fingerprints every finding as **(exception class + ClickHouse error code/name from the `Caused by:` chain, reporting oracle, first sqlancer stack frame)** and groups equal fingerprints. - The report gets one row per *distinct* failure with the individual findings and their logs nested underneath, plus `failures/analysis.txt` (all families, loudest first, and a per-finding index). The failure *message* is deliberately **not** part of the fingerprint: for most oracles it is the generated SQL, unique to every finding, which would defeat the dedup. To keep that safe, every family lists all of its occurrences by database name and up to three distinct *message shapes* (literals → `'S'`, numbers → `N`, generated identifiers such as `c0`/`t3`/`database7` → `id`), so a family that merged more than one bug is visible as such. The job info line becomes, for example: ``` sqlancer main @ 3a66cc5ce597; 1,407k queries; 43 finding(s) in 13 distinct failure(s): PivotedQuerySynthesisBase/Code 241 x20, NoREC/Code 241 x8, TLPDistinct/AssertionError x3, ... ``` and the rows: ``` Failure analysis [analysis.txt] PivotedQuerySynthesisBase / AssertionError / Code 241 (MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED) / at SQLQueryAdapter.checkException:176 (x20) |- database0 [database0.log] \- ... TLPDistinct / AssertionError / at ComparatorHelper.assumeResultSetsAreEqual:127 (x3) |- database48 [database48.log] \- ... ``` If the analysis script itself fails, the job still fails and attaches the raw reproducer logs, so a bug in it can never swallow a finding. #### 3. A finding now marks the job failed Praktika derives the GitHub job conclusion from the job script's **exit code** (`res = run_code == 0` in `ci/praktika/runner.py`); the result file's status only drives the HTML report. Both SQLancer scripts exited 0 unconditionally, so a finding could not turn the nightly red. They now exit non-zero whenever anything was found: - a reproducer log; - a sanitizer report or `<Fatal>` message in the server logs (this job runs an ASan+UBSan build) — checked before the server is stopped, so a leak report emitted during shutdown does not turn every run red; - a dead or unreachable server; - a non-zero sqlancer exit code; - a run that produced no execution statistics at all (silently broken run). `sqlancer_pp_job.sh` additionally wrote the invalid status tokens `success`/`failure` instead of `OK`/`FAIL`, which made praktika render its result as "completed but unknown". Concretely, the [2026-08-13 nightly](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/31674904130) reported **green** while the SQLancerPP job had failed on the `WHERE` and `NoREC` oracles. Its per-oracle logs are now attached to their own rows too. ### Testing The scripts' logic was exercised directly, without a real fuzzing run: - `ci/jobs/scripts/sqlancer_failures.py` against **43 real reproducer logs** from a saved SQLancer run: 43 findings → **13 distinct failures**, grouped the way they are actually triaged (PQS memory-limit noise x20, NoREC memory-limit x8, TLPDistinct row-count mismatch x3, TLPSetOp `UNION_DISTINCT` mismatch x1, TLPSetOp NPE x1, CODDTest Code 27 x1, …). Empty and missing log directories yield `no findings` and an empty fragment. - `ci/jobs/sqlancer_job.sh` end to end against stubbed `java`/`wget`/`git`/`mvn`/`clickhouse` binaries: clean run → `OK`, exit 0, 18 console lines; run with findings → `FAIL`, exit 1, 36 console lines and valid nested result JSON; UBSan `runtime error:` → `FAIL` while benign ASan boilerplate stays `OK`; server death, sqlancer crash, missing statistics, runtime-build failure (falls back with a warning), the 50-file upload cap, >10 MB log compression and a deliberately broken analysis script all behave as described. The real verification is the next nightly run of this workflow. ### CI validation (2026-08-14) Validated by dispatching `NightlySQLancer` twice from a throwaway branch on top of this one (short fuzz runs; branch deleted since). **[Run 31825081436](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/31825081436) — clean path, 20 min fuzz.** Workflow conclusion `failure`, driven by SQLancerPP (see below). - Docker image with the new Dockerfile built (by this PR's own CI) and reused from the registry here. - Runtime clone + rebuild of `ClickHouse/sqlancer` `main`: **11 s**, commit `3a66cc5ce597`, no fallback (the warm maven repo in the image is doing its job). - **93 oracles** exercised, versus 31 with the old pinned commit. - 4 progress lines on the console for the whole fuzz run; job info `sqlancer main @ 3a66cc5ce597; 56k queries; no findings`; exit 0, job green. - The job's report entry is populated for the first time: status `OK`, `duration: 1243`, the info line and 5 artifact links. For comparison, the same entry in the [2026-08-13 nightly](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/REFs/master/45cb8371bbe63a39f7d0c655543563e8f15e5a40/result_nightlysqlancer.json) is `{"results": [], "links": [], "duration": null}`. - SQLancerPP went `failure` with per-oracle rows (`WHERE`, `QUERY_PARTITIONING` assertions; `FUZZING` → server not responding), each with its logs — and the **workflow status became `FAIL`**. The identical failure reported green on 2026-08-13. **[Run 31830811184](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/31830811184) — failure path, 15 min fuzz** with `TextIndexDirectRead` re-included, since it reliably fires on the open ClickHouse#107186. - **37 findings deduplicated into 1 distinct failure**: `TextIndexDirectRead / java.lang.AssertionError / at ClickHouseTextIndexDirectReadOracle.check:95 (x37)`, one report row listing all 37 databases with 10 reproducer logs attached, plus the `Failure analysis` row with `analysis.txt`. - `analysis.txt` per-finding index carries the full assertion for each one (`ClickHouse#107186`, tokenizer, preprocessor, predicate, the diverging key sets and the DDL). - A downloaded reproducer (`database0.log`, 2035 lines) starts with the assertion plus stack trace and ends with the exact `CREATE TABLE ... INDEX idx (s) TYPE text(tokenizer = 'splitByNonAlpha', preprocessor = lower(s))` + `INSERT` that reproduces it. - Job info `39k queries; 37 finding(s) in 1 distinct failure(s)`, job red, workflow `FAIL`. Two fixes came out of this validation and are included: the result-name bug above, and `SQLancerPP` no longer listing per-oracle logs that were never written (praktika replaces the whole job `info` with `WARNING: File [...] was not found`, which buried the result). One observation, not addressed here: the ASan+UBSan server writes ~10 MB of `DB::Exception` stack traces to stderr per 20 minutes (~150 MB projected over 5 h), from logging every failed fuzzer statement at error level. Dropping the mounted `log_level.xml` to `fatal` would remove it while keeping `<Fatal>` and sanitizer detection intact.

signal.title: Support arrayElement and arraySlice for QBit
signal.text: arrayElement(qbit, n) (and the qbit[n] operator) reconstructs the n-th vector element at the full precision of the QBit element type, reading only the bit planes of the stride group that contains the element. Out-of-range indices follow the Array semantics: default value for arrayElement, NULL for arrayElementOrNull, negative indices count from the end. arraySlice(qbit, offset[, length]) returns a QBit over the selected dimensions (projection to a subset of dimensions). The offset and length must be constants because the dimension of a QBit is part of its type. A slice aligned to stride-group boundaries keeps the stride and reuses the stored bit-plane streams without copying; an octet-aligned slice is a pure byte move; any other slice repacks the bits, reading only the planes of the stride groups it overlaps. Possible follow-up: an analyzer pass (similar to DistanceTransposedPartialReadsPass) could rewrite these functions to read only the needed bit-plane subcolumns from disk, extending the "only needed strides" guarantee from the in-memory execution down to storage I/O. Closes #109942 ### Changelog category - New Feature ### Changelog entry Functions `arrayElement` (the `vec[n]` operator) and `arraySlice` now work for the `QBit` data type: `qbit[n]` returns the n-th vector element at full precision, and `arraySlice(qbit, offset, length)` returns a projection to a subset of dimensions. Both read only the bit planes of the stride groups they need, and slices aligned to stride-group boundaries reuse the stored streams without copying. This closes #109942.

signal.title: Flaky test: 04625_hash_table_sizes_stats_table_expression_modifiers reports zero preallocated sizes
signal.text: 🕵 `04625_hash_table_sizes_stats_table_expression_modifiers` fails regularly on master and on many pull requests: the hash-table-sizes statistics come back as zero, so the test prints ``` final-prealloc 0 no-final-prealloc 0 ``` instead of the expected `520000` / `650000`. Per CIDB it failed 8 times on master in the last 30 days (most recently 2026-08-13 22:32:26), plus on 42 distinct pull requests, across every build flavour (`Fast test`, `arm_binary`, `amd_debug`, `amd_tsan`, `amd_msan`, `amd_llvm_coverage`), so it is not tied to a particular sanitizer, storage, or analyzer configuration. It also survives the automatic reruns ("Failed 3 out of 3 reruns"), which makes it look like a real regression in a job that hits it. Query for the history: ```sql SELECT toStartOfDay(check_start_time) AS day, count() AS failures, groupUniqArray(pull_request_number) AS prs FROM checks WHERE check_start_time >= now() - toIntervalDay(30) AND test_name = '04625_hash_table_sizes_stats_table_expression_modifiers' AND test_status IN ('FAIL', 'ERROR') GROUP BY day ORDER BY day DESC ``` The test was last touched by 9650bb8cd624 (2026-07-23) "Fix flaky ... under randomized external aggregation", so the earlier flakiness fix looks incomplete. Example report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105987&sha=77de23431cd96d94d5370923e65911c42dc65480&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_llvm_coverage%2C%20old%20analyzer%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20DBReplicated%2C%20WasmEdge%2C%20parallel%2C%201%2F3%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105987

signal.title: Add SeaweedFS object storage integration guide
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Documentation (changelog entry is not required) ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes Adds an integration guide for using SeaweedFS as S3-compatible object storage with ClickHouse, alongside the existing MinIO and Tigris pages: a one-container local setup, the S3-backed MergeTree disk configuration with a cache disk and storage policy, `s3` table function reads and writes, and `BACKUP`/`RESTORE` to a SeaweedFS endpoint. Registers the page in the connectors navigation. Every step is verified directly against ClickHouse 26.7.3 and the current `chrislusf/seaweedfs` image, using the exact commands and configuration shown: the docker run and bucket-creation commands, `s3()` insert, read, and glob reads, MergeTree create/insert/merge/select on the S3 disk (including the cache disk and data surviving a server restart), and a `BACKUP`/`RESTORE` round trip with matching row counts and sums. One cross-link points to the SeaweedFS catalog guide added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114255, so that PR should merge first.

signal.title: The trivial GROUP BY LIMIT optimization returns wrong results with DISTINCT, QUALIFY, window functions or arrayJoin in the projection
signal.text: The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT` optimization (`optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`, default `true` since 26.5) rewrites eligible queries to `max_rows_to_group_by = n + offset` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`, so the aggregation keeps only the first `n + offset` distinct keys. That is only sound when the LIMIT directly cuts the produced groups. The shape check misses four constructs that consume or filter the groups **between** the aggregation and the LIMIT, and each of them returns wrong results with default settings (verified on current master, top-level queries, multi-threaded): **`DISTINCT`** — collapses the projected groups before LIMIT. 100000 groups yield 4 distinct values, `LIMIT 3` must return 3 rows; with the rewrite the aggregation is cut at 3 keys and the distinct set shrinks to 1 value: ```sql SELECT DISTINCT intDiv(k, 25000) FROM (SELECT number AS k FROM numbers_mt(100000)) GROUP BY k LIMIT 3 SETTINGS max_threads = 16, max_block_size = 100; -- returns 1 row instead of 3 ``` **A window function in the projection** — is evaluated over all groups. `hasWindow()` only catches the named `WINDOW` clause, not inline `OVER ()`: ```sql SELECT count() OVER () AS w FROM (SELECT number AS k FROM numbers_mt(100000)) GROUP BY k LIMIT 5 SETTINGS max_threads = 16, max_block_size = 100; -- returns w = 100 instead of w = 100000 ``` **`arrayJoin` in the projection** — can drop rows (empty arrays), so `n + offset` kept groups may produce fewer rows than the LIMIT while more groups exist: ```sql SELECT arrayJoin(if(k % 1000 = 0, [k], [])) FROM (SELECT number AS k FROM numbers_mt(100000)) GROUP BY k LIMIT 10 SETTINGS max_threads = 16, max_block_size = 100; -- returns 1 row instead of 10 ``` **`QUALIFY`** — filters the groups after the aggregation, so the kept groups may not contain enough qualifying ones (a `QUALIFY` on plain group keys alone is pushed down below the aggregation and is not affected; a window function keeps it in place): ```sql SELECT count() OVER (PARTITION BY k % 2) AS w FROM (SELECT number AS k FROM numbers_mt(100000)) GROUP BY k QUALIFY k >= 99000 LIMIT 10 SETTINGS max_threads = 16, max_block_size = 100; -- returns 0 rows instead of 10 rows with w = 50000 ``` All four have the same root cause: the pass checks `HAVING`/`ORDER BY`/`WINDOW`/`LIMIT BY`/`GROUP BY` modifiers/aggregate functions, but not `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window function nodes or `arrayJoin` in the projection. Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104473 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114690 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #114695 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1479` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Parquet and ORC do not push predicates into Tuple subcolumns
signal.text: ### Describe the issue Parquet and ORC filter pushdown works for a top-level column but is lost when the identical values are stored in a `Tuple` subcolumn. With one million ordered rows: | Format and predicate | Input read | |---|---:| | Parquet: `id = 555555` | 1 of 91 row groups | | Parquet: `tup.1 = 555555` | all 91 row groups | | ORC: `id = 555555` | 10,000 rows | | ORC: `tup.1 = 555555` | 1,000,000 rows | `id` and `tup.1` contain identical `UInt64` values. ### Version `26.8.1.404` ### Reproducer The automated reproducer generates both fixtures, captures `--print-profile-events`, prints the result counts and reader metrics, and asserts the differences: Run python script [repro_format_nested_and_orc_cast_pushdown.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30543252/repro_format_nested_and_orc_cast_pushdown.py) Output: ```text case result selected_rows_raw rows_per_pass read_row_groups pruned_row_groups parquet_direct 1 3372 1686 1 90 parquet_tuple 1 2000000 1000000 91 0 orc_direct 1 20000 10000 0 0 orc_tuple 1 2000000 1000000 0 0 orc_noop_toUInt64 1 2000000 1000000 0 0 All result and ProfileEvents assertions passed. ``` `clickhouse-local` includes both schema inference and query execution in `SelectedRows`, so the script prints the raw counter and the corresponding per-pass value. Parquet row-group counters are emitted directly. Expanded manual steps follow. Generate the files: ```bash clickhouse local \ --output_format_parquet_row_group_size 10000 \ --output_format_parquet_data_page_size 4096 \ --output_format_parquet_write_page_index 1 \ --output_format_parquet_write_bloom_filter 1 \ --query " SELECT number AS id, tuple(number, toString(number % 31)) AS tup FROM numbers(1000000) INTO OUTFILE '/tmp/nested_pushdown.parquet' TRUNCATE FORMAT Parquet" clickhouse local \ --output_format_orc_row_index_stride 10000 \ --query " SELECT number AS id, tuple(number, toString(number % 31)) AS tup FROM numbers(1000000) INTO OUTFILE '/tmp/nested_pushdown.orc' TRUNCATE FORMAT ORC" ``` Compare Parquet predicates: ```bash clickhouse local --print-profile-events --query " SELECT count() FROM file('/tmp/nested_pushdown.parquet', Parquet) WHERE id = 555555 SETTINGS max_threads=1 FORMAT Null" clickhouse local --print-profile-events --query " SELECT count() FROM file('/tmp/nested_pushdown.parquet', Parquet) WHERE tup.1 = 555555 SETTINGS max_threads=1 FORMAT Null" ``` Relevant output: ```text # id = 555555 ParquetReadRowGroups: 1 ParquetPrunedRowGroups: 90 # tup.1 = 555555 ParquetReadRowGroups: 91 ParquetPrunedRowGroups: 0 ``` Compare ORC predicates: ```bash clickhouse local --print-profile-events --query " SELECT count() FROM file('/tmp/nested_pushdown.orc', ORC) WHERE id = 555555 SETTINGS max_threads=1 FORMAT Null" clickhouse local --print-profile-events --query " SELECT count() FROM file('/tmp/nested_pushdown.orc', ORC) WHERE tup.1 = 555555 SETTINGS max_threads=1 FORMAT Null" ``` Relevant output, including the schema-inference pass: ```text # id = 555555 SelectedRows: 20000 # tup.1 = 555555 SelectedRows: 2000000 ``` ### Parquet statistics are present `ParquetMetadata` reports valid min/max statistics for physical path `tup.1`. The nested scan is therefore not caused by missing file statistics. ### Expected behavior Predicates on supported primitive Tuple/Nested subcolumns should be translated to their physical Parquet/ORC paths and used for row-group or row-index pruning, the same as equivalent top-level columns. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #113383 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1477` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: [CI crash] Pure-virtual call in dumpPipeline/printPipeline for a streaming (STREAM) query on teardown (debug build)
signal.text: ## Description The `AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted)` job crashes with `SIGABRT` (a pure-virtual call) while dumping the pipeline for a streaming (`STREAM`) query over a `MergeTree` table. This is unrelated to the codec whose test the targeted fuzzer mutated — the crashing query reads no data columns (`SELECT 'Int32' FROM t_pco STREAM`), and the crash is entirely inside generic streaming-query + pipeline-diagnostics code. Found via the targeted fuzzer on PR https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110613 (report: `PR -> AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted)`, sha `7898ce1800f75471f816553d3e341f7adbe61719`). ## Crash ``` (from thread 1165) (query_id: ae177a58-...) (query: SELECT 'Int32' FROM t_pco STREAM) Received signal Aborted (6) ... 6. libcxxabi/src/abort_message.cpp:66 7. libcxxabi/src/cxa_virtual.cpp:16 (__cxa_pure_virtual) 8. src/Processors/IProcessor.h:139 DB::IProcessor::getUniqID() const 9. src/QueryPipeline/printPipeline.h:74 DB::printPipeline<...>(...) 10. src/Processors/Executors/PipelineExecutor.cpp:771 DB::PipelineExecutor::dumpPipeline() const 11. src/Processors/Executors/PipelineExecutor.cpp:229 DB::PipelineExecutor::execute(...) 12. src/Processors/Executors/CompletedPipelineExecutor.cpp:43 DB::threadFunction(...) ``` ## Root cause In a debug build, `PipelineExecutor::execute()` wraps the run in `try/catch`, and on any exception it logs `dumpPipeline()` (guarded by `#ifndef NDEBUG`, `PipelineExecutor.cpp:229`). `dumpPipeline` → `printPipeline` walks the graph and, for every output port, calls `next.getUniqID()` on the connected downstream processor (`printPipeline.h:74`). `getUniqID` calls the virtual `getName()` (`IProcessor.h:139`). The pure-virtual dispatch (`__cxa_pure_virtual`) means a processor reachable through a port is being destroyed / no longer alive at the time of the dump. For a long-running streaming query that is cancelled or torn down (here the query had been running ~4 minutes and the crash coincides with the server being shut down at the end of the fuzzer run — the client log shows `Connection reset by peer` / `Connection refused` around the same time), the pipeline graph still references a processor whose derived part has already been destructed. This is a **debug-only** path: release builds do not call `dumpPipeline`, so they surface the original exception instead of crashing. It is also **codec-independent** — it reproduces for any `MergeTree` table (`SELECT '...' FROM <mt> STREAM` returns rows on a release build; the crash needs the debug diagnostics + teardown timing). ## Reproduction - Debug build. - `SET enable_streaming_queries = 1;` - A `MergeTree` table `t`. - `SELECT '<const>' FROM t STREAM` while the query is cancelled / times out / the server shuts down mid-execution, so `PipelineExecutor::execute()` throws and reaches the `dumpPipeline()` diagnostics path. ## Notes - `enable_streaming_queries` is an experimental feature (`STREAM` table modifier). - Fix direction: `dumpPipeline`/`printPipeline` should not dereference processors reachable only through ports without a guaranteed lifetime, or the streaming-query teardown must keep the graph's processors alive until the executor stops; alternatively, the diagnostics should tolerate a partially-destroyed graph.

signal.title: [CI crash] Segfault in ContextData destructor during MetricLog flush
signal.text: ### Overview Segfault at address `0x50` (null pointer with offset) during `MetricLog` flush in the `SystemLog` saving thread. The crash occurs during `ContextData::~ContextData` when destroying Context objects held by `InsertDependenciesBuilder`. **CI report**: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=98677&sha=ad456bbcb213b8e58952cf24390b4c6fe282fefb&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_release%29 ### Stack trace ``` sdallocx_default operator delete(void*, unsigned long) DB::ContextData::~ContextData() std::__shared_ptr_pointer<DB::Context*, ...>::__on_zero_shared() std::__hash_table<..., std::shared_ptr<DB::Context const>, ...>::__deallocate_node() DB::InsertDependenciesBuilder::~InsertDependenciesBuilder() DB::QueryPlanResourceHolder::~QueryPlanResourceHolder() DB::QueryPipeline::reset() DB::BlockIO::reset() DB::BlockIO::~BlockIO() DB::SystemLog<DB::MetricLogElement>::flushImpl() DB::SystemLog<DB::MetricLogElement>::savingThreadFunction() ``` ### Analysis - The crash is at address `0x50`, which is a null-like address — a `ContextData` member's internal pointer was corrupted before destruction. - The MetricLog flush thread is likely a victim of heap corruption originating from another source. The code path itself (`SystemLog::flushImpl` → `InterpreterInsertQuery` → `InsertDependenciesBuilder` context lifecycle) appears correct on inspection. - This occurred in the Stress test (arm_release) job, which is a release build without sanitizers. An ASan or TSan reproduction would be needed to identify the actual corruption source. - PR #98677 is CI-only (adds ARM stress tests), so this is a pre-existing bug exposed by new test coverage. - The crash happened ~1.5 hours into the stress test during normal operation (not during shutdown). Only one crash event, no prior fatal errors. - Version: 26.3.1.776, git hash: `92a2b37d5ab51b4d5d0042ea9876727e112727ec`, architecture: aarch64.

signal.title: `IcebergLocalDefinition::object_storage_type` incorrectly set to `azure` instead of `local`
signal.text: _Found via ClickGap automated review. Please close or comment if this is incorrect or needs adjustment._ _Retrospective finding from a historical scan of [PR #68210](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68210) (merged 2024-08-27). Confirmed on current codebase — close with a note if already fixed._ ### Describe what's wrong `icebergLocal` table function throws `BAD_ARGUMENTS: Disk type doesn't match with table engine type storage` when used with a Local object storage disk via `SETTINGS disk = 'local_disk_name'` **Root cause:** StorageObjectStorageDefinitions.h:77 — `IcebergLocalDefinition::object_storage_type = "azure"` is a copy-paste error from `IcebergAzureDefinition`. Should be `"local"` to match `DeltaLakeLocalDefinition` and `IcebergLocalClusterDefinition`. **Why we believe this is a bug:** TableFunctionObjectStorage::getConfiguration (line 108-114) validates that Definition::object_storage_type matches the disk's object storage type. For icebergLocal with a Local disk: Definition::object_storage_type='azure' != 'local', causing the check to fail. **Affected locations:** - `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/StorageObjectStorageDefinitions.h:77` — object_storage_type = "azure" in IcebergLocalDefinition - `src/TableFunctions/TableFunctionObjectStorage.cpp:114` — Validation throws BAD_ARGUMENTS when object_storage_type != "local" **Impact:** Users cannot use `icebergLocal` table function with a Local object storage disk. The `SETTINGS disk = 'local_disk'` feature is completely broken for `icebergLocal`, while it works for `deltaLakeLocal` and `icebergS3`. ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `9821949fd80`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Using clickhouse client to reproduce: -- First verify a Local object storage disk exists: -- SELECT name, object_storage_type FROM system.disks WHERE object_storage_type = 'Local' -- Then run: -- SELECT 1 FROM icebergLocal(path = 'test', SETTINGS disk = '<local_disk_name>') -- Expected: should proceed to check if path exists -- Actual: BAD_ARGUMENTS: Disk type doesn't match with table engine type storage ``` ### Expected behavior ``` Should proceed past disk type validation (and then fail on path not existing or similar) ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Code: 36. DB::Exception: Disk type doesn't match with table engine type storage. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` ### Additional context **Suggested fix:** Change `object_storage_type = "azure"` to `object_storage_type = "local"` in `IcebergLocalDefinition` struct at StorageObjectStorageDefinitions.h:77. **Analysis details:** Confidence HIGH | Severity P1 | Testability: `STATELESS_SQL` Found during automated review of [PR #68210](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68210). --- _ClickGapAI · Confidence: HIGH · Severity: P1 · Finding: `h_pr68210_001`_

signal.title: Add experimental cuckoo_filter and binary_fuse_filter skip indexes
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Related Issue: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101795 (Cuckoo Filter) https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104466 (Binary Fuse Filter) ### Changelog entry: Added experimental `cuckoo_filter` and `binary_fuse_filter` skip index types for MergeTree tables. Both are gated by experimental settings and documented as workload-dependent alternatives to `bloom_filter`, with stateless size-benchmark coverage; the binary-fuse CI benchmark also includes a tiny pruning sanity check. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) --- ## Summary This PR implements and benchmarks two experimental probabilistic filter structures for MergeTree skip indexes: **`cuckoo_filter`** and **`binary_fuse_filter`**. Both structures are based on published research on compact approximate membership filters for large static sets. Benchmark results in the stateless tests show that they are **not general replacements for `bloom_filter`** in ClickHouse's current skip-index model. In particular, at skip-index `GRANULARITY = 1` and a common target FPR such as `0.025`, both filters are often larger than `bloom_filter` because of fixed structural overhead on small per-index-granule key sets. The feature remains experimental and gated. `bloom_filter` remains the recommended default skip index unless workload-specific benchmarks show an advantage for one of these filters. ## Implemented Index Types ### 1. `cuckoo_filter` Based on Fan et al., "Cuckoo Filter: Practically Better Than Bloom" (ACM CoNEXT 2014), with secondary-index motivation from Kipf et al., "Cuckoo Index" (PVLDB 2020). **Parameters:** Single argument — target false positive rate, for example `0.01`. **Experimental setting:** Requires `allow_experimental_cuckoo_filter_index = 1`. ### 2. `binary_fuse_filter` Based on Graf & Lemire, "Binary Fuse Filters: Fast and Smaller Than Xor Filters" (arXiv:2201.01174, 2022). **Parameters:** Single argument — target false positive rate, for example `0.025`. **Experimental setting:** Requires `allow_experimental_binary_fuse_filter_index = 1`. ## Benchmark Results Both filters were evaluated against `bloom_filter` in `04104_cuckoo_filter_benchmark.sql` and `04204_binary_fuse_filter_benchmark.sql`. **Methodology:** 10,000 rows per table, table `index_granularity = 8192`, skip-index `GRANULARITY = 1`, `OPTIMIZE FINAL`, then `sum(secondary_indices_uncompressed_bytes)` from `system.parts`. Each file covers **18 core scenarios**: 6 cardinality regimes × 3 FPR values. `04204` adds representative CI-friendly extensions (lower FPR snapshot, skip-index `GRANULARITY` sensitivity, distribution-sensitive cases, and a tiny pruning sanity check). ### Cuckoo Filter vs Bloom At skip-index `GRANULARITY = 1` and `fpr = 0.025`, `cuckoo_filter` was larger than `bloom_filter` in all six tested cardinality regimes (`04104` reference). | Scenario | FPR | Bloom | Cuckoo | Ratio | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | single value | 0.025 | 2 B | 15 B | **7.5x** | | 1% distinct | 0.025 | 101 B | 139 B | **1.4x** | | 10% distinct | 0.025 | 1,002 B | 2,061 B | **2.1x** | | 50% distinct | 0.025 | 5,002 B | 8,205 B | **1.6x** | | 90% distinct | 0.025 | 9,002 B | 16,397 B | **1.8x** | | all distinct | 0.025 | 10,002 B | 16,397 B | **1.6x** | Observed range at `fpr = 0.025`: **1.4x–7.5x larger than Bloom**. At the lower `fpr = 0.001` (where the requested FPR is rounded up to the nearest supported fingerprint width), `cuckoo_filter` remains larger than `bloom_filter` in every tested cardinality regime as well (`04104` reference): | Scenario | FPR | Bloom | Cuckoo | Ratio | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1% distinct | 0.001 | 189 B | 267 B | **1.4x** | | 10% distinct | 0.001 | 1,877 B | 4,109 B | **2.2x** | | 50% distinct | 0.001 | 9,377 B | 16,397 B | **1.7x** | | 90% distinct | 0.001 | 16,877 B | 32,781 B | **1.9x** | | all distinct | 0.001 | 18,752 B | 32,781 B | **1.7x** | ### Binary Fuse Filter vs Bloom At skip-index `GRANULARITY = 1` and `fpr = 0.025`, `binary_fuse_filter` was also larger than `bloom_filter` in all six core cardinality regimes (`04204` reference). | Scenario | FPR | Bloom | Binary Fuse | Ratio | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | single value | 0.025 | 2 B | 12 B | **6.0x** | | 1% distinct | 0.025 | 101 B | 187 B | **1.9x** | | 10% distinct | 0.025 | 1,002 B | 1,396 B | **1.4x** | | 50% distinct | 0.025 | 5,002 B | 6,293 B | **1.3x** | | 90% distinct | 0.025 | 9,002 B | 11,029 B | **1.2x** | | all distinct | 0.025 | 10,002 B | 12,309 B | **1.2x** | Observed range at `fpr = 0.025`: **1.2x–6.0x larger than Bloom**. However, `binary_fuse_filter` can be smaller in specific FPR regimes where its fingerprint width is favorable. For example, at `fpr = 0.001`: | Scenario | FPR | Bloom | Binary Fuse | Ratio | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1% distinct | 0.001 | 189 B | 187 B | **0.99x** | | 10% distinct | 0.001 | 1,877 B | 1,396 B | **0.74x** | | 50% distinct | 0.001 | 9,377 B | 6,293 B | **0.67x** | | 90% distinct | 0.001 | 16,877 B | 11,029 B | **0.65x** | | all distinct | 0.001 | 18,752 B | 12,309 B | **0.66x** | Additional representative CI-friendly coverage in `04204_binary_fuse_filter_benchmark.sql`: lower-FPR snapshot (`fpr = 0.005`), skip-index `GRANULARITY = 1 / 8 / 64`, distribution-sensitive scenarios, and a tiny hit/miss pruning sanity check. `04104` covers the full 18-scenario size matrix for cuckoo but does not include those extensions. ## Root Cause Analysis The common issue is **structural overhead in small-set regimes**: - **`cuckoo_filter`**: per-index-granule bucket count rounds up to a power of two; fixed overhead from slot structure, load-factor requirements, and fingerprint-width choices cannot amortize well for small distinct-key counts. - **`binary_fuse_filter`**: whole-byte fingerprints and power-of-two segment alignment introduce step changes in size. This can be favorable in some FPR regimes, but unfavorable at common settings such as `fpr = 0.025`. Both structures are designed for larger static sets where structural overhead is easier to amortize. ClickHouse skip indexes often operate on much smaller per-index-granule key sets, so the benefit is workload- and parameter-dependent. ## Why keep this experimental implementation? Although the MergeTree skip-index results are workload-dependent, these implementations provide reusable probabilistic filter structures that may be useful beyond the current skip-index model, for example for runtime filters or future index layouts with larger key sets. The user-facing skip-index integrations remain experimental and gated, and the documentation describes the measured limitations instead of presenting these filters as general `bloom_filter` replacements. ## Test Files - `04077_cuckoo_filter_skip_index.sql` — focused cuckoo predicate coverage vs `bloom_filter`: scalar equality/`!=`/`NOT IN`, scalar `IN` (including a forced miss set), `hasAny`/`hasAll`, tuple expression indexes, and map key paths; EXPLAIN sanity for scalar equality - `04299_binary_fuse_filter_skip_index.sql` — same focused predicate coverage for `binary_fuse_filter` - `04319_experimental_skip_index_json_isnotnull_nested.sql` — JSON path-presence correctness: bare `isNotNull(json.path)` uses the index; nested forms such as `isNotNull(json.path) = 0` do not - `04078_cuckoo_filter_skip_index_bad_args.sql` — cuckoo bad-argument validation, experimental-setting gates, and unchanged-index ALTER behavior - `04205_binary_fuse_filter_bad_args.sql` — same for `binary_fuse_filter` - `04104_cuckoo_filter_benchmark.sql` — full 18-scenario Cuckoo vs Bloom size benchmark (`04104` reference) - `04204_binary_fuse_filter_benchmark.sql` — 18 core scenarios plus representative CI-friendly extensions for Binary Fuse vs Bloom - `04103_cuckoo_filter_vs_bloom_filter_equivalence.sql` — PREWHERE scalar-equality count equivalence vs `bloom_filter` - `04203_binary_fuse_filter_vs_bloom_filter_equivalence.sql` — same for `binary_fuse_filter` Both benchmark files use the same core methodology: same schema/data pattern, `OPTIMIZE FINAL`, then reading `secondary_indices_uncompressed_bytes` from `system.parts`. ## Predicates Covered The implemented index-condition paths follow existing `bloom_filter` skip-index semantics **where applicable**, while unsafe or unsupported forms fall back conservatively to avoid false negatives. Covered paths exercised by the stateless tests include: - scalar equality (`=`) - scalar `IN` (including a forced miss set in `04077` / `04299`) - array predicates `hasAny` and `hasAll` - tuple expression indexes (`x = … AND y = …` on a tuple index) - map key access paths (`m['key'] = …` with a `mapKeys(m)` index) - bare JSON path-presence checks such as `isNotNull(json.path)` (`04319`) Not claimed as index-backed in tests: - nested boolean forms such as `isNotNull(json.path) = 0` - negation / inversion paths such as `!=`, `NOT IN` — compared against `bloom_filter` for result parity, but not forced through the skip index More complex boolean forms should fall back to normal scanning rather than being forced through the skip index. ## Example Usage ```sql SET allow_experimental_cuckoo_filter_index = 1; SET allow_experimental_binary_fuse_filter_index = 1; CREATE TABLE t ( k UInt64, INDEX idx_cuckoo k TYPE cuckoo_filter(0.01) GRANULARITY 1, INDEX idx_bfuse k TYPE binary_fuse_filter(0.025) GRANULARITY 1 ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k;

signal.title: Bound the waits in 02932_refreshable_materialized_views_1 and report refresh state on expiry
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105987 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105987 Requested by @ alexey-milovidov in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105987#issuecomment-5302349211, after a private-sync run of `Stateless tests (amd_asan_ubsan, distributed cache, meta in keeper, s3 storage, parallel, 2/2)` hung in this test with the active query `select * from rmv_a order by x`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description **The problem.** Every wait in this test is an unbounded loop with no deadline and no diagnostic, and some predicates can never become true: the first waits for a refresh to succeed, but with `refresh every 2 second` a failing refresh retries forever, so the predicate never holds and the `exception` column that says why is never read. The test just times out, naming nothing. `-- $LINENO` was also single-quoted at two of the three sites emitting `select * from rmv_a order by x`, and the third had no marker, so the one query a report can quote was untraceable. **The change.** One `wait_for` helper for all ten client-side waits and the unguarded read. Each poll is capped by the budget remaining, a failing client fails the wait rather than being retried as a mismatch, and on expiry the test prints the awaited query, expected and actual values, why the wait expired and `system.view_refreshes` including `exception`, then exits 1. All three `order by x` sites now carry a line number. I bound every wait, not just the two loops I first offered on that thread: the observed hangs pin lines 42, 91 and 145. One wait costs at most 30s (20s polling, then SIGKILL grace and the bounded dump), inside the 60s Fast test cap, against a slowest measured wait of 2.65s on ASAN. It bounds one wait, not the script, since the harness timer is per-test. `SYSTEM WAIT VIEW` is left alone: `RefreshTask::wait` has no deadline and no cancellation check, so bounding it client-side would park a server thread. **Validation.** With a failing refresh armed, the test previously spun silently until killed; it now reports in 20s with the pinned line and the exception. Passing-path stdout is byte-identical to the unchanged `.reference`; 50/50 runs pass on debug and ASAN.

signal.title: Retry transient GitHub errors in the `good-prs` skill
signal.text: Make the `good-prs` skill survive transient GitHub API errors. A full report makes roughly two GraphQL calls per pull request — several hundred per run — so hitting at least one transient GitHub failure is close to certain. The script aborted the whole run on the first one, which threw away all the API quota already spent. Three consecutive runs died this way: on `HTTP 503`, on `API rate limit already exceeded`, and on `HTTP 504`. This adds a shared `gh_retry` wrapper used by both per-pull-request helpers: - Transient failures (`HTTP 408`, `429`, any `5xx`, gateway timeouts, connection resets, TLS handshake errors) are retried with exponential backoff. - Secondary rate limits back off more aggressively. - A primary rate-limit rejection waits for the hourly window to reset, using the unmetered `rate_limit` endpoint, capped so a run always terminates. The fail-loud design is preserved. An error that will never fix itself (auth, unknown pull request, bad flag) still aborts on the first attempt, and a transient error that outlives every retry still aborts — in both cases with the original `gh` diagnostic. A row is never silently dropped from the report. Two tests were added to `test.sh`: a pull request whose checks fail twice with `HTTP 503` is retried and still rendered (exactly three calls), and a permanent error is attempted exactly once. `GH_RETRIES` and `GH_RETRY_DELAY` make the suite exercise the retry path without sleeping. All tests pass. This only touches `.claude/skills/good-prs/`, a developer-facing helper script; there is no change to ClickHouse itself. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1472` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Populate the submodule working trees in parallel in the build job
signal.text: The build job populated the submodule working trees with a bare `git submodule update` on a submodule cache hit, which walks the submodules one at a time on a single core. In `Build (arm_tidy)` on master that step takes 39 s at ~3% CPU of a 32-core `m8g.8xlarge` — an otherwise idle machine waiting on one `git` process, right before the equally single-threaded cmake configuration and long before `ninja` can saturate the box. The first 253 s of that job produce no compilation at all; this is one of the three serial phases in it. Report the numbers come from: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=03ad5002ff1501ceb5d584b6d0bb028674b276e7&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Build%20%28arm_tidy%29 Fan the checkouts out over the idle cores instead, the same way the cache-miss branch right below it (`contrib/update-submodules.sh --max-procs 10`) and `ci/jobs/fast_test.py` already do: feed the submodule paths from `.gitmodules` to `xargs --max-procs`. The submodule list is read with `get_output_or_raise` and asserted non-empty, so failing to enumerate `.gitmodules` fails the step rather than silently checking out nothing — `xargs --no-run-if-empty` would otherwise exit 0 on an empty pipeline. Measured on a synthetic superproject with 40 submodules and a populated `.git/modules` (the CI cache-hit state): **2.13 s serial vs 0.16 s** with `--max-procs=20`, both producing an identical working tree and a clean `git status`. In CI the win is bounded by the largest submodule rather than by the sum of all of them, so expect the step to shrink to roughly the cost of `contrib/llvm-project` alone; the `Checkout Submodules` duration in this PR's build reports against 39 s on master is the real measurement. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1473` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Iceberg: propagate table UUID from REST catalog to avoid metadata cac…
signal.text: REST catalog inline responses already contain the table UUID and metadata location. Propagate the UUID through DataLakeSpecificProperties -> StorageObjectStorageConfiguration.catalog_uuid_hint -> initializePersistentTableComponents so the metadata cache is checked before fetching metadata.json from network storage. ### Performance mechanism **Before:** On first table initialization, `getMetadataJSONObject` is called without a known UUID. The cache probe is skipped (`table_uuid == nullopt`), so metadata.json is always fetched from remote storage as a cold read. Even if the same table is initialized again later, the cache was never populated on the first pass. **After:** The REST catalog provides the table UUID upfront via `catalog_uuid_hint`. `getMetadataJSONObject` probes the cache with `uuid:path` key before doing any remote I/O. If the metadata was previously cached (e.g., by a prior query that retroactively populated it), the cold read is eliminated entirely. If not, the cold read still happens but the result is cached with the correct UUID for future lookups. **Impact:** Deterministic reduction in remote `metadata.json` fetches for REST catalog tables. Each avoided fetch saves one round-trip to S3/GCS/ABFS plus deserialization overhead. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve Iceberg catalog metadata caching by using table UUID from catalog responses to warm the metadata cache, avoiding a redundant remote metadata.json read on table initialization. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes Improve Iceberg catalog metadata caching. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Medium risk because it changes Iceberg metadata cache key composition and the metadata-loading path to use a new UUID hint, which could affect cache hit rates or correctness if UUIDs/paths are inconsistent. > > **Overview** > **Improves Iceberg REST catalog metadata caching** by propagating the table UUID from REST inline responses through `DataLakeSpecificProperties` into `StorageObjectStorageConfiguration` as `catalog_uuid_hint`, so the first metadata fetch can probe the metadata cache before doing extra remote IO. > > Updates metadata loading to accept an optional known UUID, capture raw metadata JSON for reuse, and retroactively populate the cache once the real UUID is discovered. Also fixes potential cache-key collisions by changing `IcebergMetadataFilesCache::getKey` to use a `uuid:path` delimiter, and adds gtest coverage for key uniqueness and cache hit/miss behavior. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 2e7400b8dc007641c702d41b3fd6cafdc10eb823. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: Fix signed integer overflow reading Iceberg decimal bounds
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114929 Decoding a `Decimal` column bound from an Iceberg manifest ran in `int64_t` regardless of how wide the bound was, in `deserializeFieldFromBinaryRepr` (`src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/ManifestFileIterator.cpp`). Three steps overflow: * the big-endian accumulation `unscaled_value = (unscaled_value << 8) | byte`, once the bound is more than eight bytes wide; * the sign extension `sign_extension <<= (str.size() * 8)`, which shifts by 64 or more for a bound of eight bytes or more; * the scaler loop `scaler *= 10`, which computes `10^scale` and leaves `int64_t` at scale 19. A `Decimal(38, 30)` column reaches all three: its bounds are 14 bytes wide. Bounds are parsed for every column of a manifest entry, so any query with a filter is enough and the filter does not have to touch the decimal column. A build with the undefined behaviour sanitizer aborts, as reported in the issue. Only `Decimal32` and `Decimal64` bounds are ever turned into a `Field` (everything else already returned `std::nullopt` a few lines below), and both fit into `Int64`. So the fix decodes exactly those and rejects anything wider before the arithmetic, which keeps the observable behaviour: a bound that used to be computed and then discarded is now not computed at all. Two smaller defects in the same expression are fixed along the way: * the sign extension is skipped when the value already fills all 64 bits. Previously it shifted an `int64_t` by 64, which is undefined; on the usual targets the shift count is taken modulo 64, so `-1` was left unchanged and OR-ing it in turned every eight-byte negative bound into `-1`. That is a wrong bound, not just undefined behaviour, and a wrong bound prunes files that do contain matching rows. * the widening `unscaled_value += scaler` and the narrowing to `Int32` are range checked. The bound comes from the manifest and is not validated against the declared precision, so a malformed manifest could otherwise wrap it into a bogus bound. ### Testing `tests/queries/0_stateless/04907_iceberg_decimal_bounds_overflow.sh` reads a `Decimal(38, 30)` Iceberg table with a filter. The table is the one attached to the issue, produced by Spark, repacked without the Spark checksum files and embedded as base64: ClickHouse cannot write a decimal column to Iceberg (`Unsupported type for iceberg Decimal(38, 30)`), so the test cannot build it itself. Because the overflowed bound was discarded anyway, the query results are the same before and after this change; the test fails before the fix only under the undefined behaviour sanitizer, and pins the results everywhere else. I verified the reproducer and the resulting query output against the official master build `26.8.1.1463`; I have not built this branch locally, so the compile and the sanitizer runs are left to CI. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes reading Iceberg tables whose manifests carry `Decimal` column bounds that do not fit into 64 bits, such as those of a `Decimal(38, 30)` column. Such a bound is now ignored instead of being decoded into a meaningless value, and a negative bound stored in eight bytes is no longer read as `-1`, which could skip files that do contain matching rows.

signal.title: Recover a dead py4j gateway in ResilientSparkSession
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112175 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112175 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Requested on #112175 as a separate PR. Every test in a spark-dependent integration module can error at fixture setup with `Py4JError: SparkConf does not exist in the JVM`, losing the module's coverage and failing the job. Seen on `Integration tests (amd_asan_ubsan, db disk, old analyzer, 5/6)`, 6 of 805 ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112175&sha=5af55d5ac9dbe8d076e99c2022053c89a17accd9&name_0=BackportPR&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%2C%20db%20disk%2C%20old%20analyzer%2C%205%2F6%29)). CIDB, 21 days: 11 rows, that shard only, none on master. **Root cause.** The message is not a missing class: py4j's `GatewayClient.send_command` swallows a `Py4JNetworkError` and returns `proto.ERROR`, which `JVMView.__getattr__` re-labels (`java_gateway.py:1722-1725`): the gateway socket is dead. pyspark caches that socket in class state and relaunches the JVM only `if not SparkContext._gateway` (3.5.5 `context.py:435-437`). Neither `stop()` clears it, so once the JVM dies no relaunch happens in that process, and xdist reuses it across modules. The wrapper could not recover either: `_is_alive` guards an already-built wrapper, but the failure is in `__init__`. **Change.** Probe the cached gateway before building a session and discard it only when it stops answering. The probe is conditional: the JVM survives `stop()` (the failing job's log shows it answering 10 minutes later), so an unconditional reset would orphan a live JVM per module. `_restart()` shares the path, so restarting on a live gateway still reuses the JVM. It recovers from the death, not prevents it; the trigger is not recoverable from the artifacts. Also drops a dead `builder._options` line. **Validation.** Reproduced in the runner image on the CI-pinned pyspark, with the message and frame above. The new test fails on pristine master at its recovery arm and passes with the fix, 10/10 stable; mutants confirm the arms are live. It reports the relabel as `SparkSession$`, not `SparkConf`: `getOrCreate` asks for that name first while `_instantiatedSession` is set (`session.py:502`). Out of scope: `test_sts.py:42` and `test_storage_delta_shuffles/test.py:121` bypass the wrapper, and `retry_ok` is consumed only under LLVM coverage. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.841` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.4.45` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: toUnixTimestamp() in ORDER BY silently loses primary-key pruning starting in 26.7 (regression from 26.6)
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour For a MergeTree table whose sorting key includes `toUnixTimestamp(<DateTime64 column>)`, a plain range filter on the raw column (e.g. `WHERE event_ts >= '2026-06-15'`, no cast, no function wrapper) uses the primary key to prune granules on ClickHouse `26.4` through `26.6`. Starting with the first `26.7` release, the identical query against the identical table and data no longer prunes via the primary key at all. `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` shows `PrimaryKey Condition: true`, meaning every granule in the matched parts is read. This persists through the current 26.8 master build. Partition-level (Min-Max) pruning is unaffected in all versions; only the primary-key contribution is lost starting in 26.7. No exception is thrown and no incorrect results are returned. This is a silent loss of an optimization, not a correctness bug. ORDER BY keys using `toDate(<col>)` or `toStartOfHour(<col>)` on the same table/data do not show this regression — they continue to prune correctly on every version we tested, `26.4` through `26.8`. The issue appears specific to `toUnixTimestamp()`. I also checked the new `use_partition_minmax_for_primary_key_pruning` setting (present in `26.8`, absent in `26.5`) as a possible cause, since its description sounded related. Toggling it on/off made no difference to the broken query, so it does not appear to be the cause. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Not affected: `26.4.5.143, 26.5.6.113, 26.6.1.1193, 26.6.2.160` Affected (regression introduced here): `26.7.1.1315` (first `26.7` release) — confirmed present through `26.7.3.19` and the current `26.8` master build (`26.8.1.1181, built ~2026-08-11`) The break happens between the `26.6` branch cut and the first `26.7` release. ### How to reproduce How to reproduce - Interface: clickhouse local (also reproduces in clickhouse-server; tested via official release binaries downloaded from GitHub Releases for each version, arm64) - Non-default settings: index_granularity = 128 on the table (lowered only so a 100k-row table produces enough granules to observe pruning; not related to the bug) - Minimal repro (single-column ORDER BY, no composite key needed) `CREATE TABLE t (id UInt8, ts DateTime64(3)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY toUnixTimestamp(ts); INSERT INTO t SELECT number, now() - toIntervalDay(180) + toIntervalMinute(number) FROM numbers(1000000); EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT count() FROM t WHERE ts >= now() - toIntervalDay(30);` - Full repro matching the original investigation (composite key, closer to a real schema): `CREATE TABLE events_base ( platform String, application String, event_name String, event_ts DateTime64(3, 'UTC'), user_id String ) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO events_base SELECT ['ios','android','web'][1 + rand() % 3] AS platform, ['checkout','billing','onboarding'][1 + rand() % 3] AS application, ['click','view','purchase','error'][1 + rand() % 4] AS event_name, toDateTime64('2026-03-01 00:00:00', 3, 'UTC') + toIntervalSecond(rand() % 14083200) AS event_ts, toString(rand()) AS user_id FROM numbers(100000); CREATE TABLE events_tounix ( platform LowCardinality(String), application LowCardinality(String), event_name LowCardinality(String), event_ts DateTime64(3, 'UTC'), user_id String ) ENGINE = MergeTree() PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(event_ts) ORDER BY (platform, application, event_name, toUnixTimestamp(event_ts)) SETTINGS index_granularity = 128; INSERT INTO events_tounix SELECT * FROM events_base; EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT sum(length(user_id)) FROM events_tounix WHERE event_ts >= '2026-06-15';` On 26.4, 26.5, and 26.6, the PrimaryKey block of the EXPLAIN output is: `PrimaryKey Keys: toUnixTimestamp(event_ts) Condition: (toUnixTimestamp(event_ts) in [1781481600, +Inf)) Parts: 3/3 Granules: 283/340` On 26.7.1.1315 and every version since, the same query against the same table gives: `PrimaryKey Condition: true Parts: 3/3 Granules: 340/340` ### Error message and/or stacktrace Expected performance: `toUnixTimestamp(event_ts)` should continue to be usable by the primary key for range pruning when the query filters on the raw `event_ts` column, exactly as it did on 26.4–26.6 and as demonstrated in ClickHouse's own docs example at https://clickhouse.com/docs/knowledgebase/why_is_my_primary_key_not_used (which uses `ORDER BY (code, toUnixTimestamp(timestamp))` as its worked example). On affected versions, queries that previously read a few hundred granules out of many thousand now read every granule in the matched parts, which will show up as a significant, silent latency/cost regression for anyone using this documented pattern. ### Related issues and pull requests Related: - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97746 - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/95125 - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/docs/knowledgebase/why_is_my_primary_key_not_used (Not confirmed as the same root cause, but same subsystem/time window: PR #97746, merged Feb 25 2026 into 26.3.1.43+, reworked KeyCondition.cpp's handling of monotonic-function atoms for DateTime64 columns. In review, @nihalzp explicitly flagged toUnixTimestamp() as having a known, deliberately-deferred issue — a DECIMAL_OVERFLOW on out-of-range values used as a PARTITION BY key — left for a follow-up PR. That's a different symptom (partition key, thrown exception) from this regression (ORDER BY key, silent loss of pruning, no exception), but it's the same function and the same code path, so it may be relevant context for whoever picks this up.) ### Additional context The issue might surface if we run a diff on `src/Storages/MergeTree/KeyCondition.cpp` between the v26.6.1.1193-stable and v26.7.1.1315-stable tags, since the regression is present in the very first 26.7 release.

signal.title: Fix SimpleAggregateFunction Native header dropping an explicit nested aggregate version
signal.text: Fix SimpleAggregateFunction Native header dropping an explicit nested aggregate version Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes reading a `SimpleAggregateFunction` column whose value type holds an `AggregateFunction` declared with an explicit version `0`, such as `SimpleAggregateFunction(anyLast, AggregateFunction(0, sumMap, Array(UInt64), Array(Decimal32(2))))`. The `Native` type header omitted that version, so a reader re-parsing the announced type saw the function's default instead and could not read the data back: `SELECT` failed with `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` on `StripeLog`, and the column could not be reloaded by `Set`/`Join`, restored from a `Memory` backup, or read from a `Native` file, which was left empty. ### Description **Root cause.** `SimpleAggregateFunction(f, T)` is stored as the storage type `T` plus a custom name caching its own copy of `T`. Version `0` is never printed, so a leaf declared `AggregateFunction(0, ...)` prints a versionless spelling, and the alias rebuilds its value type by parsing that spelling back, where the missing token reads as the function's default. The version walker leaves an explicit version alone, so nothing corrects it: the header announces the default over a version-`0` payload, and for `sumMap` the two versions differ in width, so the reader over-consumes. **The change** stays at the transport boundary. `NativeWriter::write` renders the header from both type trees: syntax from the cached side, which alone remembers spellings such as `Nested(...)`, and versions from the live side. One rendering feeds the stream and index headers so they cannot drift apart. `getName()`, the type factory, the version walker and `NativeReader` are untouched, so `CREATE`, `ATTACH` and on-disk data are unchanged. **Scope after #112052.** That PR made the walker re-version the alias customization, which covers a leaf pinning no version: it is stored with the default spelled out, so header and payload already agree. What remains, and what this PR fixes, is the explicit version-`0` declaration. Verified against a master build carrying #112052 and none of this change: that case fails `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` there and round trips here. The test marks its regression arms; the wrapper and engine cases stay as round-trip coverage. **Known adjacent gap.** The same shape below a `Variant` fails identically on plain master. Covering it means mirroring the walker's discriminator-order and refuse-on-collapse semantics for an experimental type, which is a separate change; `NativeFormat.mdx` records the behaviour.

signal.title: Fix lazy materialization OOB and a Merge LOGICAL_ERROR from unused text index virtual columns
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111422 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix an out-of-bounds read (release) / logical error (debug) in the lazy materialization optimization, and a logical error in `Pipe::unitePipes` for `Merge` tables, when the direct-read-from-text-index optimization leaves an unused index virtual column in the read header of a `MergeTree` table with multiple `text` indexes. ### Description Closes #111422. `TextIndexDAGReplacer::replace` rewrites text-search predicates into `__text_index_*` virtual columns, recording one per rewritten node, then runs `removeUnusedActions()`. When the rewrite keeps a different index's virtual column (or the original expression), the first virtual's input becomes unreferenced, but `result.added_columns` was not re-filtered, so `createReadTasksForTextIndex` still appended that orphaned column to the `ReadFromMergeTree` output header. `removed_columns` was already reconciled against the surviving inputs; `added_columns` was not, and that asymmetry is the bug. The fix drops from `added_columns` any virtual column whose input did not survive, reusing the surviving-inputs set already computed for `removed_columns`. The reading step's header then matches what the plan consumes, and a redundant index read goes away. One orphaned column causes two user-visible failures, both fixed: 1. **Lazy materialization out-of-bounds read** (the reported issue). `optimizeLazyMaterialization2` builds its `required_columns` mask positionally from the input headers above the reading step, which never contain a read-only virtual column. The mask ends up shorter than that step's header and the pass indexes a `std::vector<bool>` past its end: out-of-bounds read in release, `cols.size() == required_columns.size()` assertion in debug. 2. **`Merge` table logical error.** With `text` indexes on both `mapKeys(map)` and `mapValues(map)`, the `mapKeys` virtual wins the predicate and the `mapValues` one is left registered but unreferenced. Under `SELECT count()` nothing else is read, so the dead virtual becomes the indexed child's only output column while a non-indexed sibling's header stays empty. `Pipe::getCommonHeader` picks the first non-empty header and `unitePipes` asserts the empty sibling against it: `Block structure mismatch in Pipe::unitePipes stream`, a server abort in debug and sanitizer builds. `02346_text_index_bug111422` covers the first shape. The new `04563_text_index_merge_heterogeneous_children` covers the second, which the first cannot reach (no `merge()`, no bare `count()`). It pins the two runner-randomized settings it depends on per setting, not with a blanket tag. <details> <summary>Validation of the new test</summary> Debug build of this branch, memory-capped server, per-slot ports. | arm | build id | result | |---|---|---| | master `f9801d5649` (no fix) | `c29b56ab…` | aborts: `Block structure mismatch in Pipe::unitePipes stream: different number of columns` (`Block.cpp:308` <- `Pipe.cpp:316` <- `QueryPipelineBuilder.cpp:263`) | | this branch, reconciliation loop removed | `fd96fd28…` | aborts: `Column __text_index_idx_map_values_equals_… already added for reading` (`ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4765`); via the test runner: `ClickHouse server died` | | this branch, unmodified | `a0a422da…` | passes byte-for-byte, and 50/50 randomized runs | The pre-fix signature differs between the two bases because this branch's merge-base predates the `already_has_direct_read` re-entry gate (`optimizeDirectReadFromTextIndex.cpp`, `6253632d8da4`): without that gate the pass visits the step twice and the same over-registration trips the duplicate guard before a pipe is united. Same defect, two assertions. Both pinned settings were verified load-bearing and effective: with the pins removed, a client injecting `query_plan_direct_read_from_text_index=0` or `query_plan_text_index_add_hint=0` turns the `EXPLAIN` assertion vacuous (`1 0` -> `0 0`); with the pins present the test matches the reference under either injection and under both together. Full `text_index` suite on this branch, base vs with the new test: 157 -> 158 tests, 7 -> 6 failures, **zero new failures**. All shared failures are environmental on a bare slot server (missing stateful `test.hits` dataset, no `localhost:9000`, and four debug-build 600s timeouts). </details>

signal.title: Support specifying or auto-assigning Parquet field_ids for output columns
signal.text: ### What this PR does Two related knobs for writing Parquet files with column `field_id` metadata — needed for Apache Iceberg compatibility, which identifies columns by `field_id` rather than by name. Both knobs can be used independently or together. #### 1. Explicit per-column overrides New setting `output_format_parquet_column_field_ids : Map(String, Int32)`. ```sql SET output_format_parquet_column_field_ids = '{"col_a": 10, "col_b": 20, "col_c": 30}'; INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('data.parquet') SELECT 1::UInt32 AS col_a, 'x'::String AS col_b, 42::Int64 AS col_c; ``` Each output column gets the id specified in the map. The map must cover every output column (unless auto-assign below is enabled to fill the gaps), and ids must be unique; violations raise `BAD_ARGUMENTS` with specific messages. #### 2. Auto-assign (Iceberg writer convention) New setting `output_format_parquet_auto_assign_field_ids : Bool`, default `false`. When enabled, every output column is assigned a unique sequential `field_id` starting at `1`, matching the convention used by Apache Iceberg writers. ```sql SET output_format_parquet_auto_assign_field_ids = 1; INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('iceberg.parquet') SELECT 1 AS a, 'x' AS b, 42 AS c; -- a -> 1, b -> 2, c -> 3 ``` #### 3. Mixed mode The two settings compose: override-map entries win for the columns they mention; auto-assign fills the remaining columns with the smallest unused positive ids. ```sql SET output_format_parquet_auto_assign_field_ids = 1, output_format_parquet_column_field_ids = '{"b": 1}'; INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('mixed.parquet') SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS b, 3 AS c; -- b -> 1 (override), a -> 2, c -> 3 (auto-assign skipping 1) ``` ### Implementation - `src/Core/FormatFactorySettings.h` — declare both settings. - `src/Formats/FormatSettings.h` — carry a `std::vector<std::pair<String, Int32>>` of overrides and the `auto_assign_field_ids` bool; no string parsing on the hot path. - `src/Formats/FormatFactory.cpp` — convert the `Map` setting into the pair vector, with structural validation (tuple shape, string keys, integer values in `Int32` range). - `src/Processors/Formats/Impl/ParquetBlockOutputFormat.cpp` — `buildColumnFieldIds()` resolves overrides against the actual output header, auto-assigns unused ids if the flag is on, and rejects unknown columns, duplicate ids, and non-covering overrides. ### Test `tests/queries/0_stateless/04321_parquet_column_field_ids.sh` writes Parquet files with `clickhouse-local`, reads the `field_id` metadata back with `pyarrow`, and covers: - Explicit per-column overrides. - Auto-assign only. - Mixed override + auto-assign. - Writing with neither setting (no `field_id`s, unchanged behavior). - Nested types: auto-assign and dotted-path overrides for `Array.element`, `Tuple` subfields, and `Map.key`/`Map.value`. - Geo columns written as WKB under GeoParquet (the `Point`/`Array`/`Tuple` shape collapses to a single top-level field). - Error cases: unknown column, non-covering map (top-level and nested), duplicate id, non-integer value, negative id, and a dotted top-level name colliding with a nested path (in both auto-assign and override modes). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58753 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry: Added `output_format_parquet_column_field_ids` (`Map(String, Int32)`) to set explicit Parquet `field_id` overrides per column and `output_format_parquet_auto_assign_field_ids` (`Bool`) to auto-assign sequential `field_id`s to every output column, matching the Apache Iceberg writer convention. The two settings can be combined. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches the Parquet write path and schema generation to emit `field_id` metadata, which could affect interoperability and schema expectations; defaults are preserved unless new settings are enabled. > > **Overview** > Adds two new Parquet output settings to control column `field_id` metadata for Iceberg compatibility: `output_format_parquet_column_field_ids` (explicit per-column overrides) and `output_format_parquet_auto_assign_field_ids` (sequential auto-assignment starting at 1). > > `FormatFactory` now parses/validates the `Map` setting into typed overrides up-front, while `ParquetBlockOutputFormat` resolves the final `field_id` mapping (including error checks for unknown columns, duplicates, negative ids, and incomplete coverage when auto-assign is off) and explicitly rejects using these settings when a datalake writer provides its own column-id mapping. > > Documentation and a new stateless test are added to verify correct `field_id` emission via `pyarrow` and expected failure modes. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit ce5f371493174b5b0ee58307dfc05f5df32af0b2. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
