signal.title: Fix data race on DataTypeAggregateFunction version during Native serialization
signal.text: Related: found by the `arm_tsan` and `azure, amd_tsan` Stress tests (STID 3977-4818, ThreadSanitizer data race). No existing issue. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/94859 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not for changelog. ### Description A single `DataTypeAggregateFunction` instance is shared across query result blocks: it lives once in the table's column description and is aliased by shallow column copies. `NativeWriter`/`NativeReader` called `setVersionToAggregateFunctions`, which walked to the leaf type and wrote its `mutable version` field in place. Two concurrent `Native` serializations of the same aggregate-function-typed column then raced on that field, and the version written for one old connection stayed on the shared type, so every later query read the states at that version - for `sumMap` over `Decimal32` that returns wrong values. Reports: * https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109496&sha=62eeb400eafe86cedff9b5a4e9a36aa722633cda&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 * https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=b59441bd06c2fcb6b103a30874528cc398afc723&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28azure%2C%20amd_tsan%29 **That fix has since landed on `master`** through #94859 and #112052: `setVersionToAggregateFunctions` now replaces every versioned nested type instead of mutating it, and `replaceNestedSimpleTypes` carries the custom names (`Nested`, `SimpleAggregateFunction`) over the rebuild. This branch is therefore resolved in favour of that implementation, and what it added on top of it - an `IDataType::transformChildren` override per container type, and the `unique_ptr` to `shared_ptr` switch of `DataTypeCustomNamePtr` - is dropped as duplicate machinery. What remains here is what `master` does not have, and it keeps this PR's intent - the race cannot come back, because the version can no longer be assigned in place at all: * `DataTypeAggregateFunction::setVersion` and `updateVersionFromRevision` are removed, and `version` is no longer `mutable`. Both mutators were left without callers by the rewrite on `master`; the version is now set only at construction (parsed from AST, decoded from the binary type encoding, or chosen by `setVersionToAggregateFunctions`, which builds a new type). * Unit and functional coverage of the behaviour, which `master` has only indirectly. ### Testing * `gtest_aggregate_function_version_race` (14 tests) pins the type-level behaviour: the shared type object is not mutated; a wrapper is rebuilt only when a leaf was actually replaced; the `Point`, `Nested` and `SimpleAggregateFunction` custom names survive, including a `Tuple`-backed `SimpleAggregateFunction`; a `Variant` keeps its discriminator order and throws when two alternatives would collapse; a `JSON` typed path keeps the version spelled in its own type name; and an 8-thread x 2000-iteration stress over one shared type object is race-free. * `04612_aggregate_function_version_custom_type_names` round-trips `Nested`, `SimpleAggregateFunction` and a wrapper-named type through `Native` (which assigns the version in the writer and again in the reader) and through `DETACH`/`ATTACH`, and checks that a deeply nested `Nested` stays linear in the nesting depth. * `04613_aggregate_function_version_not_sticky` asks for a `Native` response at a revision below the one that introduced versioning and then checks the column again, so a version pinned for that one response would be visible both in the values read back (`sumMap` over `Decimal32`) and in `system.columns`. The revision is pinned explicitly and the type name the response carries is asserted, so the test cannot pass without that path having run.

signal.title: Follow-ups for CREATE HANDLER: parse limits of the stored query, docs, refactoring
signal.text: Follow-ups from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106231 (`CREATE HANDLER`). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106231 **Requested in review of #106231:** - The two predicates over `IAST::QueryKind` that describe the `readonly` mode - whether a query of that kind is rejected under it, and whether `readonly = 2` still lets it produce side effects - moved out of `SQLDefinedHandlerFromAST` into `Interpreters/QueryKindUnderReadonly.h`; `queryKindRequiresMutatingMethod` is renamed to `isQueryKindRejectedUnderReadonly` after the property it reports. The handler code keeps the statement-level refinements and the HTTP-method fences. - `currentHandler` and `currentRequestURL` were registered with `IntroducedIn` 26.6 (the development version when they were written); they are released in 26.8. **The one unresolved review finding:** a request could still lower the parse limits of a handler's query. `HTTPHandler::processQuery` relaxed `max_parser_depth` / `max_parser_backtracks` *before* applying the settings the request supplies, and a request names settings freely - so `GET /h?max_parser_depth=1` put the caller's value back and broke a handler the server itself had accepted. The relaxation now happens after the request settings. `max_query_size` had the same hole and did not even need a hostile request: a stored query longer than its default value is creatable and reloadable (both parse without a size limit) but failed on every invocation; it is now raised to fit the query text - not disabled, because `executeQuery` also uses `max_query_size` to decide how much of the request stream to read ahead in search of the query text, where `0` would make it read a single byte. New tests `04897_handler_request_parser_limits` and `04898_handler_large_query_invocation`, both verified to fail without the fix. **Documentation:** the `CREATE HANDLER` page was written into `docs/en/sql-reference/statements/create/handler.md` - a path in the legacy Docusaurus tree that `9440ca729a3` had already removed - so the only documentation of `CREATE HANDLER` / `ALTER HANDLER` / `DROP HANDLER` was published nowhere. It moves to `docs/reference/statements/create/handler.mdx`, with the frontmatter and internal links converted to that tree's conventions and the page registered in `docs/reference/navigation.json`. `docs/en/operations/system-tables/handlers.md` was a leftover copy of the generated `docs/reference/system-tables/handlers.mdx` whose hand-written `SHOW HANDLERS` / secret-masking paragraph had been lost; that paragraph is restored and the legacy copy deleted. The statement is now cross-referenced from the HTTP interface page, the `DROP` page and the `ALTER` overview, and the anchored (`RE2::FullMatch`) semantics of `URL REGEXP` are documented. Verified locally: all 30 SQL-defined-handler stateless tests pass against a server built from this branch (the 31st match of the `handler` filter, `03354_tcp_handler_async_insert_bug`, is unrelated and needs a writable `/var/lib/clickhouse/user_files`), and `04844_handler_deep_query_invocation` still passes without the fix, confirming it covered only the session-level limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed HTTP handler invocation so request-level `max_parser_depth`, `max_parser_backtracks`, and `max_query_size` no longer break stored handler queries, and published the `CREATE HANDLER`, `ALTER HANDLER`, and `DROP HANDLER` documentation.

signal.title: Fix `bloom_filter` index skipping granules for a `FixedString` constant
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112693 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `hasAny`, `hasAll`, `has`, `indexOf`, `mapContainsKey`, `mapContainsValue` and `mapContains` returning too few rows, or failing with `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE`, when a `bloom_filter` index is queried with a `FixedString` constant. The index hashed the padded form of the constant while the function compares the unpadded one, so a matching granule was skipped. ### Description A `bloom_filter` skip index silently returns too few rows when the constant is a `FixedString`, and in four cases raises `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE` on a query that succeeds without the index: ```sql CREATE TABLE k (id UInt64, v Array(String), INDEX idx v TYPE bloom_filter GRANULARITY 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id SETTINGS index_granularity = 1; INSERT INTO k VALUES (0,['V0']),(1,['V0\0']),(2,['X']); SELECT count() FROM k WHERE hasAny(v, [toFixedString('V0',3)]); -- 0, wrong SELECT count() FROM k WHERE hasAny(v, [toFixedString('V0',3)]) SETTINGS use_skip_indexes=0; -- 1 ``` Root cause: the array-search functions coerce the constant with CAST before comparing it to the elements (`hasAny`/`hasAll`, and `has`/`indexOf` over a `FixedString` element, cast both sides to the least supertype; `has`/`indexOf` over a `LowCardinality` element cast the constant straight to the dictionary type), and a CAST of `FixedString` to `String` strips the trailing zero padding. The index instead converted the constant with `convertFieldToType`, which keeps the padding, so it hashed a value the function never compares and pruned granules that match. The error cases are the same cause: an oversized `Field` passed through unchanged and reached a column `insert` during index analysis. The fix replicates the coercion at the `Field` level, which is exact because the string casts involved are fully predictable: strip the padding of a `FixedString` constant, re-pad it to the width of the element type (the stored form of every element the function can match), and decline the index when the constant has no stored representation, so a runtime `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE` stays reachable instead of becoming a silent empty result. The direct cast to a dictionary type rejects an over-wide `FixedString` constant before stripping, while the supertype cast strips first - that one ordering difference is the only divergence between the two coercions, so it is a `bool` rather than a second code path. `has`/`indexOf` over a plain `String` element compare the constant's raw padded bytes (`executeString`) and keep the old conversion, as does `has(<constant array>, <indexed scalar>)`, whose runtime compares `Field`s directly. #### `Map` predicates `mapContainsKey`, `mapContainsValue`, `mapContains` and `has` over a `Map` are adapters of the same `arrayIndex.h` machinery, so a `bloom_filter` index on `mapKeys`/`mapValues` needs the same coercion - and it needs to pick the mode from the `Map` type rather than from the index header, because the `mapKeys`/`mapValues` index expression strips `LowCardinality` from the key/value type while the `mapContains*` adapters run over the keys/values subcolumn, which keeps it. Reading the mode from the stripped header alone would still prune a matching granule on `Map(LowCardinality(String), ...)`, which is broken on `master` today independently of the constant's width. `has` over a `Map` is the one exception, and it goes the other way: `FunctionArrayIndex::executeMap` rewrites the map to an array of its keys and calls `recursiveRemoveLowCardinality` on both arguments before `executeArrayImpl`, so it compares the raw padded bytes exactly like `has` over an `Array(String)`, unlike `mapContainsKey` on the same column. Its element type is therefore stripped of `LowCardinality` before the mode is read. The direct array spellings `has(mapKeys(m), ...)` / `indexOf(mapValues(m), ...)` need no special handling: `mapKeys`/`mapValues` return a full `Array` with `LowCardinality` stripped from the type, so the index header type is already the type the runtime compares against. This supersedes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112693 with a smaller implementation of the same semantics (one `Field`-level helper instead of a two-mode column-cast round-trip through `getLeastSupertype` plus a batched clone of `createColumnFromConstantArray`). The array test - 115 assertions over the full element-type/function/constant-width matrix, including granule-pruning and `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE` reachability assertions - is taken unchanged from that pull request and passes byte-identically, so the two implementations are behaviorally equivalent on the covered surface. Three further tests cover the `Map` predicates, the direct `mapKeys`/`mapValues` array spellings, and `has` over a `Map` with `LowCardinality` keys; each compares the indexed answer against an unindexed oracle.

signal.title: Support DEFINER / SQL SECURITY for dictionaries
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85293 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support `DEFINER` and `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` for dictionaries, like for views. A dictionary with a local `CLICKHOUSE` source can name the user whose privileges its load runs with, instead of storing a user and password in `SOURCE(...)`. Rotating that user's password no longer breaks the dictionary. ### Description A dictionary with a `CLICKHOUSE` source authenticates every load with the credentials in `SOURCE(...)`, so rotating that password breaks all later reloads. A deployment issuing short-lived credentials must embed a long-lived one, or load as `default` with excess authority. Name the identity instead: `DEFINER = dict_owner`, with no `USER`/`PASSWORD` in `SOURCE(...)`. The load then runs with that user's privileges, consults no credential, and is bounded by the definer's settings constraints. It reuses the view definer machinery, inheriting the `SET DEFINER` grant check and the guard against dropping a live definer. `04869_dictionary_definer.sh` covers rotation against a stored-credential control, privilege and settings bounding, `SET DEFINER`, the metadata round trip, every rejection, and locality both ways, each arm mutation-verified. Scoped to a **local** `CLICKHOUSE` source, as @ pufit confirmed on the issue: any other authenticates against a foreign system with credentials a locally resolved identity cannot replace, so the clause is rejected at `CREATE` time. Locality is decided on the effective configuration, resolving named collections and `PORT tcpPort()` first; an unprovable source is rejected too. `DEFINER` is the only accepted type and must name somebody: `INVOKER` because a dictionary loads from a background pool with no invoker, `NONE` because nothing consults the type at load time. A dictionary without the clause is unchanged; `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = Dictionary(...) SQL SECURITY ...` keeps failing closed. Three limits come from the shared UUID-keyed definer registry, and each is master's behaviour for views today: an ephemeral `<user>:definer` clone can go uncollected when a `CREATE` is rejected late or the object leaves a UUID-bearing database; drop protection does not apply in `Memory` or `Ordinary` databases; and a `DROP USER` racing a `CREATE` can pass its dependency check before the object registers (over 60 attempts, 21 hits for views on master against 2 for dictionaries here).

signal.title: SAS token in the URL argument of AzureBlobStorage / azureBlobStorage is not masked in SHOW CREATE, engine_full and query_log
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** An Azure SAS token embedded in the URL argument of the `AzureBlobStorage` engine / `azureBlobStorage` table function is not masked: the full token, including the `sig=` signature, appears verbatim in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, `system.tables.engine_full`, and `system.query_log.query` at default `format_display_secrets_in_show_and_select = 0`. The URL-with-SAS spelling is a documented, working authentication form: when the URL contains `?`, everything after it is used as `sas_auth` (`src/Disks/DiskObjectStorage/ObjectStorages/AzureBlobStorage/AzureBlobStorageCommon.cpp`, `processURL`), and the integration test `test_storage_azure_blob_storage/test.py::test_sas_token` exercises exactly this form. A SAS token is a bearer credential — anyone holding it gets the granted container access until expiry. The equivalent connection-string spelling (`...;SharedAccessSignature=...`) IS masked (as `[HIDDEN]`), and the positional `account_key` argument IS masked, so the URL spelling is the one gap: `FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder` masks designated secret argument positions, and a URL argument is treated as non-secret even when it carries the credential. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduced on master 26.8.1.1448 (official build). 20/20 deterministic. **How to reproduce** No Azure endpoint is needed — with SAS auth the engine skips the container existence probe, so the CREATE succeeds against an unreachable address: ```sql CREATE TABLE sas_leak (k Int64) ENGINE = AzureBlobStorage('http://127.0.0.1:1/devstoreaccount1/cont/?sv=2025-01-05&sp=rl&sr=c&sig=SYNTHETICSIGNATUREVALUE', '', 'data.parquet', 'Parquet'); SHOW CREATE TABLE sas_leak; -- ENGINE = AzureBlobStorage('http://127.0.0.1:1/devstoreaccount1/cont/?sv=2025-01-05&sp=rl&sr=c&sig=SYNTHETICSIGNATUREVALUE', '', 'data.parquet', 'Parquet') -- the token is verbatim; expected [HIDDEN] for the SAS query string SELECT engine_full FROM system.tables WHERE name = 'sas_leak'; -- same verbatim token -- the table function leaks through the query log even when the query itself fails: SELECT count() FROM azureBlobStorage('http://127.0.0.1:1/devstoreaccount1/cont/?sv=2025-01-05&sp=rl&sr=c&sig=SYNTHETICSIGNATUREVALUE', '', 'data.parquet', 'Parquet'); -- fails, endpoint unreachable SYSTEM FLUSH LOGS query_log; SELECT count() FROM system.query_log WHERE query LIKE '%SYNTHETICSIGNATUREVALUE%' AND query LIKE '%azureBlobStorage%'; -- >= 1 ``` Contrast (masked correctly): ```sql CREATE TABLE conn_ok (k Int64) ENGINE = AzureBlobStorage('DefaultEndpointsProtocol=http;AccountName=a;BlobEndpoint=http://127.0.0.1:1/a;SharedAccessSignature=sv=2025-01-05&sig=SYNTHETICSIGNATUREVALUE', 'cont', 'data.parquet', 'Parquet'); SHOW CREATE TABLE conn_ok; -- ENGINE = AzureBlobStorage('[HIDDEN]', 'cont', 'data.parquet', 'Parquet') ``` **Expected behavior** The SAS query string in a URL argument is masked the same way the connection-string `SharedAccessSignature=` spelling and `account_key` are — at minimum the `sig=` parameter value. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/75045 Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signal.title: Azure data lake table engines (IcebergAzure, DeltaLakeAzure, PaimonAzure) do not mask credentials in SHOW CREATE TABLE and system.tables.engine_full
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** The Azure data lake table engines — `IcebergAzure`, `DeltaLakeAzure`, `PaimonAzure` — do not mask credentials in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, `system.tables.engine_full`, or any other surface that formats the engine arguments with secrets hidden. Both the connection-string form (the `AccountKey=...` stays verbatim inside the string) and the 5-argument form (the `account_key` positional stays verbatim) leak, at the default `format_display_secrets_in_show_and_select = 0` and without the `displaySecretsInShowAndSelect` privilege. Any user who can run `SHOW CREATE TABLE` or read `system.tables` sees the storage account key. The `AzureBlobStorage` engine with the very same argument shapes masks correctly (`AccountKey=[HIDDEN]` inside the connection string, `'[HIDDEN]'` for the positional), and so do all the Azure *table functions* (`azureBlobStorage`, `icebergAzure`, `deltaLakeAzure`, `paimonAzure` and their `*Cluster` variants) — a `CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT * FROM icebergAzure(...)` masks fine. Only the three lake *engines* leak. **Affected versions** Reproduced on master `26.8.1.1448`; by code inspection the gap exists on every version that has the engines — the release tags `v26.4.2.10-stable` and `v25.3.1.2703-lts` both register `IcebergAzure` (26.4 also `DeltaLakeAzure`) while their `findTableEngineSecretArguments` dispatch lists neither, and `git log -S "IcebergAzure"` over the secret finder's history is empty, so the engines were never masked since their introduction (not a regression). **How to reproduce** The engine needs a reachable Azure endpoint to create the table, so the repro uses Azurite (`npm install azurite`) and creates the container named `test`. > Note: the `Eby8vdM02...` account key below is NOT a real credential — it is the well-known public account key of the `devstoreaccount1` emulator account, documented by Microsoft, shipped by every Azure storage emulator, and already used throughout this repository's own tests (e.g. `tests/queries/0_stateless/03582_azure_double_free.sh`). It is used here precisely so the repro works against Azurite out of the box. ```bash npx azurite-blob --blobHost 127.0.0.1 --blobPort 10000 --location /tmp/azurite --silent & python3 -c " from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient key = 'Eby8vdM02xNOcqFlqUwJPLlmEtlCDXJ1OUzFT50uSRZ6IFsuFq2UVErCz4I6tq/K1SZFPTOtr/KBHBeksoGMGw==' BlobServiceClient.from_connection_string('DefaultEndpointsProtocol=http;AccountName=devstoreaccount1;AccountKey=' + key + ';BlobEndpoint=http://127.0.0.1:10000/devstoreaccount1;').create_container('test')" ``` ```sql CREATE TABLE ice_az ENGINE = IcebergAzure('DefaultEndpointsProtocol=http;AccountName=devstoreaccount1;AccountKey=Eby8vdM02xNOcqFlqUwJPLlmEtlCDXJ1OUzFT50uSRZ6IFsuFq2UVErCz4I6tq/K1SZFPTOtr/KBHBeksoGMGw==;BlobEndpoint=http://127.0.0.1:10000/devstoreaccount1;', 'test', 'ice') AS SELECT toInt64(number) AS k FROM numbers(10) SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; SHOW CREATE TABLE ice_az; -- ENGINE = IcebergAzure('DefaultEndpointsProtocol=http;AccountName=devstoreaccount1;AccountKey=Eby8vdM02xNOcqFlqUwJPLlmEtlCDXJ1OUzFT50uSRZ6IFsuFq2UVErCz4I6tq/K1SZFPTOtr/KBHBeksoGMGw==;BlobEndpoint=http://127.0.0.1:10000/devstoreaccount1;', 'test', 'ice', 'Parquet') -- ^^^ raw account key SELECT engine_full FROM system.tables WHERE name = 'ice_az'; -- same raw connection string CREATE TABLE az (k Int64) ENGINE = AzureBlobStorage('DefaultEndpointsProtocol=http;AccountName=devstoreaccount1;AccountKey=Eby8vdM02xNOcqFlqUwJPLlmEtlCDXJ1OUzFT50uSRZ6IFsuFq2UVErCz4I6tq/K1SZFPTOtr/KBHBeksoGMGw==;BlobEndpoint=http://127.0.0.1:10000/devstoreaccount1;', 'test', 'plain.parquet', 'Parquet'); SHOW CREATE TABLE az; -- ENGINE = AzureBlobStorage('DefaultEndpointsProtocol=http;AccountName=devstoreaccount1;AccountKey=[HIDDEN];BlobEndpoint=http://127.0.0.1:10000/devstoreaccount1;', 'test', 'plain.parquet', 'Parquet') -- ^^^ masked, same DDL shape ``` The 5-argument form leaks the same way: `IcebergAzure('http://.../devstoreaccount1', 'test', 'ice', 'devstoreaccount1', '<account_key>')` keeps the raw key in `SHOW CREATE`, while `AzureBlobStorage` with the same positionals shows `'[HIDDEN]'`. **Mechanism** The table-engine dispatch in `FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder::findTableEngineSecretArguments` (`src/Parsers/FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder.cpp`) lists the S3-family lake engines (`DeltaLake`, `DeltaLakeS3`, `Hudi`, `Iceberg`, `IcebergS3`, `Paimon`, `PaimonS3`, `S3Queue`) in the S3 branch and `AzureBlobStorage` / `AzureQueue` in the Azure branch, but `IcebergAzure`, `DeltaLakeAzure` and `PaimonAzure` appear in neither, so none of their arguments are ever marked secret. The *table function* dispatch in the same file does cover `icebergAzure` / `deltaLakeAzure` / `paimonAzure` (routing to `findAzureBlobStorageFunctionSecretArguments`), which is why views over the table functions mask while the engines leak. `IcebergAzure` (`DeltaLakeAzure`, `PaimonAzure`) presumably just need to join `AzureBlobStorage` / `AzureQueue` in the engine branch (they take the same leading argument shape). Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signal.title: Paimon incremental read: the unfenced processing_lock lets a second consumer silently duplicate acknowledged rows after a session expiry
signal.text: ## Describe what's wrong The Paimon incremental-read stream state (`allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine`) coordinates competing consumers that share one `paimon_keeper_path` with an ephemeral `processing_lock` znode. That lock has **no fencing**, so if the lock is lost while a consumer is mid-read (the usual cause being a Keeper session expiry that auto-removes the holder's ephemeral node), a second consumer acquires the freed lock and re-reads the same committed snapshot range. Both consumers then deliver the same committed data — an at-least-once **duplicate of already-acknowledged rows, with no error logged anywhere**. The `processing_lock` exists precisely to make the read/commit critical section mutually exclusive, so this defeats its only purpose. The unfenced-ness is visible in three places in `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Paimon/PaimonStreamState.cpp` (line numbers on `master`): 1. Acquire writes the owner's `replica_name` into the lock node but it is **never read back** anywhere — the value is dead (`acquireProcessingLock`, lines 70–90): ```cpp keeper->create(processing_lock_path, replica_name, zkutil::CreateMode::Ephemeral); ``` 2. Release is an **unconditional** `tryRemove(path, -1)` whose return code is discarded, so it deletes whatever node is at the path — including an ephemeral created by a *different* session (`removeProcessingLock`, lines 269–274): ```cpp keeper->tryRemove(processing_lock_path, -1); ``` 3. The watermark advance is a **blind** `makeSetRequest(..., -1)` in its own standalone `tryMulti` with no check op on the lock and no monotonicity guard, so it succeeds regardless of whether the caller still holds the lock or whether another consumer moved the watermark underneath it (`setCommittedSnapshot`, lines 214–238): ```cpp ops.emplace_back(zkutil::makeSetRequest(committed_path, toString(snapshot_id), -1)); ``` For contrast, the sibling `is_active` node in the *same file* is fenced correctly — it reads the node back with its `Stat` and removes it version-checked (`tryGet(is_active_path, existing_identifier, &stat)` then `tryRemove(is_active_path, stat.version)`, lines ~159 and ~165) — so applying the same discipline to `processing_lock` is clearly feasible. Note this is distinct from the documented "at-most-once" window (a *loss* on crash between watermark advance and delivery): the issue here is a **duplicate with no crash**, produced by a routine session expiry, which an at-most-once contract does not permit. ## Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes, reproduces on current `master`. The Paimon storage engine is experimental (`allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine`, default off). ## How to reproduce Two ClickHouse instances (two Keeper sessions), each with a Paimon incremental-read table over the **same** warehouse and the **same** `paimon_keeper_path`: ```sql -- on both servers CREATE TABLE c (id Int64, v String) ENGINE = PaimonLocal('/warehouse/db.db/t1') SETTINGS paimon_incremental_read = 1, paimon_keeper_path = '/paimon/stream', paimon_replica_name = 'ra'; -- 'rb' on the second server ``` 1. Commit snapshot 1 to the warehouse; consumer A drains it, so `committed_snapshot` = 1. 2. Commit snapshots 2 and 3 (ids above the watermark). 3. Consumer A starts an incremental read: it acquires `processing_lock`, reads `committed_snapshot` (still 1), and plans the read of snapshots 2–3. 4. Consumer A's Keeper session expires (network blip / GC pause / Keeper failover exceeding `session_timeout_ms`). A's ephemeral `processing_lock` is auto-removed, but A's in-flight read continues (its server process is alive; the ZooKeeper client reconnects on a fresh session). 5. Consumer B polls: it acquires the now-free `processing_lock`, reads `committed_snapshot` (still 1, because A has not advanced it yet), and delivers snapshots 2–3. 6. Consumer A finishes: its blind `setCommittedSnapshot(3)` succeeds (version `-1`), and A also delivers snapshots 2–3. Both consumers have now delivered snapshots 2–3 — the same committed rows twice, with no error. The window in step 3–4 is deterministically reproducible by pausing A's `setCommittedSnapshot` multi to Keeper and deleting the `processing_lock` znode during the pause (which is exactly what a session expiry does to the ephemeral), then letting B poll and finally releasing A. ## Expected behavior Each committed snapshot is delivered to at most one consumer. A consumer that lost its `processing_lock` (session expiry, or the node otherwise gone) must not silently commit over another consumer's progress: the watermark advance and the lock release should be fenced by lock ownership (e.g. a version/session check, as `is_active` already does) so that a stale holder fails loudly instead of duplicating acknowledged data. ## Error message and/or stacktrace None — this is the problem. No exception is thrown and nothing is logged; the duplication is silent. ## Additional context The three call sites above are all in `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Paimon/PaimonStreamState.cpp`.
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: Paimon incremental read: a Keeper watermark left ahead of the warehouse (e.g. after restore) silently and permanently skips committed data
signal.text: ## Describe what's wrong A Paimon table read with incremental reads enabled (`paimon_incremental_read = 1`, which keeps a consumed-snapshot watermark in Keeper at `<paimon_keeper_path>/committed_snapshot`) can **silently and permanently skip durably-committed data** if the Keeper watermark is ever left ahead of the warehouse's latest snapshot id — for example after the Paimon warehouse is restored from an older backup, or is rolled back / truncated by another engine, while the ClickHouse Keeper cursor is not correspondingly reset. `PaimonMetadata::collectIncrementalDataFiles` resolves the resume point by comparing the Keeper watermark to the warehouse's current latest snapshot id, and treats "watermark `>=` latest" as an unconditional no-new-data case: ```cpp else if (*committed_snapshot_id >= state->snapshot_id) // PaimonMetadata.cpp:825 { LOG_DEBUG(log, "Snapshot {} already processed (committed={}), no new data", // :828 state->snapshot_id, *committed_snapshot_id); return {}; // :830 } ``` There is no read-repair and no error on this path — it returns an empty file list at `LOG_DEBUG`. So every snapshot the writer commits after the restore whose id is `<=` the stale watermark is never delivered to any consumer, with no exception and no user-visible log. Snapshots committed *above* the stale watermark resume normally, which makes the loss a silent hole rather than a total stall. The table-identity guard `validateTableIdentity` does not catch this: it re-reads schema-0 `timeMillis`, which is unchanged by a byte-copy restore, so the guard passes and the stale watermark is trusted. This is distinct from the *documented* At-Most-Once loss (`PaimonStreamState.h:35-37`), which concerns the window between advancing the watermark and finishing consumption *within a single poll*; here durably-committed data that no consumer ever received is dropped at resume time. This surface is behind the experimental setting `allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine` (default off). ## Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — reproduced on `26.8.1.1`; the code on current `master` is identical (`PaimonMetadata.cpp:825-830`). ## How to reproduce Requires the experimental Paimon engine and a Paimon warehouse (e.g. written with `pypaimon`), read via `PaimonLocal` with incremental reads and a Keeper cursor: 1. Create a warehouse with snapshots 1..3 (300 distinct rows) under the server's `user_files/`. Back up the warehouse directory at the snapshot-1 point. 2. `CREATE TABLE pt (...) ENGINE = PaimonLocal('<table_path>') SETTINGS paimon_incremental_read = 1, paimon_keeper_path = '/paimon/cursor', paimon_replica_name = 'r1'` with `allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine = 1`. 3. Poll `SELECT ... FROM pt` incrementally — all 300 rows are delivered and the Keeper watermark reaches 3. 4. Restore the warehouse directory from the snapshot-1 backup (schema unchanged). Have the Paimon writer append two new snapshots of new, distinct rows — these become snapshots 2 and 3 again (ids `<=` the stale watermark 3). 5. Poll again (and once more): **zero of the new rows are returned, no error is raised**, and the Keeper watermark stays 3. 6. Append one further snapshot (snapshot 4, id `>` 3): only snapshot 4's rows are returned — confirming the consumer is alive and the loss is confined to the snapshots at id `<=` the stale watermark. Controls that isolate the cause: reading the same restored-and-re-appended warehouse under a **fresh** `paimon_keeper_path` delivers all the new rows (so the warehouse content is intact and readable); and without the restore, appending snapshots above the watermark delivers normally. ## Expected behavior When the committed watermark is ahead of the warehouse's latest snapshot id (the warehouse has moved backwards relative to the cursor), ClickHouse should detect the disagreement and either fail loudly or reset the cursor to the warehouse state, rather than silently returning no data and permanently skipping every subsequent commit at id `<=` the stale watermark. ## Error message and/or stacktrace None — the defining property is that the skip is silent (only a `LOG_DEBUG` "no new data" line).

signal.title: Fix DPsub join reordering silently dropping single-table ON-clause filters
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111898 The `dpsub` join-order algorithm silently dropped single-table filter and constant predicates that live in a `JOIN ... ON` clause (e.g. `t1.value = 'x'`), returning extra rows. `greedy` uses a different placement path and was unaffected. The predicates are placed in `collectJoinEdgesMask`. Two placement conditions there each silently dropped such a predicate: - `two_relations` required the whole join step to be exactly two relations, so the predicate was dropped whenever its relation was introduced against an already-multi-relation subplan (e.g. `t1` at the top of `t1 JOIN (t2 JOIN t3)`). - `fromLeft() || fromRight() || fromNone()` dropped the predicate for any single-table filter on a relation whose id is >= 2, because `fromLeft`/`fromRight` test relation ids 0 and 1 specifically (they describe the two inputs of a binary join step, not "references a single relation"). The predicate is now attached at the join that introduces its relation (the split whose one side is exactly that relation), and pure constants at the earliest two-relation join. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `dpsub` join-order optimization (`query_plan_optimize_join_order_algorithm = 'dpsub'`) silently dropping single-table filter conditions from a `JOIN ... ON` clause, which could return extra rows.

signal.title: Reuse the previous row's result for equal consecutive rows in Set execution
signal.text: The per-row execution of `x IN <set>` (`Set::executeImplCase`) hashes the full key for every row — SipHash128 for hashed multi-column keys. When the key columns are clustered (e.g. they are a primary-key prefix, so the data arrives sorted), consecutive rows form long runs of equal values, and the previous row's result can be reused after a cheap raw-byte comparison instead of repeating the hash+probe. With this change, when all key columns are non-nullable fixed-width (tuples are flattened element-wise), each row's raw bytes are compared with the previous row's, and on equality the previous result is reused, skipping the hash+probe entirely. Motivation: in SQL transpiled from PromQL selectors over `TimeSeries` tables, the per-row `id IN (tags subquery)` filter computes SipHash128 of a 24-byte `Tuple(UInt64, UUID)` per row into a `HashSet<UInt128>`. On tsbench, a PromQL benchmark over the ClickHouse `TimeSeries` engine (30 days of scrape data at 15s step, scale 1 = 1.06 billion samples / 6112 series, Ryzen 9950X, query result cache disabled, best of 3), this filter took ~17.5% of CPU of a 30-day rate query scanning 69M rows. With this change the hashing disappears from the profile (~3% of cheap byte comparisons remain), and raw-selector benchmark queries improved 1.4–2.3x. The optimization is generic: any `IN` over clustered/sorted key columns benefits; for unclustered data the added cost is a few loads per row. Bitwise comparison is applied only to POD column layouts (fixed-width raw bytes in one contiguous buffer, tuples flattened element-wise), where bitwise equality implies key equality; strings, arrays, `Nullable` and other non-POD layouts keep the existing path. The new performance test `tests/performance/set_in_clustered_keys.xml` covers both the clustered case (runs of equal consecutive keys) and the unclustered regression control (consecutive rows always differ). Note: tsbench scale-64 validation is in progress; numbers will be added before merge. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up execution of `IN` over clustered (e.g. sorted by primary key) columns by reusing the previous row's result for equal consecutive rows.

signal.title: Fixed a use-after-free in async callbacks scheduled from borrowed `ThreadGroup` scopes
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107030 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108577 CI: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105890&sha=3dc0e76362eb18e27f1fffcd3f61ca9f13725fe8&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20sequential%2C%201%2F2%29 Fixes a use-after-free risk in asynchronous work scheduled while a borrowed `ThreadGroup` is current. Borrowed `ThreadGroup` objects used by materialized view and async insert flush paths point their `performance_counters` and `memory_tracker` to the parent query group, so they are valid only while that parent group is alive. Async callbacks could capture such a borrowed group and later attach it on a pool thread after the parent query group had finished. Instead of keeping the parent `ThreadGroup` alive with a `shared_ptr`, this change keeps borrowed accounting scoped. Borrowed groups are marked explicitly, async callback capture drops borrowed groups, and thread pool callback runners capture the normalized group at task enqueue time rather than when a potentially long-lived runner object is created. This preserves synchronous borrowed accounting, but async work started from a borrowed scope runs under normal thread/global accounting instead of writing into, or prolonging the lifetime of, an already finished query group. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a memory safety issue where asynchronous work scheduled from materialized view processing could keep using query-level accounting after the query had finished.

signal.title: Add cardinality estimation for `startsWith`, `endsWith` String predicates
signal.text: The condition selectivity estimator previously handled string predicates poorly: `startsWith` / `endsWith` fell back to the generic unknown-condition factor (0.33), and every `LIKE` pattern got one flat factor (0.1) regardless of shape. This PR estimates both families through one shared mechanism. These two predicate families must land together: the analyzer pass `LikePerfectAffixRewritePass` (enabled by default via `optimize_rewrite_like_perfect_affix`) rewrites `col LIKE 'p%'` → `startsWith(col, 'p')` and `col LIKE '%s'` → `endsWith(col, 's')` *before* the where-optimizer runs. Only with both halves present does the same logical predicate get the same estimate regardless of that setting. ## What's included **`startsWith` / `endsWith` estimation** (all 8 variants, incl. `CaseInsensitive`/`UTF8`): pattern-shape heuristics scaled by literal length (UTF8 variants count code points), with statistics-based NULL-share handling for `Nullable` columns and FixedString(N) impossibility detection (needle longer than N ⇒ 0 rows). **Constant `LIKE` / `ILIKE` / `NOT [I]LIKE` pattern classification:** | Pattern shape | Estimate | |---|---| | `'abc'` (exact, case-sensitive) | equality range — uses real per-column statistics (uniq/countmin) | | `'abc'` (exact, ILIKE) | equality heuristic (`default_cond_equal_factor`) | | `'abc%'` / `'%abc'` / `'%abc%'` | prefix 0.25^n / suffix 0.35^n / contains 0.45^n (n = literal length, capped at 4), never above the legacy 0.1 fallback | | `'%'`, `'%%'` | matches every non-NULL row | | `x LIKE NULL` | SQL NULL for every row ⇒ 0 TRUE rows, NOT-safe | | `LIKE ... ESCAPE 'c'` | normalized via `likePatternWithCustomEscapeToLikePattern`, same argument restrictions as `FunctionsStringSearch` | | `'_'`, multi-segment (`'%a%b%'`), trailing `\` | unsupported ⇒ legacy 0.1 fallback | Escape-sequence semantics of the classifier mirror `likePatternToRegexp()` exactly (`\%`, `\_`, `\\`; unknown escapes keep the backslash literal). Exact `LIKE` on `FixedString(N)` is only treated as equality when the literal is exactly N bytes, because `=` ignores trailing NUL padding while `LIKE` matches all N bytes. **Three-valued-logic correctness for same-column combinations:** the `Selectivity` model tracks how each predicate behaves on the column's NULL rows, so combinations like `col LIKE '%' AND col IS NOT NULL` or `(pred OR col IS NULL) AND col IS NULL` are estimated with NULL-domain correlation instead of assuming independence. **Bug fix in clause merging:** `RPNElement::tryToMergeClauses` now counts `column_selectivities` carriers in its single-carrier merge arm. Without this, a nested same-column sub-clause such as `(startsWith(ns, 'abc') OR ns IS NULL) AND ns IS NOT NULL` flattened through the opposite logical operator and lost its grouping, estimating 0 rows instead of ~117/10000 (this was visible as a failing expectation in `Statistics.StringPredicateFunctionSelectivity`). ## Testing - `Statistics.StringPredicateFunctionSelectivity` — startsWith/endsWith across String, Nullable(String), FixedString, UTF8, negation, and same-column `IS [NOT] NULL` combinations (AST and DAG paths). - `Statistics.LikePatternSelectivityWithMetadata` — exact/prefix/suffix/contains/match-all, NULL patterns, ESCAPE normalization, escaped wildcards, FixedString length rules, and nested same-column OR/AND grouping. - `04266_statistics_basic_prewhere` — end-to-end EXPLAIN-based PREWHERE ordering checks for both predicate families, including nullable correlation and FixedString exact-length cases. ## Limitations / follow-ups - ILIKE affix patterns reuse the case-sensitive constants; a case-insensitive match is somewhat less selective, but the estimator has no case-distribution statistics yet. - LIKE literal length is counted in bytes (the UTF8 `startsWith`/`endsWith` variants count code points). - Padding-aware FixedString exact-LIKE estimates (matching a `String` equality literal against NUL-padded values) are left for a follow-up, noted in code comments. - Multi-segment patterns (`'%a%b%'`) keep the legacy fallback; they could later be estimated as a product of contains factors. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve PREWHERE condition ordering by using statistics-based selectivity estimates for `startsWith` and `endsWith` string predicates, including case-insensitive and UTF-8 variants.

signal.title: Measure the compressed size of aggregate states in `estimateSizeOfCompressedState`
signal.text: `Aggregator::estimateSizeOfCompressedState` estimates how many bytes the aggregate states would take when a replica sends them to the initiator, which is how automatic parallel replicas decides whether distributing a query pays off. It builds a `CompressedWriteBuffer` over a `NullWriteBuffer`, but serializes the sampled states into the `NullWriteBuffer` directly and then reads that buffer's counter: ```cpp NullWriteBuffer wb; CompressedWriteBuffer wbuf(wb); // never written to ... aggregate_functions[j]->serialize(place + offsets_of_aggregate_states[j], wb); ... wbuf.finalize(); res += it ? static_cast<size_t>(table.size() * wb.count() / ((it + period - 1) / period)) : 0; ``` So nothing is ever compressed and, despite the function's name and its own `We only interested in the size of compressed state` comment, it returns the plain serialized size. `recordAggregationStateSizes` then stored that single number as all three of `bytes`, `sample_bytes` and `compressed_bytes`, which pins the compression ratio of the aggregation-state statistics to 1. `recordAggregationStateColumnSizes`, documented as `Mirrors the logic of Aggregator::estimateSizeOfCompressedState` for in-order aggregation, feeds the same `AggregationState` counters via `estimateCompressedColumnSize` and does measure the compressed size - so two producers of one statistic disagreed on what it means. This change serializes the sample through the compressing buffer and returns the sample's uncompressed and compressed sizes alongside the extrapolated total, letting the existing compression-ratio machinery in `RuntimeDataflowStatisticsCacheUpdater` apply the states' real ratio. Taking the ratio from the sample rather than compressing the extrapolated size also keeps the per-compressed-block framing overhead out of the extrapolation, where multiplying it by `table.size() / num_samples` would have inflated it. **Effect on the estimate.** Only queries whose output is dominated by compressible aggregate states move. That is exactly the shape that showed up as a CI failure of `03634_autopr_output_bytes_estimation` on master: `query_28` (`MIN(Referer)` states over a two-level hash table with many groups) estimated 59335657 bytes against a recorded 23722663, a ratio of 2.4996 that left the test's 2.5x bound no margin. Reading the estimates out of the failing job's server log, the ten other queries in that test match their recorded values within 1.00..1.41x, because their output is dominated by aggregation keys or by output columns, both of which were already measured compressed. So the recorded values expect the compressed size and this defect is why that one entry looked wrong. **Two small-sample corrections found while validating this in CI.** The compressed format writes a checksum and a block header in front of every block, so a sample of a few bytes comes out of `CompressedWriteBuffer` larger than it went in and the derived ratio drops below one, *inflating* the estimate. With an early conversion to a two-level hash table (`group_by_two_level_threshold=1`, which the test randomization sets) every one of the 256 buckets holds a handful of states and every per-bucket sample is dominated by that framing, which is what made `04034_autopr_dataflow_cache_reuse_between_different_queries` fail on the first run of this pull request: the two cache-reusing queries lost parallel replicas. When the states are really sent, the framing is amortized over `min_compress_block_size` of data, so such a sample is now reported as incompressible rather than as expanding, keeping the ratio at 1 - exactly what the caller assumed before the ratio was measured at all. The new test `04653_autopr_state_size_estimate_small_buckets` pins `group_by_two_level_threshold` to 1 and fails without that. Reviewing the same statistic end to end also turned up the mirror-image defect on the in-order-aggregation side, reported in review: `recordAggregationStateColumnSizes` totalled `IColumn::byteSize`, which for a `ColumnAggregateFunction` whose states live in a foreign arena (as `AggregatingInOrderTransform` hands them over) counts one pointer per row, so arena-backed states - `min(String)`, `groupArray`, `uniqExact` - were under-counted. That column is now sized from its serialized states too, sampling at most as many of them as the hash-table producer samples per bucket. **Recorded values.** The values in `03634_autopr_output_bytes_estimation` are empirical and need `test.hits`, so they are re-measured from this PR's own CI run rather than guessed - the test reports every query that lands outside the 2.5x band, and I will update whatever it reports. `query_1` and `query_20` are single `count()` states whose estimate becomes the ~29-byte compressed-block framing instead of a 2-3 byte varint; the test's `NOT (res.2 < 100 AND res.3 < 100)` guard already covers those. Verified so far: both changed translation units pass a full `-fsyntax-only` typecheck against master. The estimate itself is validated by CI, since reproducing it needs the stateful dataset. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111981 That PR is the interim, test-only fix for the master CI failure linked below: it re-records `query_28` as the ~58 MB the estimator currently reports. **The two changes touch the same line and are mutually exclusive.** If #111981 merges first, this PR must set `query_28` back to the post-fix measurement (expected to land near the original 23722663); if this PR merges first, #111981 should be closed as unnecessary. https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=5baed0f5a10c333cd220b9646d6ef4647425079d&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%20parallel%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the estimation of the size of aggregate states used by automatic parallel replicas: it measured the serialized size of the states instead of their compressed size, overestimating how much data a replica would send for queries that aggregate into large, compressible states.

signal.title: Support trailing commas in PromQL grouping labels
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Accept trailing commas in PromQL grouping label lists.** ### Description The current Prometheus operators guide explicitly documents trailing commas in label lists. Both `(label1, label2)` and `(label1, label2,)` are valid syntax. Prometheus has supported this since 2.16.0. The upstream change was merged in [PromQL: Support trailing commas in grouping opts](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/6480) and is listed in the [Prometheus changelog](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). It followed an upstream request for consistency with trailing commas already supported in label matchers ([issue #6470](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/6470)). This is useful for generated or templated queries where a label list can be assembled with a final comma. ClickHouse previously rejected these valid PromQL queries. The shared ANTLR `labelNameList` rule now accepts one optional trailing comma for `by`, `without`, `on`, `ignoring`, `group_left`, and `group_right`. Examples: - `sum by (job,) (up)` - `sum by (job, instance,) (up)` - `foo + on(job,) bar` - `foo + ignoring(instance,) bar` ### References - [Prometheus operators guide](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/operators/) - [Prometheus implementation PR #6480](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/6480) - [Prometheus issue #6470](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/6470) - [Prometheus changelog](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) ### Tests - **Coverage:** `PromQLParser.TrailingCommasInGroupingLabelLists`. - **Coverage:** one-label and multi-label trailing commas. - **Coverage:** malformed empty and double-comma lists with rejection assertions. - **Generated artifacts:** the ANTLR parser artifacts. - **Checks:** parser smoke tests for all six forms and malformed empty/double-comma lists.

signal.title: Do not deserialize a skip index whose on-disk type is stale
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112213 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106988 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes reading a stale secondary (skip) index after an `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN` type change whose mutation never ran, for example because `KILL MUTATION` removed it: the granules on disk were written with the old type but decoded with the new one, raising `LOGICAL_ERROR`, requesting multi-exabyte allocations, or silently returning a wrong result. Also fixes a wrong result from an index over an expression whose meaning changes while every stored byte stays identical, so no mutation is created at all: a `MODIFY COLUMN` altering only a `DateTime` timezone, or only a custom type name such as `UInt8` to `Bool`. Such an index is now skipped for the affected part. Closes #112213. ### Description `MODIFY COLUMN` updates table metadata at once and schedules a mutation to rewrite the parts. Until it runs, a part's granules hold bytes written with the OLD type while index analysis decodes them with the NEW one. The read gate `canUseIndex` infers that mismatch from a *pending mutation entry* and fails open when there is none. Six measured ways reach the deserializer anyway, including `KILL MUTATION` having removed the entry (the report) and conversions for which no mutation is ever created, being metadata-only for the column but not for the index. The top-k minmax read had no gate at all. **The fix** asks the durable question instead: do the part's bytes match the type about to decode them? It lands in `IMergeTreeIndex::getDeserializedFormat`, which already receives the part, so one predicate covers every read path. Physical discovery splits off into a virtual `getPhysicalFormat`, leaving `getDeserializedFormat` **non-virtual** so no override bypasses it. Each required column's part-side type, taken from the part's own list rather than the type-erasing interned cache, is compared against the metadata type: only representation-preserving differences pass, plus a `getName()` same-meaning check on the equals-equal path. The walk recurses pairwise through `Array`, `Nullable` and `LowCardinality`; adding or dropping a wrapper is refused. A non-trivial expression index is refused on any difference. Over-firing costs pruning, not correctness. Two `MergeTask` text-index sites share the predicate, so a stale text index is rebuilt during a merge instead of hardlinked forward. **Out of scope:** index *identity* staleness (a changed expression, a name reused after a killed `DROP INDEX`), which no type check detects. <details><summary>Measured symptoms on master, and validation</summary> | target type | observed on master | |---|---| | `Nullable(UInt64)` | `LOGICAL_ERROR: Sizes of nested column and null map ... not equal after deserialization` | | `Nullable(UInt64)` release / `UInt64` / absent-column part | `Code: 241`, 4 / 2 / 4 EiB | | `Array(UInt64)` | `Code: 33`, "read just 38 of 18005230136" | | `Int8` to `Enum8` | wrong: prunes a granule the unindexed read rejects (`Code: 691`) | | `DateTime('UTC')` to `DateTime('Asia/Tokyo')`, `INDEX toHour(dt)` | wrong: 0 vs 3 | | `UInt8` to `Bool`, `INDEX toString(v)` | wrong: 0 vs 32 | | `Tuple(x UInt8)` to `Tuple(x Bool)`, `INDEX toString(p.x)` | wrong: 0 vs 32 | `04165_skip_index_stale_type_after_alter.sql`: 29 cases covering the above, whose 21 control fixtures carry 25 `explain ILIKE` granule assertions pinning the over-fire direction (a simple single-column index across the timezone and `Bool` ALTERs, an unchanged subcolumn index, an unchanged `JSON(a DateTime)` column). On the base commit the test **kills the server** with the reported stack (`SerializationNullable.cpp:178` <- `MergeTreeIndexGranuleSet::deserializeBinary` <- `MergeTreeIndexReader::read` <- `filterMarksUsingIndex`); with the fix it passes 50/50. 36 mutations each confirm one line is load-bearing. A 462-test A/B sweep against pure HEAD leaves the failure set unchanged (27 in both arms, all needing infra this sandbox lacks). Perf over 250 parts and 4 indexes is inside noise. No setting or format changes. #110050 overlaps these files and its helper asks the *physical* question, so it should forward to `getPhysicalFormat` on rebase. My #109616 has since merged and independently reached the same physical-vs-usability split, so it needs no forwarding. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108096&sha=25f51f1fddd05350d9c5aa1231aa0e7ee6fc676f&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 </details> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1470` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Do not run the server-side AST fuzzer on the stress harness's own queries
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or improvement (changelog entry is not required) The stress test aborts with `Test script failed` before running a single test: ``` Error on processing query: Timeout exceeded while receiving data from server. Waited for 15 seconds, timeout is 15 seconds. (query: SELECT value FROM system.server_settings WHERE name = 'cannot_allocate_thread_fault_injection_probability') ... subprocess.CalledProcessError: ... returned non-zero exit status 159. ``` The fail-close verification in `install_thread_pool_fault_injection` (added in #104782) ran a single `clickhouse client` query with `--receive_timeout=15` and no retry, so one slow answer killed the whole job. The first commit retries it, mirroring `call_with_retry`, keeping the fail-close semantics: persistent failure or a zero probability still aborts the run. Retrying alone is not enough, because the server is not slow. The stress profile (`stress_tests.lib`) enables the server-side AST fuzzer for the `default` user with `ast_fuzzer_runs=5` and `ast_fuzzer_any_query=true`, and that also applies to the maintenance queries of the harness itself. The fuzzer runs as a query-finish callback, so the connection thread executes the five mutated follow-up queries before the response completes. In [Stress test (arm_release) on #113224](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113224&sha=297082adba654b8bafac191c6c61b5023bcc76ef&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm%5Frelease%29) (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113224) the verification query read its 439 rows in 67 ms and the handler returned after 16.3 s, past the client's 15-second `receive_timeout`: ``` 21:12:45.393 executeQuery: Read 439 rows, 131.72 KiB in 0.067 sec. 21:12:45.395 ASTFuzzer: Fuzzed query: SELECT value FROM system.server_settings WHERE name = ... ... 5 fuzzed follow-up queries ... 21:13:01.597 TCPHandler: Processed in 16.274 sec. ``` Every one of the five queries the fuzzer fired on in that run was the harness's own: the `SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG` and the verification query of `stress.py` (11.3 s and 16.3 s in the connection thread), the two `SELECT 1` readiness probes and the `SYSTEM STOP DISTRIBUTED SENDS` of `stress_tests.lib`. No test query was fuzzed, because `clickhouse-test` runs are already started with `ast_fuzzer_runs=0`. The second commit pins `ast_fuzzer_runs=0` on the harness's own queries, in `stress.py` and in `stress_tests.lib`. That is what `clickhouse-test` already does for its infrastructure queries (`clickhouse_execute_http`) and what `stress.py` already did for the smoke check and the hung check. An explicit value on the command line is marked `changed` even though it equals the default, so the client sends it and it overrides the profile. Besides the timeouts this also stops two hazards that `ast_fuzzer_any_query` made possible: * A fuzzed `DETACH DATABASE` / `KILL QUERY` from `prepare_for_hung_check`, or a fuzzed `SYSTEM STOP DISTRIBUTED SENDS` during shutdown, running some other statement. * Fuzzed copies of a `system.processes` query showing up in the very processlist the hung check is about to inspect. A fuzzed readiness probe can also burn most of the 30-second `receive_timeout` of `start_server`, which reports `Cannot start clickhouse-server` for a server that is up. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109496 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113224 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104782
signal.author: alexey-milovidov

signal.title: Stale set skip index read after ALTER MODIFY COLUMN whose mutation was killed aborts index analysis
signal.text: ## Describe the bug A `set` skip index over a column that has had `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN` change its type can be read against parts that still hold the old serialization, aborting the server in debug and sanitizer builds: ``` Logical error: 'Sizes of nested column and null map of Nullable column are not equal after deserialization (null map size = 1, nested column size = 0)' ``` ``` SerializationNullable::deserializeBinaryBulkWithMultipleStreams src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationNullable.cpp:178 MergeTreeIndexGranuleSet::deserializeBinary src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexSet.cpp:129 MergeTreeIndexReader::read src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexReader.cpp:167 MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor::filterMarksUsingIndex src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor.cpp:2710 ``` The `Nullable` wording is incidental. With a non-Nullable target type the same defect surfaces as `Code: 12 PARAMETER_OUT_OF_BOUND` in `ColumnVector<T>::insertRangeFrom`, so keying on the `Nullable` message understates the bug. ## How to reproduce ClickHouse version: `master` (reproduced on 26.8.1.1, debug build). ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, value String, INDEX i (value) TYPE set(0) GRANULARITY 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id PARTITION BY id SETTINGS add_minmax_index_for_numeric_columns = 0, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, '10'), (2, '20'), (3, '300'); SYSTEM STOP MERGES t; SET alter_sync = 0, mutations_sync = 0; ALTER TABLE t MODIFY COLUMN value Nullable(UInt64); -- the ALTER mutation is removed before it materializes KILL MUTATION WHERE table = 't' SYNC FORMAT Null; SELECT count() FROM t WHERE value = 300; -- aborts ``` This is not transient. Every later query against the table aborts until the parts are rewritten. `OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL` clears it, and `SETTINGS use_skip_indexes = 0` returns the correct answer. Reading the column itself still works, so the data is intact and the fault is confined to skip-index analysis. ## Expected behaviour The type-incompatible index is excluded from index analysis for parts that predate the type change, and the query returns the correct result, as it does when the mutation is allowed to finish. ## Root cause Exclusion is driven by `getAlterConversionsForPart(...)->getAllUpdatedColumns()` feeding `canUseIndex` (`MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor.cpp:1108-1117` and `:764`). `canUseIndex` returns success unconditionally when that name set is empty, so the stale granule is read. Two independent situations leave the name set empty: 1. The mutation is still pending, but the read snapshot drops it, because `MergeTreeData.cpp:12000` sets `need_alter_mutations = apply_mutations_on_fly || apply_patch_parts`. With both off the `READ_COLUMN` entry is absent from the snapshot. This is what https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106988 fixes. 2. The mutation was killed. The entry is gone from `system.mutations` entirely, so the name set is legitimately empty regardless of `need_alter_mutations`, while the table metadata keeps the new column type and the old parts keep the old index. Not covered by #106988. Measured on a debug `master` build: | case | result | |---|---| | killed mutation, `Nullable(UInt64)` | abort, `null map size = 1, nested column size = 0` | | killed mutation, plain `UInt64` | `PARAMETER_OUT_OF_BOUND` in `ColumnVector::insertRangeFrom` | | killed mutation, `alter_column_secondary_index_mode` at default | abort | | pending mutation, `apply_mutations_on_fly = 0, apply_patch_parts = 0` | abort (case 1) | | pending mutation, default settings | correct result | | mutation allowed to finish, or no ALTER at all | correct result | `alter_column_secondary_index_mode` is not required to trigger this, so it is not specific to the recent index-rebuild work. The exclusion decision currently trusts a mutation entry that `KILL MUTATION` can remove. A durable fix should compare what the part actually holds against what the table metadata now declares, rather than inferring it from pending mutations. ## CI history 35 rows across 24 distinct pull requests since 2026-05-01, of which 4 have `pull_request_number = 0` (`master`), on `arm_tsan`, `amd_tsan`, `amd_debug`, `arm_debug`, `arm_release`, `amd_msan` and `arm_asan_ubsan`. STIDs `6726-6874`, `6726-6444`, `6726-6673`, `6726-36f1`, `6726-4d8b` and `6726-38f2` are this same defect in different buckets. On 2026-08-07 alone the message produced all of `6726-6874` (11 rows), `6726-6444` (5), `6726-6673` (4), `6726-4d8b` (3) and `6726-38f2` (1), so searching on any single STID misses most of the family. In CI the kill is not issued by the failing test. On the occurrence below, an unrelated concurrent test (`02558_system_processes_elapsed.sh`, running `kill query where current_database = currentDatabase()`) had its statement mutated by the AST fuzzer into `KILL MUTATION WHERE current_database = currentDatabase() SYNC`, which removed 9 mutations across three databases, including those of the victim table in `03702_alter_column_modify_secondary_index_drop.sh`, two seconds before the abort. That cross-database reach is why the carrier pull request is always unrelated. Example report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108096&sha=25f51f1fddd05350d9c5aa1231aa0e7ee6fc676f&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 Reported from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108096#issuecomment-5098842183. Related but distinct: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101832 is in the same function, but `block.clear()` there runs only on the `rows_to_read == 0` early return and costs filtering effectiveness downstream. Here the fault is upstream of any granule reuse. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #112484 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1470` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Race condition on `StorageObjectStorageConfiguration::(get/set)Paths`
signal.text: ClickHouse S3 related functions, when not using hive partitioning, supports writing multiple files to the same file path by appending a numbered counter at the end when using `s3_create_new_file_on_insert=1`. ``` create table s3_table (id UInt32) engine=s3(s3_conn, filename='root/file.parquet'); insert into s3_table values 1 SETTINGS s3_create_new_file_on_insert=1; insert into s3_table values 2 SETTINGS s3_create_new_file_on_insert=1; select _file, id from s3_table; "root/file.parquet", 1 "root/file.parquet.1", 2 ``` The way this has been implemented is through an in-memory vector keeping the paths produced by this function/ table so that the next insert knows the next filename and upon reading it is possible to enumerate all files. When the server re-starts, this information is lost and ClickHouse relies on a slow retry-mechanism to get the latest inserted file path. When looking at https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/87592, I realized the `StorageObjectStorageConfiguration::getPaths/setPaths` methods are not thread safe. AFAIK, `StorageObjectStorage::write` can be executed in parallel and does not impose any locking mechanism - which might result in the `paths` object being modified simultaneously. The obivous answer is to add protection around `(get/set)Paths`, but honestly wouldn't it be better if we just deprecated it since [hive partitioning is becoming the default](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86746)? The downside tho is that we would no longer support multiple writes to a fixed location without a partition strategy. Actually, it could also break the wildcard partition strategy in case the user is also relying on `s3_create_new_file_on_insert`
signal.author: arthurpassos

signal.title: Is ATTACH PARTITION FROM ... ON CLUSTER safe on replicated tables, or should we execute on a single replica?
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Question We are designing a staging-to-target partition promotion flow on our on-premise, bare-metal cluster using ReplicatedMergeTree with ClickHouse Keeper. We are confused by two conflicting recommendations regarding DDL distribution: 1. **The Official ClickHouse Blog** ([ClickLoad Series](https://clickhouse.com/blog/supercharge-your-clickhouse-data-loads-part3)): It recommends using `ON CLUSTER` for sharded clusters: > > "The MOVE PARTITION operations must run on all shards in a sharded cluster, e.g., by utilizing the ON CLUSTER clause." > > However, on a replicated cluster, `ON CLUSTER` distributes the `ATTACH PARTITION FROM` DDL to **every single replica** of every shard, executing them concurrently. 2. **The Community Guide** ([OneUptime Detach/Attach in Replication](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-clickhouse-replication-detach-attach-partitions/view)): It explicitly notes that `ATTACH PARTITION` and `ATTACH PARTITION FROM` are automatically replicated: > > "You only need to run the command on one replica - the other replicas will perform the same operation automatically." > > ### My Questions: - If `ATTACH PARTITION FROM` is automatically replicated under `ReplicatedMergeTree`, doesn't using `ON CLUSTER` (as recommended in ClickLoad) cause race conditions or duplicate execution issues among replicas of the same shard? - Does this mean we should avoid `ON CLUSTER` and instead build a custom orchestrator to target and execute the query on exactly one replica per shard? - Is there any plan to make `ATTACH/MOVE PARTITION ... ON CLUSTER` replication-aware so it automatically delegates to a single replica per shard?

signal.title: Do not abort the server when a loader worker cannot be spawned
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110174 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a server abort that happens when the global thread pool is momentarily saturated while tables are still loading. `AsyncLoader` now keeps running if it cannot spawn an extra loader worker and some worker will still drain the queued jobs, instead of calling `std::terminate`. ### Description `AsyncLoader::spawn` wrapped `scheduleOrThrowOnError` in `NOEXCEPT_SCOPE`, whose handler is unconditionally `std::terminate()`. A transient `CANNOT_SCHEDULE_TASK` from a saturated global thread pool therefore killed the server (`Received signal 6`) during table loading. Seen 4 times over 4 unrelated PRs and 4 build flavours in 30 days, e.g. [`Stress test (arm_tsan)`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108468&sha=27a154474608ee82636207020a9bd13beb8c9449&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29), whose stack is `terminate_handler()` -> `std::terminate()` -> `AsyncLoader.cpp:908` `spawn()` -> `:744` `enqueue()`. A spawn must succeed only when nothing else will drain the pool's ready queue, so it now tells three states apart: - a worker that entered `worker()` and is not inside `wait()` drains the queue now; - a worker inside `wait()` on *another* pool's job resumes draining once that job runs; - neither of those means nobody ever will. In the first two cases `spawn` uses the non-throwing `trySchedule`, rolls back its `Pool::workers` increment on failure, warns and returns false. Only the last case keeps the fatal path, byte for byte: the queued jobs would be stranded, and throwing is not an option because `schedule` marks that region non-exception-safe. Covering it needs rollback-and-retry across the loading DAG, out of scope here. All 4 observed rows are recoverable. `BackgroundSchedulePool` narrows the same way (`929227464f9736b`). Two counters are added because `Pool::workers` also counts a worker still queued in the global pool, which drains nothing, and one blocked in `wait()`, which cannot take its own pool's jobs. A saturated pool is remembered so the failing thread creation happens once per episode, not once per queued job, counted by the new `AsyncLoaderSpawnFailures` event; entering `wait()` clears the memo. Tests are gtests asserting which branch was taken, not just that the process survived. A SQL test cannot reach the line: on master the whole call sits under `blockFaultInjections()`. Related: #110174, which removed the mask that hid this exception.

signal.title: Adaptive Aggregator
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New adaptive algorithm for parallel `GROUP BY` (controlled via setting `enable_adaptive_aggregator`, enabled by default): each thread aggregates into its own hash table until it holds `adaptive_aggregator_freeze_threshold` keys and then freezes it, so frequent keys keep updating the small cache-resident tables with no coordination, while rare keys are routed by their hash into per-bucket backlogs and aggregated exactly once, inside the bucket-parallel merge. ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1465` (included in `26.8` and later)

signal.title: Array subscript operator supports array of integers as index.
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108095 The array subscript operator now accepts an array of integers as the index, so `arr[indexes]` gathers the elements at all of those positions at once. It is equivalent to `arrayMap(i -> arr[i], indexes)`, including the result type, the handling of negative indexes and the value produced for an out-of-range position, but it has its own implementation: a constant source array is not materialized per row, and numeric element types are gathered through the `PODArray` directly. ```sql SELECT [10, 20, 30, 40][[2, 4, 1]]; -- [20,40,10] SELECT [10, 20, 30][[1, 5, -1]]; -- [10,0,30] SELECT arrayElementOrNull([10, 20, 30], [1, 5]); -- [10,NULL] SELECT [10, 20, 30][[1, NULL, 2]]; -- [10,NULL,20] ``` The positions may be nullable, and a `NULL` position produces `NULL`, just as for a scalar index. The main use case is a lookup table: a constant dictionary array indexed by a per-row array of positions. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The array subscript operator supports an array of integers as the index: `arr[indexes]` returns the elements at all of the given positions, equivalently to `arrayMap(i -> arr[i], indexes)`. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1466` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Write wide integers in Parquet as Decimal
signal.text: Previously UInt128/UInt256/Int128/Int256 were written as `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY`, but as little-endian. Since little-endian is not lexicographically sortable, there were no statistics and no way to prune row groups and pages. This was not intentional, but rather an accidental artifact from when Parquet serialization was first introduced in ClickHouse. However, we cannot just change the endianness and break existing code/data. Here instead we switch to `DECIMAL` encoding in Parquet, which is big-endian. This enables row group and page pruning for querying for queries that use filtering on wide integer columns. The encoding is a little bit akward with 17 or 33 bytes per integer, but it enables other data consumers to have a correct data interpretation hint. Since the new data cannot be read by older versions, this new serialization mode is behind `output_format_parquet_wide_integer_as_decimal` setting, which defaults to `0` to preserver backward compatibility. The new version can still read old data (but not the other way around). <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add opt-in Parquet serialization of UInt128/UInt256/Int128/Int256 as DECIMAL to enable row group and page pruning. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1464` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->
