signal.title: Do not run 04726_kill_undrop_table_busy_wait on database engines without UNDROP support
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/56062 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `04726_kill_undrop_table_busy_wait.sh` has no `# Tags:` line, so the stateless runner admits it into the `--replicated-database` lane. There `InterpreterUndropQuery::executeToTable` rejects the query outright with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` before the busy-wait the test exists to exercise ever starts, so the test's own assertion fires with `UNDROP TABLE was not cancelled with QUERY_WAS_CANCELLED`. Deterministic, not flaky: in that check 1771 of its 1776 `OK` results carry the failure text, against 0 of the 27000+ results in every other check, continuously since the explicit assertion was added on 2026-08-09. It stays invisible because that coverage job relabels diagnosed-flaky results to `OK`; the [master report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=432b1ae96183f5b085835f4b0aece8d95ce9ce73&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_llvm_coverage%2C%20old%20analyzer%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20DBReplicated%2C%20WasmEdge%2C%20parallel%2C%202%2F3%29) that exposed it escaped only because a concurrent server death skipped the diagnostics rerun. That relabel is pre-existing and intentional; noted as disclosure, not touched here. `Ordinary` is a second carrier: `DatabaseAtomic` is the only engine that registers dropped tables for undrop, and `Ordinary` does not override `DatabaseOnDisk::dropTable`, so nothing is put into `tables_marked_dropped` and the undrop throws `UNKNOWN_TABLE`. Both rejections verified directly against a server. All three sibling UNDROP tests already tag both engines; 04726 was the only omission. Validation on one binary: the failure reproduces 100% on the pre-fix tree through the real runner; with the tag the test is `SKIPPED` in that lane and under `--db-engine Ordinary`, and still passes in the default `Atomic` lane, 50 of 50 with randomization. Negative controls (tag names typo'd, or the reason comment kept while the `# Tags:` line is deleted) re-admit the test and it fails again, so the tag is load-bearing rather than silently inert. `Related:` is context only; this PR does not implement UNDROP for Replicated. @ alexey-milovidov reached the same conclusion from the same report in PR 114884, which was closed unmerged over its unrelated `ThreadGroup` half, so this tag never landed.

signal.title: Parallelize single-level to two-level conversion in Aggregator::prepareVariantsToMerge
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114640 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107490 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/pull/1360 When some per-thread aggregation states convert themselves to two-level mid-scan, `Aggregator::prepareVariantsToMerge` converts all the remaining single-level variants **sequentially on one thread**. Initializing a two-level variant allocates and zeroes 256 bucket tables, and there is one variant per query thread, so on machines with many cores this serial loop dominates short aggregation queries. This regime became reachable after #107490: the accurate aggregation memory accounting makes `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes` (default 50 MB) engage for queries with **few groups but heavy states** (e.g. `uniqExact` over ~300 groups, where the states sum to hundreds of MB while the hash tables stay tiny). Previously the query-tracker delta under-reported such memory (each thread batches up to `max_untracked_memory` before propagating), so the threshold effectively never fired for this shape. Once it fires mid-scan, only the variants that happen to execute a block after the crossing convert themselves (measured: ~25 of 192 on ClickBench Q11), and the merge preparation then serially converts the remaining ~170. Effect on ClickBench (`c7a.metal-48xl`, 192 cores), hot runs, bisected and measured via manual ClickBench dispatches (evidence and result files in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/pull/1360): | build | Q10 | Q11 | |---|---|---| | master `c79b0d9227e` (4 min before #107490) | 0.133 | 0.092 | | master `32129f76fca` (4 min after #107490) | 0.297 | 0.165 | | master 07-11 (`ab8535b3ab0`) | 0.391 | 0.213 | | master 07-11 + `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes=0` | 0.093 | 0.102 | | pre-#107490 + `group_by_two_level_threshold=1` (uniform early conversion) | 0.132 | 0.095 | The last two rows show the cost is specifically the serial merge-prep conversion after a mid-scan flip: disabling the bytes trigger recovers fully, and uniform early conversion (which happens in parallel, each thread converting its own variant during the scan) is also fast. The daily ClickBench dashboard shows the same regression on both `c7a.metal-48xl` and `c8g.metal-48xl` (192 physical cores) since 2026-07-19, and not on machines with 96 or fewer physical cores. The fix converts the remaining single-level variants in parallel on the aggregator thread pool, following the existing `ThreadPoolCallbackRunnerLocal` pattern used elsewhere in the file. Converting distinct variants concurrently is safe: `AggregatedDataVariants::convertToTwoLevel` touches only the variant's own members. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Parallelize the single-level to two-level conversion of per-thread aggregation states before merging. This fixes a 2-3x regression of short `GROUP BY` queries with heavy aggregate states (e.g. `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)`, ClickBench Q10/Q11) on machines with very many cores, introduced in 26.7 development builds when the aggregation memory accounting was made accurate. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1469` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Extract reusable `ActionsDAG` lineage
signal.text: Extract a reusable `ActionsDAG` lineage computation into `actionsDAGUtils`. The new `traceActionsDAGLineage` traces every `ActionsDAG` output to at most one input via a single iterative, memoized traversal. Each hop is classified as `Identity`, `ValuePreserving`, or the weaker `DistinctValuesBound` (output NDV bounded by input NDV plus `ndv_delta`), and results are keyed by input/output positions, so they stay unambiguous under duplicated column names. `remapColumnStats` in the join-order optimizer is rewired onto the new API, replacing its hand-rolled `propagatesNdv`/`backTrackColumnsInDag` walk. Besides the extraction, this improves the call site: - One lineage walk per `ActionsDAG` instead of one full DFS per statistics column: complexity drops from `O(#stats × DAG)` to `O(DAG + #outputs)` when several columns carry statistics. - No wasted walks for statistics names that match no DAG input — previously the full DFS still ran and its result was discarded. - The common case of absent statistics stays free by construction: an explicit `mapped.empty()` guard skips the (now unconditional) lineage walk entirely. - The remap itself becomes a straight loop over the lineage vector with two hash lookups per traceable output, dropping the per-name set/map bookkeeping. The computed statistics values are unchanged: the hop classification is ignored by `remapColumnStats` (only traceability and `ndv_delta` matter there), and the `ndv_delta` logic — NULL-collapsing hops add one distinct value, with the same overflow guard — is identical. The position-based keying is a robustness property of the reusable API for future consumers; this consumer still keys statistics by column name. New unit tests cover the lineage kinds (`Identity` vs `ValuePreserving` vs `DistinctValuesBound`) and the position-based disambiguation of duplicated input/output names. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): - Not for changelog

signal.title: Do not read FINAL merging columns that the output header no longer carries
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/91849 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` ("Unexpected number of kept output positions after removing unused columns from `ReadFromMergeTree`") raised by a `SELECT ... FINAL` whose `PREWHERE` uses a column that `FINAL` needs for merging (`ver`, `is_deleted`, `sign`) and which does not select that column. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/91849 ### Description A `SELECT ... FINAL` whose `PREWHERE` consumes a merging column it does not select fails with `LOGICAL_ERROR: Unexpected number of kept output positions after removing unused columns from ReadFromMergeTree`. `removeUnusedColumns` added back to the read set every `getColumnsRequiredForMergingFinal` column, including ones `PREWHERE` had consumed and the output header no longer carried. `kept_output_positions` is sized from the old header, so the header recomputed from the widened read set was longer and tripped the count assertion. That widening is redundant: `initializePipeline` already appends the sorting-key columns plus `is_deleted`/`sign`/`version` for `FINAL`, and passes `original_column_names` separately so the extras are projected back off. So retain a merging column at analysis time only when the output header has it. The header keeps its size, `kept_output_positions` stays correct, and the assertion is kept. This is option 1 of the two I put to @antaljanosbenjamin above, reached by not widening the read set at all, so no position mapping is rebuilt and no grown root header has to be reconciled. Say so if you would rather the general fix (option 2) land. It also drops the first version's `canRemoveUnusedColumns` exclusion, so pruning now applies where that version declined it. The merge still gets its key columns: `is_deleted` stays in the read set, and every merging mode returns the same deduplicated rows as with `query_plan_remove_unused_columns = 0` on multi-part tables. Test `04906` covers both entry points, four merging modes, the optimizer-moved `PREWHERE`, the two late header rebuilds and duplicate output names, and asserts pruning still applies. Found by the AST fuzzer and the stress test on unrelated pull requests; also reproduces on a plain `FROM t FINAL`. - `AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107305&sha=1a49e7372d0f969cd06d7ba237d8eb3b3461e814&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29 - `Stress test (arm_asan_ubsan, s3)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108069&sha=77f495e71c33bb2c27441fa12f9deb0fdb7e24f2&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1463` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Paimon tables partitioned by `TIMESTAMP` cannot be read: "scale 6 is not supported, only support scale <= 3"
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong Any read of a Paimon table that is partitioned by a `TIMESTAMP` column with precision greater than 3 fails with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`, before a single row is produced: ``` Code: 36. DB::Exception: scale 6 is not supported, only support scale <= 3. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` Precision 6 is not an unusual choice — it is what everybody gets by default: * In Paimon, a bare `TIMESTAMP` is `TIMESTAMP(6)`. * Spark's `TIMESTAMP` and `TIMESTAMP_NTZ` always map to Paimon `TIMESTAMP(6)`, so no Spark DDL can produce a partition column that ClickHouse is able to read. * ClickHouse itself defaults to precision 6 when the Paimon type string carries no precision (`Types.h`). So in practice *every* timestamp-partitioned Paimon table is unreadable. Only partition values are affected: the same column reads fine when it is not a partition key. ### How to reproduce * Which ClickHouse server versions are incompatible: 26.8.1.491 (`e61186d9a13`), master * Non-default settings: `allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine = 1` Create the table with Spark (`pyspark` 4.0.2, `org.apache.paimon:paimon-spark-4.0_2.13:1.4.1`): ```python spark = ( SparkSession.builder .config("spark.sql.extensions", "org.apache.paimon.spark.extensions.PaimonSparkSessionExtensions") .config("spark.sql.catalog.p", "org.apache.paimon.spark.SparkCatalog") .config("spark.sql.catalog.p.warehouse", WAREHOUSE) .config("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "UTC") .getOrCreate() ) spark.sql("CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS p.d") spark.sql("CREATE TABLE p.d.ts6 (id INT, ts TIMESTAMP_NTZ) PARTITIONED BY (ts)") spark.sql("INSERT INTO p.d.ts6 VALUES (1, TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456')") # Control: the same column type, but not a partition key. spark.sql("CREATE TABLE p.d.plain (id INT, ts TIMESTAMP_NTZ)") spark.sql("INSERT INTO p.d.plain VALUES (1, TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456')") ``` The written schema confirms the precision: ```json { "id" : 1, "name" : "ts", "type" : "TIMESTAMP(6)" } ``` Then read both tables: ```sql SET allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine = 1; SELECT * FROM paimonLocal('<warehouse>/d.db/ts6'); -- Code: 36. DB::Exception: scale 6 is not supported, only support scale <= 3. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) SELECT * FROM paimonLocal('<warehouse>/d.db/plain'); -- 1 2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456 ``` ### Expected behavior `SELECT * FROM paimonLocal('<warehouse>/d.db/ts6')` returns `1 2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456`, like the non-partitioned control table does. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 5. Paimon::BinaryRow::getTimestamp(int, int) @ BinaryRow.cpp:192 6. Paimon::getPartitionString(Paimon::BinaryRow&, DB::PaimonTableSchema const&, String const&) @ Utils.cpp:246 7. Paimon::getBucketPath(String const&, int, DB::PaimonTableSchema const&, String const&) @ Utils.cpp:293 8. DB::PaimonManifestEntry::DataFileMeta::DataFileMeta(...) @ PaimonClient.h:203 9. DB::PaimonManifestEntry::PaimonManifestEntry(...) @ PaimonClient.h:287 11. DB::PaimonTableClient::getDataManifest(...) 12. DB::PaimonMetadata::getManifest(String const&, long) const @ PaimonMetadata.cpp:520 ... 17. DB::DataLakeConfiguration<DB::StorageLocalConfiguration, DB::PaimonMetadata>::iterate(...) ``` ### Root cause `BinaryRow::getTimestamp` only implements Paimon's *compact* timestamp encoding and gives up otherwise — `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Paimon/BinaryRow.cpp:185`: ```cpp DateTime64 BinaryRow::getTimestamp(Int32 pos, Int32 scale) { if (scale <= 3) { return DateTime64(getFixedSizeData<Int64>(pos)); } /// TODO: support larger precision throw DB::Exception(ErrorCodes::BAD_ARGUMENTS, "scale {} is not supported, only support scale <= 3", scale); } ``` Paimon splits the value once the precision exceeds 3 (`BinaryRow.getTimestamp` → `MemorySegmentUtils.readTimestampData` in `paimon-bundle-1.4.1`): the 8-byte field slot then holds `(sub_offset << 32) | nanoOfMillisecond`, and the epoch milliseconds live in the variable-length area at `offset + sub_offset`. That layout is visible in the manifest of the table above — the partition blob is ``` 00000001 0000000000000000 40F5060010000000 7BD75A6198010000 arity null bits field slot millis ``` i.e. `sub_offset = 16`, `nanoOfMillisecond = 456000`, and the `Int64` at `offset(4) + 16 = 20` is `1753980000123` = `2025-07-31T16:40:00.123` — together, `2025-07-31T16:40:00.123456`. ### A second defect on the same path Accepting the wider encoding is not sufficient on its own: both callers of `getTimestamp` hardcode scale 3 for the value they get back, so the partition value would then be off by three orders of magnitude. * `Utils.cpp:164` — `DecimalField<DateTime64>(partition.getTimestamp(i, type->getScale()), 3)` * `Utils.cpp:246` — `formatDateTime(partition.getTimestamp(i, type->getScale()), 3, type->getTimeZone())` The second one builds the partition directory name, which must reproduce byte for byte what Paimon wrote. Paimon names partition directories with Java's `LocalDateTime.toString()` (`Timestamp.toString()` → `toLocalDateTime().toString()`), which drops the seconds when both they and the fraction are zero and prints 0, 3, 6 or 9 fractional digits depending on the value. The directories written by the reproducer show all of those cases: ``` ts=2025-07-31T16%3A00 -- 16:00:00 ts=2025-07-31T16%3A40 -- 16:40:00 ts=2025-07-31T16%3A40%3A00.000456 ts=2025-07-31T16%3A40%3A00.123 ts=2025-07-31T16%3A40%3A00.123456 ``` Passing `type->getScale()` instead of the literal `3` covers precision up to 6, because `writeDateTimeText<..., /*cut_trailing_zeros_align_to_groups_of_thousands=*/true>` already reproduces that rule. It does not cover precision 7 to 9: `writeDateTime64FractionalText` only ever emits 3 or 6 digits, so a nanosecond partition value is silently truncated rather than printed with 9 digits. ```sql SELECT toDateTime64('2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456789', 9, 'UTC') SETTINGS date_time_64_output_format_cut_trailing_zeros_align_to_groups_of_thousands = 1; -- 2025-07-31 16:40:00.123456 (Java would print 2025-07-31T16:40:00.123456789) ``` ### Impact Read-only failure, no data loss and no abort.

signal.title: Mask the Azure shared access signature carried in a url argument
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114946 A storage account url is a documented, working way to authenticate: when the url contains a `?`, `processURL` (`src/Disks/DiskObjectStorage/ObjectStorages/AzureBlobStorage/AzureBlobStorageCommon.cpp`) takes everything after it as `sas_auth`, and `tests/integration/test_storage_azure_blob_storage/test.py::test_sas_token` exercises exactly that form. `maskAzureConnectionString` (`src/Parsers/FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder.cpp`) skips any argument starting with `http`, so the token stayed verbatim in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, in `system.tables.engine_full` and in `system.query_log.query` at the default `format_display_secrets_in_show_and_select = 0`. The same credential spelled as a connection string (`...;SharedAccessSignature=...`) was hidden, and the positional `account_key` was hidden, so the url spelling was the one gap. A shared access signature is a bearer credential: whoever holds it gets the access it was issued for until it expires. This masks the `sig` parameter, the HMAC over the signed fields and the only part of the token that cannot be guessed. The remaining parameters (`sv`, `sp`, `se`, `sr`, ...) grant nothing without it and stay visible, which keeps the url diagnosable, the same way `maskPresignedURLParameters` keeps a presigned S3 url readable. The new `maskAzureSASSignature` sits next to it in `src/Common/maskURIPassword.h` and is written the same way. The url argument is replaced in place (`result.replaced_arguments`) rather than hidden whole, and the function keeps returning `false`, so a positional `account_key` in the same call is still masked by the caller. That is the mechanism the S3 url masking already uses, and it composes with the other masking. All the call sites of `maskAzureConnectionString` are covered by the one change: the `AzureBlobStorage` and `AzureQueue` engines, and the `azureBlobStorage` table function with its `*Cluster` and named collection forms. If masking the whole query string is preferred over masking only `sig`, that is a one line change here; I went with the narrower one because the other parameters are not secret and are useful in a log. ### Testing `tests/queries/0_stateless/04909_azure_sas_url_secret_mask.sql` covers the engine through `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and `system.tables.engine_full`, and the table function and its cluster variant through `EXPLAIN QUERY TREE run_passes = 0`, which leaves them unresolved so nothing is read. A url with no signature in it is asserted to be left alone. The `CREATE` needs no reachable endpoint: with a shared access signature the engine skips the container probe. Against the official master build `26.8.1.1463` every one of those surfaces prints the signature verbatim; the committed reference is the same output with `sig=[HIDDEN]`. I also compiled `maskAzureSASSignature` standalone and checked it over multiple occurrences, a fragment, an empty value, a missing `=`, and the near-miss names `signature`, `xsig` and `SIG`. I have not built this branch, so the compile and the test run are left to CI. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): When an Azure shared access signature is passed inside the url of the `AzureBlobStorage` engine or the `azureBlobStorage` table function, its `sig` value is now hidden in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, `system.tables.engine_full` and `system.query_log`. Previously the whole token was stored and displayed in plain text, even though the equivalent connection string spelling was already hidden. The rest of the signature stays visible so the url is still readable in a log.

signal.title: Serial single-level to two-level conversion in aggregation merge prep regressed ClickBench Q10/Q11 2-3x on 192-core machines (exposed by #107490 memory accounting)
signal.text: Between the official ClickBench mainline runs of 2026-03-27 (≈26.3) and 2026-08-11 (latest stable, 26.7.x) on `c7a.metal-48xl` (192 vCPU), the `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` queries regressed while overall hot performance stayed flat (hot geomean 0.97): | query | hot 2026-03-27 | hot 2026-08-11 | ratio | |---|---|---|---| | Q10 `SELECT MobilePhoneModel, COUNT(DISTINCT UserID) AS u FROM hits WHERE MobilePhoneModel <> '' GROUP BY MobilePhoneModel ORDER BY u DESC LIMIT 10` | 0.114 s | 0.196 s | **1.7x** | | Q11 `SELECT MobilePhone, MobilePhoneModel, COUNT(DISTINCT UserID) AS u FROM hits WHERE MobilePhoneModel <> '' GROUP BY MobilePhone, MobilePhoneModel ORDER BY u DESC LIMIT 10` | 0.078 s | 0.257 s | **3.3x** | | Q37 (possibly related) | 0.023 s | 0.042 s | 1.8x | `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` maps to `uniqExact` by default (`count_distinct_implementation`), and the evidence points at `uniqExact` state merging at high thread counts specifically: - The versions benchmark (`c7a.4xlarge`, 16 vCPU) shows **no** regression on these queries across 26.3 → 26.7 → master — but it substitutes `uniq(UserID)` for `COUNT(DISTINCT UserID)` (oldest-compatible query set), so it does not exercise `uniqExact` at all. - On a 96-core aarch64 box with the same 100M-row dataset, 26.7.1.1315 and current master both run Q10/Q11 in ~0.07 s hot — no regression at 96 threads. - So the degradation manifests only on the 192-vCPU machine, i.e. it scales badly with thread count rather than being a general codegen regression. Q10/Q11 have few groups (mobile phone models) with large per-group `uniqExact` states over ~100M rows — the merge of many per-thread large states is the hot path. A bisect of the 26.3 → 26.7 window on a high-core-count machine is needed; candidates are changes to parallel aggregation state merging or `uniqExact`-specific merge paths. Found while investigating the ClickBench dashboard delta for PR #81944 — this regression is unrelated to that PR but inflates the hot side of its dashboard comparison. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944#issuecomment-5280709772 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #114691 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1469` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Mask credentials of the Azure data lake table engines
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114939 `IcebergAzure`, `DeltaLakeAzure` and `PaimonAzure` appear in neither branch of the table engine dispatch in `FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder::findTableEngineSecretArguments` (`src/Parsers/FunctionSecretArgumentsFinder.cpp`): the S3 branch lists the S3 family lake engines (`DeltaLake`, `DeltaLakeS3`, `Hudi`, `Iceberg`, `IcebergS3`, `Paimon`, `PaimonS3`, `S3Queue`) and the Azure branch lists `AzureBlobStorage` and `AzureQueue`. With no branch matching, none of the three engines has any argument marked secret, so the storage account key stays verbatim in `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, in `system.tables.engine_full` and in the logged query text, at the default `format_display_secrets_in_show_and_select = 0` and without the `displaySecretsInShowAndSelect` privilege. Both spellings leak: the `AccountKey=` inside a connection string and the positional `account_key` of the five argument form. The three engines take the same leading arguments as `AzureBlobStorage`, and `findAzureBlobStorageTableEngineSecretArguments` already handles both spellings, so this routes them to it. The Azure *table functions* (`icebergAzure`, `deltaLakeAzure`, `paimonAzure` and their `*Cluster` variants) were already dispatched there, which is why a `CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT * FROM icebergAzure(...)` masked while the engine did not. As the issue notes, this is not a regression: `git log -S "IcebergAzure"` over the secret finder's history is empty, so the engines were never masked. `findBackupNameSecretArguments`, the other dispatch in the same file, is left alone: it resolves a `BACKUP ... TO` destination, and the lake engines are not backup destinations. ### Testing `tests/queries/0_stateless/04908_azure_lake_engines_secret_mask.sh` covers all three engines and both argument spellings against an unreachable endpoint, so no Azure endpoint or emulator is needed: * `DeltaLakeAzure` defers reading the table when the columns are given, so its `CREATE` succeeds and `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and `system.tables.engine_full` are asserted directly. * `IcebergAzure` and `PaimonAzure` read their metadata while the table is created, so theirs fail against that endpoint. The masking happens when the query is formatted for the log, before the failure, so for those two the assertion is that the logged query text carries no key. Against the official master build `26.8.1.1463` the test prints the raw account key in all four `SHOW CREATE` and `engine_full` rows and reports 4 logged queries containing it; the committed reference is the masked output with 0. I have not built this branch locally, so the compile and the test run are left to CI. The Azure part of `tests/integration/test_mask_sensitive_info/test.py` is untouched: it runs against Azurite, and these three engines need a real table to exist there, which the unreachable-endpoint approach above avoids. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `IcebergAzure`, `DeltaLakeAzure` and `PaimonAzure` table engines now hide the Azure storage account key in `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and in `system.tables.engine_full`, as the `AzureBlobStorage` engine already did. Previously any user allowed to run `SHOW CREATE TABLE` or read `system.tables` could see the key of such a table.

signal.title: Add a Row(...) data type for bundling columns into one stream
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add a `Row(name1 T1, name2 T2, ...)` data type that bundles several columns into a single row-oriented stream on disk. A query-plan optimization automatically reads covered columns from the wrapper, speeding up narrow and point/scattered lookups over wide schemas while the original columns keep their columnar storage. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) ### Motivation Columnar storage excels at analytical workloads but is inefficient when reading a small subset of rows across many columns: each column lives in its own file, so a scattered point lookup pays one open/seek per column per granule. This reworks the original table-level "hybrid storage" idea into a user-declared, column-scoped construct. A new `Row(...)` data type stores its fields together as one binary record per row (one `.bin`/`.mrk` pair), in contrast to `Tuple` which stores one stream per element. It is typically declared as a `MATERIALIZED tuple(...)` mirror of the bundled columns, so the wrapper is populated automatically on insert and the originals keep their own columnar storage. A query-plan rule (`query_plan_use_row_wrappers`) rewrites reads that the wrapper covers to read the single wrapper stream and unpack the requested fields. In benchmarks the biggest win is the target case, a small number of rows scattered across many granules, where bundling ~20 columns into one file cut file opens ~19x and bytes read ~9x. It is most useful for moderate column counts read together; very wide full scans are better left columnar. ### Example use ```sql CREATE TABLE events ( id UInt64, timestamp DateTime, user_id UInt32, event_type String, payload String, combined Row(user_id UInt32, event_type String, payload String) MATERIALIZED tuple(user_id, event_type, payload) ) ENGINE = MergeTree() ORDER BY (timestamp, id); -- Reads user_id, event_type and payload from the single `combined` stream. SELECT user_id, event_type, payload FROM events WHERE id = 12345; ```
signal.author: raimannma

signal.title: Fall back to local execution when a plan step does not support distributed execution (`make_distributed_plan`)
signal.text: `make_distributed_plan=1` builds a multi-stage distributed plan whose fragments are shipped to workers by serializing the query plan. Not every `IQueryPlanStep` supports serialization: the base class already has `isSerializable` (default `false`, `src/Processors/QueryPlan/IQueryPlanStep.h`), and `assertFragmentSerializable` in `src/Processors/QueryPlan/QueryPlan.cpp` checks each stage fragment up front. However, when a non-serializable step is found, the query **fails** with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED`: `make_distributed_plan cannot distribute this query: step '...' is not serializable for remote execution`. There are also several ad-hoc throws for other unsupported shapes (`WITH TOTALS` / `ROLLUP` / `CUBE` / extremes in `optimizeTree.cpp`, `GROUPING SETS` and `max_rows_to_group_by` in `makeDistributed.cpp`, etc.). **Proposal** Introduce a systematic check of all steps of the plan for distributed-execution support before distributing it, and if any step is unsupported fall back to normal local execution, exactly as if `make_distributed_plan=0`, instead of throwing: 1. Run the check once on the whole plan before the `tryMakeDistributed*` transforms (not per-fragment after the fact), based on `isSerializable` plus the existing ad-hoc conditions, so the decision is made before the plan is rewritten with exchanges. 2. On failure, log the offending step (as the parallel-replicas fallback already does: `Keeping the plan fragment local: step '...' is not serializable for remote execution` in `applyParallelReplicas.cpp`) and continue with the ordinary single-node plan. 3. Keep a way to get the old strict behavior (e.g. a setting like `distributed_plan_fallback_to_local_execution`, or reusing the error under a "throw" mode), so tests and users who want to be sure the plan is actually distributed can still assert it. 4. Convert the scattered `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` throws in `optimizeTree.cpp` / `makeDistributed.cpp` / `assertFragmentSerializable` to the same mechanism, so the supported/unsupported decision lives in one place.

signal.title: Support animated PNG in the `PNG` format
signal.text: Support animated PNG in the `PNG` format. If the result has a `t` column of an integer type, the format produces an animated PNG (`APNG`) instead of a still image. Records are grouped into frames by the value of `t`, which is the relative time offset of the frame. Every frame is an independent image: the canvas is empty at the start of each frame, and in the implicit coordinate mode the cursor restarts from the top-left corner. The `t` column can be combined with either coordinate mode. The unit of `t` is set by the new settings `output_format_image_time_multiplier_seconds` (default 1) and `output_format_image_time_divisor_seconds` (default 60), so one unit of `t` is 1/60 of a second by default. A frame is displayed until the next one begins, and the last frame is displayed for as long as the frame before it. The new setting `output_format_image_streaming_animation` (default `false`) writes each frame out as soon as the next value of `t` is seen, instead of buffering all the frames in memory, so a viewer can display the frames while the query is still running. It requires `t` to be non-decreasing and throws otherwise. It defaults to `false` because of a constraint of the format itself: the `acTL` chunk must precede the first `IDAT` and must declare the total number of frames, which a forward-only writer does not know. This is why the `APNG` muxer of `ffmpeg` seeks back to patch `acTL` and warns when the output is not seekable; a ClickHouse `WriteBuffer` cannot seek. The streaming mode therefore declares an upper bound rather than the exact count. Measured behaviour of real decoders on such a file: - Firefox plays it. The `APNG` patch of `libpng` emits a non-fatal `png_warning("Number of actual frames fewer than expected")` at `IEND`. - Chrome plays the real frames, but keeps the image in the "still loading" state: `SkPngRustCodec::parseAdditionalFrameInfos` maps the frames that never arrive to `kIncompleteInput`. - `Pillow` reports the declared count and then raises `OSError: Truncated File Read` past the last real frame. With the default `false` the frame count is exact and the output conforms to the specification. The `sixel` protocol cannot represent an animation at all, and the Kitty graphics protocol animates only through a separate flow of per-frame commands, so both reject a result with a `t` column. The `iterm` protocol carries the whole datastream as a single payload, so the frames cannot reach the terminal early there; since that payload is fully buffered before it is sent, the exact frame count is patched into `acTL` and the payload conforms to the specification even in the streaming mode. ```sql SELECT number % 60 AS t, toInt32(intDiv(number, 60) % 64) AS x, toInt32((number * 7) % 64) AS y, toUInt8(255) AS v FROM numbers(60 * 64) INTO OUTFILE 'animation.png' FORMAT PNG SETTINGS output_format_image_width = 64, output_format_image_height = 64; ``` ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support animated PNG in the `PNG` output format. A `t` column turns the result of a query into an animation, with the time scale of `t` set by `output_format_image_time_multiplier_seconds` and `output_format_image_time_divisor_seconds`, and `output_format_image_streaming_animation` to write the frames out as the query produces them instead of buffering them in memory. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1267` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Add RadixHashJoin: a radix-partitioned hash join
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106023 `parallel_hash` probes one shared two-level hashtable. Once the build side outgrows last-level cache every probe lookup is a cold miss, and after the per-slot maps are merged at the end of the build phase the two-level split does nothing to shrink the working set. This adds `radix_join`: radix-partition the build side into many small hashtables that each stay cache-resident, then stream the probe side against them in budgeted waves, so that while a leaf table is in cache it is hit by a long run of probe rows instead of one lookup at a time. Each leaf is a real `HashJoin`, so join semantics aren't reimplemented — only the partitioning and the scheduling around it. v1 handles `INNER ALL` equi-joins with a single equality clause (no `OR`) over fixed-width columns; anything else falls back to `parallel_hash`. Design notes are in `RadixHashJoin.h`. ## The probe side is not fully materialised This is the part that departs from a textbook radix join, and it is the point of the design. A classic partitioned hash join shuffles the *entire* probe side down to leaf depth before it probes anything, which puts its memory floor at `|build| + |probe|` and means no output appears until the whole probe input has been read and scattered. Here the probe side is buffered only up to a budget. When the budget fills, that wave of buffered rows is scattered, probed against the leaves it touches, and emitted; the probe buffer is dropped, and the cycle repeats. The leaf hashtables persist across waves — only the probe buffer is recycled. So transient memory is bounded by the budget rather than by probe cardinality, and rows start flowing downstream well before the probe side has been consumed. The budget is `radix_join_probe_buffer_fraction` of the bytes the build side accumulated (stored rows plus leaf tables), default **0.15**, with a floor of `radix_join_probe_buffer_min_bytes` (default 512 MiB) and an optional cap from `radix_join_probe_buffer_max_bytes`. On the sweep below that works out to a 0.5-6.9 GiB probe buffer; at the widest shape measured, a classic fully-materialising implementation would instead have had to hold ~119 GiB of shuffled probe stream. The trade-off is time, and it is worth being explicit about the direction: full materialisation scatters the probe side once and touches each leaf table once, whereas a leaf that receives rows in several waves gets re-read once per wave, so bounded memory is bought with extra cache traffic. Turning `radix_join_probe_buffer_fraction` (or `radix_join_probe_buffer_max_bytes`) up trades back toward the classic behaviour, and at a budget large enough to hold the whole probe stream the eviction cycle never fires and this degenerates to a classic partitioned hash join. Every number below is at the default budget; I have not measured the fully-materialising end of that range. ## Benchmarks ### What was measured Two generated tables joined on one `UInt64` key, `INNER JOIN ... USING (k)`. Three properties of the join were varied: - **How big the build side is** — 32M, 64M, 128M, 256M or 500M rows. - **How much bigger the probe side is** — 1, 2 or 4 probe rows per build row. - **How wide the rows are** — every row is the 8-byte key plus 0, 1, 3 or 7 further 8-byte columns, so **8, 16, 32 or 64 bytes per row**, chosen independently for the two sides. Only the columns counted here are projected out of the join, so these widths are what the join actually moves. That is 5 x 3 x 4 x 4 = 240 join shapes, each run at `max_threads` of 16, 32, 64 and 96: **960 measured points**. Every point is checked against `parallel_hash` for an identical result (960/960 completed, zero checksum mismatches). Hardware: 4 identical ARM64 VMs — Neoverse-V2 (Graviton 4), 96 cores on one socket and one NUMA node, 64 KiB L1d and 2 MiB L2 per core, 36 MiB shared L3, 371 GiB RAM. Sweep tag `radix-sweep-202608140814`. Settings pinned: `join_algorithm` to the algorithm under test, `enable_analyzer = 1`, `enable_join_runtime_filters = 0`. Multiplying row counts by row widths gives the one quantity that organises every result below — **how many bytes the probe side carries for each byte of build side**: probe bytes / build bytes = (probe rows x probe row width) / (build rows x build row width) Across the sweep this spans 1/8 (a 64-byte build row against an equal number of 8-byte probe rows) to 32 (an 8-byte build row against four times as many 64-byte probe rows). It does not depend on how big the build side is, which is why build size below is a separate axis from it. Speedup always means `parallel_hash` time / `radix_join` time, so above 1 is a `radix_join` win. Aggregates are geometric means. ### Why this range of shapes The build sizes start high enough that every point is already past the cache cliff this algorithm exists to address: at the bottom of the range, a 32M-row key-only build reserves a 1 GiB leaf-table budget — 28x the 36 MiB L3 — so there is no point in the sweep that `parallel_hash` could have kept cache-resident. From there the range spans 16x in build size, enough to put both the crossover and the peak inside it. It stops at 500M rows because the per-row costs of both algorithms have flattened out well before that (see below), not because of a hardware limit — the heaviest single point peaks at 63.6 GiB, 17% of the box. ### Headline `radix_join` wins **793/960 (82.6%)**, median winning factor 1.62x. | threads | radix wins | gmean speedup | gmean latency, radix | gmean latency, `parallel_hash` | |--------:|-----------:|--------------:|---------------------:|-------------------------------:| | 16 | 200/240 | 1.28x | 2676 ms | 3421 ms | | 32 | 197/240 | 1.31x | 1634 ms | 2145 ms | | 64 | 193/240 | 1.47x | 1202 ms | 1770 ms | | 96 | 203/240 | 1.88x | 1133 ms | 2133 ms | The best single point is 5.73x: 96 threads, 500M build rows, one probe row per build row, a 64-byte build row and a 16-byte probe row — 3446 ms against 19747 ms. The worst is 0.14x, in the band described under "Known weak spot". ### Where it wins How many bytes the probe side carries per byte of build side predicts the outcome almost by itself, monotonically across two and a half orders of magnitude: | probe bytes per byte of build side | 1/8 | 1/4 | 1/2 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | gmean speedup | 2.93x | 2.67x | 2.08x | 1.74x | 1.41x | 1.19x | 1.04x | 0.99x | 0.91x | | radix wins | 20/20 | 60/60 | 112/120 | 164/180 | 173/200 | 145/180 | 83/120 | 31/60 | 5/20 | That ordering is what the algorithm predicts. `radix_join` shuffles both sides. The build-side shuffle is amortised — paid once, then repaid by every probe row that hits a cache-resident leaf. The probe-side shuffle is pure added cost, repaid by nothing. So the advantage decays as the probe side grows relative to the build side, and the crossover sits near 8: `radix_join` is ahead while the probe side carries up to roughly 8 bytes per byte of build side, and behind past that. Per side, the same thing stated two ways: a **wide build row** is the strongest predictor of a win (64-byte build rows win all 240 of their shapes, gmean 2.57x; key-only 8-byte build rows manage 1.05x), and a **wide probe row** is the strongest predictor of a loss (8-byte probe rows average 1.87x, 64-byte probe rows 1.29x). Build size is the second axis, and it is not monotone: the advantage rises sharply from 32M to 64M rows, peaks around 128M-256M, and gives some back at 500M. The low end is the algorithm not having enough build side to pay back the partitioning, plus the bug below. The decline at the top bounds how far this result extrapolates. Two measured facts produce it, pulling in opposite directions: 1. **`parallel_hash`'s cost per build row is already flat across the whole sweep** — 17.97, 18.17, 18.44, 18.44, 17.07 ns per build row at 32M, 64M, 128M, 256M and 500M. Whatever penalty it pays for falling out of cache is fully saturated before the sweep even starts, which is what the 28x-L3 figure above would predict. A larger build side therefore hands `radix_join` no additional penalty to recover. 2. **`radix_join`'s own cost per build row climbs after 128M** — 10.40, 10.64, 11.42 ns per build row at 128M, 256M and 500M. One curve flat and the other rising is the whole arithmetic of the decline: the speedup falls 12-15% from 256M to 500M in every band, and extrapolating, the two would meet somewhere above this sweep. I have not measured where. I also have not investigated *why* (2) happens — it is an observation, not a diagnosis. The number of leaf partitions does grow with the build side over that range (8192, 16384 and 32768 for a key-only build side), which is the obvious thing to look at first, but I have not confirmed it is the cause. What it is *not* is a change in the depth of the radix plan: that is two passes at every point in this sweep, and a third pass would need more than 1024^2 partitions, which is around 10^10 rows away. ### Thread scalability This is the case the algorithm was built for. Going from 64 to 96 threads, `parallel_hash` gets *slower* on 197 of the 240 shapes — 20% slower in the geometric mean, 1770 ms to 2133 ms pooled — while `radix_join` keeps improving on all but 20 of them. The regression is a build-side effect, and the sweep can show that much without a phase breakdown. It scales cleanly with how wide the build row is — 96-thread over 64-thread latency of 0.97, 1.19, 1.30, 1.41 for 8-, 16-, 32- and 64-byte build rows — while being flat in probe row width (1.19, 1.19, 1.23, 1.21) and *shrinking* as probe rows per build row grows (1.29, 1.22, 1.11 for 1, 2 and 4). A cost that tracks build-side bytes and gets diluted by added probe work sits on the build side. `radix_join`'s build side writes only per-lane block stores, never a shared map, and its leaf tables are immutable once built. ### Known weak spot Of the 167 losing points, 52 fall in one reproducible band. With a 32M-row build side and a build row of 16 or 32 bytes, `radix_join` costs 40-73 ns per build row, against 3-7 ns for the *same shape* at every larger build size — up to 14x its own family: | probe rows per build row | build row | probe row | at 32M rows | at 64M+ rows | factor | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 2 | 16 B | 8 B | 60.8 ns/row | 4.3 ns/row | 14.3x | | 2 | 32 B | 8 B | 72.9 ns/row | 5.7 ns/row | 12.7x | | 1 | 32 B | 16 B | 45.4 ns/row | 4.4 ns/row | 10.3x | Two things point at plan selection rather than bandwidth. It is non-monotonic in the build row width at a fixed byte ratio — 8-byte build rows are healthy, 16 and 32 are pathological, 64 is healthy again — and the affected points do not respond to threads at all: 1.04x going from 16 to 96 threads, against 1.92x for the healthy 32M points. That suggests the leaf-count/pass-plan heuristic picking a bad plan in a narrow band of small build sizes. These are the visible sub-parity outliers in the first plot. Not diagnosed further. The remaining 115 losses are mostly the regime the model expects to lose: 68 of the 72 losses at 64M build rows and above are where the probe side carries 4 or more bytes per byte of build side, and the probe-side shuffle cannot be repaid. Excluding only the 52 pathological points, the sweep reads 793/908 (87.3%) at gmean 1.60x. ### Memory `radix_join` costs 1.35x peak memory over `parallel_hash` on average (median 1.34x, worst 1.83x), from holding the scattered build side plus the leaf tables. It is highest on the smallest build sides (32M rows: 1.49x) and lowest on the largest (500M: 1.21x). ### Reproducing The harness is in this PR: `bep/tools/join_mergetree_bench.py` runs the SQL sweep above — the four axes are `--cardinalities`, `--ratios`, `--build-payload-columns` / `--probe-payload-columns` (the 0/1/3/7 extra columns per row) and `--threads`. `src/Common/benchmarks/hash_join_bandwidth_model.cpp` is the standalone build/probe/scatter bandwidth microbenchmark. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental JOIN algorithm `radix_join`, a radix-partitioned hash join for joins whose build side is too large to stay cache-resident. Enable with `SET join_algorithm = 'radix_join'`. It supports `INNER ALL` equi-joins with a single equality clause whose key and payload columns are all fixed-width, non-nullable and non-`LowCardinality`; other queries fall back to `parallel_hash`.

signal.title: Fix cubic complexity of planning a JOIN with a `merge` table
signal.text: Planning a query that joins a `Merge` table with something else could take minutes and hundreds of megabytes of memory, and it was interruptible neither by `max_execution_time` nor by `KILL QUERY`, because all of it happens inside `QueryPlan::optimize`. `ReadFromMerge::createChildrenPlans` builds a separate child query tree for every source table. When the `Merge` table takes part in a JOIN, this goes through `replaceTableExpressionAndRemoveJoin`, which rebuilds the projection list from the required column names. Every column there was resolved by its own `QueryAnalysisPass` run, and every such run rebuilt `AnalysisTableExpressionData` for all the columns of the `Merge` table. The structure of a `Merge` table is the union of the structures of its source tables, so the cost of planning was cubic in the number of source tables. All the required columns are now resolved with a single `QueryAnalysisPass` run. For 40 tables with 20 distinct columns each, a `SELECT *` joined with `merge` goes from 18 seconds down to about a second in a release build; the results are byte-identical before and after. This is what made the `Hung check` fail in a stress test: the AST fuzzer produced `SELECT * FROM (SELECT number AS a FROM numbers(11)) AS t1 PASTE JOIN merge('system', '') AS t2 LIMIT 294` for `02933_paste_join.sql`, and the query spent more than 16 minutes inside `QueryPlan::optimize` under TSan. https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=dd1e53dfe2715c22d4b7e63c2459bc9eec994581&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed cubic complexity of query planning for a JOIN with a `Merge` table over many tables with different structures. Such queries could previously spend minutes in query planning without responding to `max_execution_time` or `KILL QUERY`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1462` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Implemented SIEVE eviction in cache framework
signal.text: Implements the `SIEVE` cache eviction policy in the cache framework (`CacheBase`), available alongside the existing `LRU` and `SLRU` policies. `SIEVE` is a simple, scan-resistant eviction algorithm: a single "hand" walks a FIFO queue of entries and evicts the first entry whose `visited` flag is clear, clearing the flag as it passes set entries. See the paper for details: https://junchengyang.com/publication/nsdi24-SIEVE.pdf This continues the original work by @Vectorshine, brought up to date with `master`: - Reworked `SIEVECachePolicy` to match the current `ICachePolicy` interface (`CurrentMetrics` tracking, `maxCount`, `contains`, per-entry `OnRemoveEntryFunction`), mirroring `LRUCachePolicy`. - Fixed a bug in `remove` where the stored queue iterator was advanced in place and the wrong node was erased. - Added unit tests in `gtest_sieve_cache.cpp`, including a step-by-step test of the eviction logic. - Randomized the mark and uncompressed cache policy across `LRU`, `SLRU` and `SIEVE` in stateless functional tests (`ci/jobs/functional_tests.py`) and the stress test (`tests/docker_scripts/stress_runner.sh`). `SIEVE` is only implemented for the `CacheBase`-backed caches, so the filesystem cache (backed by `FileCachePolicy`) is not randomized to it, and it is excluded during bugfix validation, which runs downloaded master-side binaries. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58910 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new cache eviction policy `SIEVE`. It can be selected for the in-memory caches backed by `CacheBase`, such as the mark cache and the uncompressed cache, via the corresponding `*_cache_policy` server settings (for example, `mark_cache_policy` and `uncompressed_cache_policy`). It is not available for the filesystem cache. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: fix: error message for ALTER DROP COLUMN of a key column
signal.text: <!-- PR title: Fix error message for ALTER DROP COLUMN of a column used in a key expression --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/71776 Related follow-up issues: #114481, #114181 `ALTER DROP COLUMN` and `ALTER CLEAR COLUMN` behaved inconsistently on a column that belongs to `ORDER BY`, `PRIMARY KEY` or `PARTITION BY` An `ALTER` is validated by building the new table schema first and inspecting it afterwards. Once the column is gone the sorting key cannot be resolved, so building the schema fails before the check that knows the real reason. That check is now done first, on the current schema, where the key columns are already known. It understands all the ways a key can refer to a column: the column itself, a column inside a key expression, a subcolumn (`ORDER BY a.x` for `a Tuple(...)`) and a whole nested group dropped by its common prefix Examples: 1. Basic ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64, b UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN a; -- before: Code: 47. Missing columns: 'a' while processing: 'a' ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) -- after: Code: 524. Trying to ALTER DROP key a column which is a part of key expression. (ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN) ``` 2. Dropping a column that is used only in a TTL expression now also reports which TTL expression it breaks Note: `ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN` would be wrong here. Dropping a column used in a `TTL` is not always forbidden - `ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN d, MODIFY TTL a + INTERVAL 1 DAY` is valid and passes. And this is a wrapper not a check: the same step returns `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` for `MODIFY COLUMN d Array(UInt8)`, which `ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN` would mislabel ```sql CREATE TABLE t (d Date, a UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a TTL d + INTERVAL 1 DAY; ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN d; -- before: Code: 47. Missing columns: 'd' ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) -- after: Code: 47. Cannot apply ALTER because it breaks the TTL of the table: Missing columns: 'd' ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) ``` 3. For a key column the command is rejected whatever the partition is, so the old error only sent the user to fix something that would not help ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64, b UInt64, c UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY b ORDER BY a; ALTER TABLE t CLEAR COLUMN a IN PARTITION 'nonsense'; -- before: Code: 53. Cannot convert string 'nonsense' to type UInt64. (TYPE_MISMATCH) -- after: Code: 524. Trying to ALTER CLEAR key a column ... (ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN) ``` 4. With `share_nested_offsets` enabled, a name that is not a column of the table denotes the whole nested group `<name>.*`, and `DROP`/`CLEAR` of the group is now rejected the same way when any column of the group is used in a key. Before, this was worse than a confusing message: the checks compare names exactly and did not see the group, so `DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS n` destroyed the group's data with a mutation that then failed halfway and `CLEAR COLUMN n` on a non-empty table left a mutation that can never finish (a key column cannot be rewritten) in `system.mutations` until `KILL MUTATION` ```sql CREATE TABLE t (`n.a` UInt64, `n.b` UInt64, x UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY `n.a`; ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN n; -- before: Code: 47. Missing columns: 'n.a' while processing: '`n.a`' ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) -- after: Code: 524. Trying to ALTER DROP whole Nested group n whose columns (`n.a`) are part of key expression. (ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN) ALTER TABLE t CLEAR COLUMN n; -- before: accepted, data of `n.a` and `n.b` is zeroed and the mutation stays in system.mutations forever -- after: Code: 524. Trying to ALTER CLEAR whole Nested group n whose columns (`n.a`) are part of key expression. (ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN) ``` Groups with no key columns inside are dropped as before, and with `share_nested_offsets = 0` the name does not denote the group and the check does not apply. The remaining group/exact-name mismatches (silent data destruction for groups without key columns, dependent views, races with background mutations) predate this PR and are reported separately with reproductions ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN` of a column that is used in the sorting, primary or partition key now fails with `ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN` and an explanation, the same as `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR COLUMN` does. Previously it failed with a confusing `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER: Missing columns` error coming from the recalculation of the key expressions. The same applies to dropping or clearing a whole `Nested` group by its common prefix when a column of the group is used in a key; previously that could silently destroy the group's data or leave a mutation that never finishes. Dropping a column that is used only in a `TTL` expression now also reports which TTL expression it breaks

signal.text: Scope WITH aliases to the SELECT that declares them when adding the default database <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104972 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104972 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed table names not being qualified with the default database when a `WITH` alias elsewhere in the same query happened to share the name. `ALTER TABLE other_db.t UPDATE v = (WITH RECURSIVE src AS (SELECT 7 AS id) SELECT max(id) FROM src) + (SELECT max(id) FROM src)` failed with `UNKNOWN_DATABASE`, the same expression through `UPDATE ... SET` silently read the session's `src` instead of `other_db.src`, and a view whose `UNION` branch referenced such a table could not be read from another database. Closes #104972. ### Description `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` records `WITH RECURSIVE` aliases so it does not qualify a name that is a CTE rather than a table. That record was one set shared by the whole visitor instance and never cleared, so an alias declared inside one `SELECT` kept suppressing qualification for every identifier seen afterwards, including a genuine physical table. The leak is forward-only: a colliding name before the CTE is fine. The set becomes a stack of scopes, one pushed per `ASTSelectQuery` and popped by a destructor, so a `SELECT`'s subtree inherits the enclosing aliases and nothing outside it does. Lookups walk it innermost-first. Three cases follow: - The `WITH` list is now walked in the non-recursive case too. A recursive alias is registered before its element is visited, since it may reference itself; a plain alias after, so inside its own definition the name still denotes a table. This mirrors `ApplyWithSubqueryVisitor`, and matters because `ApplyWithGlobalVisitor` copies a first branch's `WITH` list into later `UNION` branches without the `RECURSIVE` flag. - Enclosing scopes are searched for a plain name only when `enable_global_with_statement` is set, matching the resolver: without it the analyzer clears `allow_to_check_cte` for parent scopes. A recursive name is searched unconditionally, since its self-reference resolves inside its own definition. The setting is read per `SELECT`, by replaying the clauses reaching it as `QueryTreeBuilder` does, so a repeated setting takes its last value and `compatibility` is honoured. - `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY QUERY` and `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` expand a plain CTE reference into a copy of its body first. Inside that copy the name denotes a table, so that binding is masked. Fixing the visitor covers all 13 construction sites at once. Validated on 40 arms, with eight mutants pinning the scope stack, the clone mask, the registration and lookup order, and the setting handling.

signal.title: DeltaLake Logical error: 'No version found in table state snapshot'
signal.text: ### Describe the bug Seems not related to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/102037 Reading a persistent DeltaLake (or Iceberg) table through a code path that does **not** call `updateExternalDynamicMetadataIfExists()` reaches `IDataLakeMetadata::iterate()` with a storage snapshot whose `datalake_table_state` is empty. `iterate()` treats this as impossible and throws `LOGICAL_ERROR`, which aborts the server: ``` <Fatal> : Logical error: 'No version found in table state snapshot'. DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel::iterate (DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel.cpp:331) -> DataLakeConfiguration<…, DeltaLakeMetadata>::iterate (DataLakeConfiguration.h:294) -> StorageObjectStorageSource::createFileIterator (StorageObjectStorageSource.cpp:287) -> ReadFromObjectStorageStep::createIterator / initializePipeline ``` Found by BuzzHouse on master `26.6.1.694` via `SELECT * FROM d2.t284` on a `DeltaLakeS3` table that had been through many ALTER/mutation/cluster-function operations. ## Root cause A persistent data-lake table's in-memory metadata gets its snapshot version pinned (`setDataLakeTableState`) only inside `updateExternalDynamicMetadataIfExists()` (`StorageObjectStorage.cpp:397`). The analyzer calls it on the table it resolves (`IdentifierResolver.cpp:335`), so a *direct* SELECT is fine. But several read paths build the child storage snapshot straight from `getInMemoryMetadataPtr()` **without** that call: - `StorageMerge` — `StorageMerge.cpp:730` (and `:414`) - cluster/distributed table-function reads on the executing node - (the materialized-view target path used to have this bug; it was fixed by adding the update call — `StorageMaterializedView.cpp:400`) When the table is reached first through one of these, the snapshot carries no `datalake_table_state`, and `iterate()` throws instead of falling back. The throw is also asymmetric with its sibling in the *same file*: `DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel::prepareReadingFromFormat()` (`DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel.cpp:505-511`) handles the identical missing-version case **gracefully** by falling back to the version from settings. `iterate()` should do the same. Iceberg is identical: `IcebergMetadata::iterate()` (`IcebergMetadata.cpp:1023`) throws `"Can't extract iceberg table state from storage snapshot"` under the same condition. ## Relationship to prior findings Same bug *class* as the Iceberg over-assertions filed in #107316 — a `LOGICAL_ERROR` guarding an invariant that is actually reachable from normal SQL. signal.title: Heap-use-after-free: Parquet v3 prefetcher reads and writes through a `ReadBuffer` freed by `IInputFormat::onFinish`
signal.text: 🕵️ ## Describe what's wrong `ParquetV3BlockInputFormat` does not override `resetReadBuffer()`, so `IInputFormat::onFinish()` frees the format's owned `ReadBuffer` while the Parquet `Prefetcher`'s IO tasks are still reading through it on the prefetch thread pool. The tasks then dereference freed memory. ASan on a plain `clickhouse local` run of the reproducer below (master, 26.8.1.1310): ``` ==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x7112bd001800 WRITE of size 1048576 at 0x7112bd001800 thread T9 (ParquetPrefetch) #3 in DB::ReadBuffer::next() src/IO/ReadBuffer.cpp:113:15 #5 in DB::ReadBuffer::read(char*, unsigned long) src/IO/ReadBuffer.h:169:37 #6 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::readSync(...) src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/Prefetcher.cpp:113:29 #7 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::runTask(...) src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/Prefetcher.cpp:540:13 #8 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::scheduleTask(...)::$_0::operator()() src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/Prefetcher.cpp:435 #15 in DB::ThreadPoolCallbackRunnerFast::threadFunction() src/Common/threadPoolCallbackRunner.cpp:225:13 ``` It is a **1 MiB write into freed heap**, so this is memory corruption, not only a bad read. The same defect was hit independently by the `La Casa Del Dolor (arm_asan_ubsan)` CI job, where the report is a read and carries the full free/allocation stacks: ``` ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0xfcdd2aec39c0 READ of size 8 at 0xfcdd2aec39c0 thread T423 (ThreadPool) #0 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::readSync(...) Prefetcher.cpp:110:21 <- reader->setReadUntilEnd() #1 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::runTask(...) Prefetcher.cpp:523:13 #2 in DB::Parquet::Prefetcher::scheduleTask(...)::$_0::operator()() Prefetcher.cpp:424:17 #9 in DB::ThreadPoolCallbackRunnerFast::threadFunction() threadPoolCallbackRunner.cpp:225:13 0xfcdd2aec39c0 is located 0 bytes inside of 272-byte region freed by thread T468 (ThreadPool) here: #1 in std::default_delete<DB::ReadBuffer>::operator()(DB::ReadBuffer*) #7 in std::vector<std::unique_ptr<DB::ReadBuffer>>::~vector() #8 in DB::ISource::work() src/Processors/ISource.cpp:140:13 ... #18 in DB::IPolygonDictionary::loadData() src/Dictionaries/PolygonDictionary.cpp:337:8 previously allocated by thread T468 (ThreadPool) here: #2 in DB::FileDictionarySource::loadAll() src/Dictionaries/FileDictionarySource.cpp:60:19 ``` `ISource.cpp:140` is the `onFinish()` call inside the `catch (...)` handler, and the freed 272-byte region is the `ReadBufferFromFile` that `FileDictionarySource::loadAll` handed to the format via `addBuffer`. ## How to reproduce Reproduces on master (26.8.1.1310) with the official `build_amd_asan_ubsan` binary, **8 out of 10 runs, with no ThreadFuzzer and no unusual settings**. Under ThreadFuzzer it hit on the first run. Run Fiddle: https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/06f26a34-d286-40a1-85f5-7d3e952d47b8 On a release build this prints only the load error and exits 53: `Code: 53. CAST AS Array can only be performed between same-dimensional Array ... While executing ParquetV3BlockInputFormat. (TYPE_MISMATCH)` — the 1 MiB write into freed memory is silent. On an ASan build the process dies with the report above instead (5/5 runs of exactly the commands above; 8/10 in an earlier variant, so it is a race, but a very wide one). The polygon dictionary is only a convenient way to make the pipeline throw mid-read while owning its `ReadBuffer` — the defect is in the format, not in the dictionary. ## Root cause `Prefetcher` protects only *its own* lifetime. `scheduleTask` captures the shutdown handle and each task takes `std::shared_lock(*_shutdown, std::try_to_lock)`; `~Prefetcher` calls `shutdown->shutdown()` (`ShutdownHelper`, `src/Common/threadPoolCallbackRunner.h:507`), which blocks until every in-flight task has released. As its own comment says, "`this` is safe to access as long as `shutdown_lock` is held". But `Prefetcher::reader` points at a `ReadBuffer` owned by `IInputFormat::owned_buffers`, an unrelated lifetime that the handshake does not cover: - `IInputFormat::onFinish()` -> `resetReadBuffer()` -> `resetOwnedBuffers()` -> `owned_buffers.clear()` - `ParquetV3BlockInputFormat` overrides `resetParser()` and `onCancel()`, but **not `resetReadBuffer()`**. `resetParser()` happens to be safe only because it destroys the reader *before* delegating to the base. `resetReadBuffer()` has no such ordering, so the buffer dies while the `ReadManager` -> `Reader` -> `Prefetcher` chain is still alive with tasks running. Three routes reach it: `onFinish()` from the `catch (...)` in `ISource::work()` (the one above), `onFinish()` on the normal completion path (`ISource.cpp:133`) with speculative prefetches still outstanding, and `IInputFormat::setReadBuffer` when a format is reused across files. ## Suggested fix Mirror what `resetParser()` already does, so `~Prefetcher` drains the IO tasks before the base frees the buffer: ```cpp void ParquetV3BlockInputFormat::resetReadBuffer() { /// ~Prefetcher waits for in-flight IO tasks, which read through the buffer that /// IInputFormat::resetReadBuffer() is about to free. { std::lock_guard lock(reader_mutex); reader.reset(); } IInputFormat::resetReadBuffer(); } ``` ## Additional context Distinct from #109678 / #112573. That was a data race on `AsynchronousBoundedReadBuffer::prefetch_future` consumed by concurrent `readBigAt` (the `RandomRead` branch, `Prefetcher.cpp:102`). This one is a lifetime bug in the `SeekAndRead` branch, which already holds `read_mutex` — locking cannot help once the object is freed — and the freed buffer here is a plain `ReadBufferFromFile`, so `AsynchronousBoundedReadBuffer` is not involved at all. The binary used above already contains #112573 (merged into 26.8.1.1240). Found by this Dolor run: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=94148&sha=a2ef409981fc77a168eaf8cc68d7ddf67c9fadec&name_0=PR&name_1=La+Casa+Del+Dolor+%28arm_asan_ubsan%29 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #114668 - Backported to: `26.7.4.42`, `26.5.7.56`, `26.3.18.30` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Custom-key parallel replicas over a Merge table with a Distributed child: children are offloaded to a finalized stage (CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE, logical error in GroupingAggregatedTransform)
signal.text: 🕵 Reading a `Merge` table (or the `merge` table function) with custom-key parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_mode = 'custom_key_sampling'` or `'custom_key_range'`) fails with an exception when the common processing stage of the children is `WithMergeableState` — for example, when one of the underlying tables is a `Distributed` table. ```sql CREATE TABLE t_mrg_ck_1 (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k AS SELECT number FROM numbers(100000); CREATE TABLE t_mrg_ck_2 (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k AS SELECT number FROM numbers(100000); CREATE TABLE t_mrg_ck_3 (k UInt64) ENGINE = Distributed('test_shard_localhost', currentDatabase(), 't_mrg_ck_1'); SET enable_parallel_replicas = 1, max_parallel_replicas = 3, cluster_for_parallel_replicas = 'test_cluster_one_shard_three_replicas_localhost', parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree = 1, parallel_replicas_mode = 'custom_key_sampling', parallel_replicas_custom_key = 'k'; SELECT count() FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t_mrg_ck_'); ``` ``` Code: 70. DB::Exception: Conversion from UInt64 to AggregateFunction(count) is not supported: while converting source column `count()` to destination column `count()`: Child table: default.t_mrg_ck_1. (CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE) ``` Depending on the aggregate function, it instead trips an assertion in the pipeline — an exception in debug and sanitizer builds (found by the AST fuzzer, STID `3970-479a`): ```sql SELECT 47, quantileExactInclusive(visibleWidth(['1', '2'])) IGNORE NULLS FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t_mrg_ck_') GROUP BY ALL LIMIT 973; ``` ``` Logical error: 'Chunk should have AggregatedChunkInfo/ChunkInfoWithAllocatedBytes in GroupingAggregatedTransform.'. ``` **Root cause.** The `Distributed` child reports `WithMergeableState` from its `getQueryProcessingStage`, so `StorageMerge::getQueryProcessingStage` sets the common stage of all children to `WithMergeableState`, and `ReadFromMerge::createPlanForTable` plans each `MergeTree` child through an interpreter with `SelectQueryOptions(WithMergeableState)`. Inside that child interpreter, the custom-key branch of `PlannerJoinTree` (`src/Planner/PlannerJoinTree.cpp`, the `canUseParallelReplicasCustomKey` block) offloads the child query to the replicas at the hard-coded stage `WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`, ignoring the requested `to_stage`. The child plan therefore produces finalized rows (post-aggregation, post-`LIMIT`) where the parent `ReadFromMerge` pipeline expects partial aggregation states: `convertAndFilterSourceStream` throws `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` when the finalized type differs from the state type, and when the types coincide structurally, the chunks without `AggregatedChunkInfo` reach `GroupingAggregatedTransform` and trip the assertion. Only the analyzer path is affected (`enable_analyzer = 0` returns correct results). Reproduced on current master (verified on a binary with no unrelated changes); found by the targeted AST fuzzer on https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972 (which is unrelated: the failure reproduces without `parallel_replicas_allow_merge_tables`, a setting that does not exist on master), report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110972&sha=ac0a584ce316ace31f4dbc16b38e1262a2344751&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29 The custom-key offload should be skipped when the requested `to_stage` is below `WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`: a plan that must stop at a partial stage cannot accept a finalized remote read. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972 <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #113742 - Backported to: `26.7.4.29`, `26.6.3.42`, `26.5.7.52`, `26.3.18.31`, `25.8.30.19` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Keep the function name of a stack frame attributed to a libc++ `__functional` header
signal.text: Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/57201 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100419 `collapseDemangledNames` replaced a stack frame's function name with `?` whenever the frame's source location was a file in a directory ending in `functional`. The intent was to hide `std::function` plumbing frames, whose demangled names spell out the whole captured lambda type and say nothing the neighbouring frames do not already say. But the file of a frame is the source line the *instruction* maps to, which is not necessarily where the enclosing function is defined. An ordinary function can have individual instructions attributed to a libc++ `__functional` header - an inlined `std::function` operation, or compiler-generated code reported with line 0 - and then its name was dropped too, which loses the only useful part of the frame. This PR requires the symbol to name the `std::function` plumbing as well: the type-erasing wrappers (`std::__function::__func`, `__value_func`, `__policy_func`, ...) and the type erasure of `std::function` itself - its `operator()`, its copy, move and callable-taking constructors and assignment operators, and its destructor. The ordinary members of `std::function` (`swap`, `target_type`, `operator bool`, the `nullptr` reset `operator=(std::nullptr_t)`, the empty-constructing `function()` / `function(std::nullptr_t)`, ...) do work of their own, so they keep their names too. Those are still displayed as `?`, exactly as before; every other frame keeps its name - not only an ordinary `DB` function, but also a meaningful libc++ symbol that happens to live in a `__functional` header, such as `std::hash<String>::operator()` from `__functional/hash.h`, or the generic invocation helpers `std::invoke` / `std::__invoke` / `std::mem_fn`, which are not `std::function`-specific and whose frames can name the callable they dispatch to. This is much more likely in a build with ThinLTO enabled, where `std::function` calls are inlined across translation units, so it went unnoticed for a long time: `amd_cfi` is the only integration-test build with ThinLTO on, and its `test_crash_log` failure is what surfaced it. In that build, the frame that actually terminated the server was displayed as ``` 8. contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__functional/function.h:0:7: ? @ 0x1c01f41f ``` both in the fatal log and in `trace_full` in `system.crash_log`, where `0x1c01f41f` is inside `DB::executeQuery` (the symbol resolves correctly - only the display suppressed it). Official release builds also use ThinLTO, so the same frames were being anonymised for users. `collapseDemangledNames` becomes a static member of `StackTrace` so that the heuristic is covered by a unit test in every build, rather than only by the weekly ThinLTO job. Fixes `test_crash_log/test.py::test_crash_log_extra_fields[terminate_with_exception-trace_full]` and `[terminate_with_std_exception-trace_full]`, seen in https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=b05161aa67d75ad84151a392f3e87156efd42842&name_0=WeeklyCFI&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28amd_cfi%2C%202%2F4%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a stack frame being displayed as `?` instead of its function name in fatal log messages and in the `trace_full` column of `system.crash_log`. It affected frames of ordinary functions that have code attributed to a libc++ `__functional` header, which is common in release builds. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1334` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.4.44`, `26.5.7.57` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.text: `DatabaseCatalog::checkTableCanBeRemovedOrRenamedUnlocked` skips dependent tables from the same database when the removal comes from `DROP DATABASE`, and carried a TODO asking for the tables to be unloaded in reverse topological order instead.
