signal.title: Row policy on the shard-local table is bypassed with `serialize_query_plan = 1` on a non-local replica
signal.text: 🕵 **Describe the bug** With `serialize_query_plan = 1`, a read shipped to a non-local replica of a `Distributed` table bypasses the row policy defined on the shard-local table: the receiving server deserializes an already-built read plan, so it never applies its own row policies. With `serialize_query_plan = 0` (text shipping) the same query is filtered correctly. This matters because defining the policy on the underlying local table is the documented way to filter reads that go through a `Distributed` table (`docs/en/sql-reference/statements/create/row-policy.md`), so the workaround silently returns unfiltered rows in this mode. **How to reproduce** Version: 26.8.1.1 (reproduced on `master`, commit `bde560d7b00`). Server config: a cluster `self` with one replica pointing back at the server itself, and `<process_query_plan_packet>1</process_query_plan_packet>`. ```sql CREATE TABLE rp_leaf (x UInt32, y UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x; INSERT INTO rp_leaf SELECT number, number FROM numbers(10); CREATE TABLE rp_dist AS rp_leaf ENGINE = Distributed('self', currentDatabase(), rp_leaf); CREATE ROW POLICY rp_l ON rp_leaf FOR SELECT USING y < 5 TO CURRENT_USER; SELECT count() FROM rp_dist SETTINGS prefer_localhost_replica = 0, serialize_query_plan = 0; -- 5, correct SELECT count() FROM rp_dist SETTINGS prefer_localhost_replica = 0, serialize_query_plan = 1; -- 10, policy skipped SELECT count() FROM rp_leaf; -- 5, correct ``` **Expected behavior** Both remote reads return `5`. Either the shipped plan carries the filter, or the receiving server re-applies its local row policies to the deserialized plan, or plan shipping is refused when the shard-local table has a row policy that applies (fail close). **Additional context** Two stateless tests already pin `serialize_query_plan = 0` for exactly this reason: - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04498_row_policy_role_scope_interserver.sh` - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04652_nested_merge_prewhere_type_mismatch.sql` (added by https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112326) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112326

signal.title: Delete Iceberg table files on DROP with iceberg_delete_data_on_drop
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108524 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `DROP TABLE` on an Iceberg table with `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop = 1` not deleting the table's files, which made re-creating a table at the same path fail with `TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS`. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108524 With `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop = 1`, `DROP TABLE` on an Iceberg table left the underlying files in place, so a later `CREATE TABLE` at the same path failed with `Iceberg table with path ... already exists (TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS)`. Long-standing (reproduces at least down to v25.9), not a recent regression. Two independent bugs, both in the self-managed Iceberg drop path: 1. `IcebergMetadata::drop` listed the files to delete with the table path passed as both the listing base and the prefix (`listFiles(..., table_path, table_path, "")`). `listFiles` keys on `path / prefix`, so it looked under `table_path/table_path` and matched nothing. Fixed by using an empty prefix so everything under the table path is enumerated (this matches the existing `create` and `Hudi` callers). 2. `StorageObjectStorage::drop` runs in a background pool and read `iceberg_delete_data_on_drop` from the global context, where it is always the default `false`, so the deletion never ran even after bug 1 was fixed. The value is now captured from the query context in `checkTableCanBeDropped` (called on the drop path with the query context, on the same storage object) and applied to a copy of the global context passed to the background drop. This is the same `mutable`-flag pattern `StorageNATS`/`StorageRabbitMQ` already use for drop-time state. Both the self-managed engine path (`Iceberg`/`IcebergLocal`) and the `DataLakeCatalog` database path go through the same `checkTableCanBeDropped` -> `drop()` on one storage instance, so both are covered. With the setting off (default) files are left in place, as before. Regression test `04365_iceberg_delete_data_on_drop_108524` fails without the fix (files survive the drop, re-create fails) and passes with it; it also checks the default-off behavior is unchanged.

signal.title: Do not install standalone symlinks for multi-call-only subcommands
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/36588 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/36588 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Build/Testing/Packaging Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Stop installing standalone `clickhouse-<name>` symlinks for subcommands that no package ships. This removes useless work from the CMake install step without changing the produced packages. ### Description Step 1 of #36588. `ninja programs/install` copied a `clickhouse-<name>` symlink into the packaging root (`<build>/root/usr/bin/`) for every subcommand registered via `clickhouse_program_install`. nfpm builds every package strictly from the explicit `src:` entries in `packages/clickhouse-*.yaml` (no globs), and 14 of those symlinks are referenced by no manifest, so installing them only populated the staging tree. This splits the helper into: - `clickhouse_program_link(name lib)` - link the subcommand library into the multi-call binary and create the `clickhouse-<name>` symlink in the build directory (no install); - `clickhouse_program_install(name lib [aliases...])` - the same, plus install the standalone symlink (and aliases) for packaging. 14 subcommands are switched to `clickhouse_program_link`: `check-marks`, `checksum-for-compressed-block`, `disks`, `docker-init`, `git-import`, `oom-canary`, `packed-io`, `static-files-disk-uploader`, `su`, `zookeeper-dump-tree`, `zookeeper-remove-by-list`, `keeper-data-dumper`, `keeper-utils`, `keeper-bench`. The criterion is the packaging reference, not the invocation surface. Two of the 14, `clickhouse-disks` and `clickhouse-git-import`, are also symlinked by `clickhouse install` from its own `tools` list in `programs/install/Install.cpp`. That path is unaffected: it symlinks from the binary it has just copied itself, and never reads this staging tree. The build-tree symlinks and the multi-call dispatch table in `programs/main.cpp` are unchanged, so `clickhouse <name>` keeps working. Verified by configuring the tree with and without this change, everything else identical: the installed set drops exactly those 14 symlinks and gains none, and all 30 build-tree `create_symlink` commands are still generated. Packages are unaffected. Step 2 of the issue (dropping CMake `install` entirely in favour of direct build-directory paths in the packaging YAML) is a deliberate follow-up.

signal.title: Fix `rows_before_limit_at_least` under parallel replicas local plan (#113279)
signal.text: ### Problem Closes #113279 With parallel replicas enabled (`parallel_replicas_local_plan = 1`, the default), queries with a `LIMIT` incorrectly report `rows_before_limit_at_least = 0`, even when `exact_rows_before_limit = 1`. Under `parallel_replicas_local_plan = 0` or standard non-parallel execution, the exact total rows before limit is correctly reported. ### Root Cause When building the local replica plan for parallel replicas, the query is planned at `QueryProcessingStage::WithMergeableState`. However, `createLocalPlanForParallelReplicas` (`src/Processors/QueryPlan/ParallelReplicasLocalPlan.cpp`) previously initialized `select_query_options.is_local_shard_plan` checking only `processed_stage == QueryProcessingStage::WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`. Because `is_local_shard_plan` evaluated to `false`, `addPreliminaryLimitStep` in `src/Planner/Planner.cpp` did not invoke `limit->markAsShardLimit()` on the local branch's preliminary `LimitStep`. During pipeline initialization in `initRowsBeforeLimit` (`src/QueryPipeline/QueryPipeline.cpp`), this unmarked limit transform was treated as a query-level accounting boundary rather than an internal shard limit, terminating the processor traversal early without attaching the rows-before-limit counter to the local input pipeline. Consequently, when the reading coordinator routed read granules to the local replica, the statistics counter remained 0. ### Solution In `createLocalPlanForParallelReplicas`, mark `select_query_options.is_local_shard_plan` as true when `processed_stage` is either `WithMergeableState` or `WithMergeableStateAfterAggregationAndLimit`. This ensures the preliminary limit on the local replica branch is recognized as a shard limit, allowing `initRowsBeforeLimit` to traverse through it and attach the counter to the local input stream, matching remote replica behavior. ### Test Plan - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/02590_parallel_replicas_local_plan_rows_before_limit.sh` and reference asserting `rows_before_limit_at_least` returns the correct row count under `parallel_replicas_local_plan = 1`.

signal.title: `WindowTransform`: stream `lagInFrame` via `StreamingLagTransform` to…
signal.text: This is the first time I'm creating a PR in ClickHouse respository, there might be things not correct. Please forgive and I'll correct the issues. It involves several classes. Motivation This is for issue: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105466 Queries of the form: SELECT sum(prev_count) FROM (SELECT lagInFrame(Count) OVER (PARTITION BY MetricName, Attributes, ResourceAttributes ORDER BY TimeUnix) AS prev_count On a MergeTree table ordered by (MetricName, TimeUnix) previously required a FinishSortingTransform that buffered all rows within each MetricName group before sort-completing them by Attributes and ResourceAttributes. For wide partitions this means O(rows per prefix group) peak memory and an O(N log N) sort pass — even though lagInFrame with offset 1 only needs the single previous row per partition key. Approach Introduces StreamingLagTransform, a new ISimpleTransform that replaces the FinishSortingTransform + WindowTransform pair when: All window functions are lagInFrame with offset 1 (one-, two-, or three-argument form; offset argument must be a constant equal to 1). The SortingStep is in FinishSorting mode (storage ordering already covers the partition prefix). The prefix description is a strict prefix of the window PARTITION BY. The transform keeps a small hash map — one Field per distinct suffix-partition key, keyed by SipHash128 — and emits the stored previous value on each row. When the prefix key changes (e.g. MetricName changes), the map is cleared. A new SortingStep::Type::MergeOnly replaces FinishSorting in the activated path: it merges K sorted input streams into one (by the full storage ORDER BY) without finish-sorting, so StreamingLagTransform receives rows in the correct per-partition window order. The optimization is gated by query_plan_reuse_storage_ordering_for_window_functions (default off) and wired in as a bottom-up pass in optimizeTree after the existing read-in-order pass. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry: Added a streaming execution path for `lagInFrame(col, 1)` window functions when data is already read in storage `ORDER BY` order. Instead of buffering an entire prefix group in `FinishSortingTransform` + `WindowTransform`, a new `StreamingLagTransform` processes rows in a single pass with a small per-partition hash map, reducing peak memory from O(rows per prefix group) to O(distinct partitions per prefix group). Enabled via `query_plan_reuse_storage_ordering_for_window_functions = 1`. Performance Before (master): SELECT sum(prev_count) FROM ( SELECT lagInFrame(Count) OVER (PARTITION BY MetricName, Attributes, ResourceAttributes ORDER BY TimeUnix) AS prev_count FROM ch_metrics_histogram_table ) 1 row in set. Elapsed: 1.939 sec. Processed 3.00 million rows, 873.63 MB (1.55 million rows/s., 450.56 MB/s.) Peak memory usage: 2.57 GiB. After (this PR): SELECT sum(prev_count) FROM ( SELECT lagInFrame(Count) OVER (PARTITION BY MetricName, Attributes, ResourceAttributes ORDER BY TimeUnix) AS prev_count FROM ch_metrics_histogram_table ) SETTINGS query_plan_reuse_storage_ordering_for_window_functions = 1, max_threads = 4 1 row in set. Elapsed: 4.317 sec. Processed 3.00 million rows, 873.63 MB (694.99 thousand rows/s., 202.39 MB/s.) Peak memory usage: 154.85 MiB. Peak memory: 2.57 GiB → 154.85 MiB (17× reduction). The streaming path trades read parallelism for memory — reads are serialized per prefix group so rows arrive pre-sorted, which is the correct trade-off for workloads hitting OOM.

signal.title: Fix vertical merge nested default corruption
signal.text: ### Summary --- Vertical merge gathers columns one at a time. When a column has `DEFAULT` that references another column which is absent from all source parts and has no `DEFAULT` itself – that dependency is already expired and won't be in the block during evaluateMissingDefaults. Expression engine substitutes a typeless empty value for it, the resulting column gets wrong outer array dimensions, and this corrupts shared Nested offsets when written to the merged part. This is challenge (1) from [#91127](https://github.com/germiBest/ClickHouse/issues/91127). Fix extends existing column expiration logic to transitively expire columns whose DEFAULT depends on already-expired column. Since these columns were never present in any source part, read path was already computing them on-the-fly with full column context available – so expiring them during merge changes nothing for the end user. Fixes [#86123](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/86123). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix silent data corruption during vertical merge when a Nested subcolumn added via ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN has a DEFAULT expression that depends on another missing column without a default. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Stop exchange sinks when the consumer needs no more data
signal.text: A distributed-plan query with a satisfied `LIMIT` kept all upstream stages running to completion: an exchange sink consumed and dropped the rest of the stream after the consumer sent `NoMoreDataNeeded`, so the client received the result while the query kept running until cancelled. Now the sink closes its input instead, and the stop propagates backward through the stages the same way a local `LimitTransform` stops its producers. The in-memory exchange reader also detaches when its output port is closed, not only on cancellation. The new test covers a `LIMIT` in the middle of the plan: the stage that satisfies it finishes early and the stop crosses two exchange layers down to the scans. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A distributed plan query (`make_distributed_plan`) now stops its upstream stages when a `LIMIT` is satisfied, instead of computing the full result and discarding it. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

I can try to fix this in the next few days 🙏 ### Describe what's wrong When using `DataLakeCatalog()` engine to connect to Apache Polaris REST catalog with vended S3 credentials, ClickHouse incorrectly constructs the S3 object path by duplicating the table location path. The table path However, the table path already includes the full location, resulting in duplication. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce **Prerequisites:** 1. signal.title: Report RabbitMQ container recreations absorbed by the startup retry
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114415 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114434 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description #114415 made the RabbitMQ readiness waiter recreate a container that fails to start and try again, turning a 21-case module abort into a passing run. When the second attempt succeeds, every channel that could record the first failure closes at once: artifact collection is gated on a failing suite (`if failed_suits:`), the report log strips setup logs from passed tests (`--report-log-exclude-logs-on-passed-tests`), and `job.log` never carried harness logging. The recovered failure survives only as an anomalous duration on the module's first test: +123.5 s against a p99 of 13.4 s over 7774 runs of that test and lane. So a retry-absorbed run discards exactly the diagnostics #114415 added to show where a hang is stuck. Now: - the waiter copies the failed attempt's `rabbit.log` out of the instance directory before recreating the container (that directory is removed on teardown) and emits a stable `RABBITMQ_RECREATE` token. The copy is named per process, cluster, waiter call and attempt, because S3 upload keys use the basename alone; - at job end the script counts those tokens across the per-worker pytest logs, puts the count in `Result.info` and attaches the preserved logs, whatever the outcome. The failure-gated paths are left alone. A recreation is not itself a verdict, so only `info` and `files` are touched: status and labels stay as the test results set them, and the count is appended after the job's own `Failures: N/M` summary rather than replacing it. Forcing a retry on a healthy host passes, and the count reaches `result_*.json` with the 107,336 B broker log attached. The same run with the reporting removed attaches nothing; a run that never retried writes no count; a forced-red run keeps its `Failures: 1/1`. `test_system_stop.py` is 21 passed. Both sides are unit-tested, each arm checked against a mutation of the code it pins.

signal.title: Test: merge memory is not bounded by max_memory_usage (merge OOM repro)
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107389 --> Draft. A test demonstrating that a background merge's memory is **not** bounded by the per-query `max_memory_usage` setting. ### Motivation In the AST fuzzer run for #107389 ([CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107389&sha=ec12cb3ce0a49a403226cb0668b092f02a2fa3f6&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29)) the server was OOM-killed even though the fuzzer runs queries **sequentially** and no single query peaked above 1.69 GiB. During the steepest part of the memory climb there were *zero* foreground queries running — only background merges. The fuzzer's `INSERT`s left behind parts (large arrays from `arrayResize`, very wide schemas up to 1796 columns) that the background merge subsystem then combined; that memory accumulates across query boundaries and is governed by the global / background-pool trackers, not by the per-query limit. A merge runs under its own memory tracker — a child of the global `Background process (mutate/merge)` tracker — created in `ThreadGroup::createForMergeMutate`. `configureMemoryTrackerFromSettings` never installs `max_memory_usage` as the merge tracker's hard limit, so the per-query limit does not constrain a merge at all. ### What the test does - Creates a `MergeTree` table and inserts two parts of large arrays (forcing a horizontal merge). - Sets a tiny `max_memory_usage` (20 MB). - Runs `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` — the merge **completes** despite the limit. - Confirms via `system.part_log` that the merge's `peak_memory_usage` (~110 MiB observed) is far above the per-query limit. The test asserts behavior with a generous margin, so it does not literally OOM-kill the CI server (that would be destructive and flaky). It reliably reproduces the *condition* that leads to OOM: a merge consuming memory the per-query limit never sees. It is intended as the regression/repro basis for extending the memory-overcommit mechanism to merges (today `OvercommitTracker` only selects victims from `ProcessList`, i.e. user queries; merges — which are restartable and therefore cheaper to cancel than queries — do not participate). ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Do not disable the query condition cache for materialized lightweight deletes
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107145 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113239 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/83259 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104985 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a performance regression where a single lightweight `DELETE` disabled the query condition cache for the whole table. Repeated selective queries over a table that had ever been touched by a lightweight delete stopped pruning granules and fell back to reading every mark. ### Description #### The regression Deleting **one row** stops the query condition cache from pruning anything, for the entire table, permanently. ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, val String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toString(number % 97) FROM numbers(1000000); DELETE FROM t WHERE id = 0; -- the whole trigger SYSTEM DROP QUERY CONDITION CACHE; SELECT count() FROM t WHERE val = 'nope_nope'; -- run this 3 times ``` `ProfileEvents['SelectedMarks']` per run: | version | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 | |---|---|---|---| | 26.3 (before the backport) | 122 | **0** | **0** | | 26.4 / 26.6 / master | 122 | **122** | **122** | Same behaviour with `mutations_sync = 2`, so this is not a pending-mutation window: it persists after the delete is fully materialized. This was found on a production table (24M rows, 5 parts) where exactly one part carried `has_lightweight_delete = 1`. That part has 4318 marks; the four small parts have 6 between them. The affected version pruned the four small parts and read all 4318 marks of the big one on every repetition, turning a **0.03 s** query into **0.8-2.0 s**. An `INSERT ... SELECT *` copy of the same table into a fresh table did not reproduce, which is what pointed at `_row_exists` rather than the schema or the data. Bisected to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107145. #### Root cause `MergeTreeReadPoolBase` appends two different kinds of thing to the same `mutation_steps` list: ```cpp if (reader_settings.apply_deleted_mask && has_lightweight_delete) read_task_info.mutation_steps.push_back(createLightweightDeleteStep(...)); // committed part data if (read_task_info.alter_conversions->hasMutations()) ...append... // pending, per-query ``` and `appliesMutationsBeforePrewhere()` was `!info->mutation_steps.empty() || !info->patch_parts.empty()`. The reasoning in #107145 is correct for anything whose effect varies between queries: a mark emptied by an on-fly mutation must not be attributed to the predicate, or a later `apply_mutations_on_fly = 0` query reusing that entry loses rows. A **materialized** `_row_exists` mask is not that. It is committed part data, every query reading the part observes exactly the same rows, and a mark it empties is attributable to the predicate like any other. The read path already draws this line correctly - it bypasses on `hasDataMutations()` and `hasPatchParts()`, but not on `hasLightweightDeletedMask()`. So the write side was not actually made symmetric with the read side; it was made stricter. #### The fix **Part 1 - key the check off the source of the filter, not the resulting step list** (`MergeTreeReadTask.cpp`). Patch parts and mutations coming from the mutations snapshot stay disqualifying. `alter_conversions->hasLightweightDelete()` keeps an *unmaterialized* lightweight delete disqualifying, because that one really is applied from the snapshot at read time and varies with `apply_mutations_on_fly`. A materialized mask no longer disables the cache. This is a narrowing of an over-broad condition; every case #107145 set out to cover is still covered. **Part 2 - keep `apply_deleted_mask = 0` out of the cache** (`MergeTreeIOSettings.cpp`, `MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor.cpp`). Part 1 leaves exactly one way for the mask to vary between queries. Only one direction is unsound: - `apply_deleted_mask = 1` writes, `= 0` reads: **unsound**. The writer saw fewer rows and may record "no match" for a granule whose only matching rows are deleted; the reader must return those rows. - `= 0` writes, `= 1` reads: sound. The writer saw a superset, so its verdict is conservative. `apply_deleted_mask` is a debugging aid, so such queries simply do not read or write the cache. That is cheaper and easier to reason about than splitting the key space, and it costs nothing on the default path. #### Tests New `04669_query_condition_cache_lightweight_delete`: - a materialized lightweight delete still prunes on a repeat query (fails before this change: the second run reads every mark) - an `apply_deleted_mask = 0` read does not consume an entry written by a normal read, and the reverse order is also correct - results stay correct with the cache warm - a repeated `apply_deleted_mask = 0` query does not prune, which is the one behaviour Part 2 gives up. Pinned deliberately: keying entries by `apply_deleted_mask` instead of excluding them (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113239) has to update that block. The effectiveness assertions demand that the repeat reads *no* marks rather than fewer marks than the first run. Only the part holding the deleted row carries the mask, so with a weaker assertion a multi-part table would satisfy it through the other parts pruning and the test would pass with the bug present. New `04670_query_condition_cache_unique_key` covers `UNIQUE KEY` tables, which is where the one internal reader that turns the mask off lives (building a part's dense index reads its `UNIQUE KEY` columns with `apply_deleted_mask = 0`, in `UniqueKeyDenseIndexOps::readUniqueKeyColumns`). Two independent reasons keep such tables away from anything this PR changes, and the test pins both: - a `UNIQUE KEY` read never uses the cache. `ReadFromMergeTree` disables it for both the write and the consult side, because the cache is CSN-oblivious while the delete bitmap is not; there is a `TODO(unique-key)` to revisit it with a snapshot-aware cache. - no `UNIQUE KEY` part can carry a materialized mask, because mutation-class commands are rejected on such tables, `DELETE FROM` included. Re-enabling the cache for `UNIQUE KEY` reads now has to come past this test, which is the point: that work has to look at the mask and bitmap interaction rather than only flipping the flag. The unmaterialized/on-fly direction is already covered by `03229_query_condition_cache_on_fly_mutations`, added by #107145, which must keep passing. #### Backports #107145 was backported to `26.5.6.46`, `26.4.5.134` and `26.3.17.50`, so every one of those lines is affected and needs this fix. Note `26.3` is LTS and is affected from `26.3.17.50` onward. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Backported to: `26.7.3.13`, `26.6.3.2` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions `sort()` and `sort_desc()`
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `sort()` and `sort_desc()`. ### Description Implements two PromQL functions that were previously rejected with a not-implemented error: - `sort(v instant-vector)` — returns vector elements sorted by their sample values in ascending order. - `sort_desc(v instant-vector)` — same, but descending. These functions do not modify sample values; they only affect the output ordering of instant queries (range query results always have a fixed ordering, as in Prometheus). The implementation adds a `sort_direction` field to `SQLQueryPiece` (0 = none, 1 = ascending, -1 = descending). A new `applySortFunction` converter acts as a pass-through: it forwards the argument's `SQLQueryPiece` unchanged and sets `sort_direction` accordingly. `finalizeInstantVectorAsSQL` then appends `ORDER BY value ASC/DESC` to the final SQL when `sort_direction` is set. Nesting behaviour matches Prometheus: the outermost sort wins (`sort(sort_desc(up))` produces ascending output). The metric name is preserved (sort does not drop `__name__`), consistent with Prometheus. Sort composed with a math operator (e.g. `sort(up * 2)`) correctly reflects the operator's metric-name dropping in the output tags. No parser changes were needed — the ANTLR grammar already accepts any function name, and `getFunctionResultType` already returns `INSTANT_VECTOR` for `sort`/`sort_desc`. **Testing**: new parser cases in `gtest_PromQLParser.cpp` for `sort(v)`, `sort_desc(v)`, and `sort(abs(v))`; new stateless test `04550_promql_sort_sort_desc.sh` covering `sort(up)`, `sort_desc(up)`, `sort(sort_desc(up))`, and `sort(up * 2)` against a 3-series TimeSeries table with deliberately unsorted values (30, 10, 20).

signal.title: Apply HAVING without aggregation in the old analyzer
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113760 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results with `enable_analyzer = 0` when a query has a `HAVING` clause but no aggregation: the condition was silently ignored and excluded rows were returned. `HAVING` is now merged into `WHERE` for such queries, matching the new analyzer. ### Description With `enable_analyzer = 0`, a `SELECT` that has a `HAVING` clause but no aggregation silently discarded the condition and returned rows it excludes. Over a MergeTree table holding 1, 2, 3: ```sql SELECT a FROM t HAVING a > 999 SETTINGS enable_analyzer = 0, enable_optimize_predicate_expression = 0; -- returned 1, 2, 3; the new analyzer returns nothing ``` Root cause: the old analyzer builds and executes a `HAVING` filter only in its aggregation branch (`appendHaving` is called under `if (need_aggregate)`, and `executeHaving` is reachable only from inside `else if (expressions.need_aggregate)`), so without aggregation the clause is never applied. What normally hides this is `PredicateExpressionsOptimizer` moving non-aggregate conjuncts to `WHERE`, i.e. a performance optimizer was load-bearing for correctness with no interpreter fallback. It also fails at default settings when a stateful conjunct makes `tryMovePredicatesFromHavingToWhere` bail out, so `HAVING a > 999 AND blockNumber() >= 0` reproduces with `enable_analyzer = 0` alone. This merges `HAVING` into `WHERE` in `TreeRewriter::analyzeSelect` when the query does not aggregate, the canonicalization the new analyzer already performs in `Planner.cpp:2231-2238`. The interpreter, `ExpressionAnalyzer` and `PredicateExpressionsOptimizer` are unchanged. The site sits after `getAggregates` and `getWindowFunctions` so `NOT_AN_AGGREGATE` and `ILLEGAL_AGGREGATION` keep being raised, after `PredicateExpressionsOptimizer` so the default path is a no-op, and outside the `ast_optimizations_allowed` gate so it also applies on shards. Validation: `EXPLAIN` shows no `Filter` step before; after the fix the predicate reaches the storage and prunes (`Parts: 0/1`). 33 query shapes now agree across the old analyzer, the old analyzer with the rewrite enabled and the new analyzer; 20 disagreed before. `NOT_AN_AGGREGATE`, `ILLEGAL_AGGREGATION` and the `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` for `WITH TOTALS` without aggregation are unchanged and pinned by the new test. Distributed and `remote()` queries were checked on a two-shard cluster. The 44 stateless tests setting `enable_optimize_predicate_expression` pass, 589 further `HAVING` and `*analyzer*` tests show no regression.

signal.title: Coordinate a read with pinned block numbers in classic parallel replicas
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114263 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/97557 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results when a `SELECT` with `select_sequential_consistency = 1` on a `ReplicatedMergeTree` table runs with classic (task-based) parallel replicas. Every replica performed a complete local read clamped to the quorum boundary instead of a coordinator-assigned slice, so rows were returned once per participating replica. ### Description `StorageReplicatedMergeTree::read` routes a `select_sequential_consistency = 1` query into `readLocalSequentialConsistencyImpl`, which called `MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor::read` with `enable_parallel_reading` hardcoded to `false`. The setting is propagated to the followers, so each follower took that same branch: `read_task_callback` was never installed, the follower never announced its parts, and it read the whole pinned range locally. The initiator then merged N complete copies. On a 5-part `ReplicatedMergeTree` with a pinned boundary of 12000 rows and `max_parallel_replicas = 3`, `count()` returned 36000 and `sum()` was likewise tripled, with no exception and no warning. It scaled exactly linearly with `max_parallel_replicas`, and `uniqExact` stayed correct, confirming pure per-replica duplication. Reaching the defect requires turning off one of the optimizations that would otherwise bypass this read path: `optimize_trivial_count_query = 0` for `count()`, since at its default the planner serves the count from `totalRows()` and disables parallel replicas, or `parallel_replicas_local_plan = 0` or `parallel_replicas_prefer_local_replica = 0` for data reads. All three are documented, settable per query, and leave the wrong result silent. The fix passes `canUseParallelReplicasOnFollower()` at that call site, exactly as the sibling `readLocalImpl` already does for the non-pinned path, so the pinned read participates in coordination instead of being silently excluded from it. The boundary stays computed and applied: when it binds it comes from ZooKeeper and is identical on every replica (measured on two replicas holding different part sets, 7 and 6 active parts, both clamping to the same block), and with no quorum node it is the replica's own maximum, which excludes nothing it owns. Validation: new test `04912_pr_classic_pinned_block_numbers` fails on master and passes with the change, 50/50 green under randomized settings. Full matrix in the validation-gate comment below. Out of scope, neither introduced nor altered here: the plan-based path with `parallel_replicas_local_plan = 0` (#114263), and divergent part sets with no quorum node (#105710).

signal.title: Reject `arrayJoin` in a mixed JOIN ON condition in hash joins
signal.text: Reject `arrayJoin` in a mixed JOIN ON condition in hash joins <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104785 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104785 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112831 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a logical error and wrong results when a non equi `JOIN ON` condition that is evaluated during the join contains `arrayJoin`. A `hash`, `parallel_hash` or `grace_hash` join now rejects such a condition with `INVALID_JOIN_ON_EXPRESSION`. Where the expansion depends on one side only, move it into an `ARRAY JOIN` in a subquery before the join; a condition whose `arrayJoin` argument reads columns from both sides has to be restructured. ### Description A non equi `JOIN ON` condition that mixes columns from both sides becomes a residual filter which `buildAdditionalFilter` evaluates once per probe batch, after which `joinRightColumnsWithAdditionalFilter` indexes the resulting mask by row position. That requires the condition to preserve the number of rows. `arrayJoin` does not. `ActionsDAG::ActionType::ARRAY_JOIN` is the only row-count-changing action, and nothing removes it from the residual when the condition spans both sides. Two user-visible effects. An `arrayJoin` over an empty array makes the mask shorter than the batch, which reads past the end of a `PaddedPODArray` and raises a logical error, aborting the server in debug and sanitizer builds. An `arrayJoin` that multiplies rows makes the mask longer, so flags pair with the wrong rows and the query silently returns wrong results. Found by the stress test, STID `2508-224e`: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111493&sha=2054925548cba91a78383141bd49da2126f92307&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29). The fix rejects such a condition in `HashJoin::validateAdditionalFilterExpression`, which already enforces this expression's contract. One-sided `arrayJoin` is hoisted into a pre-join step and keeps working, so the supported shapes of #104785 are unaffected, as is a plain `INNER` join, which pushes the condition down instead of building a residual. Most refused shapes only look plausible: measured against a pre-join oracle with a selective residual they diverge there too. One does not. A single element `arrayJoin` does preserve the number of rows and returned the oracle value, and it is refused anyway, because the replication factor is only known while the expression runs, so there is no static row-count property to test at this point. <details> <summary>Documented behavior impact</summary> The restricted surface is `arrayJoin`, including its `unnest` alias, in a `JOIN ON` condition evaluated during the join. No setting, syntax element, engine argument or error code changes. Two documented flows promised the old behavior and are updated here: `docs/en/sql-reference/functions/array-join.md` and `docs/en/sql-reference/statements/select/join.md`, plus their published `docs/reference/` counterparts and the `arrayJoin` function documentation. No other page promises this shape. Migration path: an `ARRAY JOIN` in a subquery before the join, which covers every refused shape whose expansion depends on one side only; a bilateral argument such as `arrayJoin(arrayConcat(t1.arr, t2.arr))` cannot be expanded by either input subquery and has to be restructured. `ClickHouse/clickhouse-docs` holds only translated mirrors, regenerated by the docs team. Fleet usage of the refused shape is not quantified here; please run that scan before this reaches a Cloud release branch. </details>

signal.title: Support PromQL timestamp() function on both vector selectors and general expressions
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: `timestamp()` is now implemented for both direct selectors and general expressions, matching Prometheus 3.5.0 semantics. ### Description `timestamp(<expression>)` previously threw `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. This PR implements `timestamp()` support for both direct vector selectors and general instant vector expressions (e.g. `timestamp(test)`, `timestamp(test offset 1m)`, `timestamp(test * 1)`, `timestamp(-test)`, `timestamp(timestamp(test))`). Matching Prometheus 3.5.0 semantics: - For direct instant vector selectors (plus optional direct `offset`/`@` modifiers), extracts the raw sample timestamp from storage via `timeSeriesTimestampToGrid`. - For general instant vector expressions (binary math, unary operators, comparisons, nested `timestamp()` calls), evaluates the argument as an instant vector and returns the query step evaluation timestamp ($T_{\text{eval}}$) for each present sample. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0**, including the timestamp-unit conversion (seconds, not milliseconds). **Testing**: Added integration test cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering bare vector selectors, offset/@ modifiers, binary math, unary minus, and nested `timestamp()` calls.

signal.title: optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup does not work with views
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the situation `optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup` (#91164) rewrites `dictGet(dict, attr, key) = const` into a key-column filter that the primary index can use. This rewrite happens when the `dictGet(...)` call is written directly in the query. It does not happen when the same predicate is expressed as a filter on a **view** column that is itself defined as `dictGet(...)`. The view case falls back to a full-table scan. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Found on 26.7 ### How to reproduce ```sql CREATE TABLE dim_source ( dim_id UInt64, dim_code String ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY dim_id; INSERT INTO dim_source SELECT number, substring(lower(hex(sipHash64(number))), 1, 8) FROM numbers(1000); CREATE DICTIONARY dim_dict ( dim_id UInt64, dim_code String ) PRIMARY KEY dim_id SOURCE(CLICKHOUSE(TABLE 'dim_source')) LAYOUT(HASHED()) LIFETIME(MIN 0 MAX 0); CREATE TABLE fact ( dim_id UInt64, created_at DateTime, metric Float64 ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY dim_id; INSERT INTO fact SELECT number % 1000, now() - number, rand() / 1e9 FROM numbers(1000000); INSERT INTO fact SELECT number % 1000, now() - number, rand() / 1e9 FROM numbers(1000000); INSERT INTO fact SELECT number % 1000, now() - number, rand() / 1e9 FROM numbers(1000000); CREATE VIEW fact_v AS SELECT dim_id, dictGet('dim_dict', 'dim_code', dim_id) AS dim_code, created_at, metric FROM fact; ```sql SET optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup = 1; -- (1) works: dictGet() written directly in the query EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT * FROM fact WHERE dictGet('dim_dict', 'dim_code', dim_id) = assumeNotNull((SELECT dim_code FROM dim_source WHERE dim_id = 723)); -- ┌─explain──────────────────────────────────┐ -- 1. │ Output: dim_id, created_at, metric │ -- 2. │ │ -- 3. │ ReadFromMergeTree (rnorgren.fact) │ -- 4. │ Read type: Default │ -- 5. │ Parts: 3 | Granules: 3 │ -- 6. │ Output: dim_id, created_at, metric │ -- 7. │ Prewhere filter │ -- 8. │ Prewhere filter column: dim_id = 723 │ -- 9. │ Indexes: │ -- 10. │ PrimaryKey │ -- 11. │ Keys: │ -- 12. │ dim_id │ -- 13. │ Condition: (dim_id in [723, 723]) │ -- 14. │ Parts: 3/3 │ -- 15. │ Granules: 3/369 │ -- 16. │ Search Algorithm: binary search │ -- 17. │ Ranges: 3 │ -- └──────────────────────────────────────────┘ -- (2) fails: identical predicate, but via a view column aliasing dictGet() EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT * FROM fact_v WHERE dim_code = assumeNotNull((SELECT dim_code FROM dim_source WHERE dim_id = 723)); -- ┌─explain───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ -- 1. │ Output: dim_id, dictGet('rnorgren.dim_dict'_String, 'dim_code'_String, dim_id), created_at, metric │ -- 2. │ │ -- 3. │ ReadFromMergeTree (rnorgren.fact) │ -- 4. │ Read type: Default │ -- 5. │ Parts: 3 | Granules: 369 │ -- 6. │ Output: dim_id, dictGet('rnorgren.dim_dict'_String, 'dim_code'_String, dim_id), created_at, metric │ -- 7. │ Prewhere filter │ -- 8. │ Prewhere filter column: dictGet('rnorgren.dim_dict', 'dim_code', dim_id) = '4810f1b6' │ -- 9. │ Indexes: │ -- 10. │ PrimaryKey │ -- 11. │ Condition: true │ -- 12. │ Parts: 3/3 │ -- 13. │ Granules: 369/369 │ -- 14. │ Ranges: 3 │ -- └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` ### Expected performance Both `EXPLAIN` plans show the primary index pruned to the matching `dim_id`, e.g.: ``` PrimaryKey Condition: (dim_id in [723, 723]) Parts: 3/3 Granules: 3/369 ``` ## Actual behavior Query (1) prunes correctly. Query (2) does not — `PrimaryKey Condition: true`, all parts and granules are read, despite the `Prewhere filter column` being identical to query (1)'s once the view's `dim_code` alias is inlined. This suggests `InverseDictionaryLookupPass` runs before the query-plan-level predicate pushdown that inlines a view's projection expression into the outer filter, so it never sees the combined `dictGet(...) = const` shape when the predicate originates outside the view. ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions clamp(), clamp_min(), clamp_max() and round()
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `clamp`, `clamp_min`, `clamp_max`, and `round`. ### Description Implements four PromQL functions previously reported as not implemented: - `clamp(v, min, max)`, `clamp_min(v, min)`, `clamp_max(v, max)` — new `applyClampFunction` converter mapping to `greatest`/`least` SQL with explicit guards, because vectorized `least`/`greatest` in ClickHouse treat NaN as the largest value and ignore NULLs, which would corrupt NaN sample values and missing points. Prometheus special cases are reproduced exactly: `min > max` returns an empty vector, and a NaN bound propagates NaN. - `round(v[, to_nearest])` — new `applyRoundFunction` converter; replicates Prometheus inverse arithmetic (`floor(v * (1/to_nearest) + 0.5) / (1/to_nearest)`), including ties rounding toward `+Inf` and NaN propagation for `to_nearest = 0` or NaN. Both drop the metric name from results, matching Prometheus. Non-constant scalar bounds (for example, `clamp(v, time()*0-1, 2)`) are supported. No parser changes were needed; arity is enforced by each converter. The embedded support matrices for `prometheusQuery` and `prometheusQueryRange` list the new math functions and retain the implemented range functions `increase`, `changes`, and `resets`. **Semantics verified against Prometheus 3.5.0** for bound combinations `(0, 1)`, `(0, 1e12)`, `(1e12, 0)`, `(1e12, 1e12)`, and fractional `to_nearest`. **Testing**: adds `test_clamp` and `test_round`, plus conversion and aggregation regressions for empty scalar handling and a runtime scalar `quantile` parameter outside `[0, 1]`.

signal.title: Share one referenced input subplan across sibling correlated subqueries
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a query plan growing exponentially with the number of correlated subqueries in one expression when `correlated_subqueries_use_in_memory_buffer` is disabled, which made such a query spend minutes in planning and consume tens of gigabytes. A query with eight sibling correlated subqueries now builds 226 plan steps instead of 6895. ### Description A `WHERE`/`SELECT` expression containing several correlated subqueries decorrelates them one at a time. `addExpressionStep` validates all of them against the header captured *before* that loop, but each subquery referenced the input subplan root as it stood *during* its own iteration, so subquery `k` referenced a subtree already containing subqueries `1..k-1`. When the referenced result is not buffered, the materialization pass clones each referenced root together with the references nested inside it, and the node count doubles per subquery. Measured plan steps for N sibling subqueries (`correlated_subqueries_use_in_memory_buffer = 0`): 415 at N = 4 rising to 6895 at N = 8, i.e. exactly `2^N`, reaching 68 GB of resident memory at N = 8. The buffer is also disabled whenever `correlated_subqueries_default_join_kind = 'left'`, so the blow-up is reachable by changing that one setting alone; `make_distributed_plan = 1` forces the buffer off as well (`SettingsQuirks.cpp`). Found as a `Stress test (arm_tsan)` hung check, where a cancelled `INSERT ... SELECT` sat 426 s in plan optimization with 1,670,597 plan nodes (N of about 17, for a `SELECT` repeating one correlated alias 20 times). CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114072&sha=08c0cd1e799e63d9cf42a2402776fa2ce09c9bc7&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 The fix creates one referenced root per expression and reuses it for every sibling. It is used only when the in-memory buffer is not in play, because the buffer optimization replaces the referenced step in place, and only when the shared root's header already carries the subquery's correlated columns. Both cases fall back to today's per-subquery root. After the fix the same plans are 226 steps at N = 8 and grow linearly. The default buffered path is untouched, and results are unchanged over both settings values. Cancellation inside the materialization pass is still not checked; with the plan now linear that pass takes milliseconds, so it is not addressed here.
signal.author: groeneai

signal.title: DeltaLake: trivial `SELECT count()` over a table with deletion vectors counts the deleted rows (`numRecords` summed, DV cardinality ignored)
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** A Delta table where a `DELETE` was persisted as a deletion vector (the default for Spark/Databricks-written tables with `delta.enableDeletionVectors = true`) returns a wrong `SELECT count()`: the trivial-count path answers from file-level `numRecords` statistics and never subtracts the deletion vector's `cardinality`, so every DV-deleted row is still counted. Any query that actually scans the data (`sum`, `min`/`max`, a selective predicate) returns the correct result — the deletion-vector *scan* path works — which makes the wrong `count()` inconsistent with every other answer the same table gives. Version-pinned reads via `delta_lake_snapshot_version` have the same wrong count. `optimize_trivial_count_query = 0` is a workaround. `optimize_count_from_files = 0` does **not** help — the shortcut is the storage's `totalRows`, not the files-count path. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1448 (also checked master snapshots back to 26.8.1.820). **How to reproduce** Write a table with a deletion vector using Spark (`pip install pyspark==3.5.3 delta-spark==3.2.1`, needs a JRE): ```python from delta import configure_spark_with_delta_pip from pyspark.sql import SparkSession b = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[1]") .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension") .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")) spark = configure_spark_with_delta_pip(b).getOrCreate() spark.sql("CREATE TABLE t (k BIGINT, v BIGINT) USING delta LOCATION '/tmp/dv_table' TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableDeletionVectors = true)") spark.sql("INSERT INTO t SELECT id, id*10 FROM range(300)") spark.sql("DELETE FROM t WHERE k < 50") # persisted as a deletion vector, cardinality 50 spark.sql("INSERT INTO t SELECT id, id*10 FROM range(300, 310)") ``` The table now holds 260 rows (Spark: `SELECT count(*)` → 260, `VERSION AS OF 2` → 250). Then: ```bash clickhouse local -q "SELECT count() FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/dv_table')" # 310 <- wrong, counts the 50 DV-deleted rows clickhouse local -q "SELECT count(), sum(k), min(k) FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/dv_table')" # 260 46670 50 <- scan path, correct clickhouse local -q "SELECT count() FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/dv_table') SETTINGS optimize_trivial_count_query = 0" # 260 <- workaround clickhouse local -q "SELECT count() FROM deltaLakeLocal('/tmp/dv_table') SETTINGS delta_lake_snapshot_version = 2" # 300 <- wrong; Spark's VERSION AS OF 2 says 250 (a scanning query with the same pin correctly returns 250) ``` An `strace` of the wrong read shows neither the data files nor the `deletion_vector_*.bin` file is ever opened — only the `_delta_log` JSON files. **Expected behavior** `SELECT count()` returns 260 (and 250 at `delta_lake_snapshot_version = 2`), matching what the same queries return when they scan. **Actual behavior** 310 and 300: the count is answered from metadata as the plain sum of `numRecords` across add actions, ignoring each file's `deletionVector.cardinality`. **Mechanism** `DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel::totalRows` serves the trivial-count from `TableSnapshot::getTotalRows`. Both row-accumulation sites in `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/DeltaLake/TableSnapshot.cpp` (the scan callback that fills `data_files`, and the `StatsVisitor` stats-only path) receive the file's `dv_info` handle from delta-kernel, yet unconditionally do `total_rows.value() += stats->num_records`. Fail-close would be setting `total_rows = std::nullopt` whenever `dv_info` is present (forcing the scan path); the precise fix is subtracting the deletion vector's cardinality. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/93852 --- Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: Vector similarity pk partial filter
signal.text: Fixes the case where `vector_similarity` skip indexes were not used when a primary key condition left only a subset of marks in a part. Previously, that situation skipped vector index analysis entirely, so reads could not use the HNSW granule to narrow work the way the index is intended. This PR keeps running vector index analysis under partial PK pruning and passes surviving PK `MarkRanges` into USearch `filtered_search` as a predicate, so graph traversal only keeps neighbors whose rows map to PK-allowed data marks. Motivated by #104122. Typical pattern: a long-retention table (for example tickets by time in the primary key) plus a narrow time predicate and `ORDER BY` vector distance with `LIMIT` — partial PK on the part plus vector search. When other skip indexes (minmax, set, text) run earlier in the pipeline and narrow `MarkRanges`, the vector path still sees that reduced `ranges` input, so behavior stays conjunctive without extra glue. `limit` is oversampled with `vector_search_index_fetch_multiplier` when `row_filter` is set, using the same rule as `additional_filters_present` and rescoring. `filtered_search` can still return fewer than `limit` hits if the PK slice removes almost all rows inside a granule. Stateless: `04217_vector_similarity_pk_partial_pruning`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Vector similarity skip indexes are used when the primary key leaves only a subset of marks in a part: neighbors are filtered with USearch `filtered_search` to PK-allowed data marks instead of skipping the vector index for that case. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Changes MergeTree mark filtering and vector-search hint propagation during query execution; mistakes could cause incorrect pruning or `_distance` ordering behavior under mixed PK/skip-index conditions. > > **Overview** > Enables `vector_similarity` skip index usage even when primary key pruning leaves only a subset of marks in a part, by passing PK-surviving row intervals into USearch `filtered_search` and restricting ANN hits to those ranges. > > Updates vector-search hint handling to **merge per-granule ANN results into part-global row offsets**, conservatively dropping `_distance` hints if any non-empty granule lacks distances, and adds per-`index_mark` caching to avoid repeated ANN work when marks are referenced by multiple PK ranges. > > Adds new `VectorSearchUtils` types (`GranuleRowFilter`, `ANNSearchOverrides`) and adjusts tests to expect index usage under partial PK pruning, plus a new stateless regression test (`04217_vector_similarity_pk_partial_pruning`). > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 082abd37613ee9945aca26aa69f3bdb4cc27f978. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: Reintroduce borrowed threadgroup async uaf fix
signal.text: Reintroduce #108988 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107030 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108577 CI: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105890&sha=3dc0e76362eb18e27f1fffcd3f61ca9f13725fe8&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20sequential%2C%201%2F2%29 Fixes a use-after-free risk in asynchronous work scheduled while a borrowed `ThreadGroup` is current. Borrowed `ThreadGroup` objects used by materialized view and async insert flush paths point their `performance_counters` and `memory_tracker` to the parent query group, so they are valid only while that parent group is alive. Async callbacks could capture such a borrowed group and later attach it on a pool thread after the parent query group had finished. Instead of keeping the parent `ThreadGroup` alive with a `shared_ptr`, this change keeps borrowed accounting scoped. Borrowed groups are marked explicitly, async callback capture drops borrowed groups, and thread pool callback runners capture the normalized group at task enqueue time rather than when a potentially long-lived runner object is created. This preserves synchronous borrowed accounting, but async work started from a borrowed scope runs under normal thread/global accounting instead of writing into, or prolonging the lifetime of, an already finished query group. Full ASAN reports https://gist.github.com/filimonov/1ec59047c65e3a5367c5c83f6021cc27 Compared to #108988 - added one commit with code comments + fix of the test failure https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109841 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a memory safety issue where asynchronous work scheduled from materialized view processing could keep using query-level accounting after the query had finished.

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions max_over_time() and min_over_time()
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `max_over_time()` and `min_over_time()`. ### Description Implements `max_over_time(v range-vector)` and `min_over_time(v range-vector)`, previously reported as not implemented. Unlike `sum`/`count`, max/min are not invertible monoids, but they are commutative and associative (merge = `max(a, b)`/`min(a, b)`), so the new header (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesExtremumOverTime.h`, templated on a bool `is_max_`) reuses `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSlidingSum`'s existing non-invertible sliding-window fallback (the same two-stacks/recompute machinery already shipped and tested via `deriv`/`predict_linear`) — no new windowing logic was needed. `Bucket == Summary` directly, following `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesToGridSparse`'s (`last_over_time`'s) simplest-case shape, since max/min don't depend on sample order. The comparison is NaN-aware (`candidate > current || isnan(current)`), matching Prometheus's own "a NaN currently held as the running extremum is unconditionally overwritten by the next sample" semantics. Registered `timeSeriesMaxToGrid`/`timeSeriesMinToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the two `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`, matching `rate`/`increase`/`delta`'s convention. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0.** **Testing**: new SQL-level test (`04628_max_min_over_time_timeseries_functions.sql`) including an `AggregatingMergeTree` serialize/deserialize/merge round-trip, plus cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering both functions over a series with decreases (so results differ meaningfully from `last_over_time`), including a more complex nested query. This flips 13 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed.

signal.title: Respect filesystem_prefetches_limit when prefetching JSON substreams
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113380 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113380 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `filesystem_prefetches_limit` being compared against the number of columns instead of the number of prefetches it is documented to bound. Reading a `JSON` column from a Wide part issued one prefetch, each with its own read buffer, per substream, so a single-column read could allocate thousands of buffers and fail the query with `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`. The limit is now enforced where the prefetches are issued; `0` still means unlimited. ### Description `MergeTreeReaderWide::prefetchForAllColumns` admits prefetching by comparing `filesystem_prefetches_limit` against `num_columns`, the number of columns in the block. But the prefetches are issued per SUBSTREAM: `prefetchForColumn`'s `enumerateStreams` callback calls `buf->prefetch()` for each one, and each call resizes that stream's own read buffer, which then lives in the reader's `streams` map for the reader's lifetime. A `JSON`/`Object` column expands into arbitrarily many substreams through `SerializationObject` -> `SerializationDynamic` -> `SerializationVariant`, so reading one such column allocates one live buffer per substream while the admission test compares the limit against `1`, which cannot fire at any non-zero limit. The plain read pool has no `filesystem_prefetch_max_memory_usage` budget either, so nothing bounds the fan-out. Seen in CI on `Stateless tests (amd_debug, distributed plan, s3 storage, parallel)`: `SELECT count() FROM t_wide WHERE length(JSONAllPaths(j)) > 0` failed with `Query memory limit exceeded: would use 4.66 GiB (attempt to allocate chunk of 1.25 MiB)` while running with `filesystem_prefetches_limit = 10`. This counts the prefetches actually issued and stops at the limit, at both issuance sites (data path and structure-prefix path). The counter is a reader member reset wherever `prefetched_streams` is cleared, so its lifetime tracks the live buffer set. The existing column-count early-out is kept, so this can only issue fewer prefetches than before. A skipped prefetch is a synchronous read later, never a failure; results are unchanged. Measured on one JSON column in a Wide part, counting `ProfileEvents['RemoteFSPrefetches']` for a single reader batch: at limit 10, 122 prefetches -> 10; at limit 5, 122 -> 5; at `0`, 122 (still unlimited). Capping at the default of 200 can reduce prefetching for very wide JSON reads; that is the setting's purpose, and `0` restores the old behaviour. #113380 touches the same callback but removes three specific shared-data substreams, so the two changes are complementary.

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions stddev_over_time() and stdvar_over_time()
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `stddev_over_time()` and `stdvar_over_time()` (population standard deviation/variance). ### Description Implements `stddev_over_time(v range-vector)` and `stdvar_over_time(v range-vector)`, previously reported as not implemented. **Key Technical & Numerical Stability Highlights**: 1. **Welford's Algorithm & Chan's Parallel Merge**: Uses a running centered-moment `{count, mean, m2}` accumulator ($M_2 = \sum (x - \bar{x})^2$) in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesVarianceOverTime.h` updated per sample via Welford's formula and merged pairwise via Chan et al.'s parallel merge algorithm. This avoids catastrophic cancellation on large-magnitude counter series (e.g. byte counters $\sim 5 \times 10^8$, where raw $\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2 / N$ loses all precision and produces false zeroes or negative variances). 2. **Prometheus Staleness Handling**: Implements full Prometheus stale-marker (`0x7ff0000000000002`) semantics. Stale markers are flagged at ingestion (`is_stale_marker`), excluded from range-vector aggregations (`WHERE NOT is_stale_marker`) so target disappearance does not pollute range windows with NaNs, while remaining detectable by instant selectors to correctly report series absence. 3. **Non-Invertible Two-Stacks / Recompute Strategy**: Avoids floating-point `unmerge` subtraction on moments to prevent numerical cancellation and drift over long sliding windows. Registered `timeSeriesStddevToGrid`/`timeSeriesStdvarToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the two `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`. **Verified numerically against Prometheus 3.5.0**: verified bit-for-bit accuracy against Prometheus 3.5.0 live responses, including cross-architecture (ARM64 vs x86_64) ULP tolerance handling in CI. **Testing**: SQL-level test (`04628_variance_timeseries_functions.sql`) covering empty/single/multi-sample windows and `AggregatingMergeTree` round-trips, plus integration cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` (including stale-marker ingestion and instant/range evaluations). This flips 12 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed.

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions absent and count_values
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented `absent` and `count_values`, including range queries and `by`/`without` aggregation modifiers. ### Description Implements two PromQL operations that previously returned a not-implemented error and require result construction beyond transforming a fixed per-series values array. - `absent(v instant-vector)` aggregates sample presence across all input series independently at every grid point and emits one synthetic sample with value 1 only where the input is empty. For a direct selector, including `offset` and `@` modifiers, it performs Prometheus-compatible equality-matcher label inference while excluding `__name__`; complex expressions produce an unlabeled result. Label inference deliberately mirrors Prometheus's historic monotonic `has` map: after the first accepted equality matcher for a label name, a later matcher can delete the inferred label but cannot unlock that name for another equality matcher. An empty exact-match value is canonicalized as label absence, matching Prometheus `labels.Builder::Set`. - `count_values(label, v instant-vector)` unrolls each series' grid values, sets or overwrites the requested value label, groups by label set, grid point, and formatted sample value, counts each bucket, and repacks sparse counts into nullable grid arrays. Both `by (...)` and `without (...)` are supported, including removing the generated label or using `__name__` as the destination. Destination label names follow Prometheus 3.x UTF-8 validation—non-empty valid UTF-8—rather than the legacy ASCII label-name pattern. A new internal `timeSeriesPrometheusValueToString` function reproduces Go's fixed shortest-roundtrip formatting used by Prometheus, including `-0`, `NaN`, `+Inf`, and `-Inf`. The supported-function documentation for `prometheusQuery` and `prometheusQueryRange` is updated accordingly. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0** with direct response comparisons covering sparse range points, inferred labels (including equality/regex/equality ordering and empty exact-match values), grouping modifiers, empty inputs, metric-name and non-legacy UTF-8 destination labels, floating-point label strings, and result ordering. **Testing**: added `test_function_absent` and `test_aggregation_operator_count_values` integration coverage in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py`. All six modified C++ translation units compile locally with zero warnings or errors. The focused queries were exercised against a local `TimeSeries` table and compared with Prometheus 3.5.0. The clean-master integration module collects all 25 tests, including both additions, but no test body ran locally because the Docker daemon was unavailable and the module-scoped cluster fixture failed during setup; containerized integration execution is left to CI.

signal.title: Query Result Cache: Allows cached query results to disk
signal.text: Adds an optional persistent on-disk tier to the query result cache. Query-level settings control disk reads and writes; entries survive restarts, preserve user isolation, and can be managed independently from the memory tier. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/52141 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow using a disk for the query result cache. The `enable_writes_to_query_cache_disk` and `enable_reads_from_query_cache_disk` settings control on-disk query-cache writes and reads.

signal.title: Fix server abort on a corrupt ORC stripe footer
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114674 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/orc/pull/25 Reading a corrupt ORC blob aborts a debug or sanitizer server instead of raising `INCORRECT_DATA`: ``` generated_message_tctable_lite.cc:228] Check failed: VerifyHasBitConsistency(msg, table) is OK (INTERNAL: Has bits mismatch for Type=orc.proto.StripeFooter Field=1 ``` Found by the AST fuzzer (`AST fuzzer (amd_debug, targeted)`, [report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114267&sha=08273e65417c8b6a4fe95d2c2cdad899ea17d041&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29)), and reproduced on pristine master with default settings by `SELECT c0 FROM format(ORC, 'c0 DateTime64(3)', unhex('4f524311...524317'))`, so any user-supplied ORC bytes reach it. **Root cause.** ORC's `DecompressionStream` throws where protobuf's `ZeroCopyInputStream::Next` contract requires a `false` return, so the exception originates inside protobuf's parse loop. `TcParser` keeps has-bits in a register-cached local and writes them back only on its own exit paths, so the unwind skips that write-back and leaves `StripeFooter` with the repeated field `streams` appended to and its has-bit clear. Since the v35.1 protobuf bump the generated destructor checks that invariant, so destroying it aborts. `DebugHardenCheckHasBitConsistency()` gates it on `!NDEBUG` or a sanitizer, so release builds are unaffected, hence a CI fix. **Change.** A submodule bump only. ORC's parse boundary now wraps the caller's stream in an adapter that captures anything escaping `Next`/`BackUp`/`Skip`/`ByteCount`, returns the contract's failure value, and rethrows the original exception once the parser has returned consistent. One header covers all nine `parseProtobufFromStream` call sites, including embedder streams such as ClickHouse's `ORCInputStream`. **Validation.** The blob aborts (RC 134) before the change and afterwards reports `Code: 117 ... Read past EOF in DecompressionStream::readBuffer ... (INCORRECT_DATA)`, byte-identical to master release today, so no user-visible message or code changes. New test `04856_orc_corrupt_stripe_footer` passes 50/50 randomized and fails on the unfixed binary with the has-bits tokens. A 183-case corruption sweep and the full `orc` suite show no behaviour change. `ProtobufZeroCopyInputStreamFromReadBuffer` (Prometheus remote-write) has the same shape, but is unreported and I could not reproduce a failure there, so it is untouched.

signal.title: Add a type-aware Bloom filter index for JSON
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113376 The original design used `JSONAllValues` as the input to a Bloom filter. `JSONAllValues` serializes each value as text. It does not preserve the runtime type. This loss of type information is important for `Dynamic` values. ClickHouse can compare JSON values with different runtime types. Some type pairs can match after conversion. Other type pairs can return an exception. A Bloom filter that stores only text cannot safely model these rules. It can skip a granule that contains a match. It can also hide an exception. `JSONAllValues` remains useful for text search, but it is not a safe base for this index. This PR replaces that design with `jsonbf_v1`. The new index creates tokens from these components: - JSON path - Container role - Runtime type - Binary value The container role separates scalar values, array elements, and map values. The index also processes nested JSON objects and named tuple fields. For `Dynamic` values, the index stores type-presence and complex-value presence tokens. Query analysis uses exact value tokens only when the comparison is safe. If analysis cannot prove safety, ClickHouse reads the granule. Container roles are preserved through nested tuples, and nested casts are handled conservatively. The index supports: - Equality and typed `IN` conditions - `has`, `hasAny`, and `hasAll` for arrays - Typed map values by key - Nested JSON objects and tuples The index does not optimize range conditions or whole-container equality. It also rejects unsafe comparison paths, such as Decimal-to-Float comparisons. An unsupported `Dynamic` runtime type disables skipping for its granule. In a one-million-row JSONBench test, the index reduced reads from 123 granules to 12–15 granules. Selected string equality queries were 1.6–2.3 times faster. Indexed inserts were approximately 2.9 times slower in the checked-in performance test. A local performance test produced these median results: | Operation | Without index | With `jsonbf_v1` | Difference | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Numeric equality, matching value | 13.05 ms | 10.99 ms | 1.19 times faster | | Numeric equality, missing value | 13.25 ms | 10.80 ms | 1.23 times faster | | String equality | 24.49 ms | 12.90 ms | 1.90 times faster | | Array `has` | 24.71 ms | 12.78 ms | 1.93 times faster | | Insert | 20.51 s | 40.87 s | 1.99 times slower | The small performance test shows limited benefit for numeric scalar equality and larger improvements for string equality and array membership. The larger JSONBench data set benefits more because the index skips more granules. Token generation and Bloom-filter construction increase insert time. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Adds the `jsonbf_v1` data-skipping index for type-aware equality and array membership on `JSON` values.
